OF THE

VOL. 22.

By the KING,

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS our Parliament (lands prorogued to Tuesday the Fifth Day of December next: We, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued on the said Fifth Day of December to Tuesday the Sixteenth Day of January next ensuing; and we have given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain, to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do hereby further declare our Royal Will and Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on

the said Sixteenth Day of January next, be held, and fit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important AfTairs: And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminsterl on the said Sixteenth Day of January next.

Given at our Court at St. James's, the Thirtieth Day of November 1732, in the Sixth Year of our Reign.

GOD fave the KING.

Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy 1 which he read to the House, and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is a great Satisfaction to me, that the prefect Situation of Affairs both at home and abroad makes it unnecessary for me to lay before you any other Reasons for my calling you together at this time, but the ordinary Dispatch of the publick Business; and that I may have an Opportunity of receiving your Advice upon such Affairs as may occur to you, and shall require the Care and Consideration of Parliament.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I will order the proper Officers to lay before you the Eliimates for the Service of the current Year; and I make no doubt but that you will, with the same Chear-fulness as I have always experienced in you, effectually raise such Supplies as you shall judge necessary for the Honour, Safety, and Defence, of the Kingdom: And I cannot but recommend it to you, as a Consideration worthy the Commons of Great Britain, that, in all your Deliberations, as well upon railing the annual Supplies, as the Distribution of the public Revenues, you pursue such Measures as will most conduce to the present and future Ease of those you represent.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

You muii be sensible, that it is very desirable to give all possible Dispatch to the public Business; and that nothing can give more Weight and Credit to all your Resolutious, than to avoid unreasonable Heats and Animosities; and not to suffer yourselves to be diverted, Vol. 22*

by any specious Pretences, from ftedfaflly pursuing the true Interest of your Country: Let that be your first and principal Care, and the People will be sensible of the Benefits they shall receive from your Wisdom and Resolution, in preferring their Eafej and the public Good, to all other Considerations*

A Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to return his Majesty the Thanks of this House for his most gracious Speech from the Throne; to express the Satisfaction of this House at the present Situation of Adairs both at home and abroad; and to assure his Majesty, That this House will, with all possible Duty to his Majesty, and just Regard and Concern for those we represent, chearfully and effectually raise such Supplies as shall be necessary for the Honour, Safety, and Defence, of his Majesty, and his Kingdoms; and that, in all our deliberations upon raffing the annual Supplies, and the Distribution of the public Revenues, we will pursue such Measures as will most conduce to the present and futureeafeofour Fellow Subjects; and that, in order to £ivethe necessary Dispatch to the publick Business, and that our Proceedings may carry with them that weight and credit in the Nation which ought always to attend the Resolutions of the Commons of Great Britain, we will endeavour to avoid all unreasonable Heats and Animosities; and not suffer ourselves to be diverted, by any specious Pretences whatsoever, from ftedfaflly pursuing the true Interest of our Country, which shall, upon all Occasions, be our first and principal Care;

An Amendment was proposed to be made to the Quef-tion, by inferring, after the Words " our Fellow Subjects," these Words, "and such as shall be consistent " with the Honour and Justice of Parliament, and the " Trade, Interest, and Liberties, of the Nation

And the Question being put, That those Words be there inserted;

It was resolved in the Affirmative:

Then the Question, so amended, being put;

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any uiual Right to give his Vote in the Election of any Member, Orders, to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge atiy Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, a Mem* ber of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery,

or

6 GeoJ- II. r 7° Jwiuarii.

or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdeameanour, and this House will proceed with the utmost Sever t v against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House wilt proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members, to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do from time to time take into his Custody any Stranger or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House, is fitting; and that no Person, so taken into Custody, be discharged out of Custody, without the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That the Back-door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning, at the Sitting of the House, and the Key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any Person whatsoever, without Order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do take care to clear the Speakers Chamber every Day, before the Door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger or Strangers into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables, and other Officers, of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that from Ten of the Clock in the Morning to Four in the Afternoon, during this Session of Parliament, the Passages through the Streets, between Temple-bar and Westminster-hall, shall be kept free and open; and that no Obstruction be made by Cars, Drays, Carts, or otherwise, to hinder the Passage of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Arms, attending this House, do give Notice of this Order to the Officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in Westminster-hall, or the Passages leading to the House, during the Sitting of Parliament; and that there be no Annoyance by Chairmen, Footmen, or otherwise, therein, or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the High Bailiff of Westminster; and that he do fee the same put in Execution.

Ordered, That no Footmen be permitted to be within the Lobby of the House, or upon the Stairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care, that there be no Gaming, or other Disorders, in the Room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his Custody such Footmen as shall presume to disobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of Custody, but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That, to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the Person appointed to bring Letters from the General Post Office to this House, or some other Person to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do, for the future, every Day, during the Session of Parliament, Sundays Vql. 22.

exempted’, constantly attend from Ten of the Clock in the Morning till One in the Afternoon; and for Two Hours, at the Teaft, immediately after the Riling of the House; and also on every Friday, Monday, and Wed-liefday, from Five of the Clock in the Afternoon till Seven, at the Place appointed for the Delivery of the said Letters; and take Care, during his stay there, to deliver the same to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known Servant or Servants, or others, bringing Notes under the hands of the Members fending for the fame.

Ordered, That the said Officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered; and that no Letter be delivered but within the Hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be sent to the Postmaster General.

Ordered, That when any Letter or Pacquet, di retied to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame; and acquaint the House, at their next Sitting, with the Contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, when the House is going to Prayers, give notice thereof to all Committees: And that all Proceedings of Committees in a Morning, after such Notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the Printing thereof: And that no other Person, but such as he shall appoint, do presume to print the fame.

Resolved, That this House will receive no Petition for private Bills after the Second Day of March next.

Mr. Henry Bromley reported from the Committee appointed Yesterday, to draw up an Address, to be presented to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, humbly beg Leave to return your Majesty our most sincere and hearty Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

The Situation of Affairs both at home and abroad gives your faithful Commons the highest Satisfaction, and fills their Hearts with the deepest Sense ot Gratitude to your Majesty; being fully sensible, that the present Happiness we enjoy is the intire Effect of your Majesty’s Wisdom and Resolution.

Such Supplies as shall be necessary for the Honour, Safety, and Defence, of your Majesty, and your Kingdom, shall chearfully and effectually be raised, by your faithful Commons, with all possible Duty to your Majesty, and a just Regard and Concern for those we represent.

We also beg Leave to attire your Majesty, That, in all our Deliberations, as well in raising the Supplies, as in the Distribution of the public Revenues, we will pursue such Measures as will moll conduce to the present and future Ease of our Fellow Subjects $ and such as, agreeably to your Majesty’s known Goodness, and gracious Intentions towards your People, and the constant Endeavours of your faithful Commons, shall be confident with the Honour and Justice of Parliament, and with the Trade, Interest, and Liberties, of the Nation.

That our Proceedings may carry with them the Weight and Credit which ought always to attend the Resolutions of the Commons of Great Britain, and that the necessary Dispatch may be given to the publick Business, we will use our utmost Endeavours to avoid all unreasonable Heats and Animosities; nor suffer our-selves to be diverted, by any specious Pretences whatsoever, from stedfastly pursuing the true Interest of our Country, which, in pursuance of your Majesty’s most gracious Recommendation from your great Example, and our own indispensable Duty, shall, upon all Occasions, be our first and principal Care.

The said Address, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the 1-Joufe.

Peebles A Petition of Sir Alexander Murray, of Stanhope, was

Election. prefen'ted to the House, and read; setting forth, That, on Friday the 28th of April 1732, being the Day appointed for electing a Knight of the Shire to serve in Parliament for the County of Peebles, in the room of the honourable Mr. John Dbuglas, deceased,-Sir James Nafmish, of Pojfo, and the Petitioner, appeared as Candidates, when Alexander Murray of Cringlety, the last elected Commissioner, now living, pursuant to the Act of Parliament made in that behalf, put the Question for the Choice of a Praefes, and Clerk; and, upon the Question so by him severally put, the Honourable Mr. William Carmichael was duly elected Praefes, and Alexander Shaw duly elected Clerk, by themajority of legal Voters; bat that SivAlexander Murray, of Black bar rony, Sheriff, appointed Cnee the date of the Writ, though retrained by his Commission from naming a Sheriff Cferk, and though there was another Sheriff Clerk then existing, and lawfully intitled to act, appointed William Veitch to be Sheriff Clerk, who, by Order of the said Sheriff, put the Question for the Choice of a Praefes and Clerk; and that the said Sheriff, and the said William Veitch, by his Direction, voted in the Election of Praefes, though neither of them.were inrolled in the Roll of Freeholders: That the Petitioner required the whole Meeting to qualify by taking the Oaths appointed by Law; and though he and his Friends did accordingly qualify, the said Sheriff, and his Adherents, who appeared in the Interestof Sir James Nayfmish, refuled to qualify; and that the Roll of Electors was partially made up, by inserting the . Names of Persons not intitled to vote, and deleting the Names of such as have been duly inrolled, and had voted in former Elections: That though the Petitioner protested against this Proceeding, and was duly elected by a Majority oflegal Voters, the said Sheriff has taken upon him to return the said SirjamesNaysmith as duly elected, to serve in this present Parliament for the said County o {Peebles-, inViolation of the Freedom of Elections, and the Right of the Freeholders; and alleging, that the said Sir James Naysmith is not only unduly elected, but that his Return is void, hisEleftion not having been certified by the proper Clerk, nor the Election carried on under the Conduct of the Praefes lawfully elected; but contrary to the Voices of the Majority of habile Voters: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and to afford the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

read; complaining, That, on the Twenty-eighth of April One thousand Seven hundred and thirty-two, at a Meeting of the Freeholders of the said County, to elect a Knight of the Shire, Sir Alexander Murray, of Black-barrony, Sheriff Depute, though restrained, byhis Commission, from naming a Sheriff Clerk, appointed Mr. William Veitch, of Bog-end, to execute that Office; in Prejudice to the Petitioner, who then attended, and infilled on his Right: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to relieve the Petitioner, in such manner as to the House shall seem proper.

Wear

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Gentlemen,.and

Navigation, principal Inhabitants, of the City of Durham, was pre-

Great Admiral of England; and, upon his Application to the said Matter, Wardens, and Assistants, and their Successors; who also, by a Grant of King Charles the Second, made on the 24th Day of June, in the Seventeenth Year of his Reign, are intitled to the Soil, Gravel, and Sand, of the River Thames, with the foie Right of supplying all Ships and Vessels with Ballatt, at the Rates and Prices accustomed'; viz. Nine Pence per Ton, by all Ships employed in the Coal-trade, Twelve Pence person by all other British Ships, and Sixteen Pence per Ton by foreign Ships: That the Petitioners have continually employed Sixty Ballatt Lighters, and One hundred and twenty Men, in their Service, with an Allowance of Four Pence per Ton to the Ballatt Men, and Two Pence per Ton to the Owners of the Ballatt Lighters; and have applied the Residue of the Money received for Ballatt, deducing the Charge of Management, to the Maintenance of Ninety-three Almshouses, and the monthly Relief of many Hundred Out Pensioners, the Expence of this Charity amounting to Four hundred Pounds per Month; and the poor decayed Seamen, their Widows, and Orphans, who are the Objects thereof, being above One thousand Nine hundred; That the Petitioners, upon the Complaint of the Masters and Commanders of Ships, have endeavoured to compel the Ballatt Men to deliver dueTonnage of Ballad; but that the said Ballatt Men, not content with the ancient Prices allowed to them by the Petitioners, but pretendingthat the Deepness of the River has made their Work more difficult; and that the DearnefsofProvisions has made the Increase of their Wages necessary; and perceiving that the Knowledge of the Business, in which they are employed, is confined to themselves, have of late combined together, and infilled on Three Pence per Ton more, and have actually demanded and received the same to their own Use, from several Matters and Commanders of Ships, in Disobedience to the Orders of the Petitioners; who, notwithstanding the Subscription of the Matters and Owners of Ships to advance the Prices of Ballatt, are not warranted to increase the accustomed Rates; and therefore cannot allow greater Wages to the said Ballatt Men, without starving the Poor; and therefore, that the Trade of the Nation may not suffer by the Want of Ballatt, and the Obstructions of the said River, praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to impower the Petitioners to receive such other Sums of Money for the Prices of Ballatt, and, to make such further Allowance for the railing and delivering the fame, as shall be thought reasonable; and to compel the fai,d Ballatt Men to deliver due Tonnage of Ballatt to all Matters of Ships, ar>d subject them to such Regulation and Government, as to the House ttxall feera meet.

Mr. Gregory reported from the Committee, to whom Dun the Petition of the Undertakers for making the River Navigation. Dun, in the County of York, navigable from Holmjlile, in Doncaster, to the utmost Extent of Tinftey West ward \ and also of the Undertakers for improving the Navigation thereof, from Holmjlile a fore said, to Wiljick house, pursuant to Two several Acts of Parliament made in the Twelfth and Thirteenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House: And he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to an Order of the House dated the'20th of January lad, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations of the fame,

Mr. Thomas Radford was called: Who said. That he has been employed, as Expenditor, for Four Years last past, for the Town of Sheffield, in One of which Years he was also Expenditor for both Sheffield and Doncaster;

And he produced an Account, whereby it appeared, that there was laid out and expended, in making and improving the Navigation of the said River, the Sum 7,coo. and upwards:

He also said, That the Undertakers of the said Navigation, above Holmjlile, had made Eight chargeable Locks, and several long Cuts; and that the Undertakers of the said Navigation below Holmjlile, had made Two chargeable Locks and Dams; as also a wooden Bridge, Siathing; ^nd otl^er expensive Works:

That when the Two Corporations settled their Accounts, about Two Years ago, there appeared to be laid out £. 13,000; and the Year after there was laid out about £.2,000; and the last Year upwards of £.2,300:

That the Navigation is not yet finished; but is capable of being made very good with further Expence, which will be of great Advantage to the Manufactory of Sheffield, and all the adjacent Country near the said River:

He also said, That the Navigation will be much more easily completed by the Two Companies being united into One, which will render the said Navigation more advantageous to Trade, by a more quick and easy Conveyance of Goods and Merchandizes up and down the said River.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend Two Acts of Parliament, One made in the Twelfth, and the other in the Thirteenth Year of his late Majesty s Reign, for making navigable the River Dun, in the County of York; and for the better perfecting and maintaining the said Navigation; and for uniting the several Undertakers into One Company:

And that Mr. Gregory, Sin George Saville, Mr. Jessop,

Mr. Plumplre, and* Sir James Campbell, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Wear Mr. Hedworlh reported from the Committee, to whom Navigation, the Petition of the Commissioners of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the Count# of Durham, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter t>f the said Petition; which, as it appeared to them, they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 29th of January last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition;

And, to prove the Allegations thereof.

The Petitioners first laid before the Committee, An Act made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for Preservation and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, whereby certain Persons, therein named, were constitilted and appointed Commissioners of the said River, Port and Haven, within the Limits, with the Powers, and for the Purposes, therein mentioned, for and during the Term of Twenty-one years; and certain Duties were granted, payable from the 24th Day of June 1717, for the Space of Twenty-one Years:

The Petitioners also laid before the Committee another Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his said late Majesty, for the mo re effect ual Preservation and Improvement of the said River, Port, and Haven, whereby divers additional Powers were granted to the said Commissioners.

Then several Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. Thomas Allen: Who fair!, That the Commissioners had borrowed on the Credit of the said Acts, the Sum of £.6,800, whereof only £. 1,000 had been repaid; so that there remained due £.5,800; which Sum carries Interest:

And he being asked, What the Duties granted amounted to annually ? said. That the net Produce thereof was £ 1,200 per Annum; which, according to a Computation by him made, would scarce be sufficient to pay off the principal Money borrowed, as aforesaid, and the growing Interest thereof, before the Expiration of the Term for which the said Duties were granted; and consequently, that nothing would be left to defray the necessary Expences of repairing, and carrying on, the Works, for the Preservation, and Improvement, of the said River, Port, and Haven.

Sir Wm. Williamson, Mr. Thomas Allen, and Captain Lampion, being severally examined, laid, That, for want of a new Pier, toproteft the Harbour from the North-east Winds, Ships and Vessels have often been very much damaged; the Building of which, and erecting other necessary Works, will amount to a considerable Sum of Money more than can be raised by the Duties during the Continuance of the said Term, which expires on the24th Day o[June 1738:

And the same Witnesses proved, that the Commissioners have been often restrained from levying the Duties and Penalties imposed by the said Act, of the 3d Year of his said late Majesty, by reason the Commissioners are not thereby impowered to direct their Warrants for levying the same to any Person, but to the Cotistable of the Place where the Offence is committed, where there are very seldom Effects of such Persons as refuse, or neglect, to pay such Duties and Penalties, sufficient to answer the fame.

And it appeared to the Committee, That unless the Duties and Powers, by the said Acts of Parliament granted, be further continued, and the Acts made more effectual, the said River, Port, and Haven, cannot be eife&ually cleansed, preserved, and improved, and the Money already borrowed on the Credit of the said Acts, be repaid, with Interest.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to continue, and make more effectual, Two Acts made in the Thiid and Thirteenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for Preservation, and Improvement of the River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham: And that Mr. Hedworlh, Mr. Hilton, Mr. Burlon, and Sir Wilfrid Laufon, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Minister, Churchwardens, Over- St. George'* seers of the Poor, and other principal Inhabitants, of the ancient Parish of Si. George the Martyr, in Southwark9 r

in the County of Surrey, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the IToufe, and read; felting forth. That the Church belonging to the said Parish is very old, ruinous, and irreparable, though the Petitioners have contributed to the Repairs thereof, within the Compass of a few Years* more than the Sum of Eleven hundred Pounds, notwithstanding the great Poverty of the said Parish, occasioned by the Increase of Poor, the Rate for whose Support, in the Year 1696, amounted to no more than Two hundred Eighty-three Pounds Eleven Pence Halfpenv, hut in the Year 1729, exceeded the Sum of One thousand Pounds; which Increase of Poor is chiefly owing to the Increase of Prisoners in the Four several Prisons within the said Parish; and especially the King's Bench, the Rules whereof are of great Extent, wherein many info!vent Debtors frequently gain Settlements, and to t he present Condit ion of one Part of the said Parish, called the Mint, the Houses in which are now either empty, or inhabited by indigent Persons, not paying any parochial Duties; and that by these Means the Petitioners are disabled to defray the Expence of rebuilding the said Church; and that the Petitioners, by the Consumption of Coals in the said Parish, have, for many Years, contributed a great Sum of Money to the Fund appropriated, by several Acts of Parliament, for building, and endowing, Fifty new Churches, within the Cities of London and Westminster, proportionally with all other Parishes within the Bills of Mortality, the said Parish being included within the City of London, and under the Jurisdiction of the Lord Mayor thereof: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for appropriating such Part of the said Fund for rebuilding the said Church, as the House shall think fit; or that the Petitioners may have such other Assistanee and Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Thomas Fletcher was called: Who said, That there is a great Quantity of arable Land, Meadow and Pallure Ground, in Aston Magna, now used and enjoyed by the Petitioners in common; but, if such Common Grounds were divided and inclosed, the same would be very beneficial to all the Proprietors thereof.

York A Petition of the Proprietors of the Stock of the

Bui Mings Governor and Company for raising the Thames Water, Company, in York Buildings, assembled in their General Court held at their House in WincheJkr-street, the Twelfth Day of January 11732, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, for carrying on the Water-works of the said Company, and for purchasing several forfeited Estates in England and Scotland, as well as for undertaking and managing several Mines, and other Works and 1 rade, in Scotland, for the Benefit of the said Company, several hundred thousand Pounds were raised, and paid in, by the Proprietors of 22

Stock in the said Company; all or thegreafefl Part of which Money hath been embezzled and misapplied by the Frauds, and notorious Mi (behaviour, of the present Governor of the said Company, and others, who are, or have been, entrusted with the Management of the Affairs thereof, and their Agents; by which all the Petitioners are become groat Sufferers, and many of them reduced to the utmost Poverty and Distress: And that, though the Petitioners have already discovered many of the said Frauds, yet they are unable fully to discover all the Persons concerned therein, or to obtain a Redress of their Grievances, without the Assistance of th is House; many of the Servants and Officers of the said Company being so far under the Influence of the present Governor, that the Petitioners have not been able to prevail on them to disclose such Ci ream Ranees of the said Frauds as they are acquainted with; and most of the Books of the Corporation, from whence any Light might be obtained therein, being either secreted or kept, and made up* on purpose to prevent a Discovery: And therefore, humbly hoping, That the House, taking into Consuleration the extraordinary Circumstances of their Cafe, ami how far Credit in general may be assessed, if such prodigious Embezzlements, and such inanifeft Violations of Trust, should go unpunished, will inquire into the State of the said Corporation, and the Conduct of those who have, or have had, the Management of their Affairs; and give inch Relief to the Petitioners as to the House shall seem meet,

Resolved, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee.

Resolved, That the Number of the said Committee be Thirteen,

Resolved, That the said Committee be chosen by way of Balloting.

Ordered, That the Members of the House do, upon Tuesday next, at Twelve of the Clock, prepare Lifts, to be put into Glafies, of Thirteen Persons Names, to be the said Committee,

The other4 Order of the Day, for the House to resolve Offices and itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the Bill to indemnify Persons, who, through Ignorance of Law, have omitted to qualify themselves for Employments or OfTices, by taking the Oaths, and making and subscribing the Declaration against Transubllantiation, and receiving the Sacrament, and allowing them further Time for that Purpose, being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Monday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Bill.

And then the House adjourned tHl Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

A Petition of the Vicar, Churchwardens, and other Inhabitants, of the Parish of Ealing, in the County of Middlefer, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of the said Parish, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in the Year 1732, the Church of the said Parish becoming ruinous and irreparable, the Parishioners, who are very numerous, were obliged to aflernble, for Divine Service, in a finall, flight, Timber Tabernacle, built by the voluntary Contributions of some of the Petitioners: That, loon after the Erection of the said Tabernacle, the Steeple and Roof of the said Church fell down; and that, towards rebuilding the said Church and Steeple, and making the said Church commodious, about the Sum of Five hundred and Fifty Pounds hath been subscribed; but that the Petitioners are unable to raise the Sum required for that Purpose, amounting to Three thousand Pounds, and upwards, the said Parish, of which the Town of Old Brentford is Part, being burdened with many Poor; and many Houses, in the said Parish, which were formerly inhabited by Gentlemen, now being untenanted: And therefore, in regard, that, in the said Town of OldBrentford, several thousand Chaldron of Coals, after Payment of the Duties at the Port of London, are annually landed, and there, and in other Parts of the said Parish, consumed, praying, That some Provision may be made for rebuilding the said Church and Steeple, out of the Money appointed for building or endowing the Fifty new Churches, or that such other Relief may be given to the Petitioners, as the House shall think fit.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put. That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee.

It passed in the Negative.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tuesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the State of the Trade of his Majesty’s Sugar Colonies in America.

By the other Charter, tin* Soil, Gravel, and Sand, of the said River, and the foie Right of {'applying all Ships and Vessels therein with Ballad, at the Rates and Prices acctifiomed, were vested in the said Master, Wardens, and Assistants, and their Successors.

Then, to prove the other Allegations of the said Petition, the following Witurtles were examined; viz.

Captain John Fell, Captain JoJ'cph Kell, and Captain John Burford, all Mailers of Ships: Who severally said, That they had navigated the River of Thames, one of them for Fifty-five, and the other, two for Sixty Years; during which Time, the nfual Prices paid for Ballast have been Nine Pence per Ton, by all Masters of Ships employed in the Coal Trade, and Twelve Pence per Ton, by the Masters of all other British Ships.

Mr. John lleup said. That he had been a Husband, a Term which signifies a Broker, to several foreign Ships: That the Masters of such Ships usually paid for Ballast Sixteen Pence per Ton.

This Evidence was confirmed by Captain John Burford.

Captain Kell added further. That, for several Years last past, the Ballast-men never delivered above Ten or Twelve hundred Weight of Ballast fora 1'on.

JchnAuJl and Robert Boatjivain, Rulers of the Ballast Office, laid, That the Number of Ballast Lighters constantly employed by the Corporation of Trinity-Jioufe, during the whole Year, is Sixty, and the Number of Men in them 120; who are directed to work upon such Shelves in the River of Thames as can with the lealt Difficulty be taken up, and are mod. dangerous and obfiruftive to the Navigation of the said River:

That for taking up Badaft each Man is allowed Two Pence per 'Foil, and the Owner of every Lighter Two Pence per Ton , and that, by these means, many Obstructions to the Navigation of the River are removed; and that there is now, in several Places, 15 Feet Depth

of Water, for 300 Sail of Ships to lie, where formerly the Depth was but Three Feet.

Jeremiah Long said, Tl^t, on both Sides the River, from the Custom-house downwards, in several Places, the Water is now 13 Feet deep, where the Depth was but Four Feet formerly.

As to the Application of the net Produce of the Revenue of the Ballad Office,

Mr. John Whormby, Secretary to the Corporation of Trinity-house, was examined: Who said. That the clear Profits of that Office are paid to him by the Cashier; and that the Examinant pays it towards the Relief of the Poor maintained in Ninety-three Almf-houses, and Out-pensioners, in all One thousand Nine hundred, being decayed Seamen, their Widows and Orphans: That the whole Revenue appropriated to this Charity, and of which the Profits of the said Office are Part, amounts to upwards of £. 400 per Month.

Mr. John Gould (borough, Predeceffior to Mr. Whormby, confirmed his Evidence, as to the Application of the Money during the time he was Secretary to the said Corporation.

To prove the Endeavours of the Petitioners to prevent Frauds and Abuses in delivering short Tonage of Ballast,

Captain Burford was examined: Who said, That he never could obtain full Tonage of Ballast to be delivered to him by the Ballast-men; but that, upon Application to the Trinity-house, he always had Satisfaction from them, either by receiving an additional Quantity of Ballast, or Part of his Money, in proportion to the Deficiency.

John Aujl likewise said, That whenever Complaints were made to the Corporation of Trinity-house, of short Tonage of Ballast, by any Masters of Ships, they always obtained Satisfaction, either in Money or Ballast.

Mr. Whormby then produced a Table of Rules, made by the said Corporation, and signed by him; which Table contains Directions where Ballast shall be taken up, what Lighters shall be employed, and how marked, to prevent Frauds; and at what Prices Ballast shall be delivered; with several other Directions for preventing and redressing Abuses:

He likewise produced Three of the London Gazettes, the First dated the 24th of July 1731, the Second the 23d of May, and the lait the 14th of November 1732; in the Two first of which, the said Corporation have pub-liffied Advertisements, giving Notice to all Masters of Ships toobserve the Marks of the Ballast Lighters, wh.cn they come and return from the Ships Sides; and directing them where to apply for Red refs of any Abuses; and, in the last, an Advertisement is published, mentioning the Prices for Delivery of Ballast, forbidding Persons to exact any further Payment, and inviting all Persons who are willing to be employed in the Ballast Service, to apply to the Office for that Purpose.

Mr. John Willis, Clerk to the Ballast Office, being called, produced One of the printed Receipts, which, he said, are always given to Masters of Ships, when they pay for Ballalt, at the Office; in which Receipts, the Marks of the Lighters are described, and Directions are given to Masters of Ships, how they may discover Frauds, and where to apply upon such Occasions for Redrels.

John Aujl, being again examined, said, That, about Midsummer last, the Ballast-men entered into a Combination not to work, unless they were paid Three Pence per Ton more; since which Time, several Masters of Ships have willingly paid it, and received fuller Tonage than before: That this additional 3d. per Ton the Ballast-men receive clear to themselves, no Part of it being brought to Account:

And the Examinant said further, That Two Ballast-men being ordered to deliver Ballast on Board the Ship of one Captain Friend, they demanded of the Captain the additional Price, and, upon his refusing to pay it, carried the Ballast back again; whereupon Complaint

Mr Whormby, being examined in relation to Money given for Relief of poor Seamen, and others, said, That, at Christmas lad, the Income of the Corporation falling short, and it being usual every Christmas to relieve such as are called accidental Poor, several of the Elder Brethren of Trinity-house raised among themselves, for that Purpose, a Contribution of Twenty Pounds, Ten Pounds, and Five Pounds, each, which, amounted, in the Whole, to a considerable Sum above^. 100.

The Committee then took into Consideration the Petition of the Ballad-men of the River Thames, referred to them, by Order of the House dated the 7th of February Indant:

And the Petitioners, to prove their Allegations, called the following Witnesses:

Robert Park: Who said, He had been a working Ballad-man on the River of Thames above Twenty Years: That the said River being now much deeper than it was formerly, the Ballad-men are obliged to go further down to take up Ballad; and that Four Men cannot now take up so much in OneDayas Two usually did heretofore: He further said, That, not being able otherwise to support themselves, they condantly demand for Ballad an additional Rate of 3d. per Ton; and that, even at that Rate, they can scarce earn Ten Shillings a Week: That all the Ballad which they take is out of the River; and that, in delivering of it, they are detained by the Maders of Ships so as often to lose a Day’s Work.

Thomas Pardor, Wm.Martin, and Robert Park, said. That Baliaft being now taken up lower down the River than it was heretofore, the Owners of Lighters are obliged to build them dronger, and to rig them with Masts and Sails.

John West, another working Ballad-man, said. That the Ballad-men mud lie under very great HaixWhips 22

and Oppression, Aould they be obliged to give full Tonage at the usual Rates: And

That the Owners of the Lighters have no Part of the additional Three Pence per Ton now paid by Maders of Ships.

A Petition of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Westminster Church of St.Peter, in Westminster, was presented to the Abbey. HoUfe, and read; setting forth. That, by Two A 61s of Parliament, one made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, and the other made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Ami'e, an annual Sum, for a certain Number of Years, out of the Duties on Coals, was applied towards repairing the said Collegiate Church, the said Church being left, in many Parts, unfinished, at the time of the Dissolution of the Monadery; and those Parts which had been edeemed to be completed, being, through Badness of Materials, and Length of Time, and from other accidental Mischiefs, become ruinous, there being no Provision of Fabrick Rents, or other Emoluments* to enable the said Dean and Chapter to complete or repair, the fame; and the Money set apart for those Uses being scarce sufficient to support the many other large and publick Buildings within their Precinct;, which they are obliged to keep up, and on which they have annually expended considerable Sums: That, by the Allowance of the said annual Sum, the said Dean and Chapter have been enabled to repair the most ruinous Parts of the said Collegiate Church; and to make good about Two-thirds of the whole Fabrick; but that the Term of the said Allowance is expired, and the Money arising therefrom has been all expended, and a great Part of the said Collegiate Church, with the Chapel of King Henry the Seventh, is dill in so ruinous a Condition, as not to be supported* without a further Supply granted by Parliament: And therefore hoping, That so great and good a Work, carried on, and so far advanced, by the Aid of former Parliaments, will, by the like Assistance, in the present auspicious Reign, be happily perfected; and that this venerable Pile will be edeemed a publick Concern; and be it length fmished according to its noble and in- tended Model.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That his Majesty, being informed of the Con* tents of the said Petition, had been pleased to command him to acquaint this House, That his Majesty recommends it to their Consideration, to make such Provision towards the Repairs of the said Collegiate Church, and for repairing and finishing other Buildings thereunto belonging, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Mr. Vincent reported from the Committee, to whom Horsley-the Petition of the Churchwardens, Overseers of the down new Poor, and other principal Inhabitants, of the Parish of St. Olave’Sy Southwark, in the County of Surrey, in Mainte-behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants of nance, the said Parish, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 23d of January last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations of the fame, the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. John Sherman, Surveyor, said, That the Commissioners appointed for building Fifty new Churches had built a new Church in the Parish of St. Olave's, Southwark, which is now entirely liniflied, and fit to be consecrated; and that the Commissioners have agreed upon, and fixed, a District to the said Church, for a new Parish.

Malius Ryal, Esquire, said, That the District for a new Parish w as laid out by a Vestry of both Parishes.

Mr. William Tifncll, Builder, laid, That the said Church is entirely fiuished, and fit for divine Service.

Mr. William Smith said, That the Inhabitants are very poor, most of them being seafaring Men, and Watermen, and are not able to contribute towards the Buil ling of the said Church.

Mr. Wm. Gage said, That there is not above One Family in Five who pay to the Poor’s Rate, which ' makes it fall hard upon the rest of the Parish: That the Poor’s Rate, before a Work-house was built, amounted to £.3,000 per Annum; but that now it amounts to about £. 2,000 only: That there are about 933 Families who pay to the Poor’s Rate, and about

4.000 Families who do not pay, there being a very great Increase ot Houses lately: That the old Church will not hold above 3,000 Persons in the Pews and lfles; and that the Number of Inhabitants is about 24,000.

The Reverend Mr. Wm. Richardson confirmed Mr. Gage's Evidence: And further said, That, supposing

3.000 Persons to come to Church, the)' could not all hear, by reason of the Largeness of the Church.

Mr. Wm. Turner, Clerk to the Solicitor to the Commissioners, produced to the said Committee an Instrument, signed by the Commissioners, whereunto was annexed a Plan of the Church, and Church-yard; as also a Plan of the District of the said Parish: He also proved, that the said Instrument and Plan had been duly inrolled in the High Court of Chancery.

A Petition of several Merchants, and other Traders in and about London, on behalf of them selves and others, who pay great Sums for Customs, Excise, fife. was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That his late Majesty King George the First did, by his Royal Proclamation, the Twenty-secondDay of December 1717, charge and command all his Subjects to receive and pay, at Twenty-three Shillings, and Twenty-five Shillings, and no more, the Pieces of Gold commonly called Broad Pieces, then received and paid at Twenty-three Shillings and Six-pence, and Twenty-five Shillings and Six-pence, and so proportionably for smaller Pieces of the like Gold Coin; but that, notwithstanding the said Proclamation, the Receivers of his Majesty’s Customs and Excise, and the Bank Tellers, refuse to take the said Pieces of Gold in Payment: whereby the Petitioners are put to very great Difficulties to provide other Monies for Payment of the Customs, Excise, fife.; and yet the Petitioners are obliged, by the said Proclamation, to receive the said Pieces, though much diminished by wearing, clipping, and filing; to the great Prejudice of the Petitioners, and the trading Subjects of the Kingdom: And therefore praying the 20:

House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to grant the Petitioners such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Resolved, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will immediately resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

The House, accordingly, resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Chai'les Turner reported from the Committee, That they had considered the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to move the House, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to issue his Royal Proclama-to forbid any Persons to receive or utter in Payment, by Tale, any of the Gold Coins of Twenty-five Shillings, or Twenty-three Shillings, commonly called Broad Pieces, or any Halves or Quarters thereof; and to direct the several Receivers and Collectors of the Revenues to receive the same by Weight, for the Space of One Year, at the Rate of Four Pounds and One Shilling perOunce Troy; and that his Majesty will also be pleased to authorize and require the Officers of his Mint to allow Four Pounds and One Shilling per Ounce Troy, to all such Persons as shal I bring the said Broad Pieces, or any Halves or Quarters thereof, into the Mint within the said Time, and to coin the same into the other current Gold Coins of this Kingdom:

And Sir Charles Turner moved the House accordingly.

Resolved, That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, That he will be graciously pleased to issue his Royal Proclamation, to forbid any Persons to receive or utter in Payment, by Tale, any of the Gold Coins of Twenty-five Shillings, or Twenty-three Shillings, commonly called Broad Pieces, or any Halves or Quarters thereof; and to direct the several Receivers and Collectors of the Revenues to receive the same by Weight for the Space of One Year, at the Rate of Four Poundsand One Shillingper Ounce Troy 5 and that his Majesty will also be pleased to authorize and require the Officers of his Mint to allow Four Pounds and One Shilling per Ounce Troy, to all such Persons as shall bring the said Broad Pieces, or any Halves or Quarters thereof, into the Mint, within the said Time, and to coin the same into the other current Gold Coins of this Kingdom.

Ordered, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by such Members of this House as are of his Majesty’s most honourable Privy Council.

Sir Charles Turner also reported from the said Committee, That they had come toaResolution, which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report.....Tomorrow

Morning.

Mr. Robert Hucks reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Churchwardens, Constables, Overseers of the Poor, and other principal Inhabitants, of that Part of the Parish of St.Giles, Cripplegate, as lies in the County of Middlesex, and always called or known by the Name of the Lordship Part of tiic said Parish, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Inhabitants thereof, was referred, That the Committee bad examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place, and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read, and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, bearing Date the Ninth Iullant, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, called,

Mr. Wm.Caston: Who, being examined, said, That the Commissioners, appointed for building Fifty new Churches, have built a Church near Old-street, in the Lord/])ip Part of the said Parish, which is ready for Consecration, and fit to have Divine Service performed therein.

Then the Petitioners produced and laid before the Committee, a Deed-poll, inrolled in Chancery, wherein a District is described, and appointed, for a new Parish to the said Church.

'Mr.George Tarry, being examined, said, That some of the Inhabitants on behalf of the said Parish, did make Application to the said Commissioners, that the Church and Churchyard might he walled in, and a House built for the Minister; but the said Commissioners informed them, that there was not Money, remaining in their Hands, sufficient to answer the Charge thereof, unless they were impowered by Parliament to appropriate, for that Purpose, Part of the Money appointed for Endowment of Churches.

Nathanael Blaekerhy, Esquire, Treasurer to the said Commissioners, attended the said Committee; and, being asked what Money was remaining, undisposed of, for the Building of Churches, said. That there remained £ 2,844, out of which there is now due, to several Persons, the Sum of £.2,400, and upwards; besides some other Debts not yet ascertained, which, together with the said £ 2,400, will amount to more than the said £.2,844 be sufficient to satisfy and discharge: Then being examined, as to what was remaining in the Exchequer on account of the Endowment-money, said, That there was the Sum of £.23,364 3$. 8\d.; and that, with this Church, there are Five Churches to be endowed out of the said Money.

Mr. Wm. Raiolinfon, being examined, as to the Number of Houses in the Lordship Part of the said Parish, said. That there were near Three thousand; and that there is only a small Tabernacle, not able to contain more than One-tenth Part of the Inhabitants thereof: And further said. That the whole Parish of St.Giles Cripplegate, consists of between Thirty and Forty thou-Vol. 22.

Strode, Great-grandfather of the said Infant, being seised in Fee of a Parcel of Ground called the Lambhay, contiguous to the Fort of Plymouth, and lying between the said Fort and the Town of Plymouth, whereof some Building Leases were granted, and others contracted for; and whereon also Docks, Cellars, Sic. were designed to be built; which would have been of great Advantage to the said Sir William Strode, and his Family: That the Buildings thereon erected were, in the Year 1660, by an Order of the Council, ordered to be demolished; and Part of the said Parcel of Ground was afterwards taken into the said Fort, and a Victualling Office, for the Service of the Navy, hath been built on another Part thereof, and has continued in the Possession of the Crown, without any Leave obtained from the said Sir William Strode, or any Person claiming under him, or any Satisfaction made to him, or them: That, by an Inquisition taken 16 September, 24 Car. Ild- by virtue of a Commission issued out of the Court of Exchequer, pursuant to an Order made by the Lords of the Treasury, in Obedience to the Directions of his said Majesty, upon the Application of the said Sir William Strode for a Compensation, it was found, that the said Parcel of Ground was the Inheritance of the said Sir William Strode; and that his Lessees had, at the Expence of One thousand Five hundred Pounds, erected Buildings thereon, of the annual Value of Two hundred and Twenty-seven Pounds Eleven Shillings and OnePeny; and that the Value of the Inheritance thereof was Four thousand Five hundred and Fifty-one Pounds One Shilling and Eight Pence; and that One Acre and Half, Part of the Three Acres and Sixty-five Perches, which remained, was fit for building Cellars and Docks for the King’®

Arundel A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, Port* and others, the Inhabitants of the Towns of Arundel, IMtle-hampfon, Petworthy and Places adjacent, in the County of Suffer, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Harbour of Litfle-hampton, called Arundel Forty situate at the Mouth of a navigable River, about Thirty Leagues from the Downs, Twelve from lieachyAiead, and Ten from the Isle of W ight, was formerly very useful to the adjacent Country, abounding with Corn, Timber, Iron, Wool, and other Commodities; and that the said River was formerly navigable up to the Town of Arundel; which was, on that Account, a Town of great Trade, for such Vessels ns required no more than Sixteen Feet Depth of Water; but that the said Harbour is now, by Shoals and Banks, prejudicial to Navigation, rendered in a manner useless: That the Attempts of the Commissioners of the Sewers, for the Vol. 22.

5-5

Levels of the Rape of Arundel, to restore the Use of the said Harbour, have proved ineffectual, the Land-owners in the said Levels not being able to defray the Expence of erecting the necessary Pifers for that Purpose: That the said River, venting itself into the Sea at several Places, and thereby Jofing its force, is confined to a narrow Channel, which, by Southerly Storms, and rolling Sands, is often intirely choaked up; and though cut, and plowed through, by the neighbouring Inha-, bitants, at a very great Expence, will only admit small Vessels, hired at an excessive Freight, by reason of the Uncertainty of their Passage out of the said Harbour: That, if Piers were built, and the Navigation of the said Harbour and River were restored, the said Harbour would receive outward-bound Ships that cannot reach the Jfte of Wight, make Shipwrecks less frequent, protect Merchant Ships in War, drain many Thou land Acres of Pasture Land, facilitate the Exportation of the Produce of our own Country, as well as the Importation of foreign Commodities, and be of great Advantage to his Majesty/s Revenues, Docks, and Kingdom in General; and particularly to the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House to enable the Petitioners to coll 6t a small Duty on the Vessels, Goods, and Merchandizes, to be laden, or unladen, in the said Harbour, for and towards building of Piers, restoriing, and rendering useful, the said Harbour, and making the River navigable to the Town of Arundel; or to make, and grant, such other Provision for the fame, as to the House shall feein meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confw oration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fume, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth, That by an Act of Parliament, made in the Twenty-second Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An additional Act for the rebuilding the City of London, Uniting of Parishes, and rebuilding of the Cathedral and Parochial Churches within the said City, for the further Convenience of Trade, the Channel of Bridewell Dock, from the Channel of the River of Thames to Holborn Bridge, was directed to be funk to a sufficient Level, whereby to make it navigable, under such Limitations as.are prescribed by. the said Act; and the 1 Profits arising by the Navigation of the said Channel were appropriated to- the Mayor and Commonalty, and Citizens, of the said City: That,.in pursuance of the said Act, the Channel, was soon after made navigable from the Thames to Holborn Bridge; but that the Profits arising by the Navigation thereof have not answered the Charge of making the same navigable: That Part of the said Channel, from. Fleet Bridge to . Holborn Bridge* instead of being useful to Trade, as was intended, is not only filled up with Mud, and become useless, but.is now, and for some Years past hath been, a common Nuisance; and that several Persons have lately lost their Lives by falling into the fame: That the Expence of cleansing and repairing the fume will be very great; and that a greater annual Charge will be required, to keep the same in Repair, than the Profits arising therefrom will defray, and yet the same will never answer the Intent of the said Act: And

therefore praying. That a Bill may be brought in to repeal so much of the said Act as relates to the said Channel;, and to, impower the Petitioners to fill up Part of the said Channel from Fleet Bridge to Holbont Bridge* and to convert the Ground to such Uses as they shall think fit and convenient.

Importing A Petition of several Merchants of the City of Lon-

Diamonds whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and other Traders and Dealers in Diamonds, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the City of London has, for many Years, been the Chief Mart for Diamonds, from whence most foreign Markets are supplied; and that great Quantities of rough Diamonds are now fentfrom Lisbon, and other Parts, to London, to be cut and polished; by which Manufacture only this Nation gains yearly a very great Sum: That what has contributed greatly to the Increase of this Trade, has been the fullering Diamonds to pass outwards, without Warrant or Fee; and the conveyance of them in the Mails, or Pacquet-boats, wherein the same used to be imported and exported with great Expedition and Safety; but that a Doubt has lately arisen, whether such Method of Conveyance be legal or not; That our Neighbours are so sensible of the Necessity of keeping secret the Quantities of Dia monds imported into any Country, that they suffer the Importation and Exportation thereof to be intirely free: That the Petitioners have great Reason to believe, that a much greater Quantity of rough Diamonds would be sent to England, to be manufactured, if the same were as safely and freely imported into England, as into other Nations; and that the free Importation thereof will probably confine this valuable Branch of Trade to this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and give them such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Sum of One Shilling in the Pound, and no more, be raised, in the Year One thousand Seven hundred anc^Thirty-three, upon Lands, Tenements, Here-, drtaments. From the House of Commons* 27th February 1732.

Sir,

I am commanded by the house of Commons to acquaint you, That you are, immediately upon the Receipt of this, to summon the Representatives of your County, and Boroughs within the same* to attend their Service in Parliament on this Day Fortnight the 13th Day of March next; the House of Commons intending to proceed with the utmost Severity against such of their Members as shall then neglect to attend the Service of the House; and you are to give me an Account of the Receipt of this, and what you have done thereon, upon Pain of incurring the Displeasure of the said House.

I am, Sir,

Your humble Servant,

Ar' Onslow, Speaker;

A Petition of James Duke of Atholl was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That by an Act passed in the First Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for vesting the Honour and Ettate of John Duke of Atholl in James Murray Esquire, commonly called Lord James Murray^ after the Death of the said Duke; reciting, That, by an Act of the same Session of Parliament, the Petitioner’s elder Brother, William Murray Esquire, commonly called Marquis of Tnllibarden, eldest Son and Heir apparent of John Duke of Atholl, the Petitioner’s late Father, since deceased, flood convicted and attainted of High Treal’on; and that the Petitioner, and his said Father, had con- , ilantly adhered to his late Majesty, and rendered him considerable Services; and, as a Reward of their steady Loyalty, his said late Majesty was moil graciously pleased to give his Royal Consent, That thie Honours, Titles, and Ettate, of the said late Duke, should, after his Death, be continued in his Family; it was enacted, That the said Act of Attainder should not be construed to extend to prevent anyDefcentof Honours or Ef-tatefrom the Petitioner’s said Father to the Petitioner, and his Issue; but that all and every such Honours, Titles, and Estates, should, from and immediately after his Death, defeend and come to the Petitioner, and his Issue, in such manner as the same would have done, in case the said William Murray had npt been attainted, and had died without Issue, in the Life-time of the said late Duke: That the Petitioner apprehends it was the' Intention of the Legislature, that none of the rest of the Family of the said late Duke should suffer by the said Attainder of his said eldest Son; but, by the Words of the said first-mentioned Act, it may be doubtful whether any Failure of Issue Male of the Petitioner the Honours would continue in the Family, and defeend to the said late Duke’s other Sons, who are dutiful and affeftionateto his Majesty; and whether the Petitioner, or the other Issue of the said late Duke, could'take ok

enjoy any Title or Estate that might come by collateral Descent, as they might do, if the said William Murray had not been attainted, and died without Issue, in the said late Duke’s Life-time: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, that a Bill n*ay be brought in to explain and amend the said last mentioned Act, foas that the said Attainder of the said William Murray may not be construed to extend to prevent any Descent of Honours or Estate to the Petitioner, or his Issue, or to the Issue or Heirs Male of the said late Duke.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That the same of the Petitioner having been humbly represented to his Majesty, his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, That his Majesty gives his Consent, that the House may do therein as they think fit.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill according to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Sir William Yonge, and Mr. Duncan Forbes, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Tiverton A Petition of the Mayor, Justice, capital Burgesses, Chapel and Assistants, of the Corporation of Tiverton, in the County of Devon, and of the Churchwardens of the said Parish of Tiverton; and of the principal Inhabitants residing within the said Town and Parish; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Parish Church of Tiverton aforesaid, not being capable of receiving the numerous Inhabitants of the said Parish, a Chapel of Ease hath been built, by the Subscription of the Petitioners, and by other Benefactions, on Part of the Ground purchased for the Site thereof, near a Street called St. Andrews Street; but that no Provision hath yet been made for the Maintenance of a Minister, or Mi-nifters, to officiate therein, or for defraying other incident Charges: That the said Church and Parish being divided into Four several Parts, or Portions, by the Names of Pit, Clare, Tidecombe, and Priors Quarters or Portions; which lall Quarter or Portion is appropriated to the Provost arid Fellows of King's College in Cambridge; it has been proposed, by the present Rectors of the said Portions of Pit, Clare, and Tidtcombs* and the Curate under the said College, who have, everiince the Finish'ing of the said Chapel, voluntarily, and without any Recompence, officiated therein: That they, and their Succefiois, shall, at all times hereafter, officiate in the said Chapel, by Turns, as they now do in the said Parish Church of Tiverton, provided that a competent yearly Provision or Maintenance might be made for the said Rectors and Curate for the Time being; but that no such Provision can be effected, and established, without the Aid of an Act of Parliament: And therefore praying. That a Bill may be brought in for making the said Chapel a perpetual Cure; and for providing a Maintenance for the Ministers thereof; and for such other Purposes as shall be thought fit and con-I venient in that Behalf.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of Cries, Midhell, Och- Damages terarder, Dunning, Blackfoord, and the neighbouring done by the Houses, in the Shire of Perth, was presented to the Kebels. House, and read; setting forth, That, in the Month of January 1715, the Five Villages afore-mentioned, and a considerable Number of Houses in their Neighbourhood, were burned by the Rebels in Scotland, and their whole Goods destroyed, and they exposed to the Rigour of a very severe Winter; and that the Extent of their Lodes sustained thereby hath been certified to be £.4,333. 17s. — fd. Sterling; but that the Provision made by Parliament for their Relief hath not produced any thing for that Purpose: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration, and to make such Provision for their Payment, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Petition of the Royal African Company of Eng- African

land, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, Company. That this House having, in the last Session, upon full Examination and Consideration of the Trade to Africa, granted the Sum of Ten thousand Pounds towards the Maintenance of the British Forts and Settlements belonging to the said Company, the said Sum hath been applied accordingly; and it having appeared to the House, that the said Forts and Settlements cannot be supported, and the Trade preserved, without the Aid of Parliament: Therefore praying, That such larther Provision may be made in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That his Majesty being informed of the Contents of the said Petition, had been pleased to command him to acquaint this House, That his Majesty recommends it to their Consideration, to make such farther Provision in the Premises, as the House shall think fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That the Royal African Company of England, do lay before this House the Establishment for their several Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, with the Charges thereof, for the Year 1732; distinguishing how much of the same is on account of Trade, and how much for the Maintenance and Defence of the said Forts and Settlements; and also, an Account how the Money granted in the last Session of Parliament, towards the Maintenance of the said Forts and Settlements, hath been disposed of.

Ordered, That an Estimate of the Charges of the Royal African Company of England, for the Maintenance of the several British Forts and Settlements belonging to the said Company, on the Coast of Africa, for the Year 1733, be laid before this House.

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, aWitness was called; viz.

Henry Pye Esquire: Who said, That he lived in the Town of Farringdon, through which the Road mentioned in the Petition leads; and is well acquainted with all the Road desired to be repaired; and that the same is in so ruinous aCondition, that Passengers cannot pass andrepafs, in the Win ter-season, without Danger:

And he further said, That the Road, between a Place called Eaton and Farringdon, is so bad, that such Travellers, and Carriages, as usually passed through that Road, were now' obliged to go another Way; whereby the Town of Farringdon had intirely loft its Trade.

And it appeared to the Committee, That the said Road cannot be effectually amended, and kept in Repair, by the Laws now in being, for repairing the Roads of this Kingdom, unless some further Provision be made for that Purpose.

Papists An ingrossed Bill for allowing further Time for the *wVnd Inrolfment of Deeds and Wills made by Papists, and 1 s* for Relief of Protestant Purchasers and Lessees; was read the Third time.

An ingrossed Clause was offered, to be added to the Bill, by way of Rider, That no Purchase made for valuable Considerations of any Estates, or of any Interest therein, by Protestants, and only for their Benefit, shall be impeached or avoided, by reason that any Deed or Will, through which the Title thereto is derived, hath not been inrolled as required by Acts of Parliament, so as no Advantage was taken of the want of Inrollment thereof before such Purchase was made; and so as the Purchaser had not notice, before the Purchase, that the Person who made such Deed or Will was a Papist; and so as no Decree or Judgment hath been obtained for want of the Inrollment of such Deed, Will, or Lease;

And the said Clause was thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House to be made Part of the Bill.

Resolved, That the Bill do pass: And that the Title be* An Act for allowing further Time for the Inrollment of Deeds and Wills made by Papists, and for Relief of Protestant Purchasers and Lessees.

Ordered, That Mr. Holland do carry the Bill to the Lords, and desire their Concurrence.

It appeared to your Committee, That, in pursuance of an Order of Council, made the 19th of September 1660, a Letter was wrote, by some of the then Lords of the Council, to the theu Mayor of Plymouth, and to the Lieutenant Governor of the Fort there, desiring that they would return a Report of the Situation of a House erected upon the Hoe at Plymouth, and of what Danger they conceived it was, or might be, to the Security of the Town and Harbour; and they certified, that they conceived, that the Vicinity of the many new-eredod Houses, to his then Majestys Fort, confided not with the Security of the Town and Harbour: And by°another Order of Council, of the 28th of September 1660, it was ordered, that the House built on the find/fue, or Laming, should be demolished; and that the then Mayor and Deputy Governor should fee the Order fully executed; and also cause such other Houses and Edifices, then lately built there, to be demolished, which tiood not confident with the Security of the Fort.

That, in pursuance of a Commission, dated the 19th of Jtdy, 24th Car. IIdJ issued out of the Court of Exchequer, to which the Instructious given on that Occafiou, and a Map of the Premises, were annexed, a J ury of 24 Gentlemen, of the County of Devon, was impannelled $ and an Inquisition taken the 16th of September following, and returned into that Court. It appeared to the Committee, that the Jury had viewed the Ground called the Lambhay, and Buildings thereon erected, and returned, that Sir William Strode Knight was the then Lord, Owner, and Possessor, of the Lands and Houses built on the Lambhay; and that, before the Year 1660, there had been Buildings erected thereon by his Lessees, at the Expence of £.1,500; and that the annual Value thereof was £.217. 1 is. id.; and the Value of the Inheritance £4,551. and that there remained

Three Acres and 65 Perches, which was Building-ground before the making the new Fort; and that One Acre and Half thereof was fit for building Cellars and Docks for the King’s Use, and might be improved to £.529. 1 os. Sd. per Annum, expending£.3,600 thereon.

It also appeared to the Committee, That, after the Death of Sir Wm. Strode, Richard Strode Esquire, his Son and Heir, applied by Petition to their late Majesties King William and Queen Mary, setting forth, That he and his Auceflors had been seised in Fee of the said Lands; and that Sir Wm. Strode had caused several Parts thereof to be built upon; and that there were ereCied and made some Houses, Cellars, Docks, and Quays, of a considerable yearly Value; and that he had contracted and agreed for building upon thellefidue of such Lands; but the same being, in 1660, found necessary for the Serv ice of the Crown, as well in respeCi of the Citadel there, as of Naval Affairs, his said Majesty King Charles the Second was pleased to convert the same to his own Use, declaring the said Sir William Strode should have Satisfaction for the Premises; and the said Richard Strode, by his Petition prayed, That he might have Satisfaction for the Lands and Buildings.

That this Petition was, the 27th of October 1691, referred to the then Lords Commissioners of the Treasury; and by them, the 27th of November following, referred to Mr. Taylor the then Deputy Surveyor General; who, 12th of December 1691, certified, That, before, the Year 1660, the Lessees of Sir Wm Strode had ert&ed several Houses on the said Lambhay; and that the same were ordered to be demolished as aforesaid, and the Owners forbid to erect any other Buildings; and that the same was afterwards made use of for victualling the Navy, and employed for that Service, and was then in the possession of the Crown; and he also certified, that Sir William Strode did, in November 1671, petition his then late Majesty for aCompensation for the said Piece

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the Second Day of March inilant, proceeded l to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations of the fame, the following Witnesses were called; viz.

Mr. John Smith, Surveyor: Who said. That the said Roads were in such a ruinous Condition at the time of passing the said Acts, that the Trustees were obliged to borrow a considerable Sum of Money, on the Credit of the said Acts, to make the said Roads passable; and although the Money borrowed, and also what hath been collected by the Tolls, hath been duly applied, according to the Directions of the said Acts, yet the Roads cannot be effectually repaired, and so kept, unless a further Term be granted.

Mr. William How, Treasurer to the Commissioners, said, That there is a Debt of £. 1,380 still subsisting; which) cannot be repaid, and the Roads sufficiently amended, and so kept, without a further Continuance of the Term granted by the first-mentioned Act.

Evans Dixcn, Waggoner, said. That he travels upon the said Roads often; and that the same are so bad, that they are not capable of being sufficiently repaired, without a further Continuance of the said Act; which will be of great Service to the said Counties.
