Mr. Winnington reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of John Rickefies, Gentleman, on behalf of Frances Brandon and Rebecca Brandon, Infants, Robert Heart, Brandon Heart, Thomas Peirce, and Anne his Wife, Anne Brandon, Wido\v, Brod?iax Brandon, and Mary Brandon, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame^s it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, dated the 27th Day of February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition.

And it appeared to the Committee, That William Brandon,}ate of Porlfmouth, in the County of Southampton, Grandfather of the said Frances and Rebecca Brandon, Brandon Heart, Anne Peirce, and Father of the said Brodnax, and Mary Brandon, before his Marriage, entered into such Articles, and made such Settlement and Will, as are particularly mentioned in the said Petition; and for the Purposes therein set forth; and that he died in 1704, and left the Petitioner Anne Brandon his Widow, and Issue by her the Petitioners Brodnax And Mary; and also Thomas and Charles Brandon, born after the Will was made;and likewise!eft, by his former Wives, William, Richard, James, Anne, and Elizabeth Brandon.

That the said Thomas, Charles, William, Richard, James, Anne, and Elizabeth, being dead, the Petitioners are all the Persons concerned and interested in the Estates mentioned in the said Petition.

And it also appeared to the said Committee, That the said William Brandon was Agent Victualler at Porff-mouth, at the time of his Death, and thereby became indebted to the Crown in the Sum of £.3,078. 12S. \%d; which Sum was proved to be due, and still unpaid.

That the said Sum cannot otherwise be paid than by Sale of such Part of the Estates as he died seised o($ not included in the Settlement aforesaid.

That the Money arising by such Sale will amount to a considerable Sum more than what is sufficient to pay the said Debt, and the Charges of such Sale; to which Sale the Petitioners, who are all the Parties concerned, are consenting; and that the Debt, and the Charges of such Sale, should be first satisfied out of the Purchase-money; and that the Residue thereof should be applied to the same Uses as the said Estates are subject to by the Will of the said William Brandon, and by a Covenant contained in the Articles aforesaid; but, in regard the said Frances and Rebecca are Infants, the said Estates cannot be fold without the Aid of an Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in 3 Bill for vesting in Trustees the unsettled Estates of William Brandon, deceased, to be sold, for Payment of a Debt due to the Crown; and for applying the Residue of the Money arising by such Sale for "the Benefit of his Far mily: And that Mr. Winnington, and the Lord Vere Beauclerk, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The Translations of the said Papers are as follow; viz.

Translation of the King of $/uz/Vs Cedula to his Governors in the West Indies, relating to the Spanifi Privateers; Seville, January 18th, 1732, N. S.

I the King.

Whereas the British Minister residing at this Court has represented to me, That, notwithstanding the Orders I have issued to hinder the Spanish Privateers in America from committing Hostilities against the English, and their Ships, frequenting those Seas, nevertheless, not only such Persons as have Patents from some of the Governors of the Ports in my Dominions, but also some who have no Patents at all, continue their Hostilities, under a Pretence of preventing an illicit Commerce; whilst the Governors refuse to admit of the Complaints given in by the English, who have experienced such unjust Molestations, or to indemnify them of the Losses they may have suffered thereby: My Refofution is, That the Orders already issued for that Purpose should be repeated: Wherefore, I command, by these Presents, all Governors, in any Port or Place of my Dominions in America, not to suffer any of my Subjects to molest or abuse the English, or any of their Ships, that shall fail in those Seas, as long as they keep in their proper Distances, and are not concerned in any illicit Trade; and that my Governors take special Care, that my said Subjects do conform exactly, and indispensably, to the Royal Laws and Ordinances, which treat of those Matters: And if any of my said Subjects should commit any Excess, contrary to those Laws, I command my Governors to punish them, with all the Severity that the Offence they shall have committed requires; as also, such as, without Patents, shall go to Sea, in order to commit Hostilities, and make unlawful Prizes: That the said Governors do hearken to, and admit all Complaints that shall be made to them from the Ministers, or chief Commanders, of Great Britain, either by Word of Mouth, or by Writing; taking care to do them Justice, at all times; and to give them Testimonies of all that shall be transacted; and that Satisfaction be given them for the Losses they may have sustained unjustly, by the Subjects who may have occasioned them, and who ought to make them good; for such is my Will: And the aforesaid Governors are to understand, That they shall be accountable for the Excesses committed by the Privateers; because, before they grant them Patents to go to Sea, they ought to examine who the Persons are, and infill upon proper Securities. Done at Seville, the 18th Day of January 1732.

I the King.

D. Joseph Patino.

To the Governors of the Ports in the Indies, relating to the Hostilities which the English have experienced from the Privateers of those Ports.

Translation of a Declaration, signed by the British and Spanifi Ministers, concerning the Depredations of the Spaniards in the West Indies.

Seville, February 8th, 1732, N. S.

Declaration which we, the under-written Ministers of their Britannick and Catholick Majesties, fiiike, by virtue of the Orders which we have from the Kings our respective Matters.

Whereas Complaint has been made. That, since the Arrival of his Catholick Majesty’s Orders at Carthagena, on the 22d of June 1728, and even since the Signing of the Treaty of Seville, Acts of Hostility have continued to be committed on the Part of the Subjectsof his Catholick Majesty in America; and that the Vessels and Effects of his Britannick Majesty’s Subjects have been unjustly seized, and detained; which appears to have been chiefly practised by Ships belonging to private Persons, fitted out to cruize, under the plausible Pretence of preventing a clandestine and unlawful Trade: His Catholick Majesty having agreed, by the Treaty of Seville, to cause Reparation to be made, as soon as may be, for the Losses and Damages which have been sustained on account of such Captures,

promises

6 Geo. II.

13° Martii.

87

promises and engages, parfuant to the said Treaty, and to the Declaration relative thereunto, which was signed on the Sixth of June last Year, that such Reparation shall, without Delay, be fully and effectually made, in due Form, according to the Tenor of the Treaty of Seville: And, in order to prevent the like Depredations for the future, his Catholick Majesty does moreover promise and engage, not to permit that his Vice Roys, Governors, or other Officers, in America, either by their Commissions, or in any other Manner, do encourage, protect, or authorize, such pernicious Practices; but that, on the contrary, the strictest Orders shall be sent them, to do every thing that shall be in their Power to prevent the like happening; to the End, that the lawful Commerce and Navigation of his Britannick Majesty’s Subjects, to their Colonies, and their Ports, may be carried on freely, and without Molestation, agreeable to the several Treaties upon that Subject.

His Catholick Majesty also promises and engages, by this Declaration, That whenever any Privateers shall, under the Denomination of Garde Cdtes, or any other Denomination whatsoever, have Leave to fit out for Sea, in order to prevent contraband Trade, pursuant to the Laws and Ordinances of the Indies, which have not been derogated from by the Treaties, they shall be obliged to give Security, in the Presence of the Cover-. nors of the Places from whence they shall fail, to be answerable for any Damages they may unjustly occasion; and in Default of sufficient Security, the Governors themselves shall be answerable for whatever may happen: His Catholick Majesty expecting, that proper Orders shall reciprocally be given on the Part of his Britannick Majesty, for causing the Hostilities to cease, which the Spanish Ships have met with since the 22d June 1728, and for making good the Losses and Damages which the Subjects of Spain shall have unjustly sustained.

In like manner, his Britannick Majesty promises to forbid, and effectually prevent, his said Majesty’s Ships of War from convoying, or protecting, under any Pretence whatsoever. Ships carrying on an unlawful Trade upon the Coasts of the States belonging to his Catholick Majesty, and the Governors of the Colonies from authorizing and encouraging any Landing upon his said Majesty’s Dominions; and the Catholick King promises to do the like on his Part: thereby to avoid all Cause of Complaints, which might interrupt the good Correspondence between the Subjects of the two Nations.

In Witness whereof, we, the under-written Ministers dxhvlr Britannick and Catholick Majesties, have signed the present Declaration, and put the Seals of our Arms thereto. Done at Seville, the 8th Day of February 1732. B. Keene, EL Marquis de la Paz, D. Joseph Patino. (L. S.) {L. S.) (L. S.)

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House of the 26th of February last, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

An Act, passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, for laying a Duty of Two Penies fats, or One Sixth Part of a Peny'Sterling, upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer brewed and fold within the Vou 22.

Town of Linlithgow % and Liberties thereof, in the County of West Lothian, for paying the Debts of the; said Town, and other Purposes therein mentioned, was laid before the Committee; and which Act commenced on the First Day of July 1723, and has Continuance for and during the Term of Eleven Years, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament.

The Petitioners also laid before the Committee, a List of Debts due from the said Town, to their several Creditors, at Michaelmas last, by Bonds, signed by Alexander Bell, Common Clerk of the said Burgh, and sealed with the Seal of the said Town; by which it appears, that the said Debts then amounted to a considerable Sum of Money.

And they also produced an Account of the annual Expence of the said Town; together with an Account of the annual Revenue thereof; and the Amount of the annual Produce of the said Duty; by which it appears, that the Interest of the Debts now due, and the other necessary Expences of the said Town, exceed the annual Revenue thereof, exclusive of what arises from the said Duty; whereby they are disabled to pay off the said Debt, and keep the publick Buildings and Streets in Repair.

And Mr. Michael Bell, being examined, proved ,the several Accounts produced: And said, That the publick Buildings and Streets of the said Town are much decayed, and ruinous, and the Inhabitants thereof are not able to discharge the Debts, and keep the said Buildings and Streets in Repair, unless some further Provision be made for that Purpose.

Then the Mayor of the said Town produced a Declaration, in Writing, signed by the Nobility and Gentry in that County and Neighbourhood; whereby it appeared, that they desired a further Continuance of the said Duty.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for continuing an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One Sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, upon every ScotsPint of Ale and Beer brewed and fold within the Town of Linlithgow, and Liberties thereof, in the County of West Lothian, for paying the Debts of the said Town, and other Purposes therein mentioned; and for rendering the said Act more effectual: And that Mr. Murray and Mr. Arejkine do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That, by a Clause in a Bill, now depending in this House, for providing a Maintenance for the Rector of the new Church, near Old-street, in the Parish of St. Giles, Cripplegafe; and for making that Part of the said Parish, which is called the Lordship Part, a distinct Parish; and for impowering the Commissioners for building the Fifty new Churches to apply a Sum of Money to wall in the said Church and Church Yard; and to fereft a House for the Habitation of the Rector of the said Parish, out of the Money appropriated for the Endowment of the said Fifty new Churches; which Clause provides against the Alteration or Change of the Methods or Payments for repairing the Highways in the said Parish; the Petitioners will be obliged to contribute towards the Repair of the said Highways, though all of them lie in the said District allotted for the said new-intended Parish, and are at a considerable Distance from the District remaining to the old Parish, called the Freedom Part; to the great Injury and Oppression of the Petitioners: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration x and to admit the Petitioners to be heard, by themselves* or Counsel, against the said Clause, before the said Bill pass into a Law.

A Petition of Sir John Glynne Baronet, Lord of the Manor of Harden, alias Hawarden, in the County of Flint; and also of the several Gentlemen, and others, who have thereunto subscribed their Names, being Owners awl Proprietors of, and who have Right of Common, in certain Marsh Lands called Saitney, containing many Thousand Acres, lying near to the River Dee, on the South JSide thereof; was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, upon a View of the Plan, by which the Undertakers for recovering and preserving the Navigation of the said River propose to effect the said Navigation, whereby it appears, that they intend to alter the Course of the present Chanel of the said River, and to make a new Cut, or Chanel, through the said Marsh Lands called Saitney, the Petitioners conceive, and are advrfed by able and (kilftil Persons, who have viewed the said Plan, that the Bill, depending in this House, to recover and preserve the Navigation of the River Dee, in the County Palatine of Chester, if passed into a Law, without proper Provisions for the Security and Indemnity of the Petitioners, will not only be greatly prejudicial to the Petitioners, but indanger the total Loss of their Right and Properties in and to the said Marsh Lands: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by themselves, or their Counsel, in relation to the said Bill, before the same shall pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be heard, before the said Committee, by their Counsel, according to the Prayer of the said Petition.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the said Committee, That they do admit Counsel to be heard, at the same time, iu favour of the said Bill, against the said Petition.

Dee A Petition of the Merchants, Owners and Masters of ^tvigatiort. Ships, inhabiting within, and trading from, the Town and Port of Liverpool, in the County Palatine of Lan~ cqfier, to and from his Majesty s Plantations, and other foreign Parts, whose Names are subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and many others concerned therein, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Road or Harbour called Hoyl Lake, within the Limits of the said Port, which is preserved by the outward Bank called Hoyl Sand, has been found, by long Experience, to be the most commodious Road in that Part of the Kingdom for the Reception of his Majesty’s Ships of War, as well as of Merchants Ships; and the only Safeguard for those arriving from foreign Parts, before their Entrance into the Harbour of Liverpool; and also the most convenient Road in Great Britain for Transportation of his Majesty s Forces to Ireland; and that, in case the lliver Dee be so contrafted and confined as to increase the Current out of the same into the Sea, the Petitioners apprehend that the Ebb Tide will soon cut a Puffage through the said Bank; and thereby divert the present Current, which now run9 through, and keeps open, Hoyl Lake; and, by obstructing the said Current, render that commodious Harbour intirely useless, to the Destruction of the Navigation to and from the said Town and Port: And therefore praying, That the House will be pleased to take the Premises into Consideration; and that the Bill depending in this House, to recover and preserve the Navigation of the River Dee, in the County Palatine of Chester, may not pals into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. John Mealling said, That the old Pye Road is very bad; and that the Roads from Yaxley to Eye (being about One Mile and a Half), and from Eye to Lanthorn Green (being One Mile and a Half more), are so bad, that Coaches cannot pass without Danger; and, for that Reason, Waggons have been obliged to lie ftiort of their Journey; but, if the said Roads, were repaired, it would be of great Advantage to the neighbouring Parishes: And the said John Mealling said further. That it will cost £ 200 to repair the Road between Eye and Yaxley Bull, being about Three Quarters of a Mile.

And he also said, That the Farmers carry Corn to Ipswich; and, by the Badness of the last mentioned Roads, their Cattle have received great Damage; but, if the said Roads were amended, they would constantly return loaded, which now they cannot do, and would also fetch all Plank from Ipswich:

That, if the Farmers do carry Corn to Bungy, they must deliver 21 Coomb for a Score, and at Ipswich, only 20 Coomb: And he further said, That the last mentioned Road is the Poll Road.

Mr. John Gudgeon confirmed the Evidence of John Mealling: And further said, That he had surveyed those Roads, and that they are very bad; and that the Parishes of Yaxley, Brazcnorth, and Eye, through which the said Roads lead, have constantly done their Statute work, but the same hath not been sufficient to repair the said Roads; and that, by reason of the badness of the Roads, the Expence of Carriage is now One Shilling and Six Pence, whereas there was formerly paid only One Shilling; and that the Inhabitants cannot get into the great Road without going through Eye.

And that it appeared to the Committee, That the Roads intended to be repaired by the former Act, and the additional Roads, cannot be amended and so kept, unlessfome other Provision be made for that Purpose.

It appeared to the Committee, That Process of the Court of Exchequer hath issued against the said acting Commissioners, or some of them, for the several Sums mentioned in the Petition; and this has been certified to the Commissioners of the Treasury, by the Commissioners for the Affairs of Taxes.

Mr George Payne, Assistant Secretary to the Commissioners for Taxes, attended the Committee; and proved, Thut Mr. Allen, and about Eleven more General Receivers, were ordered by the Commissioners of the Treasury not to act, till such time as they paid such Sums as were in Arrear within their respective Receiverships.

The said Mr. Payne laid before the Committee aCer-tificate, signed by the Commissioners of Taxes; whereby it appeared. That Nlv. Allen had received, and that there was due from him, the Sum of £. 4,412. 6. 11£.

It also appeared to the Committee, That the said Mr. Allen continued acting as Receiver General, without having any Commission for so doing; and that it was not known to the Commissioners, who are the Petitioners, at the time when the Money was paid to the said Mr. Allen, that he was suspended from his Employment, he being then in full Credit in the Country; and that, immediately after he had received the Money, he became insolvent, and went beyond Sea, and is finca dead.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the Bill for granting an Aid to his Majesty, by a Land Tax, to be raised in Great Britain, for the Service of the Year 1733, is committed.

They were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House, a Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Commou-counCil assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth. That the Petitioners, on Occasion of the Bill depending in this House, for repealing several Subsidies, and an Impost now payable on Tobacco of the Brit ish Plantations; and for granting an inland Duty, in lieu thereof; presume, in all Humility, to express to this House, as they have already done, in fomemeasure, by their Representation to their Members, the universal Sense of the City of London concerning any further Exjention of the Laws of Excise: That the Burden ofraxes already imposed on every Branch of Trade, however cheerfully borne, is severely felt; but the Petitioners apprehend, that this Burden will grow tooheavy to be borne, if it beincreased by such vexatious and oppressive Methods of levying and collecting the Duties, as they are assured by melancholy Experience that the Nature of all Excises muff; necessarily produce: That the Merchants, Tradesmen, and Manufacturers, of this Kingdom, have supported themselves, under the Pressure of the Excise Laws now in force, by the comfortable and reasonable Expectation, that Laws, which nothing but public Necef-iity could be a Motive to enact, would be repealed in favour of the Trade of the Nation, and of the Liberty *of the Subject, whenever that Motive should be removed; as, the Petitioners presume, it effectually is, by undisturbed Tranquillity at home, and a general Peace so firmly established abroad: That if this Expectation be entirely taken away; if the Excise Laws, instead of being repealed, are extended to other Species of Merchandize not yet excised, and a Door opened for extending them to all; the Petitioners cannot, in Justice to themselves, to the Merchants, Tradelinen, and Manufacturers of the whole Kingdom, and to the general ln^ terefl of their Country, conceal their Apprehension, that the most fatal Blow which ever was given, will be given, on this Occasion, to the Trade and Navigation of Great Britain; That that great Spring, from which the Wealth and Prosperity of the Public flows, will be obstructed; and the mercantile Part of the Nation will become not only able to trade to Advantage, but unwilling to trade at all; since no Person, who can enjoy all the Privileges of a British Subject out of Trade, even with a small Fortune, will voluntarily renounce some of the most valuable of those Privileges, by ftibjefting himself to the Laws of Excise: That the Petitioners are able to shew, that these their Apprehensions are founded both 20 in

Charitable

Corporation.

A* Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Common Council, of the Town, and County of the Town, of Nottingham, in Council assembled, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Merchants and Tradesmen dealing in Tobacco, in the said Town, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Bill, depending in this House, for repealing several Subsidies, and an Impost, now payable on Tobacco, of the British Plantations; and for granting au Inland Duty in lieu thereof j will be highly prejudicial to the Petitioners, and encroach on their Liberties and Properties; and expressing their Apprehension, that the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will subject them to great Oppressions and Inconveniencies, by the Officers frequent entering their Houses, and taking Account of their Stocks; which they may discover to any others, by being obliged to seek for, and fend, Permits with their Goods; and the Hardships thereof, with respect to Time, by not being allowed the valuable Liberty of redrelfing their Grievances by a Jury; and by the great Trouble, Charge, and Lois of Time, in weighing their Tobacco, at any time required by the Officer, and the Prejudice to their Goods, in uncalking and breaking them: And therefore beseeching the House to consider and favour their Petition; and prevent the passing a Law which will be any-ways definitive of the Trade, or dangerous to the Liberties, of the Petitioners.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Live in °s is willing, as the Petitioners arc informed, to give up his said Patent for the National Advantage, upon haying such reasonable Allowance as the House shall think fit; but thqt the present high Duty upon Salt prevents the using such a Quantity thereof as is necessary for making the said Manure in Perfection: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill, that, upon Satisfaction given to the said Mr. Liveings, his said Patent may become vacated, to the end that all his Majesty’s Subjects may make and use, or vend, the fame, without Restraint; and that such foul Salt as shall be boiled up or mixed with Soot, and other Ingredients, so as to render it unfit for any other Use than for Manure* may be subject to a less Duty; or that such other Relief may be given in the Premises, as to the House shall feerri meet.

btife Petition of the Druggists and Grocers, China-men, and others, dealing in Coffee, Tea, Cocoa-nuts, and Chocolate, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That by an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of King George the Pirft, intituled, An Act for repealing certain Duties therein mentioned, payable upon Coffee, Tea, Cocoa*Buts, Chocolate, and Cocoa-paste, imported, and for granting certain inland Duties in lieu thereof; and for prohibiting the Importation of Chocolate ready made, and Cocoa-paste; and for better ascertaining the Duties payable upon Coffee, Tea, and Cocoa-nuts, imported; and for granting Relief to Robert Dalzell, late Earl of Camwath; the Petitioners were made to hope, that the Dutiesarifing from the said Commodities would be better Secured, and the Interestof the fair Trader bettersupported; but that the Petitioners have found Vo l, 29.

themselves, frotn fatal Experience, subjected to Laws most oppressive and injurious to Trade; are deprived of the Privilege of Juries, and subjected to the judicial Determination of Commissioners, and to the Inquisition and Inspection of Persons unknown to them, who enter their Houses at Pleasure, and to whom they are made accountable for all their Dealings; and, after having paid Duty for their Goods, have not Liberty to sell the same, without Permits from the Officers of Excise, expressing the Names, and Places of Abode, of the respective Buyers and Sellers; to thfe great Damage of the Petitioners, and the exposing the Extent and Circumstances of their Trade to the said Officers, and to whomsoever they think fit to communicate the fame; and are subject to severe Forfeitures for Errors, or Neglect of Entries, in their Books, which are absolutely unavoidable; and are moreover, by a Clause in an Act of the Eleventh of King George the First, liable to be examined upon Oath, touching the Entries in theit Books; and, in case of Neglect or Refusal, are subject to severe and heavy Fines: That, by these Grievances, the Petitioners, as they conceive, are in a Worse Condition than any of his Majesty’s Subjects; and that the clandestine Importation of Tea was never at a greater Height than at present; to the Prejudice of the Revenue, and the Ruin of the fair Traders, who only are subject to these oppressive Laws: And therefore praying, That this House will give them such Relief as to their great Wisdom shall seem meet.

Mr. Thomas Tower'reported from the Committee, who were appointed to inspect what Laws are expired, or near expiring; and to report their Opinion to the House, which of them are fit to be revived, or continued; That they had inspected the Laws accordingly; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follows; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reftn of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Regulation of Juries; and also One other Act, made in the Fourth Year of the Reign of his laid present Majesty, intituled, An Act to explain and amend an Act, made in the Third Year of his Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act for the better Regulation of Juries, so far as the same relates to the County of Middlesex; and which are near expiring; are fit to be made perpetual.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Thirteenth and Fourteenth Years of the Reign of King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for Preventing of Theft and Rapine upon the Northern Borders of England; and also certain Clauses, Powers, and Authorities, contained in one other Act, made in the Eighteenth Year of the Reign of the said King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act to continue a former Act to prevent Theft and Rapine, upon the Northern Borders of England; and also in one other Act, made in the twenty-ninth and thirtieth Years of the reign of the said King Charles the Second, intituled, An Act for continuing of Two form* r Acts for preventing of Fheft and Rapine upon the Northern Borders of England', and also in one other Act, made in the twelfth and thirteenth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, intituled, An Act for continuing the Acts therein mentioned, for preventing Theft and Rapine upon the Northern Borders of England; and which are expired, or near expiring; are fit to be revived, and further continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for the more effectual punishing wicked and evil-disposed Persons going armed in disguise, and doing Injuries and Violences to the Persons and Properties of his Majesty’s Subjects, and for the more speedy bringing the Offenders to Justice; which was to continue iij force for Three Years, from the First Day of June 1723, and from thence to the end of the then next Session of Parliament; and which, by an Act, made in the Twelfth Year of the . Reign of his said late Majesty, was continued, from the Expiration thereof, for Five Years, and from thence to the end of the then, next Session of Parliament, and is near expiring; is fit to be further continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for the better regulating the Manufactureof Cloth in the West Riding of the County of York (except a Clause restraining any Person not having served Seven Years as an Apprentice to the Trade of a Broad Clothier, or

not having exercised such Trade for Two Years before the Commencement of the faij Act, except as therein is excepted, from making, or causing to be made, any Broad Cloth in the said West Riding, under the Penalties therein mentioned); which said Act was to continue in Force for the Term of Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, and is near expiring is fit to be continued.

And presented a Petition of the Corporation of the Governor and Company of Merchants of Great Britain trading to the South Seas, and other Parts of America; and for encouraging the Fishery; which was read; setting forth. That the Petitioners having, at their General Court, held the Seventeenth Day of April, taken their Affairs into Confederation, came toa Resolution to apply to Parliament, that the whole capital Stock of the said Company may be divided into Four Parts; and that Three Parts thereof may be converted into Annuities, at Four per Cent. payable by the said Company, out of their Fund, in lieu of all Dividends and Profits now payable in respect thereof: and that the remaining Fourth Part of the said Capital may continue in the Company, attended with the Residue of the said Fund* and be the trading Stock, subject to the Company’s Debt and Incumbrances, and having all the Effects, Debts, Powers, Privileges, Profits, and Advantages, which the said Company are entitled to, with proper Clauses and Provisions for the better settling, regulating, and managing; the said Company’s Affairs for the future; and that the said capital Stock, or any Part thereof, may not, without the said Company’s Consent, be further redeemed, till the present and now proposed South Sea Annuities shall be reduced by Redemption, to be equal to such Capital: And therefore praying, That the said Company may be enabled to put the Premises in Execution, in such manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill, according to the Prayer of the said Petition, and upon the Debate of the House: And that Sir James Lowlher, Sir George Cafwalt, Mr. Glanvil, Mr. Scrope, Mr. Plinner, and Mr. Walpole, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Thomas Cockfhutt, Merchants, residing in, and trading to and from, the Town and Port of Liverpoole, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many other Merchants and Traders to and from the said 16

Town and Port oT Liverpoole, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, if the Bill, depending in this House, to recover and preserve the Navigation of the River Dee, in the County Palatine of Chester, should pass into a Law, and such Works should be begun, and such new Chanej, should be made, asproposed by the Bill, the Petitioners apprehend that the same will not only be a great Prejudice to the Petitioners, and to the said Town and Port of Liverpoole, by obstructing the Navigation to and from the said Town and Port, but will greatly affect the Bay or Harbour of Hoyle Lake, which, at present, is the only convenient Harbour and Riding Place, as well for his Majesty’s Ships of War, as for all Ships trading to and from those Parts: And therefore praying. Mr. Conduit presented to the House, according td Order, a Bill to prevent the coining or counterfeiting any of the Gold Coins commonly called Broad Pieces: And the same was received; and read the First time.

Resolved, That the Bill be read a Second time.

A Representatiob of the Justices of the Peace for the County of Lanerk, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the present Laws, made to prevent the running of French Brandies into Great Britain, are rendered ineffectual by the Continuance of the Practice of exposing condemned Brandies to public Roup at the Exchequer, where such Brandies are generally bought by the Runners of the said Commodity, who, by means of Permits procured from the Officers of the Revenue, are enabled to carry on that unlawful Trade; to the great Prejudice of his Majesty’s Revenue, the whole landed Interest of the Nation, and Distillers of Spirits from Grain and Melasses; but that these Praftiees, as the Petitioners are persuaded, might be in a great measure prevented, by causing the said Brandies to be (laved, or exported for Sale to foreign Parts, upon the Condemnation thereof; and that the drawing back all the Duties on the Exportation of Spirits made of Corn, Sugar, and Melasses, will be a great Encouragement to the Distillers, tend very much to the Consumption of Grain, without any Prejudice to the Revenue: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to do what they shall think necessary for the more effectual suppressing and preventing the running of prohibited Spirits, and for the Encouragement of Distillers from Corn and Melasses.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, who are appointed to inquire into the Frauds and Abuses in the Customs; to the Prejudice of Trade, and Diminution of the Revenue.

His Majesty having received from the Prince of Orange Proposals for a Treaty of Marriage between the Princefe Royal and the said Prince; and his Majesty having been pleated favourably to accept the Instances made by the Prince; his Highnefe has font over a Minister, instructed and authorized with full Powers, to treat of and conclude the Articles of Marriage: His Majesty has therefore thought it proper to communicate this important Affair to this House; and, as he makes no doubt but this Marriage will be to the general Satisfaction of all his good Subjects, he promises himself the Concurrence and A Alliance of this House, in enabling him to give such a Portion to his eldest Daughter, as shall be suitable to the - present Occasion, and may contribute towards supporting with Honour and Dignity an Alliance that will tend lb much to the further Security of the Protestant Succession to the Crown of these Realms, and to the Protestant Interest in Europe.

Most Gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled return your Majesty our most dutiful Thanks for being graciously pleased to communicate to us your Royal Intentions of concluding a Marriage between the Prineefs Royal and the Prince of Orange.

The happy ProspeQ; of seeing this Alliance entered into, and concluded, with a Prince whose Family has always distinguished itself in support of the Protestant Religion, and in Defence of the Liberties of Europe, gives us the greatest Satisfaction: We remember, with Gratitude, the great and infinite Benefits procured to this Nation by that illustrious House; and we cannot but promise ourselves a farther Security to the Protestant Succession to the Crown of thelb Realms, from the Renewal of that Union which gave Birth to, and laid the Foundation of, this inestimable Blessing.

And we beg Leave to allure your Majesty, that, to demonstrate our Duty, Zeal, and Affection, to your Majesty, and to testify the just Sense we have of the singular Merits, and eminent Virtues, of the Princds Royal, we will enable your Majesty to give her such a Portion, as may conduce to her future Happiness, and to the supporting her Royal Highness with Honour and Dignity.

The said Address, being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed unto by the House.

Resolved, That the said Address be presented to his Majesty by the whole House.:

Complaint being made to the House, That Jonathan Evmdon, of London, Attorney at Law, John Ellithorne, his Servant, and other Persons unknown, under the Direction of the said Jonathan Evindon, came, on the Twenty-third of November last, into a Cellar in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, wherein Sir Richard Lane Knight, a Member of this House, and his Servants, were filling up several Hogsheads of Beer, the Property of a Person in the Country, for whom, upon Request, Sir Richard acted as Agent; and, after blowing out the Candles, that they might not be discovered, locked the Door upon, and violently assaulted, him and his Servants, keeping them under Confinement above an Hour; bruised Sir Richard's Hand, with other Injuries; and, by Force and Fraud, got Possession of the said Cellar and Beer, and have ever since detained the fame; in Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Ordered, That it be referred to the Committee of Privileges and Elections to examine the Matter of the said Complaint; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

--And presented to the Ho ife a Petition of the Trustees for establishing dfe Colony of Georgia in America; which was read; reciting. That his Majesty hath been plealed to take into consideration. That many of his poor Sub-jefjfcs and many Foreigners, who are willing to become . hip. Subjects,- are reduced to great necessitjes, and would gladly be settled in the British Provinces in America; where, by cultivating the Lands, at present waste and desolate', they might not only gain a comfortable Subsistence for themselves and Families, but also strengthen his Majesty’s Colonies, and increase the Trade, Navigation, and Wealth, of Great Britain: And further reciting, That his Majesty, for the more orderly carrying on the ffcid'good purposes, hath, by His Royal Charter, bearing pate the Ninth Day of June, Anno Domini 173,2, con-ftStuted a Body Politick and Corporate, by the Name of the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia in America; and hath granted unto the said Trustees, and their Successors, for ever, certain Lands and Territories in South Cai'olina, in Trust, for establishing the said Colony; and hath erected the same into an independent Province, by the Name of Georgia; and thereby ini-powered the said Trustees to take Subscriptions, and to gather and collet such Monies as should, by any Person or Persons, be contributed; which said Trustees, are, at their owp desire, restrained, by Clauses in the Charter, from receiving any Salary, Fee, or Profit, whatsoever: And letting forth, that many Saltzburghers, and other persecuted and distressed Protestants, would be glad to go and settle in the said Province of Georgia, where they may find, under his Majesty’s Protection, an Alylumfrom Perfection and arbitrary Power; but are unable, at their own Charges, to transport themselves thither; and that, as the settling them there, will be a Charity highly becoming this Profestant Kingdom, the employing them in raising rough Materials for several of our most useful Manufactures, with which none of our Plantations, at present, supply us, will be of great service to the Trade of this Nation, increase the Number of His Majesty’s Sub-

Uport' the Petition of Sir Alexander Murray, of Slari-hop, complaining of . an u.mlue Election and Return /"-of Sir James Nafmyth, erf* to serve for the County of Peebles'; and also, the Petition of Alexander Williamson, Sheriff Clerk of the said County, complaining, that on the 28th of Aprilthen latt, at a Meeting of the Freeholders of the said County,

The Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petitions.

The Counsel for the Petitioners alleged, That the Freeholders Roll had been, in favour of the Sitting Member, arbitrarily and illegally made up by the Sheriff, contrary to the Law of Scotland, made in 1681, concerning Elections for Commissioners of Shires, which ordains that Roll to be made up by the Freeholders, at the Michaelmas Head Court, yearly.

They also alleged illegal and partial Proceedings in the Sheriff; That he did return the Sitting Member; and that . there w ere Two Prtejes. and Tw o Clerks that did preside; which was contrary to Law'; and that, by taking from the Sitting Member s Poll, and adding to the Petitioner’s, they should make a Majority for the Petitioner S\r Alexander Murray:; '

That the First or Second Commissioner last elected, or, inr their Absence, the Sheriff Clerk, should alk the Voters,

That the Petitioner was duly returned, by Mr. Carmichael the Prcefes, who was elected; upon the Question put by Mr. Alexander Murray, the last Representative, and Alexander Shazv, who was duly elected Clerk, by the Majority of Voters.

And offering to prove the Minutes, which were taken at the last Election, by the said Mr. Alexande?' Shazv the Clerk;' ' - ' '

And it being alleged, That every Freeholder inrolled, or that voted at former Elections, is intitled to vote for a Prcefes at any succeeding Election, who has not legally been put out of the Roll;

And that the Right of Election for a Prcefes, at any Election for any Shire in Scotland, is in such Persons, whole Names shall be produced, in any Roll, by the Sheriff 5

Objection was made thereto; and the same not being admitted, the Committee came to the following Refo-ution: t

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election, of a Prcefes and Clerk, is in such Persons as stand upon the Roll laii made up by the Freeholders at the Michaelmas Head Court, or at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament.

That the Election of Mr. Hay, of Hayftown, to be Prafts, and Mr. Henry Balcanquall, to be Clerk, being controverted;

The Petitioner’s Counsel alleged, That there being Twenty Voters present at the Election of a Prcefes, though the Votes, upon the Minutes, appear to be Ten and Ten, they should take off Three of those Votes who voted for Mr. Hay, in Sir James Nafmyth's Favour, charging the Sheriff with Irregularities in determining the Election of Prcefes, and insisting that the Return is void.

And, to prove the said Allegations,

They insisted, That the 4th Section of an Act of Parliament, made 1 Geo. I. c. 13. might be read:

And the same being read accordingly;

It appeared thereby, That Persons, refusing to take the Oath of Abjuration, are incapacitated to vote for ^Members of Parliament in Scotland

Page 29.] And, by the said Minutes, it also appeared, That, at die Meeting to elect their Representative, the Prcefes desired the Oaths might be taken, as required by Law; and that the Return was not good, nor made up in the publick Assembly; and therefore void.

That the Petitioners Richard, William, and Elizabeth, are the natural and lawful Brothers and Sifter by the Half Blood, and next of Kin to Richard Norton, late of Southivicke, in the County of Southampton, Esquire, deceased; and that the Petitioner James is Nephew to the said Richard Norton by another of his Half Sifters; and that the Petitioners, as such, are the only persons interested in, and intitled to, a Distribution of the personal Estate of the said Richard Norton, and are the only Persons, by Law, intitled to pray, and take out, Letters of Administration of the Goods, Chattels, Rights, and Credits, of the said Richard Norton; and that if the Bill, now depending in this House, to enable proper Persons to propound certain Papers, importing to be the last Will, Codicils, and Testamentary Schedules, of Richard Norton, late of Smithwicke, in the County of Southampton, Esquire, deceased, in the Prerogative Court of Canterbury, and to sue for Administration, with the same annexed, should pase into a Law, a Right of Administration will be introduced, unknown to the Law; which may be greatly in-j urious to the Petitioners, and draw their Right and Title to the personal Estate of the said Richard Norton into Question in an extraordinary manner, and exclude them from the Right, which they at present have, of administring to the said deceased: And therefore (and as the said Bill, should it pass into a Law, would, in many other respects, be greatly injurious to the Petitioners) praying, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

A Petition of the united Company of Merchants, of Exportation England, trading to the Edfi Indies, was presented to the of Tea. House/and read; setting forth, That, by the Laws now in being, foreign Goods are not intitled to Drawbacks, unless the same are exported within the $pace of Three

Years from the Importation thereof; and that the Petitioners do annually import, and have nowin Stock, large Quantities of TeaandCofiee intended for Sale to Dealers in those Commodities, who buy as well for foreign Export as Home Consumption; and'Tfcirrhe uuufitSl Plenty of Tea and Coliee, of late Years imported into Europe by foreign Nations, frequently makes it difficult for such Buyers to find a foreign Vent for their Goods within the time limited for Exportation thereof, and consequently discourages them from buying for foreign Exports; and that the time allowed for Exportation of Tea and Coffee, has, from Experience, been found too short, and to be attended with 1‘uch Inconveniences as will, if not prevented for the future, put a Stop to the Exportation of those Commodities, and thereby cut off a Branch of Trade, which is of great Benefit to the Nation: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give such Relief therein, as to the House ilial! seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House. N

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Morning, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

Mr. Plumptre, according to Order, reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Proprietors of the Stock of the Governor and Company for raising the Thames Water in York Buildings, assembled in their General Court held at their House in Winchester-street, the Twelfth Day of January 1732, was referred, That the Committee had agreed upon a further Report of their Proceedings, which they had directed him to make; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; together with an Appendix thereunto: Where the Report was read; and is as follows; viz.

Your Committee, since their last Report laid before 24

this House, have finished their Examinations into the Mismanagements alleged by the Petitioners against several Persons who have been in the Direction of their Affairs; and agreed on the following State of the Fasts which have appeared to them.

In this Inquiry they have received some Informations from Members of this House: All other Witnesses have been examined in the most solemn manner.

Your Committee beg Leave to refer to their former Report, for the general Constitution and Regulations of this Company, which are there set forth; and shall, in this, as Occasion shall arise, take notice of the particular Orders and Provisions necessary tow ards forming a Judgment upon the several Fasts under Proof.

The First Complaint of the Petitioners, which your Committee found material to lay before the House, is, That several Persons, whilst they were in the Direction of the Affairs of the Company, have unwarrantably taken upon them to employ Part of the Calli in buying several Parcels of Stock, and also to fell several Parcels of the same; and, great Loss having fallen upon the Company by these Transactions, the Petitioners think they have Realbn to suspect, that these Bargains were at first entered into with private Views; but, proving afterwards bad, were brought to the Account of the Company.

The Petitioners have shewn, in the Calli Book of Mr. Burgess, the late Cashier, That, between the 28th of August 1721, and the 13th of February following, both Days inclusive, there was bought £. 39,800 Stock, which cost the Company £.13,041; the Entries in the Calli Book, of the several Parcels of Stock which make up this £. 39,800, express them to have been bought to supply the Third Payment of Tickets fold for the Use of the Company: There appears no written Authority for the Buying of this Stock; but Mr. Burgess has delivered in to your Committee, and attested in the most solemn manner, an Account of the Stock bought whilst the Earl of Westmorland was Governor; in which he fays, that this £. 39,800 Stock was bought by the Order of the following Persons in the Direction, Mr. Cockburn, Mr. West, Mr. Harrison, Mr. EJfmgton, Mr. Hai'vey and Doctor Welsted: and Mr. Abraham Edlin, a Broker, who, by his Account produced to your Committee, and compared with the Calli Book, appears to have been employed in buying <£. 21,000, Part of this £. 39,800 Stock, being examined, said, That he transferred the said £. 21,000 Stock to the Lord Westmorland, by Order of Mr. Cockburn, Mr. West and Mr. Efjington: The Tickets here mentioned relate to a Lottery, which will be explained in its proper Place.

There farther appear, in the Calli Book, several Parcels of Stock bought between the 14th of February 1721-2, and the 14th September 1722, both Days inclusive; making, together, £.104,950 Stock; for which the Company has paid £. 27,359 7s. 6d.; and between the 23d February 1721-2, and the 21st July 1722, there was fold £. 120,750 Stock for £. 29,058. 13*. 6d.

At the Rate at which the <£.104,950 Stock was bought, the £. 120,750 Stock fold should have produced £-3i>478 5 5; hut it yielded no more than£. 29,058 13 6. the Difference is £.2,419 11 11; to which must be added several Payments, which appear, in the Books to have been made for Differences on Bargains, and for Commission and Transers, not included in the above Sums, amounting to £. 467 95. and making the whole Loss to be £. 2,887 on.

Mr John Billingsley, who was Secretary at the time here mentioned, being examined as to these Transactions, said, That he never knew of any Authority from a General Court, or Court of Assistants, for buying and selling this Stock: That he has searched the Books, and finds no Entry of any there: That he believes this Stock was at first bought on private Persons Account, and afterwards charged to the Company: Being asked the Reason of his Belief, he said, That, at the time of a Committee of Proprietors appointed to examine into the Affairs of the Company in 1723, the Calli Books, or One of them,

had

Second Complaint.

That the Company has suffered considerable JLofies in the Management of their Lotteries, through the undue Practices of several of the Persons who were in the Direction of their Affairs.

In an Act of the Seventh Year of his late Majesty King George the First, for continuing the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, it was enacted, amongst other Things, lhat, for the better enabling the Governor and Company of Undertakers for raising the Thames Water in York Buildings, to raise and pay the Government the Price or Consideration-money for the forfeited Estates they had purchased, and intended to purchase, it should and might be lawful to and for the said Company, and their Successors, from tune to time, to grant, fell, and dispose of, Rent-charges, or Annuities, to the full Extent and Value of such of the said Estates, as were 01* should be, at any time or times, by them purchased, in or by Wav or Method of Lottery.

Under this Authority, the Company, at a General Court held the 8 th Day of August 1731, agreed on a Scheme for a Lottery for the Sale of Annuities on tingle Lives, to the Amount of £. 13,000 per Annum; some of the Terms of which were as follows: For every Ticket there was to be paid to the Company £.5; of which 30*. to be paid upon taking out the Ticket, 306*. more on or before the 9th Day of the then next September, and the remaining 40 Shillings on or before the 7th Day of the then next October; which last Payment might be made either in Money, or in the Stock of the Company, after tire Rate of jC.40 per Cent.: And, in case of Default made in the Secona or Third Payment on Ticket, within the times before-mentioned, such Ticket was to be forfeited to the Use of the Company, who might make out and dispose of another Ticket, in the room of the fame.

There were to be 56*330 Tickets, of which 11,366 Prizes, of various Values, and 45,064 Blanks, each of which would intitle the Owner to jf.5 Stock, out of the common Stock of the Company.

Soon after this, an Encouragement was given to Adventurers, by an Order of a Court of Assistants held the 23d day of August 1721, in these Words:

Ordered, That the following Advertisement be inserted in the Daily Courant, and other Papers:

Third Complaint.

That, in order to spread a deceitful Opinion of the Value of the Stock, by which particular Persons might gain Advantage, several Dividends were made, though the Company had no Profits to divide out of, and, at the times of those Dividends, was greatly in Debt.

Your Committee, in the Appendix to their former' Report, have laid before the House, a State of these Dividends; and must here observe, that, upon inspecting the Books of the Company, they find that One of the Seven Dividends, viz. the 4th, took its Rife from a Motion in the General Court, on the 6th of January 1723: The rest were declared upon Recommendations from the Court of Assistants, introduced to the General Court by Speeches from the Chair full of Representations of hopeful Prospects of Advantages to the Company.

Mr: Bishop, the Cashier, being examined, said, That, at the time of making the Three last Dividends, he believes the Company was in no Capacity of making Di-, vidends; which he judged from several Transactions that happened in relation to their Dills of Exchange: That he believes they divided out of the Capital; for if the Dividends had been made out of the Profits, he must have known something of it.

Mr. Mont cage laid, That he was Accomptant when the Dividends were made, during the time when Sir John Meres was Governor: That he believes, that they were not made out of Profits; but there was no perfect Account kept, nor is there one to this Day; and lie does not remember, that, previous to any Declaration of Dividends, the Governor and Assistants called upon him to know the State of their Accounts; and that there is no Account kept of the Profits upon the Company’s Estates in Scotland.

Mr. John Billingjley, being examined, confirmed the Evidence of Bishop and Mont cage.

Sir John Meres said, That whilst he was in the Di-reSion, the Company was never in a Way of making Profits; and, if they were to have had no Dividends, but from Profits, there must have been no Dividends at all; There were Accounts made up before Two Dividends, in his time; but that was only to fee what Calli they had to make Dividends; they knew they had no Profits: In his time they run out about £. 4,000 a Year more than their Income; and lately £. 6,000 a Year in Expences of the Company: That they sent a Person into Scotland to take an Account of the Company’s Affairs; w ho made a Report of £. 26,000 Debt in Scotland, which he knew nothing of; besides^. 20,000 An ears, which continued increasing.

Fourth Complaint.

That in the Year 1724, the Proprietors transferred to the Company One-half of their Stock; for which the Company allowed them after the Bate of £. 13 Money for every £. 100 Stock; and gave them Ponds for the lame, payable in Seven Years and a Half, with Interest at£ 4 per Cent, per Annum; by which means the Company be* came burdened with a grievous Debt, which lies on them to this Day.

To make the Evidence, produced on this Head, intelligible, it is necessary to premise, that that Half of the Company’s whole Capital, which has been shewn above to have been accepted of in lieu of a Call of £. 23 per Cent, in 1720, and to have been fold out again in 1723, was, after it w*as so fold, called new Stock: and as die Purchasbrs had Liberty to make good their Bargains in partial Payments, so much of that Stock as all the Purchase Money was paid in upon, was called new Stock completed.

The Petitioners have much insisted, That this last Paragraph was not agreed to by the General Court, but has been arbitrarily inserted'in the Minute Book by the then Governor Sir John l\lercs; and they have produced his Directions in his own Hand-writing, lent to the Secretary’s Clerk for entering the Minute as it is; but as it was admitted, that it was usual for the Governor to settle the Minutes of the General Courts after they were up; and as the Evidence given on this Matter was uncertain, your Committee apprehends it is unnecessary to lengthen this Report with the Particulars’of it; and the rather so, because the immediately preceding Resolution fiands unimpeached; by which One-half of the Capital, though under a different Description, was to be sold to the Company; and all the Milehiefs, now charged by the Petitioners on the latter Resolution, would equally have flowed from the former.

The Petitioners also objected Falsification to a Minute of the next General Court held the 2d of October 1724; which, in the Book, stands thus: "A Debate arising in " relation to the Proprietors being obliged to transfer One-half of their Stock for Bonds at Four per Cent.

" and it being put to the Vote, it was carried to adhere " to the former Minutes, that each Proprietor should he " obliged to transfer Half his old, and Half his new " Stock completed, in Trust for the Company, and to " take Receipts entitling to Bonds for the lame.*’

For this they likewise produced a Direction for entering the Minute written by Sir John Meres $ Clerk; hut the Entry in the Minute Book is not entirely a Transcript of that Direction; and the living Evidence produced of the Transactions at this Court proved contradictory: Infup-port too of this Minute, it may he observed, that, at this very Court, there came on afterwards a Ballot for a Governor and Assistants for the Year ensuing; and, by the Book, it appears, that Sir John Meres w as re-deCleu Governor without One Vote against him.

However, the fatal Consequences of this Partition complained of by the Petitioners, are very evident, and make up the Four first Articles of the Account of the Debts of the Company, annexed to the former Report of your Committee; where the principal Money in Two Articles amounts to £. 71,206 \s. 6d.; and the Interest upon it, to Christmas £. 17.32, to £. 14,3.55 4?- .* And there are these other aggravating Circumstances in this TransactioB, That the Proprietors sold to the Company Vgl. 22.

their Stock at 13 per Cent, when it would not, at the York Market, have yielded them 8 per Cent, as appears by the Buildings publick Accounts of Stocks printed at that time; and ^omPau3r that, by this Artifice, they laid a Foundation for doing what afterwards was actually put in Practice; viz. felling, in their corporate Capacity, to unwary Purchasers, that very Stock which they had secured more than the worth of to themselves, in their private Capacities.

There is, indeed, in the General Court Book, an Order, made on the 28th of July 1725, upon the Motion of the Governor, Sir John Meres, which leems adapted to prevent this Mischief: It is in these Words:

" Resolved and Ordered, That £. 600,000 of the " nominal Capital of this Corporation, transferred to " Trustees for the Company, be now absolutely reduced " and annihilated, and not liable to be transferred in the " Company’s Books; and that it be left to the Governor,

" Assistants, and Committee, of this Corporation, to <£ advise thereon, and take care that the same he forthwith " done in a proper manner; and that public Notice " be given thereon, when done:" But how' effectual this Order of Annihilation was, appears l y Two other Orders, of the same Authority, in the General Court Book; the one on the 9th of November 1727, by which £. 200,000 of the said annihilated Stock is ordered to be revived, and disposed of in the manner there mentioned at 10 per Cent.; the other of the 27th of March 1728, by which £.200,000 more of that Stock was revived, to be sold at 14 per Cent.; the Produce of neither of these Parcels of revived Stock being at all proposed to be applied to the Discharge of the Debt incurred by the Annihilation of them.

The Petitioners further urged, That, at the time when Sir John Meres proposed this Division, so beneficial to the then Proprietors, and so pernicious to the Company, lie was possessed, in his own Right, of above £. ioo, uuo Stock; and he, in his Examination, owned the fame.

Robert Inwood, Shipwright, said, That, about the Year 1728, he was sent by the York Buildings Company to Abernathy Woods, to square Timber, and make Mails: That he went through them with Captain Lloyd, and Mr. Henry Strachey to view them: That he could have picked out 60,000 Trees fit for Timber and Deals; some of them fit for Top-mails, Boltfprits, and Yards; the least of them worth 2s. 4d. a Tree as they flood, and Profit to be made by them: That they cut down about 600; of which they brought away with them about 60, that run, one with another, between 60 and 70 Foot, the Diameter, at the Butt, about 2^ Foot, or Three Foot; and, at the Middle, about 18 Inches.

William Oliver, Shipwright, said, That, in December was Five Years, he was sent by the York Buildings Company to Abernathy Woods, to fell Wood for Masts, and to square Timber, along with Captain Lloyd and Robert

Inwood: That he viewed the Woods throughout; and believes there are there 600,000 Trees fit for Timber, Planks, Deal, Top-masts, Boltfprits, and Yards, worth 28 or 29 Pence a Tree: That they brought away with them about 60 Trees; and felled about 100 more, which they left there: The squared Timber Trees were from 25 to 40 Foot long; and about 12 or 14 Inches at the Butt, when squared: The longed round Timber was about 60 Foot long, and the Girt round in the Middle about Three Foot Six Inches.

John Mackrell, Shipwright, said, That, in December, about Five Years ago, he was sent by the York Buildings Company to Abernathy YVoods, to fell and square Trees, and went along with Inxvood and Oliver: That he went through that Part of the Wood where his Work lay: That he saw a great many Trees, but cannot judge of their Number or Value.

That one Inducement to his taking the Lease was, that he understood, by Colonel Horsey, that some Gentlemen, Relations, to the Rebels, had, in the Year 1726 or 1727, entered into Terms, and made Propofols to a Knot of People, to join, and purchase all the forfeited Estates they could.

Seventh Complaint.

That the same Governor had drawn the Company into an expendve and dangerous Bargain, in taking a Lease of certain Lead-mines at Strontein in Scotland, called the Swinnard Mines for a long Term, and at an excessive Rent, certain, upon a very uncertain Prospect of Advantage to them.

The Petitioners produced to your Committee a Deed, dated 31st July 1730, between the Duke of Norfolk, Sir Gervas Clifton Baronet, Sir Robert Clifton, and Sir Robert Sulton, Knights of the Bath, Sir Archibald Grant Baronet, George Wade Esquire, William Nelson, Merchant, Richard Graham, Merchant, Peter Murdock, Merchant, and Sir Alexander Murray Baronet, on the one Part; and the Governor and Company of Undertakers for raising the Thames Water in York Puddings on the other Part: It recitqs a Lease, dated 15th February 1724, granted by the said Sir Alexander Murray, to certain Persons therein named, of all Lead Ore, Lead-mines, Rakes, Pipes, and Flats, of Lead Ore, and Copper Ore and Copper-mines, Veins and Beds of Copper Ore, and other Ore, within the Lands of him the said Sir Alexander Murray, \n the Shires of Argyll and Peebles, for 30 Years, from the 25th Day of March then next ensuing, at the Rent of One-sixth Part of the Ore, when got, and made merchantable; which Lease, and Premises, were, by several mesne Alignments, become vested in the Persons above-named: The Deed then sets over to the Governor and Company the said JPreinifes, from the 24th Day of June 1730, for the Reminder of the said Term of 30 Years; they paying to Vox. 22.

the said Alexander Murray the said Sixth Part of the said Ore, J as aforesaid, and also to the Afligriors above mentioned the annual Sum of £. 3,600; for the due Payment of which, the Company, hefides other strong Covenants, tie their Estates of Winton, Marifchall, Panmuir, Kilfyth, Aiton, Linlithgow, and South o/k.

To shew the Steps taken in managing and concluding the Bargain, and the Success they have had, and rpay expect, from it, the Petitioners have produced the following Evidence:

A Letter from Colonel Horsey to Francis Place, in North Britain, dated 28th March 1730:

In this the Colonel acquaints Place, That he has a Prospect, with some of his Friends, of purchasing some of the Shares of the Lead-mines near Fort William; and desires him to view them, and fend his Opinion, as soon as possible, left the Opportunity should be loft.

Place*s Answer to Colonel Horsey, dated 23 April 1730-

In this he gives his Remarks on the Minp; and adds, " I am satisfied that this Work wopld turn out good u Profit; but as it is managed, and to be subject to the " same for the future, I would neither be concerned, <c noradvise any Friend to be, no, not if they would "make a free Gift of a Share; but, if the Partner^ " would agree to have a proper Personof Judgment to give the necessary Directions, ’twould, I am persuaded, " answer well."

Colonel Horsey*s Letter to Place, dated id May

1730.

In this he acknowledges the Receipt of Place's Rer port of the Mines; he fays, He has made some Advances towards getting them for the Company: That the Partners say, they were once offered £. 40,000 fox* their Lease: He thinks, if he could have them for an annual Rent, not exceeding the Interest of the Money, it might be worth their while: He asks Place's Opinion, Whether this Work could be carried on, without neglecting Lord Hopton's, and Eagle, and their Iron; for, in that Cafe, he would drop the Timber, and employ their whole £. 10,000 per Annum upon their Lead and Iron Works; he cannot but think it will answer well.

Fr. Place's Letter to Colonel Horsey, dated 7th May 1730-

In this, after some Remarks on the Management and Charges, he observes, That all Mines in the World are uncertain; and after adds, concerning the se; " What " renders them less valuable, is their being loaded with " such a heavy Dish as the Sixth; there being but few " Works which either pay, or are able to afford, that €t Share: And then, if they are obliged to work during u the 30 Years, without having it in their Power to " leave off at Pleasure, *tis still worse."

Fr. Place's Letter to Colonel Horsey, dated Sth May 1730-

In this he gives a Calculation of the Profit of the Mine, which comes out at £ 2,700 a Year upon the Ore, and £. 2,100 more upon the Lead, upon a Supposition which, he fays, is uncertain; and what no Man living can be positive of: He fays, " In his Opinion " ’twould be a most extravagant Rent to give £. 2,000 " per Annum, which is the Interest of the £. 40,000 " they say has been offered for the Mines; which "is Four times more than he thinks them worth:" And he enforces the reserving a Liberty of declining the Work whenever Poverty or Accident shall require it.

Mr. Place having been sent by the Petitioners, during this Inquiry of your Committee, into Scotland, to view the Company’s Works, he was, upon his Return, examined; and said, That he had been bred up in the Bufi-neis of Mining and Smelting: That he remains now of the same Opinion he was of when he wrote his Letters to Colonel Horsey about the Swinart Mines: That he

was formerly employed by the Company looverfee those Mines; and was dismissed in August 1731: That they are now in a worse Condition than when they were first let to the Company: The bed Part of the Mine; where there is any Ore of Consequence, is under Water: He was, in his time, carrying on a Level, but that is now discontinued: He does not think that any body would ive £. 3,600 a Year and the 6th Dish for them: If !e were to take a Lease of them for m Years, he would not give above £1,000 a Year and the 6th Dith; and it would be a better Tack now than when the Company took it, by about £ 2,000; for he believes the Houses may have cost about £ 5,000; and he thinks about £ 2,000, or £ 2,500, may put the Works in a good Way again: There are many Buildings there unnecessary: That the old Proprietors had worked the Mine about Four Years; and Sir Alexander Murray about Two Years before; that he is not certain of the time; but, by their Books, he found the whole Quantity they had smelted was no more than 244 T. 6 Q.

3 qrs. 22 lb. By the Experience he has in Mines, he is convinced, that, when the Proprietors left the Work to the Company the weekly Expence exceeded the Produce: That, whilst he was there, he sent to London, in about a Year’s time, 748 T. 9 C. 1 qr. 6lb. of I>ead, and, in Potters Ore, 132 T. 3 C. 3 qrs: That no Potters Ore has been made since he left the Mines; and, between that time and the 12th of April last, there has been shipped, as entered in the Books, 537 T. 6 C. 1 q?\ of Lead; and there is in the Storehouse 82 T. 5 C\; and 170 T. has been shipped by Captain Spavin, which is not entered in the Books; but he, this Examinant, saw it: That he really believes the Work may be brought, by a great Number of Hands, to raise 1,500 Ton a Year; but can never be advantageous to agy body l iable to pay an annual Rent of £ 3,600.

The Petitioners then referred to the Account hereunto annexed, N°. II. by which it appears, that the Charges of this Mine has exceeded its Returns by £ 25,856. 6s. 7d.

Jerom Horsey Esquire, who, by the Company’s Books appears to have been chosen into the Court of Assistants the First Daj' of October 1729, and to have been continued by the annual Elections to this time, being examined, said, That, about the Begiuning of the Year 1731, he was sent to oversee these Mines, which were then under the Inspection and Management of Mr. Francis Place: That he arrived there on the 16th of April 1731; and, about Two Months after, Mr. Place was dismissed, and the whole Care was committed to him: That the Water in the Mine is but of little Hindrance to them, they agreeing with the Men who get the Ore to take it off; and for this very little additional Consideration is given: As to the Quantities of Lead made and sent away, he agreed very nearly with Mr. Place.

Lieutenant General Wade, a Member of this House, informed your Committee, That he believes these Mines are well worth what the Company gives; and the Company of Mine Adventurers would have given as much; but the Proprietors, at the time of the Bargain, thought the Credit of the York Buildings Company best.

Sir Robert Cl{flon Baronet, and Knight of the Batli^So a Member of this House, gave the like Information.

This is the Evidence, which the Petitioners brought in Support of this Head of Complaint; and they gave no Proof of any private Consideration obtained by the Governor, or any of the Assistants, in making this Bargain.

Strontein, 13 July 1730.

To the Governor and Court of Assistants.

" Tis with great Pleasure I affore you, that there is " the finest Prospect for raising Ore 1 ever saw; not c< only in those Places already wrought, but also in il many others which have not been tried; and upon " the same Vein; which I have just now put Men upon u to open; by which means I am positive the Vein will " not only have a better Appearance, but be really " richer than in any Place already discoveredMentioning Four Hearths, he fays,

Strontein, 31 July 1730.

To Colonel Horsey. u The Alterations which have been in our Works are w very much for the better; our Works being much " richer in Appearance than ever."

To Colonel Horsey. u The Works grow richer every Day since I came " here; inso much that I lower the Price per Bing upon " every Bargain 1 have set since I came; and am sure w shallfave, in set fin § them this Year, £. 1,000." Strontein, 18 September 1730.

To the Governor and Court of Assistants.

After many Instances given of the Goodness of the Works, he fays, " I could write you a Volume on this " Subject, but to what Purpose ? I rather choose to tell u you, as I can in Truth, that your Works are richer " than ever I saw them."

Strontein, 4 November 1730.

To the Governor and Court of Assistants.

" We need not fear Ore and Lead enough, provided " we can get Miners and Smelters: A few Days ago I " went with Mr. Horsey to view a new Vein, which has " lately been discovered upon the Company’s Liberty, " on the Side of a Hill, and appears rich in Ore to the " very Day: I struck the First Tool into it myself; and " in less than One Hour’s time* I broke more than a " Hundred Weight of good Ore.

Dear Colonel, Edinburgh, April 23d, 1730.

This Afternoon, at Five a Clock, I got to Town, after waiting at Kinghorne 18 Hours for Passage.

I have here the Favour of both thine of the 1 ith and 18th Instant, the Answering whereof I beg leave to defer till next Pod; and that thee will, in the mean time, be pleased to accept of the following Remarks, which I made at the Mines of Swinard.

191

Remarks on the Mines of Swinard.

April the 16th, 1730.

They were first wrought by Sir Alexander Murray; fmce wrought by General Wade, and the present Company, about Two Years.

The Vein runs W. N. W. and E. S. E.; underlays (deeps, or heads) to the South, in some Places, a Foot and a Half in Six Foot.

It is a regular Spar # Course; the deepest Place wrought is about Seven Fathom, where it is working big; and, in some Places, is Four or Five Foot over, toiled with good Ore: The present grand Work is about 50 or 300 Fathom long in the Bottoms (the Eastern End whereof is the most promising), and is, in many Places, a Foot over, solid Ore; but it is so thick set with Ore, as to be almost a Foot and a Half solid: It is shot out in many Branches, and backed with many others, to the South; all which, hitherto tried, carry Ore in sinking; and, as they have the same Direction with the mean Vein, are likdy to come together in sinking; which, if the Ground favour, mull needs make a very considerable Vein: The Rider f, which, near the Grass, is Six or Seven Foot thick, is reduced, in sinking Three Fathom, to Three Foot — The Vein, Rider, and Branches, is about Sixteen Foot wide.

The Vein has been discovered with Ore in it for about One Mile and Half in Length.

There may be Twenty Fathom of Levels gained on the Vein Point.

It is now wrought upon Bargain: There are a Eleven Sets, containing, in all,' about SeventyMen; they find their own Powder and Candles (of which, as they work all open, there are but few used): The Company find all Tools and Tackle; and give the Men for the Ore, when dressed, Fourteen Shillings per Bing ||, upon au Average; the Carriage of that Bing from the Works to the Smelting Mill (being Two Mile) costs the Company Two Shillings.

There has been sent away - 164 Ton of Lead*

And lies, of Lead, at the Mill - 13 — 177 Ton.

Potters Ore sent away - - 90

Lies at the Mill, about - - 60

At the Works, dressed and undressed, by Computation, about 300 — 450 Ton. They make their Lead by Blast; their Fuel is Pit-coal and Peats: They have lately erected a Work-house, containing Three Hearths, but they are now all out; but, when in a full Course of Working, will make Two Ton Two hundred of Lead in Twenty-four Hours with Twelve Men, whose Wages is Ten Shillings per Week.

They have been at great F.xpence in building Work- houses, which are at present unemployed, and only serve as Dwellings for the Men; but might be, with a small Charge, applied to their First Design: There is a good Outlet to the Sea by a Lock, which will bring a Ship of any reasonable Burden within little more than a Gunshot of the Smelting Mill.

The above Observations are as particular and as exact as I could make in the short Time I could spend there; and, I hope, will be agreeable to thee. I will now observe, upon the Whole, That, First, it is a regular Vein, and of great Extent, and in a good-natured Stone: That the Ore seems to grow better in sinking j and, as the Branches are likely to come into the Vein, cannot fail to enrich it very much: That, as the Rider grows smaller in sinking, the Vein will be more solid, and the Branches will thereby have the greater Liberty to unite. I have taken notice of the Quantities of Ore and Lead both sent away, and remaining behind, that thee may thereby judge of the Value they have for the Money they have spent, winch thee will find means to know by some of the Partners in London. Could I

Spar is a Sort of white Stone so called, and is common in Lead Works.

+ A Rider is a dead Rock, which comes in upon the Back of the Vein.

I A Bing is Eight hundred Weight.
