have come to the Knowledge of the Cost they have been at, 1 would have stated it in this, and not have given thee the Trouble; but that was not to be come at without a View of their Books, or discovering myself, which I carefully avoided. I am satisfied, that this Work would turn out good Profit; but, as it is managed, and to be subject to the same for the future, I would ... be concerned, nor advise any Friend to be; No; not if they would make a Free-gift of a Share; but, if the Partners would agree to have a proper Person of Judgment to give the necessary Directions, it would, I am persuaded, answer well. I have endeavoured to explain the Whole; but, if there be any thing farther wanting, hope thee will be so free as to acquaint me thereof, and I will not fail to add whatever else is in my Power.

Next Monday will put Men to work at Tartrevan, Lord Hoptoris Mines. Pray excuse me to the Gentlemen, who, no doubt, expected to hear from me during this time j but thee knows it was not practicable. I fend them a few Lines, acquainting them of my Arrival here, &c.

My good Friend, Whitehall, 2d May 1730.

I acknowledge Receipt of yours, with the Report of the Mines, last Post. I am now to tell you. That I have made some Advances towards getting them for the Company, though it is with some Management and Difficulty, because several of the present Partners say, They know the Mines to be rich, and only want to be under good Management — However, as they have been so ill conducted hitherto, I say, they never will be better while in such Hands: They were once offered 40,000 for their Lease, which is for 30 Years, paying a Sixth Dish — I think, if I could have them for an annual Rent, not exceeding the Interest of the Money, it might be worth our while: They (land for more: But 1 believe I can bring them to that; and there are several other Veins lying about, not opened, but lately discovered — I acquaint you with this, to know if we could carry on that Work without neglecting Lord Hoptoris and Eagle, and our Iron — For, in that Cafe, 1 would drop the Timber for the present. I hope for a Line at the Return of the Post; and am, with Truth,

Your affectionate and true Friend,

S. Horsey.

Do not mention what I now write to any Soul; for nobody here knows of it. — Yet, if I drop the Timber, and employ our whole £. 10,000 per Annum upon our Lead and Iron Works,

I cannot but think itmuft answer well. I have ordered this to be forwarded to you by '

Express from Edinburgh; and desire so much of an Answer as you can give by the Return of it.

Dear Colonel, Edinburgh, May the 7th, 1730. Since my last, of the 25th palt, I have been at the Works of Tartrevan; where we go on very well in clearing up the old Level upon the Lead Vein: We have now Seven Men at Work there.

Last Post I wrote Charles Gorden, giving him some Directions about Eagle; which Place I will soon fee. — Last Night I came to Town, to write my Letters; where I am favoured with both thine of the 30th past, and 2d Instant, for which am obliged — I am glad my Report of Swinard Mines has thy Approbation. In mine of the 25th, I added something more concerning the m; which suppose thou has. I observe Friend Lund has wrote you fully about setting down Works near Inverness; and I afTureyou, that, in my Judgment, no Place is more convenient, especially since Grant is so unreasonable; which he, and all the World who hears of it, must suppose to be the Reason of your altering any Part of your Scheme; which, although in some degree altered, yet. will be sufficient to burn up all your own Wood, with any other small Parcels which may be purchased in the Neighbourhood, and to work up the Iron Ore lying next the Woods; which will not fail paying all Expence, and making a handfotne Return for what is laid out: No doubt but you will soon have a Sample of Iron; and thereby convince the raoft timorous, that you are acting safely, and not moving from one Place to another without sufficient and advantageous Reasons: No question Friend Lund writes you fully on this Head; and, as I know his Care and Industry for the Interest of the Company, it would be rather impertinent than otherwise, my adding more on this Subject.

I have very maturely considered the last, relating to the Advances thee has made in getting the Mines of Swinard into the Company’s Hands; which, as they have the greateftChara&er imaginable in London, would, no doubt, add greatly to the Credit of the Company; and, in procuring them Mines, then would it justiy deserve the thankful Acknowledgements of all concerned. — -Now, dear Colonel, from a disinterested and real Regard for thy Honour and the real good of the Company, I cannot omit giving the e my Sentiments, thereon, to the best of my Judgment. There are now, as I mentioned in my Report, about 70 Men upon Bargains, who raise Ore at 14^. per Bing: There had been Bargains set upon the same Terms to others, who, not being able to raise Ore at that Price, and thereby to make Wages, had quitted their Bargains — -There is no Work where there is not some dead Ground to be wrought, which is generally done at the Expence of the Adventurers: Likewifethey are at the first Coil of the Tools, and generally keep them in Repair; as also providing Timber and Ropes, &c. and very often drawing the ’ Water where there is Occasion — All these Allowances must be made for this Work, as well as any other. As to some of the Company saying the Mines are rich, that can proceed only from Supposition in them; and the only Way they can judge of their Value, is, by comparing the Money they have laid out, wiih the Amount in Value of Lead they have made, and Ore they have by them; if they have gained, then, by so much as they have profited, they may be called rich; but if, on the other side, it must be a great deal of good Management to make them turn to Account, when they will be daily growing deeper, and consequently, will be more chargeable; and another Consideration will naturally follow, which must certainly lessen the Value they may put upon them, which is, that all Mines in the World are uncertain.

That they have been offered £. 40,000 for them I make no Doubt; but 1 am of Opinion, no People would have been so indifereet as to have made a positive Agreement for a Thing of such Conference, without having

I shall now ffiew what I think may be done with good Management, according to the present Prospect, and then leave it to thy own Judgment to determine.

I believe there might be 120 Men employed upon Bargain, and about 80 more in making Discoveries, who might, in a Year’s Time, make room for 100 more to work upon Ore, provided the other Veins the Gentlemen told thee of, and those Branches I have taken notice of myself, answer to Expectation. I shall draw up a Scheme of the Whole, which I will not fail to fend per Saturdays Post. Mean time I hope thee will accept of this as the Fruits of my good Intention; and bq^ assured, dear Colonel, that I am, with best Respects to,* thee and Mr. Horseu,

Thy sincere Friend,

Francis Place.

£.40,000, they say, has been offered for the Mines; which is Four times more than I think them worth, or that I believe they will ever get for them: If the Purchasers know what they are doing, in Buying of Works, it is customary to lay the Books before the Buyers, by which they may be Judges how much has been got by them; and, according to the Sums gained, and the present Prospect, the Mines are leis or more valuable. I think, if there was a reasonable Value put upon the Works, and that they would be content to take the Payment thereof, as it lhopld arise out of One-half the Profits, this would be the justest Way of dealing; always reserving (as I know thee will) a Power of declining the Works, whenever either Poverty or Accident shall require it. — Or, otherwise, that they have such a proportioned Payment yearly, so long as the Works are continued, as may, in 28 Years (supposed still to come of their Lease), pay up both the Charge they have been at, and the Interest thereof. This may leem an unprofitable Bargain to them; but, considering how much they have loft there already, they might have reason to think themselves well off by such an Agreement, especially since they will have all the Advantage of the Ore already risen.

I have enlarged upon this Subject beyond my First Intention, but hope thee will excuse me therein; having no other Motive thereto, than that thee may have as full and perfect a Knowledge in the Affair as I am able to give; and, if any thing herein should not be so clearly expressed as I intend, or that thou;\vouldeft have further explained, pray point it out to me, and I shall add whatever in my Power to give thee an entire Satisfaction.

Thee will fee, by this, what Money will be necessary to carry on these Mines; but considering Lead would soon be made, and brought to Market, I do believe the advancing £.4,000 the First Year, would the Work, with a much smaller Addition afterwards, sufficient to maintain all Outgoings; and considering the Methods 1 shall take to make the Trials needful at Tartrevan and Eagle, I am sure that your Rents here, provided they be regularly paid, will be sufficient to carry on all your Works here.

On Wedesday or Thursday next, I design to set out from hence, to meet the Men at Carlisle, and hope to be back in 10 or 14 Days; mean time, shall leave all necessary Directions; and you may be allured, that I shall always act with that Caution and Regard for you that I would do for myself.

I am, dear Colonel,

Sir, Winch ester-street, May 19th, 1730.

We having now the Opportunity of taking the Mines at Swinardt commonly known by the Name of Wade's Mines, we think it necessary to have your Opinion thereupon.

The Proposal is, That they give us an Assignment of the Lease now made to the present Proprietors, which has 25 Years to run: f [That we pay them an annual Rent of £. 3,600:] That we pay for all their Ore above Ground, and other Stores, by Inventory, to be taken by Two Persons, one for them, and the other for us: To have all the Tools, Materials, and Buildings, without paying for them. — By the Lease the Lord is to have a Sixth Dilh.

What we desire of you is, to consider this Matter, Whether, as the Works now stand, supposing them, for the future, to be put under a regular (kilful Management, they can produce, all Charges deducted, the Rent above-mentioned, and some Profit for our Trouble — And

Winchester-street, 21 May 1730,

Sir,

By the last Poll we wrote you a Letter, for your Opinion upon the Mines at Swinard: We trouble you with this to confirm it — and only to add, That if the present Work, in Appearance, will afford the Rent the Company is to give, we think the Prospect is exceeding great, and we ought to engage in it; especially since we know it will be under your Management, and that you will find your Profit with us, which must always be regarded; and, added to the Inclination you have, with Honelty and Justice to serve us, of which we have already had good Experience, fend us only a Calculation upon 1,000 Ton of Ore, which will be a Guide to us for the rest; to which you will add what you think the future Prospect may be.

We write this, because it is of great Importance to us to succeed in this Affair.

We are,

Your sincere Friends,

Samuel Horsey, Governor;

Benj. Foxley,

Francis Townley,

Jerom Horsey,

Ja. Wilkinson.

Whitehall, 23d May 1730.

Dear Friend,

I now acknowledge Receipt of yours to the Court of Assistants, of the 15th May, and return you Thanks for that to me of the same Date. We w ell approve of the Bargain you have made with Lord Sinclair: Your Care and Application in that, as well as the other Parts of the Affairs of the Company, immediately under your Direction, is very acceptable to us all, and particularly to me. It gives us great Satisfaction, that, in you, and our Friend Lund, we find Men who think and execute with Diligence and Application the Schemes you frame with good Judgment.

You will have received Two Letters, signed by the Court of Assistants, relating to the Swinard Mines; the Accounts I have seen, and have been given me by General Wade and Sir Robert Sutton, are very extraordinary; and I am satisfied, if we come to work there, under your Management, we shall find great Riches; for it is their Mismanagement, and the Impossibility of having it otherwise, while it remains in this Copartnership, w'ho are all Men of Quality, and not of much Application to Business, that has given us the Opportunity of taking it; in which Cafe, some of them are, and will, become large Proprietors in our Stock. I did not shew your Calculation of the 8th Inltant; because it came in a private Letter; but as you make it upon 1,000 Ton of Ore converted into Lead, that alone will pay the Rent we give; and that repeated unless you have any thing more to add, will be sufficient to satisfy some People, who are over-3 D diffidept

Edinburgh, May the 30th, 1730,

Gentlemen,

My last, of the 27th, was from Penrith* giving yon an Account, That 1 had some Men with nle; that I was so far on my Way here; and that I had draw n on Humphrey Bishop, the Company’s Cashier, for Ten Pounds, which I desire may be paid, without further Advice. 1 should have been here last Night; but that I took up some time in viewing the Lord March's Estate, which is very promising for Lead-ore, and, as it lay in my Way, was loth to lose the Opportunity.

At my Arrival in Town, this Afternoon, I have both yours, of the 19th and 2ill Inllant, for which I return you my Thanks: I observe their Contents; and shall endeavour to give you the heft Satisfaction I am able about Su'inard Mines: There is now, or lately was, employed there 70 Men, who mile Ore at Fourteen Shillings per Ling; each Bing is Eight Hundred Weight: The Vein has been cut, rich in Ore, for about a Mile and Three 20

Quarters in Length; and might be capable of taking 200 Pickmen: There are several Branches that lie to the South of their mean Working, that would tuili out good Ore; but have never been much tried, as yet: The grand Work is wrought in the deepest Place, to about Seven Fathom: The Bottoms where their chief Working has been, is about 250 or 300 Fathom long. Here follows the exaftdi Calculation I can make; which, provided the Works continue as good as I believe they now are, I have ho Doubt but they will answer.

Strontien, July 13th, 1730.

Gentlemen,

Since my last to you, from Fort William, I have been at the Works, which I have carefully viewed’; and it is with great Pleasure, I assure you, that there is the finest Prospect for raising Ore I ever saw, not only in those Places already wrought, hut also in many others, which have not been tried, and upon the same vein which I have just now put Men upon to open; by which means I am positive the Vein will not only have a better Appearance, hut he really richer than in any Place already discovered.

I found Things in the greatest Confusion imaginable, and the Works very much out of Repair; but I hope, in some time, to have them as they should be, though it will cost me much Pains, and Hazard, before I get Things on a right Footing; however, hope I shall have Patience and Resolution enough to support me, during this great Reformation w'hich is to be wrought here.

I am at a great Loss for want of fuller Instructions from you; you do not tell me whether the Ore is to be valued litre or no: However, we shall make Jthe nearest Estimation we can of the Quantity, which I will transmit to you, together with the Inventory of all the Materials; which we shall soon have completed flow', since Friend Burt is come.

When you write next, pray let me know if you are to make good the former Proprietor^ Contract with thfc Dutch, for a certain Quantity of Lead if you are, then there is about .50 Tons still to be delivered them, of which there is made, and lying here, about 32 Tons; the other 18 Tons will be made in about 10 Days; and it will be that time before I can begin tolmeltany Ore upon your own Account. When I came here I found only Three Hearths at work, and them' but indifferently followed, each producing but about 13 C. of Lead ill 24 Hours; I gave immediate Orders for a 4th Hearth, and have it in 1b good Forwardness, that 1 doubt not hut to work it next Week; which, considering we had the Bellows, and many other Things necessary, to finish, will be as soon as could possibly be done. Thele Four Hearths are wrought by One Axle-tree; and I am preparing Materials for w or king Two more; but then must build another House for that Purpose. I believe shall be able to bring them to make at each Hearth 16 or 18 C. in 24 Hours; so you may from hence Calculate how loon a Ship should come. You will, ilo doubt, inform yourselves what Sale there may be for Potters Ore in London; the Matters of Ships often carry it as Ballast to the Mediterranean. If you w ould have Potters Ore font, then I can the looner load a Ship; but pray observe always to have them obliged to lie here as many working Days as possible, that we may be clear of Demurrage. It is now a very wet Season here, which may prove ill for us, in faviftg those few Peats the former Manager thought fit to have cut for us, which are not above One-third what we shall need, and it is now too late to cut more: so We must now make up the Deficiency with Billet-wood, which we can have in this Neighbourhood of Sir Alexander Murray; which, together with the Coal, which we must have from Glasgow, may be made to do; but there has been lo little Care taken of our Interest in that Respect, that we have notHalfaTonofCoalby us now, so shall be forced to borrow of our Neighbours. Since the above, relating to the Dutch Contract, 1 understand, by a Letter-from Sir Robert Sutton and Sir Archibald Grant, to the Agent here, that we are obliged to make good all their Contracts; and therein is recommended the speedy Shipping of 40 Tons of Potters

Strontien, July 31st 1730.

Dear Colonel,

Since my last, of the 23d Instant, the Alterations which have been in our Works are very much for the better, our Works being much richer in Appearance than ever: A more particular Account thereof I shall defer until my next, at which time do suppose thee may expect to hear of the flourishing Condition we are in.

My good Friends Sir Archibald Grants and Captain Burroughs, whom I am so happy as to have with me, have been so good as to offer me the Use of any of their Stores at Moreen, which I have accepted of very thankfully; and, since I am so enabled through their Assistance, I will/ if possible, have Two Hearths more at work in about Two Months time.

The Inventory will befinished next Week. I am, dear Colonel, with the utmost Esteem and Respect to thee and Mr. Iiorfey,

Strontien, August 18th 1730.

Dear Colonel,

My last was the 12th Instant; at the same time I sent the Inventory; since u'hich I have thy Favour of the 28 th past, for which I am obliged.

It is no small Satisfaction to' me, that I have the Advantage and Pleasure of consulting my good Friends Sir Archibald Grant, and Captain Burroughs; who, I assure thee, take a great deal of Fatigue to inform themselves of the State of Affairs here, and to forward what they can; which, notwithstanding the Compliment thou art pleased to do my Capacity, yet I find very serviceable, which would render their Absence very uncomfortable to me;

but that I have good Grounds to hope for thy Company soon, since I hear thou art set out from London.

Sir Archibald Grant informs me, that there can’be nothing saved by freighting Ships from Glasgozc, seeing the y will not come here but at such Seafoirs when others may be had as cheap from London or Bristol.

I very much esteem thy Condescension in ordering feme Arms; which although I put no great Confidence in, yet they cannot he altogether useless in this Place, where the very Name of them will keep troublefoine Neighbours at their due Distance.

The Duke of Argylt % Countenance w ill be of great Service to us all here.

Last Night I had a Letter and Invoice from II. Strachey, of the Particulars sent by the Sloop, which we shall now daily expect.

All Things here go well: We begun our new’ Smelting Mill but Eight Days ago, and Two Days more will finifii all the Stone-w'ork; and we have all the Materials for the Furnace in such Readiness that I hope soon to have her at work also.

This Day 1 have sent Molds to Glenkindlafs Furnace, to have Hearth Plates cast of a different Form to what they had here formerly; wdiich will not only make more Lead in the same time, but much better than could possibly be done in the present Way.

The Works grow' richer every Day since I came here; inso much that I low^er the Price per Bing, upon every Bargain I have set since I came; and am lure shall lave, in letting them this Year, £. 1,000.

Sir Archibald, and Captain Burroughs, having nothing more to write than as above, desire thee will accept of their joint Service: We all join in williing the e a good Journey, and Health.

Last Post brought me your Letters of the 27th August and 3d Instant, for both which I thank you. I am surprised at your having no Letters from me since I came here, for I wrote you very fully July the 13th; and, as I constantly correspond with the Governor, I thought it might be sufficient; but, since you desire to be informed by me, from time to time, how your Affairs go on> 1 shall not fail to give you all the Satisfaction I can. I observe you have agreed with Captain Hudson, Butden 340 Tons, to come here for Lead and Ore: I am of Opinion that finaller Vessels would answer better; however, I will do the best I can with this when Ihe comes. I shall nowr shew what Quantity we have, and a Calculation of the Quantity we may probably make per Week; after which you will be enabled to judge exactly what Ships may be loaded, and provide accordingly.

We work now Four Hearths, which will make, when they meet with no Interruption or Accident, 15 Ton per Week; but, as we are frequently obliged to blow down at some of the Hearths, either by Smoke, wherein no Man can work, or for want of Fuel being dry, which is, to my great Mortification, often the same with our Peats, for want of Weather to dry them; so that that Quantity cannot always be depended on. I have almost finished the new Mill I wrote you of; and, although the Weather has been so intolerably bad, yet I hope to have her at work in Two Weeks, and then will ex peel from her Nine Ton per Week. Our reverberating Furnace, when (he begins to work, should make 2T. 8C. every 24 Hours. I have inclosed you what the Person, who should direfct the Building of her, fays about her being finished: If I had but 5,000 Wind-for Bricks, and 8 or 10,000 Stock Bricks, I would build a Slag Furnace, which should work upon Slugs only; and would from thence make 15 Ton per Week. I would have wrote you for Bricks before now, but was deceived by the Accounts the Gentlemen who manage the Mines at Murvai gave me; which was, that they had given Orders, when at London, for j 2,000 Windsor Bricks; so they concluded from thence, and we all depended upon that Quantity, and knew not to the contrary, till I sent for them to use her6, where we find them not above 3,000; which will, with much ado, only complete this we have already begun. — As to the Quantity of Potter’s Ore we nuiy make, that depends intirely upon the Veins throwing out Ore of such a Quality, which ffie was never more likely to do than fiow; and, if I had but a sufficient Number of good Dressers, I could make a great deal more than I now do; but, as it is impossible to get any to come here this Winter, mufo endeavour so to dispose and mix those, who are experienced, with those who are new Beginners, as to answer the same Purposes, as far as it is possible: You may be affur&l, that there is not any One Thing left undone, which can be of service in forwarding the general Good; which, next my Salvation, is nearest my Heart; and, whether I have not done as much as Man could do since here, 1 leave to the Judgment of those Gentlemen who have already been here, and to the Report of the Governor, who I daily expect, and who will be a Judge by seeing what is done. It is in vain to tell you of many Inconveniencies and Hindrances which I meet with, which neither you nor I can help thisSeafon, through the former ill Management; but are such as I will affirm shall never trouble us more. I could write you a Volume on this Subject, but to what Purpose! 1 rather choose to tell you, as I can in truth> that your Works are richer than ever I saw them. I havefet, within these few Days, 10 different Bargains, considerably cheaper than the same Ground was let for before. You will please to consider. Whether it is better to fend the Lead and Ore to London or Holland: Why I would be glad to be informed herein, is, because of the Duty, which is very considerable; and, by good Management, here may be half saved if you fend it abroad; whereas, if it comes to you, our Endeavours to save the Duty here will be but to little Purpose. As the Governor will be here before I can have your Answer, I shall be advised by him: As soon as I have loaded Captain Auchterloney, I will fend you the Bill of Lading, which you will settle with the former Proprietors, and deduct out of the Quantities mentioned in the Inventory. Whenever you happen to fend Ships from London, they should be obliged to call at Newcastle; and there to take in at least^ds of their Loading of Coals; by which means it would come to us Freight free, and be much fitter for our Purpose: We may try which will come cheapest, Whether the Deals and Timber from Norzvay, Vou 22.

or from the Woods at Abernethy; I believe from Nor-jpty; but next Summer may determine: We have now got and commissioned as much as we shall want for some time.

When we begin to work our Slags, it will be absolutely necessary to have what we call Skull Iron and Buffiel Iron; the former is about 40,?. per Ton, the latter about or £. 5 per Ton; you may get it at Win. Bowen's, Founder, at Marygold Stairs again!! White Friars; at Richard Sanders's, in New Thames street, Southwark; or at Mr. Remnant's, Founder, at Woolwich.

For every Thousand of Windsor Bricks, please to fend me a Load of Windsor Loom. Captain Anderson, in the Friendship, arrived here a few Days ago: We are now discharging her; but her Cargo of Malt is much damaged; some whereof ffie left behind at Dundee, left, by its being so wet and musty, it should spoil the rest: Just now we have unloaded her, and find the Malt so damaged, that I question whether any of it will be fit for Use: The Captain fays, that, upon searching into the Cause, he found that the Carpenter, who had fitted her last in the Thames, in place of caulking her, had only run Pitch over the Seams, which made her leaky as soon as ever ffie came to Sea; so that the Carpenter seems to be liable. I have lately had a Loading of Deals and Trees from Norway, by Captain Bradey; and have now sent him to Glasgow for Coal ;\as soon as flie returns I must let her have some Lead: And I hear there are other Two Ships coming from the Murray Firth with Provisions; and they are to be loaded like-wife; besides Two I have wrote about. One from Glasgow, or Belfast in Ireland, the other from Bristol; and to be here, if they can be procured, iu December next; so that you need not engage any more, until I can advise what Answer I have about them. I am, Gentlemen, with all due Respects,

Your sincere Friend,

Francis Place.

Strontien, 4th November 1730.

Gentlemen,

On the 19th Ult. I wrote you fully, and the 2d Instant I wrote you a ffiort Letter, per Mr Horsey, from Fort William. — I have put on' board Captain Hudson 150 Ton Lead, which is as much as the Weather would permit us to do in the time; but hope soon to complete her Lading. It is impossible to unload, and then load a Ship of her Burden, in the time you have referred; therefore you will lee the necessity of having more Lie Days before Demurage commences.

1 have sent Captain Thomson to the Firth of Forth, in order to take in the Meal we have so long expected by some of Sir Archibald Grant's Ships; if the Meal should be shipped already, then he is to take in Coal at Port Seaton: I begin to dread the consequence of not having the Meal here before now: We are already reduced to lliort Allowance, not having above 500 Bolls Meal in Store; and the weekly Cop.fumption amounts to about 50 Bolls; so that, if we have not a speedy Supply, we shall be put in a poor Condition.

- Our new Smelting Mill wrought very well until last Saturday Night, when some Villains broke in, and have cut One Set of Bellows all to Bits: I endeavour all I can to discover the Persons concerned; and, in order thereto, I have published a Reward of 20 Guineas to the Discoverer; but as.yet all is in vain.

Our Furnace, I fear, will prove of little Use to usf at lead until we get Skull or Scrap Iron, to work our Slags with.

MR. Earley according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint of a Breach of the Privilege of this House, committed

against Sir Richard Lane Knight, a Member of this House; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read.

The Report and Resolutions are as follows; viz.

The Committee have examined the Matter of the Complaint against Jonathan Evindony of London, Attorney at Law, and John Ellithorne his Servant, and other Persons unknown, under the Diredion of the said Jonathan Evindony in coming, on the Twenty-third of November last, into a Cellar in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surrey, wherein Sir Richard Lane Knight, a Member of this House, and his Servants, were filling up several Hogslieads of Beer, the Property of a Person in the Country, for whom, upon Request, Sir Richard acted as Agent; and, after blowing out the Candles, that they might not be discovered, locked the Door upon, and violently assaulted him and his Servants, keeping them under Confinement above an Hour, bruised Sir Richard's Hand, with other Injuries; and, by Force and Fraud, got Possession of the said Cellar and Beer, and have ever since detained the fame, in Breach of the Privilege of this House:

Thomas Chamberlain, being examined, said. That, about the Sixth of May 1732, One hundred Thirty-one Hogslieads, and Six Half Hogslieads, of Dorchester Beer, were landed at his Wharf, belonging to Joseph Marples; and that a Contract was entered into, and signed, by Sir Richard Lane, and George Way; and that the said Way, having the charge of the Beer, acted as Agent for Marples, as he believed:

And, being asked, Whether Way fold the Beer ? He said, he could not say he did; but he gaveTaftes of it, in order to fell it; and that several Hogslieads were carried out, by Ways Order.

Then the Purchase Agreement was produced, and read; whereby it appeared Sir Richard Lane bad purchased Fifty-two Hogsheads of the said Beer 10th June 1732, for his Son, and paid One Guinea Earnest to George Way:

The Witness further said, That the Hogslieads, on the 10th or 1 ith of June, were maked R. L.; and that, upon his asking Sir Richard Lane, who would pay the Wharfage and Warehouse-room; He answered, That he would satisfy him:

That Mr. Way had the Key, and locked up the Beer for the moil Part:

That Mr. Evindon paid the Warehouse-room, and all the other Charges, to the beginning of December last:

That he knew nothing of Sir Richard Lane's putting on a Lock; and he was not at home when the Lock was broke off; but said, a Lock was broke off:

Being shewed the Contraft, He said, he believed it to be Sir Richard's Hand; but thought the Words, " for my Son," were not; and believed the Letters to be larger than Sir Richard usually wrote.

Then Sir Richard produced Chamberlain's Letter, which Chamberlain owned to be his own Hand, dated 20th November 1732, with Proposals for Sale of the Beer, by the Assignees, inclosed.

Being cross-examined. He said. Sir Richard Lane had no Key; and that he saw Two Locks on the Cellar Door; but could not say who put them on:

That the Statute came out before the Second Lock was put on; and was pulled off'about the Tenth of November: That, when he first saw the Lock on, it was the beginning of November; believed the Lock was on about Ten Days at mod: That he went out of Town the beginning of July, and returned again in September; and that he was out of Town about Seven Weeks.

Thomas Powell said. Sir Richard came to him on the Twenty-third of November, and employed him as a Cooper: That he sent for the Key to Way's Son, who came with the Key, and let them into the Cellar; That they filled up near Thirty Hogslieads, and had removed

Mr. William Taylor produced the Agreement, which, he said, was signed by them, and left in his Hands by Consent, for the Benefit of both Parties: Which Agreement being read, it appeared. That the Property of the Fifty-two Hogsheads of Beer, claimed by Sir Richard Lane, was agreed to be determined by a Tryal at the Sittings in London.

Robert Godfrey gave Evidence, That he is the subscribing Witness to the said Contraft; and saw the Parties sign the fame, about Twelve of the Clock the same Night, after the Quarrel.

Then Sir Richard Lane, in his place, said, He admitted the Contraft; and scorned to make use of Privilege unjustly.

'Mr. William Taylor, being called in again, said. That Privilege was mentioned at the time of signing the said Agreement, and that he advised Sir Richard Lane not to make use thereof; who said, He would not, without his Consent: That, after his Return from the Circuit, Sir Richard Lane came to him, and said. He would complain, with his Consent: To which the Witness answered, That he would consent, if Sir Richard desired it.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this ^Committee, That Jonathan Evindon, Attorney at Law, is not guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House, in assaulting the Person of Sir Richard Lane, Knight, a Member of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That John Ellithorne, Servant to the said Jonathan Evin-<km, is not guilty of Breach of the Privilege of this House, in assaulting the Person of Sir Richard Lane Knight, a Member of this House.

After which, his Majesty wras pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, at followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Season of the Year, and the Dispatch yern have The King’* given to the publick Business make it proper for me to Speeh. put an End to this Session of Parliament.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my Thanks for the Provisions yon have made for the Service of the current Year: I have never demanded any Supplies of my People but what wrere absolutely necessary for the Honour, Safety, and Defence, of me and my Kingdom: and I am always best pleased, when the publick Expences ate supplied in a manner least burdensome to my Subjects.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I cannot pass by unobserved the wicked Endeavours that have lately been made use of to inflame the Minds of the People, and by the moll unjust Misrepresen tat ions, to raise Tumults and Disorders that almost threatened the Peace of the Kingdom; but I depend upon the Force of Truth, to remove the groundless Jealoulies that have been raised, of Designs carrying on again!! the Liberties of my People; and upon your known Fidelity, to defeat and frustrate the Expectations of such as delight in Confusion. It is my Inclination, and has always been my Study, to preserve the religious and civil Rights of all my Subjects: Let it be your Care to undeceive the Deluded, and to make them sensible of their present Happiness; and the Hazard they run, of being unwarily drawn, by specious Pretences, into their own Destru6lion.

King’s Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended Speech his Majesty, in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty RjwrUi1, was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; of which, Mr. Speaker said, he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followed); vis.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The War which is now begun and carried on against the Emperor, with lb much Vigour, by the United Powers ot France, Spain, and Sardinia, is become the Object Vol 22.

of the Care and Attention of all Europe; and, though I am no ways engaged in it, and have had no Part, except by my good Offices, in those Transactions which have been declared to be the principal CaulesJ and Motives of it, I cannot fit regardless of the present Events; or be unconcerned for the future Consequences of a War, undertaken and supported by lb powerful an Alliance.

If ever any Occasion required more than ordinary Prudence and Circutnfpebtion, the present calls upon us to use our utmost Precaution not to determine too hastily upon so critical and important a Conjuncture; but to consider thoroughly what the Honour and Dignity of my Crown and Kingdoms, the true Interest of my People, and the Engagements we are under to the several Powers we are in Alliance with, may, in Justice and Prudence, require of us.

I have therefore thought it proper to take Time to examine the Fabts alleged on both Sides, and to wait the Ilefult of the Councils of those Powers that are more nearly and immediately interested in the Consequences of the War; and to concert with those Allies w ho are under the same Engagements with me, and have not taken Part in the War, more particularly the States General of the United Provinces, such Measures as shall be thought most advisable for our common Safety, and for restoring the Peace of Europe.

The llesolutions of the British Parliament, in so nice a Juncture, are of too great Moment not to be carefully attended to, and impatiently expected by all, and not leal! by those who will hope to take Advantage from your Determinations, whatever they shall be, and to turn them to the Prejudice of this Kingdom. It mult therefore 3 G be

306 17° Januari'u A. 173 3

be thought most lafe and prudent, thoroughly to weigh and confide* all Circumstances, before we come to a final Determination.

As I shall have, in all iny Considerations upon this great and important Affair, the strictest Regard to the Honour of my Crown, and the Good of my People, and be governed by no other Views, I can make no Doubt but that I may entirely depend on the Support and Assistance of my Parliament, without exposing myself, by any precipitate Declarations, to such Inconveniencies as ought as far as possible, to be avoided.

In the mean time, I am persuaded you will make such Provisions as shall secure my Kingdoms, Rights, and Possessions, from all Dangers and Jnfuits, and maintain the Respect due to the British Nation. Whatever Part it may, in the End, be most reasonable for us to a ft, it will, in all Views, be necessary, when all Europe is preparing for Arms, to put ourselves in a proper Posture of Defence. As this will belt preserve the Peace of the Kingdom, so it will give us a due Weight and Influence in whatever Measures we shall take in Conjunction with our Allies: But should the Defence of the Nation not be sufficiently provided for, it will make us disregarded abroad, and may jn*ove a Temptation and Encouragement to the desperate Views of those who never fail to flatter themselves with the Hopes of great Advantages from publick Troubles 'fcrtd Disorders.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I shall order the Estimates to be laid before you of such Services as require your present and immediate Care. The Augmentation, which will be proposed for the Sea Service, will be very considerable; but, I am confident, it will be thought by you reasonable and necessary: I mult particularly recommend to your Care the Debt of the Navy, which has every Year been laid before you; but, from the present Circumstances of the times, I believe you w ill think it now requires some Provision to be made for it; which cannot well be longer poltponed, without manifest Detriment to the publick Service.

As these extraordinary Charges and Expences are unavoidable, I make no doubt but you will effectually raise the Supplies necessary for defraying of them, with that Readiness and Dispatch, and with, that just Regard to the true Interest of my People, which this Parliament has hitherto shewn upon all Occasions.

My Lords and Gentlemen, h is at all times to be wished, that the Business of Parliament might be carried on free from Heats and Animosities; and with that Temper which becomes the Justice and Wifdoui of the Nation: At this time it is more particularly to be desired, that this Session may not be protracted by unnecessary Delays, when the whole Kingdom seems prepared for the Election of a new Parliament; an Event which employs the Attention of all Europe: And I am very well pleased, that this Opportunity offers, of taking again the Sense of my People in the Choice of a new llepresentative; that the World may fee how much their true Sentiments have been mistaken, or misrepresented: Those who fee and hear only at a Distance may ealily be imposed upon; and from thence conceive false Hopes, or Fears; but, I am confident, a little time will effectually remove all groundless Sunniles; and it will be found, that Great Britain is always ready to act that Part, which the Honour and Interest of the Nation calls upon them to undertake.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right ufuaf to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve Order*, in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall adjudge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath procured himself to be elected, or returned, a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, that any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly, or indirectly, hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a hjgh Crime and Misdemeanor, and this House will proceed with the utmoti Severity against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, That any Person hath given false Evidence in any same before this H&ufe, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost Severity against such Offender.

Mr. Campbell, of Pembrokeshire, reported from the Address on Committee, appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address the King’s to be presented to His Majesty, That the Committee had sPcech-drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and lie read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the'

Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; vis.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament assembled, beg Leave to return your Majesty our humblest Thanks for your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We are truly fenlible of your Majesty’s Goodnels; and hear with the deepest Sense of Gratitude, the Concern your are pleased to express for the War unhappily begun in Europe; and acknowledge, with the highest Satisfaction, this new Proof your Majesty has given us of your great Wisdom, in waiting, at this nice and critical Juncture, the Result of the Councils of those Powers who are more nearly and immediately interested in the Consequences of this War, before your Majesty makes any final Determination for your own Conduct; not wondering, that the same Prudence and Precaution, the same Concern and Circumspection, that have guided and directed every Step, hitherto taken, in your Majesty’s happy and auspicious Reign, should now induce you to take time to examine the Facts alleged on both Sides, and to concert with those Allies who are under the same Engagements with your Majesty, without having taken Part in the War, particularly the States General of the United Provinces, such Measure as shall be thought most advilabie for the common Safety, and for restoring the Peace of Europe.

That your Majesty, in all your Transactions in this great and important Affair, will have the ftriCleft Regard to the Honour and Dignity of your Crown and Kingdom, and to the true Interest of your People, is what not only your Majesty's Royal Assurances, but our happy Experience of all your Majesty’s past Conduct, and the Prudence of your Councils and Measures on every Occasion, leave us no room to doubt.

And, as we have an entire Confidence in your Majesty’s Judgment to difeern, and Solicitude to procure, the Welfare and Interest of your Subjects; lb your Majesty may depend upon the effectual Support, and ready Assistance, of your faithful Commons, in all such Meallires as your Majesty shall find it necelikry to enter into, for attaining and securing the le great Ends.

And we beg Leave further to afiure your Majesty,

That your Commons will make such Provision for the Safety of your Kingdoms, as the present Situation of

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House attended his Majesty, on Saturday last, with their Address: To which his Majesty. was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemeh,

I return you my Thanks for this very dutiful, affectionate, and loyal Address, and for the Confidence you repose in me; which, you may be assured, shall always be employed for the Honour of my Crown, and the true Interest of my People.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Motion made on Saturday last. That a Supply be granted to his Majesty;

Ordered, That his Majesty’s most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament be referred to the said Committee.

Then the House resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner reported from the Committee,

That they had come to a Resolution; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received To-morrow1 Morning.

Complaint being made to the House, That William Privilege, Philips, Attorney at Law, and Edward Barnes, Clerk to the said William Philips, who, in the last Session of Parliament, on the Thirteenth Day of June, were ordered to be taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for a Breach of the Privilege of this House, committed against Sir John Rufhout Baronet, a Member of this House, had not been taken into Custody.

The Orders made in the last Session of Parliament, for taking the said Persons into Custody, were read:

And the Serjeant at Arms having been called upon, to inform the House what he had done in pursuance of the Orders, made in the last Session, for taking the said Persons into Custody, acquainted the House, That the said Orders being made on the last Day of the last Session, the said Persons could not be taken into Custody, because of the immediate Prorogation of the Parliament:

And the Journal of the House, of the Fourth Day of April, in the Sixth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, in relation to the Proceedings of the House upon the Petition of Samuel Powell Esquire, Serjeant at Arms attending this House; and the Standing Order of the House made thereupon, relating to Persons committed by this House, and absconding from Justice, or refuting to pay their just Fees; was also read.

Ordered, That the said William Philips, having, ok the Thirteenth Day of June last, been ordered into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for a Breach of the Privilege of this House, committed by him, and, by means of a Prorogation of the Parliament, could not, by virtue of that Order, be taken into Custody, be now taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for the said Breach of Privilege.

Ordered, That the said Edward Barnes, having, on the Thirteenth Day of June last, been ordered into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for a Breach of the Privilege of this House, committed by him, and, by means of a Prorogation of the Parliament, could not, by virtue of that Order, be taken into Custody, be now taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House, for the said Breach of Privilege.

REVENUE.

The Six-Pence a Man per Menfem, of 10,000 Seamen in the King’s Service at Sea, yields -The Six-Pence a Man per Menfem, of about 1,500 Seamen employed on board his Majesty’s Ships in ordinary, may yield -

The Six-Pence a Man per Menfem, of Seamen employed in the Merchants Service, has yielded per Annum, for these Five Years past, about The Three Light-houses on the Forelands yield, per Annum, about Rent of Houses yield about -

There is veiled in South Sea Annuities, by Order of the Court of Chancery, the Sum of £.3,974 devised to the Hospital; which Sum is to be laid out in the Purchase of Lands; and, in the mean time, the Hospital receives Interest, at £. 4 per Cent.

Revenue ffiort of the Expence

Memorandum: — The Half Pay of the Governor, and other military Officers of the Hospital, which is at present applied in Aid to the Revenue of the Hospital, and may be deducted £. s. d. from the above Deficiency, amounts to about - - 1,295 15 —

The Wages, and Value of the Provisions, allowed to the Chaplains of the Ordinary of Deptford and Woolwich, which are at present applied in like manner, they being the Chaplains of the Hospital, amount to about - 107-----

But the said Sums, being uncertain, are not brought to Account, as Part of the Revenue of the Hospital.

Note, If more than 10,000 Seamen should be allowed for the King’s Service, it is probable there will be a Decrease of Seamen in the Merchant’s Service, and a Diminution in the Produce of the Light-houses, which cannot be estimated.

Parliament, made in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, upon every Pint of Ale or Beet that shall be vended or sold within the Town of Montrose% and Privileges thereof, for supplying the said Town with fresh Water, and for other Purposes therein mentioned; by which A<5fc, a Duty, over and above the Duty of Excise, payable to his Majesty, his Heirs, and Successors, was lard upon every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer, that should be, for^ Sale, either brewed, brought in, vended, tapped, or fold, within the said Town, and Privileges thereof; and payable from the 24th Day of June 1720, for the Term of 25 Years, and to the End of the then next Session of Parliament, to the Magistrates and Town Council of the said Town, and their Successors in Office for the Time being, and their Collectors and Assigns, for the Use of the Community thereof; which Duty was, by the said A ft, directed to be applied for and towards sup-

fdying the said Town with fresh Water; and for mprovement and Preservation of the Harbour there; apd for building a convenient Dock; and for maintaining and preserving other publick Works for the Benefit of the said Town; and for paying off the publick Debts thereof; subject to the Directions in the said Act mentioned.

Then the Petitioners, in Support Of the other Allegations of their Petition, produced several Witnesses; viz.

Mr. Coutts: Who said. That the Money arising by the said Duty will not be sufficient to maintain, improve, and preserve, the publick Works; so that no Part thereof can be applied towards paying off the publick Debts of the said Town.

The said Mr. Coutts further said, That the Harbour of the said Town is capable of being made very commodious for the Receiving of such Ships and Vessels as shall from time to time, fail into, and lie in, the said Harbour; and that it is absolutely necessary, that a new Pier should be built and maintained on the EastSide of the said Harbour, for preserving such Ships and Vessels from Storms and Tempests:

He also said, That the public Streets of the said Town are in a bad Condition.

Mr. Coutts and Mr. Achterloney, being severally examined, said, That the Water, in and near the said Town, is so very bad, that the same cannot be made use of for Brewing, Malting, and Bleaching of Linen, the chief Manufacture of that Country; and that the Inhabitants of the said Town are obliged to fend a great Way for fresh Water for such and other Uses, at a great Expence; and that, to supply the Town with good fresh Water, and to make a Bason for the Reception thereof, j£. 3,000 Sterling at lead will be required.

And it appeared to the Committee, That the Money arising by the said Duties will not be sufficient to do the publick Works directed to be done by the said Act; and to build and maintain a new Pier; and to repair the Streets of the said Town; and to discharge the publick Debts thereof; unless the said Imposition, or Duty, be granted for a further Term of Years.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-Sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, upon every Pint of Ale or Beer that shall be vended or sold within the Town of Montrose, and Privileges thereof, for supplying the said Town with fresh Water; and for other Purposes therein mentioned; And that Colonel Middleton, Mr. Campbell, of Edinburgh, and Mr. Scot, do prepare, and bring in the fame.

A Petition of the Masters, Workmen, and other Per- Running of fons, concerned in the Woollen and Silk Manufactures W00L within the Cities of Londonawd Westminster, and Borough of Southwark, in behalf of them (elves, and all other Personsconcerned in the said Manufactures throughout Great Britain, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, that the Running of great Quantities of Wool to foreign Parts from Great Britain and Ireland, and the Exportation of great Quantities of Woollen Goods, completely manufactured, from Ireland, to foreign Countries, contrary to Law, are highly prejudicial to the Trade of this Kingdom, and the principal Cause of the Decay of the Woollen Manufacture: That, by this means, Foreigners are enabled to work up great Quantities of their own Wool, by mixing it with English or Irish, without the Assistance of which they could not make several Species of Goods, with which they now supply foreign Markets; and that the Petitioners are fenflble of the Zeal of this House, and of the good Laws in being to prevent the said mischievous Practice of exporting Wool and Woollen Goods ma-nufadured in Ireland; but find, by fad Experience, that all Endeavours for that Purpose have been hitherto ineffectual: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to provide such Remedies, and to give the Petitioners such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the w hole House.

A Petition of the Druggists, Grocers, China-men, and Excise others, dealing in Tea, was presented to the House, and Tea. read; alledging, That by an Act, passed in the Tenth Year of King George the First, the Petitioners were induced to hope, that the Dutyarifing from Tea would be better secured to his Majesty, and the Interest of the fair Trader be better supported; but have fatally experienced the contrary Effects, the clandestine Importation of Tea being greatly increased; to the Damage of the publick Revenue, and Ruin of the fair Trader, occasioned by the great Difference of the Value of that Commodity at this and foreign Markets, whereby the Smugglers are enabled to purchase it Abroad for less than Half the Duty paid here: That the Regulations, which the Petitioners are laid under, are most burdensome and grievous, their Ploufes being liable to be entered by Persons unknown to them, and their Properties subjected to the judicial. Determination of Commissioners: That the Petitioners are liable to severe Penalties, for Errors and Omissions absolutely unavoidable; and retrained from disposing of their Goods, after having paid Duty for the fame, without Permits, from the Officers of the Inland Duties, expressing the Names and Places of Abode of the respect ive Buyers and Sellers, exposing thereby the Extent and Circumstances of their Trade ^whereby the Petitioners conceive they are in a worle Condition than any other of his Majesty’s Subjects: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and give them such Relief, as to the House shall fcem meet.

And a Motion being made, and the Question being put, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

The House divided.

A Petition of the Governor and Company of Undertakers for raising the Thames Water in York Buildings, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, through the Frauds and Mismanagements of feme of their former Dire6iors, being reduced to the

freateft Necessities, the House was pleased, in the last eflion of Parliament to appoint a Committee to’ inquire into the State of their Affairs;’ which, by the Report of the said Committee, appeared to be in a very confuted and ruinous Condition; their Books having been* kept in fb imperfe6fc and irregular a manner, that there was no general Leidger of their Accounts; so that no certain State of their Affairs, drawn from their Books, could be depended on; and that by the said Report it appeared, that the Debts and out-standing Bonds of the Company, according to the nearest Computation, amounted to up-wards of Two hundred Forty-one thousand Pounds; though the real Debts thereof amounted only to One hundred Eighty-three thousand One hundred and Forty Pounds, many of them being secured to the Creditors by very large Deposits, or Pledges of the Company's Bonds, transferrable by Indorsement thereon; for Satisfaction of which Debts the Petitioners had nothing left, but their Estate of Widdrington, and the Reversions of certain forfeited Estates in Scotland, purchased by the Petitioners, of the Publick; and that their Debts were daily increasing by the great Number of Actions brought against them by particular Creditors: That, towards the End of the last Session of Parliament, a Bill passed in this House for their Relief in the Premises; but, tlfe Session being so far advanced j it did not pals in the House of Peers: That the Expence of the many Law-foils already brought, and daily bringing, against the Petitidners, by their Creditors, will ruin both the Petitioners, and their Creditors; and that the present Sale of the Estates of the Petitioners will be equally expensive and prejudicial to them, and their Creditors: That the Petitioners cannot make any Agreement with their Creditors, who are very numerous; und many of whom are Executors, or Trustees, for Infants, without the Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House for Leave to bring in a Bill for stating the Debts and Demands between the Petitioners, and their Creditors, and for staying, in the mean time, all Suits against the Petitioners; and to make such Agreement, as a proper Proportion of their real Creditors shall accept of, binding on the rest; and that the House will take such other Order in the :Pre mi fes, for the Relief of the Petitioners, as to the House shall seem meet.

Manufacture A Petition of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace of

of Cloth in the West Riding of the County of York, assembled at

Yorkshire. General Quarter Sessions of the Peace, held by Adjournment, ^it Wakefield, in and for the said West Riding, the 17th Day of January last, and of the Owners and Occupiers of Fulling Mills in the said West Riding) and also of the Merchants, Clothiers, and Dealers in the Manufacture of Woollen Broad Cloth made in the said West Riding, was presented to the House, and read) alleging. That the Act, made in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for the better regulating the Manufacture of Cloth in the said West Riding, which, by an Act in the last Session of Parliament, was continued for several Years yet to come, has greatly improved the Credit of the said Manufacture, and has been very advantageous to the Dealers therein but complaining, that Three hundred Pounds, and upwards, expended by divers of the Petitioners in procuring the said original Act, and a Bill, which passed this House in the Fifth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for amending the said Act, has not been repaid: That, by the said Act, the Petitioners, and other Owners and Occupiers of Fulling Mills, are made subject to great Penalties, which it is almost impossible to avoid: That the Petitioners the Clothiers have been required to pay, and have paid, for every whole Cloth sealed and stamped by the Mill Men, Four Pence; and, for every Half Cloth, Two Pence; though the said Act has only made a general Provision for the payment of Two Pence for all Cloth so sealed and stamped; One Peny thereof to be paid to the Treasurer of the said West Riding, to be applied towards the Salaries of the Searchers appointed by the said Act: That no other Fund is provided, by the said Act, for Payment of the said Salaries; and that, no Provision being made, by the said Act, to compel the Clothiers to pay to the Mill Men the said Sum of Two Pence, or the Mill Men to receive the said Peny for the said Treasurer, and to pay the same, when received, the said Fund is diminished, and’in Danger of being loft, by the Refusal of several Clothiers to pav the said Peny, and of several Mill Men to receive and pay over the fame: And therefore praying Leave to bring in a Bill for mitigating or altering the said Penalties upon the Mill Men, for compelling the Clothiers to pay the said Peny to the Mill Men, for the Treasurer of the said West Riding, and the Mill Men tp receive and pay the same to the said Treasurer; and so to explain the said Act, that the Petitioners the Clothiers may be obliged to pay to the Mill Men no more than Two Pence for the Sealing and Stamping of every Cloth, whether the same shall be a whole Cloth, or an End, or Half Cloth) and for reimbursing the Petitioners the Clothiers the said Sum of Money so by them expended, as aforesaid; or that such Provision may be made, touching the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.;

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of several Merchants, Tradesmen, and Rec< Shopkeepers, within the City of London, and Liberties l*mal thereof, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several others trading in the said City, and Liberties, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are under a Necessity of giving Credit for small Sums to great Numbers of Persons, who frequently refuse, though well able, to pay their Debts; depending on the Discouragements which the Petitioners lie under, from the unavoidable Expence of Suits, and the Delays thereof, even after Judgment obtained; and alleging, That an easy, speedy, and cheap Method of recovering Debts, will greatly tend to the Promoting of Industry, and the Support of useful Credit: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts, within the City of London, and Liberties thereof; or "that such other Relief may be given to the Petitioners in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Robert Dalzell, late Earl of Carnwath.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That the same of the Petitioner having been humbly represented to his Majesty, his Majesty had commanded him to acquaint this House, That his Majesty gives his Consent, that the House-may do therein as they think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was, on the Ninth Day of February 1715, attainted of High Treason; and thereby all his Estate, real and personal, was forfeited, and, by One or more Acts of Parliament, veiled in Trullees, for the Use of the Publick: That, by a Clause in an Act, made in the Tenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for granting Relief to the Petitioner, it was Enacted, That, out of the "Money arising from the Sale or Produce of his forfeited Estate, such a Sum might be applied for and towards the future Support of the Petitioner, and his Family, and for the Payment of his Debts, without Account, Imprest, or other Charge, as his said late Majesty, by his Sign Manual, should think fit to direct; in consequence of which Act, the Petitioner was impowered, by his said Majesty’s Sign Manual, to receive, and hath received, the sum of £. 5,000; but that the Petitioner is in Danger of losing the Produce and Benefit of the said Sum, and is exposed to many Difficulties, being incapable to sue, or maintain any Action or Suit; and is likewise disabled to take or inherit any real or personal Estate that shall or may hereafter descend or come to him; and, by reason of his said Attainder, is excluded from the Means of providing for himself, and his unfortunate Family: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for removing the Disabilities and Incapacities occasioned by his said Attainder; or to grant him such other Retief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable Robert Dalzell, late Earl of Carnwath, to file or maintain any Action or Suit, notwithstanding his Attainder; and to remove any Disability in him, by reason of his said Attainder, to take or inherit any real or personal Estate that may or shall hereafter descend or come to him, or which he was intitled unto, in Reversion or Remainder, before his Attainder: And that Mr. Earle, Sir James Grant, Mr. Thompson of

York, Mr. Drummond of Quarrel, and General Wade, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

The other Order of the Day being read;

Resolved, That this House will, upon Wednesday Morning next, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning next. Nine of the Clock.

By the Running of great Quantities of Wool from Great Britain and Breland to foreign Parts, without which, Foreigners could not work up their own Wool; 2. By the Exportation of great Quantities of W oollen Goods, completely manufactured, from Ireland, to foreign Countries; 3. By the Exportation of great Quantities of faulty and ill-wrought Goods, made by unskilful Persons, who, leaving their Employment of Husbandry, and without having served due Apprentice-ftiips or Services, apply themselves to the Combing of Wool, Weaving of Stockings, and the Making of other Woollen Goods; to the great Discredit of our Manufactures, and to the Discouragement of great Numbers of Persons duly inftrlifted in those Mysteries, who, for want of Employment at home, have been forced into foreign Countries, and have taught the Inhabitants there the many Improvements in the said Mysteries, only found out, and advanced, by the Skill and Industry7 of the Natives of this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to provide such Remedies, and to give the Petitioners such Relief, as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of Samuel Buckley was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner has, at his own foie and very great Expence, and several Years Labour, by the Assistance of some learned Persons beyond the Seas, and of this Kingdom, procured, and made, Collections of many original Papers and Letters relating to Tkuanus's History, written in Latin, in order to a new and accurate Impression thereof, with great Additions and Improvements, at London, in Seven large Volumes in Folio, on Paper imported from Holland for that particular Purpose, and with new Types and proper Ornaments; which Work is now finished: That the A & of Parliament, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for the Encouragement of Learning, by vetting the Copies of printed Books in the Authors or Purchasers of such Copies, during the Times therein mentioned, extends only

to the Authors, Purchasers, or Proprietors, of the Copy of any Book in England, ptiblished after the 10th Day of April, 1710; and, by an express Proviso, allows the Importation, vending, or felling, of any Books in Greek, Latin, or any other foreign Language, printed beyond the Seas; so that any Book first compiled and printed in this Kingdom, in any of those Languages, may be forthwith reprinted abroad, and be imported into, and fold in, this Kingdom; to the srreat Damage of the First Printer or Proprietor thereof here; and that it is the constant Practice of foreign Kingdoms and Governments, to grant to their own Subjects the foie Privilege of printing and felling Books, and to prohibit the Importation into their own Dominions of such Books reprinted in other I3!aces j which Grants, by the Confutation of such foreign Kingdoms and Governments, have the same Force there as an Act of Parliament has in this Kingdom; and therefore praying, That the Petitioner may be allowed to enjoy the same Benefits in his Copy of the said History of Thuanus, in Latin, for the Term of Fourteen Years, and no longer, as are, by the said Act, granted to the Author or Proprietor of the Copy of any English Book, subject to the several Regulations and Conditions expressed in the said Act, with respect to English Books; or in such other Manner as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill pursuant to the Prayer of the said Petition: And that Mr. Walpole, Mr. Plumptre, Mr. Winnington, Mr. Sandys, Mr. Thomas Bacon, Dr. Clarke, and Mr. Cracker ode, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Manufacture of Cloth in York (hi re.

Ordered, That Mr. Turner have Leave to make a Motion, it being after Three of the Clock.

And he moved the House accordingly.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace of the West Riding of the County of York, assembled at the General Quarter Session of the Peace, held, by Adjournment, at Wakefield, in and for the said West Riding, the 17th Day of January last, and of the Owners and Occupiers of Fulling Mills in the said West Riding, and also of the Merchants, Clothiers, and Dealers in the Manufacture of Woollen Broad Cloth made in the said West Riding, is referred, be now received.

Mr. Turner accordingly reported from the said Committee, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 7th of this inttant February, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

Mr. Caleb Jeff erf on was called: Who said, That he knew several Bonds and Notes had been given, to the Value of £. 300, or thereabouts, in order to discharge the Expence in endeavouring to obtain Acts of Parliament for Regulating the Manufacturing of Cloth in the West Riding of the County of York:

That, by a Clause in an Act of the 1 ith Year of his late Majesty, a Penalty of £. 5 is laid upon such Persons

levied, will ruin the Persons concerned, many of them being very poor; for which Reason the full Penalty has Seldom been levied.

He further said. That the Clothiers have paid Four Pence for damping the whole Cloth, and Two Pence for a Half Cloth, till Midsummer last; and that some Persons are still willing to pay the same; but that the Mill Men have refused to pay the Peny to the Treasurer, which they are obliged by the said Act to pay; and that 14 of the Mill Men now (land indicted for refusing to pay the said Peny to the Treasurer, when such Mill Men have received it for his Use.

And it appeared to the Committee, That, unless the Penalties upon the Mill Men be mitigated, the Clothing Trade in the said West Riding will be very much discouraged; and that it is necessary, upon the Clothiers paying Two Pence to the Mill Man for each whole Cloth, and One Peny for Half a Cloth, such Mill Man should be obliged to pay One Moiety of each Sum to the Treasurer.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to explain and amend an Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Firfi, intituled, An Act for the better regulating the Manufacture of Cloth in the West Riding of the County of York: And that Mr. Turnery Sir George Saville, Sir William Lowtlier9 Sir William Wentworth, Sir William Milner, Mr. Thompson of York, and Sir Thomas Ro-binfon, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

And then the House adjourned till Tomorrow Morning, Nine of the Clock.

Complaint being made to the House, That William Noble, Clerk, had asserted, in a publick Coffee-house, That Sir William Milner Baronet, a Member of this House, received a Pension from the Court; and that he, the said William Noble, knew the Person who paid it; in Dishonour of the said Sir William Milner, and in Breach of the Privilege of this House;

Mr. James Farrer, and Mr. Brudenell Greenwood attending at the Door, were severally called in, and examined touching the Matter of the said Complaint.

And then they withdrew.

Ordered, That the said William Noble, Clerk, be summoned to attend this House forthwith, to answer the said Complaint.

The said William Noble, attending, according to Order, was called in, and examined.

And then he withdrew.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That it appears to this House, That William Noble, Clerk, has publickly asserted That Sir William Milner, a Member of this House, was a Pensioner, and received £. 500 per Annum I for his voting in Parliament; and that he knew from whom he received the fame.

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the said Assertion is false and scandalous, highly reflecting upon the Honour of the said Sir William Milner, and of this House, and a Breach of the Privilege thereof.

Ordered, That the said William Noble, Clerk, be, for his said Offence, taken into the Custody of the Serjeant at Arms attending this House.

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

Then the Petitioners called,

Mr. Edward Byollin: Who said. That, at the time of passing of the said Acts, the said Highways, thereby directed to be repaired, were in so bad a Condition in the Winter-season, that the Trusteeswere under a Ne-ceflity of borrowing a considerable Sum of Money, in order to make the same passable:

And the said Edward Byollin said. That all the Money collected and borrowed hath been laid out, and duly applied, according to the Direction of the said Acts.

Then the Petitioners laid before the Committee an Account of the Receipts and Disbursements of the Tolls,

in each Year, from the 24th Day of June 17171 the time of the Commencement of the Act, to Michaelmas last; whereby it appeared, That, for Five \ ears last past, the Disbursements have annually exceeded the clear Produce of the said Tolls:

And Mr. Byollin being asked, Why the Tolls have thus decreased ? Said, That there had not, of late Years, so many People resorted from London to Harnp-stead as did formerly; and that other Roads about the City having been repaired, since the patling of the Acts aforesaid, by other Turnpikes, and being thereby made commodious, Persons went other Ways to take the Air.

And he further said. That, when the Trustees found the Income of the Toll-gates abate, they removed the Collectors of the Tolls from one Gate to another, One whereof wasdifplaced; and the Trustees examined very strictly, if any Frauds were committed.

The said Byollin being asked, In what manner Contracts were made for Ballast or Gravel ? Said, That publick Notice was given, and a Day fixed, for Persons to lay Proposals for that Purpose before, the Trustees; and that they contra6ied for the same at the lovveft Price they could, giving is. per Load, and is. 3d. per Load, for what they had on Hampstead Heath, when private Persons gave is. 3d. and 1$. 6d. per Load.

Mr. Jeffreys mid Mr. Michell, being severally examined, laid, That, about a Year ago, publick Nolice was given for supplying and carrying of Ballast; because the Trustees would not be obliged to take it from One Parish.

And Mr. Henry Bin field said. That he cont rafted to carry Ballast for repairing the Roads; but, being obliged by that Con trad to carry such Loads at so low a Price, and to go many times a Day, the Work was so hard, that he had Four Horses spoiled; and, for that Reason, would not contract for the same Purpose the last Year.

And it appeared to the Committee, That, unless the Term and Powers granted by the said former Acts be enlarged, the Money, arising by the said Tolls, will not be sufficient to pay off the said Debt of£. 8,073. 165.; and also to amend the said Roads, and keep the same in good Repair.

Then the Committee proceeded to examine the Matter of the Second Petition:

And, to make out the Allegations thereof,

Mr. Peters was called: Who said, That there is a common Highway leading from the End of the Parish of Hampstead, through Hendon, to the Parish of Elfirey, which is about Seven Miles in Length; and also a common Highway, not much used by the Inhabitants, Part of the Road leading from London to Edgware, One Mile whereof is in the said Parish of Hendon: He also said, That there are several publick cross Roads, and other Roads, making together 28 Miles, and upwards; which the Inhabitants of the Parish of Hendon are obliged to keep in Repair; and that several of the Roads lead to Market Towns, and are much frequented, except in the Winter-season, when they are bad and dangerous for Waggons and heavy Carriages, although the Inhabitants have constantly done the Statute-work upon the Roads, and raised same Years 6d. others 4d. and never less than 2|d. in the Pound, by a Rate, for 23 Years past, which amounts to £. 1,766. 45*. 3d.; and that the same has been laid out by the Parishioners in amending the Highways within their Parish.

Mr. Nicholl, being examined, did confirm the Evidence given by Mr. Peters: And further said. That the Road, leading from the Flask on Hampstead Heath, to the End of Bur rough-lane, next Edgware Road, in the Parish of Hendon, is, by reason of the many heavy Carriages travelling through the fame, become very ruinous, and this last Winter was in a worse Condition than it was ever known to be.

And Mr. Nicholl also said, That the greatest Part of the Statute-work was usually performed on that Road;
