Mr. Harvey, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Byollin, as to the Badness of the Roads mentioned in the last Petition; and said, That the Tolls collected at the Turnpike erected on Islington Road are scarce sufficient to keep the same in tolerable Repair: because a greater Number of Travellers, and heavy Carriages pass and repass that Road, than through the other Roads; and the Money collected at the said Turnpike is applicable towards repairing of other Roads of less consequence, and at a Distance from Islington; but that, if the Tolls collected there were laid out in repairing that Road, the same might be kept in very good Repair, and the Roads mentioned in the last Petition might also be amended.

A Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, Overseers Whitechapel of the Poor, and principal Inhabitants, of the Parish of Wor]j£oufej St. Mary Matfellan, alias Whitechapel, in the County of Middlesex, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the said Parish being of great Extent, and containing above 2,500 Houses, the greater Number of which are inhabited by Persons of mean Circumstances, 700 poor Pensioners, and upwards, are relieved weekly by the Rates collected within the said Parish for that Purpose, which generally amount to £. 2,000per Annum, and upwards: That the Surplusses of the yearly Sum of £. 120, payable by the said Parish, to the Trustees appointed by an Act, made in the Eighth Year of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Highways from the Stones End at Whitechapel Church, in the said County, to Shenfield, and to the furthermost Part of the Parish of Woodford, leading to the Town of Epping, in the County of Essex, have been misapplied, or not accounted for, for want of a proper Authority to oblige the Collectors thereof to account for the fame: That the clamorous Proceedings, and irregular Behaviour, of the great Multitude of Persons who generally attend the Vestry of the said Parish, in which all the Inhabitants assessed to the Relief of the Poor, being more than One thousand Persons, have a Right to vote, discourage the principal Inhabitants from attending, obstruct the Business of the said Parish, and greatly increase, as the Petitioners apprehend, the Expences thereof: That it will tend greatly to the Ease and Tranquillity of the Inhabitants, and the general Interest and Good of the said Parish, that a Workhouse be erected in the fame, for the Employment and Maintenance of their Poor; and that the said Surplusses be duly accounted for; and that the Right of voting in the Vestry be confined to such Persons as either contribute the greatest Share of the publick Expence, or have served the Office of Churchwarden, or Overseer of the Poor, of the said Parish: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the Purposes aforesaid; or that the Petitioners may have such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

Mr. Earley according to Order, reported from the Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the Complaint of a Breach of the Privilege of this House, committed against Thomas Pelham junior, Esquire, a Member of this House; and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; arid he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have examined the Matter of the Complaint, That John Whitfield did, by the Assistance of Win. Stredwick, George Apps, and Richard Jenner junior, on the Twenty-eighth Day of January last, forcibly and violently enter upon Part of an House in the Possession of Edward Kennardy Tenant to Thomas Pelham)\m\ov, Esquire, a Member of this House, and still keeps Possession thereof, in Breach of the Privilege of this House.

The Counsel for the Complainant alleged, That a Lease was let, of the Premises in question, by Edward Kennardy to Thomas Pelham junior, a Member of this House: To prove which, they called,

William Wilson: Who said, That the Lease was dated the 29th of December last: That he saw it signed and sealed the same Day 5 and that it was then delivered by Mr. Kennardto Mr. Thomas Pelham.

The Lease was read; and it appeared thereby, That the same commenced from Michaelmas last, for the Term of Nine Years, at the yearly Rent of £. 10.

Edward Kennard, being called in, was objected to, as having an'Interest therein: Which being over-ruled:

He gave Evidence of the Lease, as above; and said. That he agreed afterwards, with Mr. Pelham, for Two *7

Rooms to lay Com in, for which he was to pay Forty Shillings per Annum; That he was in Possession, and had put Corn therein, and had also carried out a Load: That, on the Twenty-eighth of January last, in the Evening, he was informed, That his Door was 'broke open, and that Richard Jenner had carried away his Corn: That, the next Morning, he inquired of Goody Kimber, who lived in the Houife, and flie told him, That Mr. Whitfield, Mr. Stredwick, and George Apps, took some Corn out: That he found a new Lock put on the Door; and some Corn left.

Being cross-examined, he denied the letting the House to Mr. Whitfield; and said. That he never declared so to Mrs. Kimber: That Whitfield was not in possession before Christmas, and had not the Key; and that he never ordered Kimber to deliver it:

That he had lit another House near to it to Mr. Whifield, for which he paid Fifty Shillings per Annum; and that he had received a Quarter’s Rent on St. Thomas's Day, being the Day it was due.

Wm. Stephens said, He knew the House let to Mr. Pelham, and saw Mr. Whitfield, and George Apps, a Carpenter, there; but did not seem to do any thing; though Mr. Whitfield said, Sure, they might get in somehow.

Benjamin Wayth said, That he was at the Castle Inn, in Lewes, the 30th of January; and that Apps the Carpenter told him, That he took off the old Lock, and put on a new one; and that Mr. Whi field was there when the old Lock was taken off.

Anne Kimber gave Evidence, That flie lived in Part of the House where Kennard had put Corn, and carried away the Key: That Mr. Whitfield, with Stredwick and Apps, came thither; and, as lhe went into the Yard, flie observed the Door was shut; but, when flie came back, the Door was open; and Mr. Whitfield, with Apps and Stredtvick, were in Possession: That there was a new Lock, but that flie did not fee it put on; and that he, Mr. Whitfield, took away a Sack of Corn: That he was in Possession the Second of November last; and that Mr. Kennard let it to him: That the Key was left with her on account of the Use of an Oveu there, which he had contracted for; and that Mr. Kennard had ordered the Key to be delivered to Mr. Whitfield, when wanted.

That Mr. Stredwick, who used to dress Dogs Meat there, left the Key with her: That Mr. Kennard, on Christmas-day last, asked her for the Key, in the Name of Whitfield: That lhe asked him to leave it; and he promised her the fume again, whenever flie wanted it: That flie said, Have you not let it to Whitfield ? And he answered, No matter for that; I have let it again:

That Mr. Kennard refused her the Key the Second of January last: That she first had the Key at Mid-summer last: That Mr. Whitfield had it in Possession till December; and that flie was denied the Key by Mr. Kennard the 2d of January last.

William Wills said. That Kennard lodged at his House, when a Sack of Oats, containing about Two Bulliels, was sent there for him, with Notice, That Mr. Whitfield had taken Possession of Kennard's House, and put a new Lock on the Door; and that Kennard told him, He designed to live in it himself.

John Apsley Esquire said, That, on the 29th of January last he met Mr. Whitfield in Lewes; who toid him what he had done the Day before, and that he had hired the House of Kennard, and gave Half a Crown Earned; That he fluce advised Mr. Whitfield to submit, and restore Possession to Kennard; and that he had heard Mr. Pelham would drop the Complaint: Who answered, He would not submit, or write about it; and that he cared not what became of the House:

Thstf it was publicly talked of, both at the Coffee-house and the Club, by raoft People, That the House was let, before the 28th of January last, to Mr. Pelham.

Edward Kennard, being called again, said, He was not there when the Room was broke open; but that he

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutiotis; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That Mr. John Whitfield, having, on the 2Sth Day of January last, forcibly and violently entered upon Part of a House belonging to Thomas Pelham junior, El'quire, a Member of this House, in the Occupation of Edward Kenward, and having cauled the Goods of the said Edward Kenward to be removed from thence, and itill keeping Possession of the said Tenement, is. thereby guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee* That William Stredwick, being aiding and aliifting in the said forcible Entry, and in directing the Goods of Edicard Kenward to be removed from the said Tenement, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That George Apps, by aiding and assisting in the said forcible Entry, is guilty of a Breach of the Privilege of this House.

Westminster Ordered, That Mr. Clayton have Leave to make a AbLfcy. Motion, it being after Three of the Clock.

And he moved, accordingly, for Leave to present to the House a Petition of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Church of St. Peter Westminster.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That Ins Majesty being informed of the Contents of the said Petition, had been pleased to command him to acquaint this House, That His Majesty recommends it to their Confederation, to make such further Provision towards the Repairs of the said Collegiate Church, as the-House shall think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the ancient Fabrick of the said Col-legiateChurch being, at the Dissolution of the Monastery, in many Parts, left unfinished; and, in those that were, advanced so far as to be esteemed completed, being, by flie Badness of Materials, Length of Time, and other Accidents, beoomedecayedandruiuous; and there being no Provision of Fabrick-rents, or other Emoluments, to enable the said Dean and Chapter to complete the unfinished Parts, or to keep in Repair what was already crofted, the Money set apart for those Uses being scarce fufljcient to maintain the many other large and publick Buildings within their Precinct, which they are obliged to keep up, and on which they have annually expended confulerable Sums; an Allowance was made to them, by Two Acts of Parliament, one of the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, and the other of the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, of an annual Sum, for a certain Number of Years, out of the Duties upon Coals, to be applied towards repairing the said Collegiate Church; by which they have been enabled to repair the most ruinous Parts, and make good about Two Thirds of the whole Fabrick; but that the Term of the said Allowance is expired, and the Money arising therefrom is all expended; and agreat Part of the said Church, with the Chapel of King Henry the Seventh, is in so ruinous a Condition, as not to be supported, without a further Supply granted by Parliament: That thg. several Sums of 4,000l. for repairing the said Collegiate Church, and 1,200l. for completing and finishing the new Dormitory, were granted in the Iaft Session of Parliament, an Account of the Disposition whereof bath been laid before this House; but that a further Supply for repairing and finishing the said Collegiate Church is still wanting: And therefore expressing their Hope, That so great and good a Work carried on, and so far advanced, by the Aid of the present and former Parliaments, will, by the like Aflifiance, be continued in the present auspicious Reign; and that this venerable Pile, wherein the Remains of the Royal Family, the Nobility, and chief Gentry, of these Realms, are deposited, will be esteemed a publick Concern, and be it length finished, according to its noble and intended Model.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, who are to consider further of the Supply granted toHis Majesty.

setting forth, That, though by the said Fire almost the whole Towh was destroyed, upon the Duplicates returned in by the Commissioners of the Land Tax acting in the North Part of Bland ford Division, the Borough and Warnership of Pimpa'ne were mentioned to be assessed to the Land Tax, in the said Year 1731, in the usual Proportion; but that, by reason of the Confusion occasioned by the said Fire, no particular Assessments were made either on the said Borough, or the said Warnership: That the said Town being divided into the said Borough, and the said Warnerlliip, which is Part of Pim-perne Hundred, the former is mentioned in the Duplicate to be assessed in the said Year 1731, the Land Tax being then Two Shillings in the Pound, £.134 os. ifL and the latter £.62 if. 3d. out of which might have been, or yet may be, collected from such Lands and Houses as were not injured by the said Fire, in the said Borough, £.46 8s. 4d.; and, in the said Warnership, £.30 of 4d; so that the Deficiency, occasioned in that Year by the said Fire, would then be, in the whole, £. 119 13*. 3d.: That, in the Year 1732, the Land Tax being but One Shilling in the Pound, the Sums returned in by the said Commissioners, in their Duplicates, were, for the said Borough, £.67 of 2d.-} and, for the said Warnership, £31 of 7 id.; but that the Rate then made, and actually collected, in the said Borough, was but £. 23 4f. 2d.; and in the Warnership but £. 15, being the Assessment on Lands and Houses not injured by the Fire; so that the Deficiency, in the Collection of the said Year, for the said Borough and Warnership, was £59 i6f. 7 %d.: That a Process hath issued out of the Court of Exchequer against the said Commissioners, who will be obliged to reaffefs the said Arrears on the Petitioners: And therefore praying, That, in Consideration of the total Dell ruftion of the Houses and Goods, in respect to which the Petitioners were returned in as assessed, as well as in regard to their great Sufferings, a CJaule may be inserted in the Land Tax Bill, now depending in this House, to exempt them from Payment of the said Arrears, and for Hopping all Proceedings, in any Court of Law, which may be commenced on Occasion thereof; or that they may have such Relief, and in such manner, as to the House shall seem meet.

Wiling A Petition of the Bailiff, Constable, Freeholders, and ifCoro. other Inhabitants of the ancient Borough of Haslemere, in the County of Surrey, was presented to the House, and read; set.ting forth. That divers Millers, and Meal-men, who have engrossed the greatest Part of the Corn Trade near the said Borough, have, within Twelve Months last pall, secretly bought great Quantities of Corn by small Samples, refuting to buy such as hath been pitched in open Market; whereby the Tolls of the said Borough, which are applied towards the Maintenance of the many poor Inhabitants thereof, have been greatly reduced, and the Trade thereof hath been almost intirely loft*, and that these illegal Practices have, of late Years, been carried on in divers Parts of England, by Millers and Mealmen combining to fix the Price and Measure of Corn, and compelling the Farmers to carry the same to their Houses, whereby the Trade of several considerable Market Towns hath been destroyed, the Laws made for punishing Regrators, Forestallers, and Engrossers, being become obsolete, or the Execution thereof being attended with great Expence and Difficulty: And therefore praying Leave to bring in a Bill for making the said Laws more effectual to prevent such Practices for the future, or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved in the Premises, as to the House iliail seem meet.

A Petition of Bandal Macdonel Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, in the Year 1728, entered upon, and hath ever since enjoyed, the Profits of certain Lands in the Kingdom of Ireland, as next Remainder Man in Tail Male, under the Limitations of Articles made the Eighth Day of Januazy 1686, on the Marriage of his Father Randal Macdonel Esquire; which Lands, subject to the said Limitations, were, by Letters Patent of the same Date granted to the Trustees, in the said Articles named, by his late Majesty King James the Second; upon whose Abdication the Petitioner's said Father, being One of his menial Servants, followed him into France, and thereby incurred an Outlawry for High Treason; in consequence whereof, by an Act, made in the 1 ith and 12th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, all his Estates were vetted in Trustees, in the said Act named, for the Purposes therein mentioned, by whose Decree, upon a Claim made the 5th Day of March 1701, by the Petitioner's Mother, on the behalf of her Children, the Remainders in Tail, limited by the said Articles, were finally and conclu-fively established: That by a private Art of Parliament, made in the First Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the Relief of Hannah Macdonel, with relation to the forfeited Estates in Ireland, it was, amongst other Things, enarted, That the said Hannahy who was the Petitioner's Mother, and her Children, should enjoy the full Benefit of the Grant made in their Favour by the Letters Patent of his late Majesty King William the Third, dated the Sixth Day of November 1696, and of the said Marriage Articles, out of the Lands in the said Grant mentioned: That, the Petitionerhaving lately entered into a Treaty for the Disposal of Part of the Premises, in order to pay off some Debts contracted by himself, and to discharge Incumbrances affecting the whole Estate, it hath been objected to his Title, that no common Recovery could bar the Reversion in Fee, expeCiant upon the Determination of the said Remainders in Tail, which was vested in the Crown by his Father’s Attainder$ and that the Petitioner hath not complied with aClause in the said Act, which disables every Person educated in the Popish Religion, and not taking the Oaths, and subscribing the Declaration, therein mentioned, within Six Months after attaining the Age of Eighteen Years, to inherit, or take by Descent, any of the Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, by any Title under the said Art; and grants the Enjoyment of the Premises, during the Life of such Persons, or until he or she shall take the said Oaths, and subscribe the said Declaration, to the next of his or her Kindred, being Protestants, without being accountable for the Profits during such Enjoyment: That the Petitioner hath proposed to abate, in the Purchase of the said Estate, any Sum at which so remote and distant a Reversion could be estimated; and hath made it appear, that hisTitle to the Lands, comprised in the said Articles, doth not depend upon the said Art, and, if it did, his Compliance with the said Clause was impossible, he having attained the Age of eighteen years above twenty years before the tim§ of coming into possession of the said Estate; and that the said Clause cannot be construed to deprive him of the Freehold, or Inheritance, of the said Estate, but of the Perception of the Profits only; and that no Person was then, or is now, in being, capable of enjoying even the Profits of the said Estate, within the Intention of that Clause; but that the Petitioner cannot proceed in the Sale of the said Estate, but upon very disadvautageous Terms; and is thereby disabled from discharging either his own Debts, or those asserting the Estate: And therefore praying the House to give Leave for the bringing in a Bill to explain the said Art made in the First Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne; and for enabling the Petitioner to fell or incumber the Premises, as he shall be advised, and fee necessary.

Roads, subscribed, appointed to put in Execution anvACt, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Roads therein mentioned, between the White Poll on Alcon-bury Hill, and Wansford Bridge, in the County of Huntingdon, called the North Division, was referred.

That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directeu him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, have examined the Matter of the said Petition:

To prove the Allegations whereof,

The Act of Parliament, mentioned in the Petition, was laid before the Committee; which Ad recitesTwo former Acts of Parliament, pasted for repairing the said Roads; takes notice of the Powers wanting to complete the same; and divides the said Roads into Three Divisions; appoints separate Trustees for each Division; and grants several Tolls to be taken separately therein:

Then,

Mr. Robert Michell was examined: Who said, That he is Clerk to the Commissioners appointed to put the said ACtin execution for the North Division of the said Roads; which Roads being very ruinous, the Trustees were under a Neceftity of borrowing, on the Credit of the Tolls, several Sums, amounting to Ore thousand Pounds; which hath all been expended in Repairs, and is now due and owing; and, unless further Provisions are. made, the said Roads cannot, by the Tolls already granted, be repaired, or the Money advanced be repaid.

Mr. John Beale, being also examined, said, That these Roads are Sixteen Miles, or thereabouts, in Length, Six Miles whereof have been repaired; but the remaining Parts are still very dangerous and bad, efprcially Three Miles thereof; and that the Materials necessary for the Repair thereof lie about Four Miles Distance; by reafort whereof the Expence of repairing One Mile of the said Roads, in the last Summer, amounted to near £. So6.

Mr.

268 5° Mart A. 1733.

Mr. Robert Michell, being again examined, said, That the Tolls collected at all the Turnpikes in the North Division produced about £. 400 per Annum; and that the Expence attending such Collection is now about Fifty Pounds per Annum; though formerly there was paid, to a Surveyor of the Roads, £.30 per Annum; and, to aTreasurer of the Monies collected. £. 14 per Annum; both which Offices are now executed by a Gentleman, who is one of the Trustees, without any Consideration, in order to reduce the Expence of Management as much as is possible.

Mr. Alderman Perry reported from the Committee, Whitechapel to whom the Petition of the Rector, Churchwardens, Workhouse, Overseers of the Poor, and principal Inhabitants of the c‘ Pari Hi of St. Mary Matfellon, alias Whitechapel, in the County of Middlesex, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table:

Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the Petitioners called,

Clifford Wm. Phillips Esquire: And he, being examined, said, That there are 2,500 Houses, and upwards, within the said Parish; the greatest Part whereof are inhabited by labouring People of small Substance, and 1,357 of that N umber are afieffed to the Poor's Rate.

Mr. Char let on, being examined, said, That he is now Overseer of the Poor; and the Number of Pensioners to be maintained by the said Parish, for this Year, amounts to 65 1 Persons, besides several Children, who are to be provided for; That the Rate afieffed amounts tof. 2,262 135*. and is made discretional, by the Vestry, on the real and personal Estates; and that, if it were a Pound Rate, the Poor would be greatly oppressed.

Mr. Phillips further said, That, if the Poor were maintained by a Pound Rate, it would fall heavy on the Innkeepers, whereof there are numbers, who pay £. 100 per Annum for their Houses; when Gentlemen, worth 30,000 or £. 40,000 live in Houses of £. 50 per Annum:

That it has been the constant method, in the Parish, to make the several Rates discretional.

Then the Petitioners laid before the Committee, an Act of Parliament, passed in the 8th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Highways from the Stones End at Whitechapel Church, in the County of Middlesex, to Sheffield, and to the furthermost Part of the Parish of Woodford, leading to the Town of Epping, in the County of Essex; by which Act the Parish is charged with the yearly Sum of £.120, to be paid to the Trustees, appointed by the said Act, towards the Repair of the said Highways; to be afieffed and collected by Agreement of the Parishioners, or the Parish Officers, or Justices of the Peace of the said Parish.

Joseph Fox, being examined, said. That, in 1724, he served the Office of Petty Constable; and collected the Turnpike Rate with Mr. John Richards, a Diflilier, then Churchwarden, who always kept the Books:

That, when they went out of the Office, the Accounts were not made up; and what became of the Books, and Surplus money, he knows not, but believes Richards funk them.

Captain John Harvey, being examined, said, That he is now Churchwarden; and collects the Turnpike Rate, which amounts, this Year, to £. 122, and is more than used to be afieffed; but, there being no Church Rate made this Year, he desired the Vestry to allow a Month’s Rate extraordinary, towards the Repair of the Church, if there should be occasion, and promised to account for the same:

That, fmee the said Act passed, Wapping has been taken out of the Parish; and they pay £.40 of the £.120:

That the Assessments have been made for £. 100 and £110; but believes there has been great Deficiencies, and the Sums afieffed never collected:

That he apprehends, by the Laws in being, the Collectors of the Turnpike Rate are not obliged to account for the fame; and does not remember, that any of the Parish Rates were mixed with this before.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House of the Fourth Day of this Instant, have examined \he Matter of the said Petition:

To make out the Allegations whereof, the following Evidence was produced:

Mr. Edward Jackson and Mr. Samuel Carte, being severally examined, said, That the City of Coventry is of large Extent, and very populous; and that the Number of such of the Inhabitants of the said City, as attended Divine Service, according to the usage of the Church of England, or were supposed to be ready and willing lb to do, in cale they had a convenient place, and Opportunity, for that Purpose, was near Sixteen thousand; and that there are only Two Parish Churches in the City, which cannot commodiously contain, at the highest Computation, above Five thousand of the said Inhabitants.

To prove that the Petitioners arc seised of the Church of Bablake, in the said City, and its Appurtenances;

An attested Copy of the Inrolment of Letters Patent, bearing Date the 13th Day of December, in the Second Year of the Reign of King Edward the Sixth, was produced to the Committee; by which it appears, That the said Church 0i. Bablake, with the Cemetery, and Appurtenances thereof, was granted by the said King to the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the City of Coventry, and their Successors.

The laid Mr. Jackson and Mr. Carte, being further examined, said, That this Church stood within the Precincts of Sponn-street Ward, in the Parish of St. Michael's, within the said City; and that the said Church of Bablake, with proper Repairs, and the adding of Galleries, may be made to contain near 2,000 Persons, and thereby rendered fit to be used as a Parish Church for the said Ward:

That formerly, in the Afternoon of the Lord's Day, during thcSeafon of Lent, Divine Service had been performed therein; but that, for about 12 Years last pal't, such Service had been dil'continued there.

The said Mr. Jackson likewise gave Evidence, That several Benefactions were given, or settled, towards Maintenance of a Minister to officiate in the said Church, whenever the same should be made parochial.

One Instance whereof was further proved by Mr. Joseph Grey, who laid before the Committee, an attested Copy of Part of the last Will of Simon Norton, formerly an Alderman of the said City, bearing Date the Second Day of July 1641; in which the said Simon Norton, among other Tilings therein contained, directs, That, out of the Rents and Profits of certain Lands and Tythes, therein mentioned, the Sum of 13/. 6$. 8d. should be paid to the Per ion officiating as Minister of the said Church of Bablake, and his Succefi’ors; and all'o, that certain other Tythes, in the said Will mentioned, should be taken by such Minister of the said Church of Bablake, if ever the same should be made parochial.

And, to shew that the Petitioners were possessed of an Estate in Trait, for the Benefit of the free Grammar School in the said City, as let forth in the Petition;

A Copy of a Deed inrolled in Chancery was produced to the Committee, and proved by the said Mr. Carte, bearing Date the 17th Day of December* in the 15th Year of the Reign of Queen Elizabeth; whereby it appears, That rth.f\ Hales, then of the City of Coventry, Esquire, did grant and convey certain Lands and El'tates, therein mentioned, to certain Persons therein named, who after-

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, proceeded to examine the Alatter of the said Petition: 1

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the Committee an Act of Parliament, passed in the First Year of the Reign of King James the First, concerning Tanners, Curriers, Shoe-Makers, and other Artificers occupying the Cutting of Leather; and also, an Act, passed in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for laying certain Duties on Hides and Skins.

By the first mentioned Act it is enacted, That no Batcher, or other Person, Hi all galli or cut any Hide of any Ox, Bull, Steer, or Cow, in Haying thereof, or otherwise, whereby the same shall be impaired or hurt, under the Penalty of 1$. 8 d. for every Hide so gaihed, Uaughtcred, or cut:

And, by the said Act of the pth of Queen Anne, the Penalty was in created to 2 s. 6 d. for each Hide lb cut or galhcd: and a Penalty was imposed of 1 s. for cutting and galliing each Culvcs-ikin, one Moiety to the Poor of the Puriili where they shall be found, or offered to Sale, the other Moiety to Inch PciToiv or Persons who shall inform, lcize, or lue, for the fame; and a Power was granted to two Justices of the Peace, to hear and detennime the lame, in a fiunmary way; but, if the Party thinks himself aggrieved, he may appeal from their Determination to the Quarter Sessions, whole Adjudication shall be final.

Then the Petitioners called,

Mr. Daniel Anderby: And he, being examined, said, That Informations have been laid against Butchers, for cutting and galhing of Hides and Calvcs-ikins; but, for want of the Hands of Tw o Justices of the Peace to the Warrant, the Offender could not be convicted: That the Penalties are so small, and difficult to be recovered, that the Informers do not think it worth their while to follow the Offender to the Quarter Sessions for the Sum of \s. 3 d.: That, by this Method of levying the said Penalties, the Practice of Cutting and Gaffiing of Hides isalmost become univerlal:

And he further said, That, at pretent, there is no Law made against cutting and galhing of Sheep and Lamb Skins, which, in England, are, for the most Part, lb ill Hayed, that they are not fit for Market, and frequently are cut up to make Glue; and inch Sheep and Lamb Skius as are dressed into Leather, are diminished Jth Part, by the bad flaying thereof: That if the same were well flayed, as they may be, each Pound would produce, Vo L. 22. -

drolTcd in Oil, 3 d.; tanned, 1 id.; and 1 { d. iti Allom; which would be of confideiable Advantage to the Revenue: That the Hides would weigh Two Pound more, one with another, than they now do, being so cut and gaffied.

Air. William Fay produced to the Committee several Pieces of Leather: And, being examined, laid, That the Back or Bend Leather is so abused, by being Cut and gaffied, and in several Places lb thin, that it is not fit for its proper Use; and in those thin Places it dries more, and weighs the lighter; whereby the Revenue is considerably diminished: That the Hides made use of for Boots and Shoes are so cut and gaffied, that it is difficult to cut a Pair of Boots out of many Hides; and the Calves-Ikins are cut and gaihed in the same manner, and many of them not fit for any Use:

And be also said, That the Lincolshire Hides, when drefifed into Leather, will fell for a Halfpenny in the Pound more than those so cut and gaffied.

Then the said Mr. Fay produced several Sheep and Lamb Skins: And said, That lotne of them were Scotch Leather, and worth 4/. per Hundred, ai\d the others, which were English, not w orth above 50s. or 3 /. although larger; and the Reason of that Difference w as, because the English Skins are cut into Holes and Flaws, which reduces the Price.

Mr. Burrell repotted from the Committee, tb whom Forfhlling the Petition of the Bailiff, Constable, Freeholders,' and Cof0# other Inhabitants, of the ancient Borough of Haslemere, in the County of Surrey, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; arid had* directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered itin at the Clerk's Table: Where, the same was read; arid is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House;. of the Second of this Instant March, proceeded to examine the Matter of the said Petition:

And the Petitioners, to prove the Allegations thereof, called,

Mr. Moorey Baxter i Who, being examined, said. That he had for 21 Years past, been a Trader in the Town of ‘Haslemere; and that the Toll of the Market held there is applied to the Use of the poor Inhabitants of that Tow n not receiving Alms 2 That, w ithin these Twb Years, between 40 and 50 Loads of Com have been pitched and fold, upon a Market-day there; but, for a Year palt, there has scarce been, one Day with another, above One Load pitched in the Market; whereby the Toll, which usually produced between £. 50 and £. 60 per Annum; and Was applied as aforesaid, is now reduced to Five Pounds per Annum; and Persons not bringing their Corn to the Market, no Carriages go back from the Town; which has not only reduced the Inhabitants thereof, but has almost entirely destroyed the Trade of the Town.

The said Baxter arid Mr. Wm. Dudman, being severally examined, said, That Corn is usually sold by Samples; whereby the Com Trade now engrossed by the Mealmen and Millers, who combine together, and fix the Price thereof, as they receive Advice from their Factors in London; and the Farmers are now obliged, contrary to former Custom, to carry their Corn to the Mills; although some of the Mills are above Six or Seven Miles farther distant from the Farmers than the Market Town is; which is a great Hardship on the Farmers:

That all Grain, except Barley, is tollable at the Market in Haslemere; and, for want of finall Quantities of Com being brought, and pitched in the Market there, the Inhabitants of the Town cannot be supplied therewith, but are obliged to buy it, at Second-hand, from the Mealmen and Millers.

And the said William Dudman further said, That formerly the Mealmen hired Carriages for the Com, from the Market; and that lie has earned between £4 70 and £, 80 I er Annum for such Carriage; which, although now favorf to the Mealmen, is at the Expence of the Farmer; for it is a clear Advantage to the Mealmen, without any Advantage to the Consumer; and the Farmers are obliged to submit to these Hard ships, by reason the whole Corn Trade is engrossed by the Mealmen, who formerly hirejl the Grinding of their Corn of the Millers; but the Mealmen are now pofi’efled of most of the Mills themselves; so that the Persons who aft as Mealmen are both Mealmen and Millers too; and that he knows that the Mealmen have combined together, under a Penalty, to buy no more Corn pitched in the Market, and that all Com should, for the future, be bought by Samples; and thereby the Mealmen, not being contented to take the Market Buthe), fix the Price of Corn on the Farmers, and the Measure too; for they oblige the Farmers to feii them so much Corn for a Buftiel as weighs 72 Pounds, which generally increases their Measure to Five Buffiel the Sack, whereas formerly a Sack held only Four Bushelsj and they resell it again to the Poor at 56 Pounds only to a Bulliel; and, by this Method, the Mealmen and Millers

7 Geo. II. 27® — 28* Martii.

293

have engrailed the whole Com Trade to themselves, and forestaN the Market*, by flopping Team* ou the Road, as they bring Corn to the Town.

And, upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutious:

Rtfotoed, That it appears to this Committee, That Meal men and Millers have combined together to fix the Price and Measure of Corn brought to the Market beM at the Borough of Hajteme in the County of Surrey, and thereby ungraded the whole Cora Trade thereof.

Refitted, That it is the Opioion of this Committee, That the Combination of Meatman and Millers, and their foreflailing of Coro*markets, tend very much to the Prejudice of the Farmers using such Markets, and to the OppreSon of the Poor, and ought to be redrafted.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie apon the Table.

Mr. ChSficellor of thO Exfchfcqher acquainted the the King. House, That he had a Message from his Majesty, to this House, signed by his Majesty: And he presented the same to the House; and, all the Members being uncovered, it was read by Mrs Speaker; and is as followeth; viz.

OGEORGE R.

His. Majesty very thankfully acknowledges the Zeal arid Affect'fe^ which this House has shewn in the early Dispatch they have already made in the necessary Supplies for the Publick Service, which his Majesty recommended to their immediate Care, at the Opening of this Selflion.

But the War which has broke out in Europe still unhappily continuing, his Majesty has nothing more at H^art than to see that Flame extinguished, and to avoid, if possible, the engaging his Subjects in the Hazards and Expence of a War; being, at the farite time, desirous neither to give any just A|arm to other Nations, nor to subject himself to any unprovoked Insults.

In this View, and to the End that his Majesty ^Endeavours, in Conjunction with his Allies, for procuring an Accommodation, may, in due time, have the desirea Effect, and that his Majesty may be in a Condition to make good such Engagements, as Honour, Justice, and Prudence, may call upon him to fulfil or contract, and that his Kingdoms may not b® left exposed to any desperate Attempts during such time as it may be im-possible for his Majesty to have the? immediate Advice and Assist^nce of hi? great Council, upon any Emergency arising from the present Posture of Affairs in Europe, which may nearly concern the Interest and Safety of these Kingdoms, his Majesty hopes that he Until be enabled and supported by his parliament, in making such further Augmentation of his Forces, either by Sea or Land, as may be absolutely necessary for the Honour and Defence of his Kingdoms, and in concerting such Measures as the Exigency of Affairs may require; whatever Expence shall be thereby occasioned Hi all be made in as frugal a manner as is possible; and an Account thereof shall be laid before the next Parliament.

A Petition of the Filazers of his Majesty’s Court of; Common Pleas at Westminster, was presented to the House* and read } setting forth, That the Filazers are Officers as ancient as the Court of Common Pleas; and that their Offices have always been granted them for Life, and enjoyed as Freeholds: That, in Right of their Offices, they make out the mesne Process of that Court, and enter the Appearances of Defendants, which isdone at a very small Charge: That if the Method proposed by the Bill now depending in this House, for the more eafyand speedy Recovery ot small Debts, takes place, the Petitioners, as they apprehend, will be so far deprived of the Ordinary Income of their Offices, that the Profits will not answer the Expence of the due Execution thereof: And therefore, in Expectation of some reasonable Satisfaction for this Loss, praying, That the House will be pleased to make them Clerks of the Bills, or Petitions, in the Bill mentioned, in the respective

Comities for which they are Filazers; or that they may be heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill, before it doth pass; or be otherwise relieved, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed: And that the Petitioners, if they think fit, he heard, by their Counsel, before the said Committee, according to the Prayer of their Petition.

kftaiiing A PETITION of the Mayor, Aldermen, and free !iCorD' Burgesses, of the Borough of Helfton, in the Coun-

ty of Cornwall, was presented to the House, and read; complaining. That, of late Years, divers Millers, Meal-men, and Bakers, who have ingrossed the greatest Part of the Corn Trade near the said Borough, have secretly bought great Quantities of Corn, by small Samples, of the neighbouring Farmers, wjio, by that means, do not bring their Corn into the Market to be sold; whereby the Tolls of the said Borough, which are applied towards the Maintenance of the many poor Inhabitants, and the Repair of the Church, thereof (there being no Rate upon the Inhabitants for either), have been greatly reduced, and the Trade thereof hath been almost entirely loft; and that these illegal Practices have, of late Years, been carried on, in divers Parts of England, by Millers, Mealmen, and Bakers, combining to fix the Price and Measure of Com; and compelling the country Farmers, the Sellers thereof, to carry the same to the Houses of the Buyers; whereby the Trade of several considerarid Towns, and especialiy of the said Borough, hath been Vot. 2*. And therefore praying the House to lake their same into Consideration; and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to prevent such Practices for the future; or that the Petitioners may be otherwise relieved in the Premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Allen and Mr. Spicer:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to prevent the infamous Practice of Stockjobbing, without any Amendment. And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bilk intituled, An Act to explain an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for the converting a further Part of the capital Stock of the South Sea Company into Annuities, redeemable by Parliament; and for settling the regaining Part of the said Stock in the said Company, so far as the said Act relates to the paying off the Bonds of the said Company, without any Amendment. And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for making more effectual an Act, passed in the Thirteenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the Fil'd, intituled, An Act for the more effectual amending the Highways leading from Rojjston, in the County of Hertford, to Wandsford Bridge, in the County of Huntingdon, so far as the same relates to the amending that Part of the Road as lies between a Place called The While Post, upon Alconbury Hill, and Wandsford Bridge, in the said County of Huntingdon, called The North Division, without any Amendment. And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting in Sir Theodore Janffen Knight and Baronet, and his Heirs, the Remainder in Fee-simple, now in the Crown, expectant on the Determination of certain Estates Tail, of and in the Manor and Advqwfon of Qxver Moigne, in the County of Dorfel, and several Lands and Hereditaments to the same Manor belonging, without any Amendment. And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting certain Lands and Tenements, lying contiguous to the Citadel of Plymouth, being the Estate of William Strode, an Infant, in Trustees, in order to sell and convey the same to or for the Use of his Majesty, without any Amendment. And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to naturalise Barlold Bull, without any Amendment. And also.

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for vesting Part of the Estate late of George Evelyn Esquire, deceased, in the County of Surrey, in Trustees, in order to sell and convey the same to Charles Boone Esquire, pursuant to an Agreement for that Purpose.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House attended his Answer Majesty Yesterday with their Address: To which his toAdduk Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer; viz.

Gentlemen,

I return you my Thanks for these Assurances of your Duty and Fidelity to my Person and Government, and for the Confidence which you repose in me: I desire only, that I may be in a Condition to support the Honour and interest of my Crown an$l People; and the Power you have given me shall be made use of t9 no other Purpose.

Edward Tumor gave Evidence, That, on the Market Day at Kainton, hearing the said Rees Griffiths was in Town, he went with the original Order, which was produced to the Committee, signed by the Chairman, and shewed it to him at the Entrance of a House where he was: That he offered him a true Copy thereof; upon which he, the said Rees Griffiths, assaulted him with his Stick, and bruised his Arm; and, with some of his Strokes, tore his Hat; and said, Damn you for a Dog, take that, and go about your Business: That he dropped the Copy of the Order within the Door; and that these Blows were given on no other Account, but for serving the said Order, he having given no other Provocation whatsoever.

" Appurtenances and Freight; and for an equal Distribution and Payment thereof amongst such Freighters " or Proprietors, in proportion to their respective Losses " or Damages, according to the Rules of Equity: Provided always, That if any such Bill shall be exhibited " by or on the behalf of the Part-owners of such Ship,

" the Plaintiff or Plaintiffs shall annex an Affidavit to " such Bill or Bills, that he or they do not collude with <£ any of the Defendants thereto; and shall thereby offer " to pay the Value of such Ship or Vessel, Appurtenances " and Freight, as such Court shall direct; and such <c Court shall thereupon take such Method for ascertaining such Value, as to them ilmll leern just; and shall " direct the Payment thereof in like manner as is now " used and practised in Cafes of Bills of Interpleader;1

After which his Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen, The King’:

I Give you my hearty Thanks for the great Dif- speech, patch you have given to the publick Business; and for the Confidence you have reposed in me, for the Honour and Security of my Kingdom: So short a Session, at so critical and important a Conjuncture, concluded with so much Unanimity, and so just a Regard for the true Interest of the Nation, will give greatWeight and Credit to all our publick Transactions, and procure that Respect and Dependence upon the Great Council of this Nation, which are so necessary to support the Honour and interest of Great Britain both at home and abroad.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I must acknowledge, in a particular manner, the Zeal and Readiness which you have fljevvn, in raising, in so effectual a manner, the necessary Supplies for the Service of the Year: The Provision you have made for paying off great Part of the Debt of the Navy, a Debt necessarily and unavoidably incurred, and carrying a higher interest than the old National Debt; and which being at a Discount, increased the Charge and Expence in all Conti acts of the Navy, and Victualling, must certainly be thought of Angular Service to the Publick.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

the Time limited for the Expiration of this Parliament drawing near, I have resolved forthwith to issue my Proclamation for the Dissolving of it, and for calling a new Parliament, that the Inconveniences unavoidably

attending

t

A. 1734-

attending a General Election may be puk an End to as soon as possible: But I should think myself inexcuf-able, if I parted with this Parliament, without doing them the Justice to acknowledge the many signal Proofs they have given, through the course of Seven Years, of their Duty, Fidelity, and Attachment, to my Person and Government, and their constant Regard to the true Interest of their Country.

The Prosperity and Glory of my Reign depend upon the Affection and Happiness of my People; and the Happiness of my People upon my preserving to them all their legal Rights and Privileges, as established under the present Settlement of the Crown in the Proteilant Line: A due Execution and ftrid Observance of the Laws are the best and only Security both to Sovereign and Subject; their Interest is mutual and inseparable, and therefore their Endeavours for the Support of each other ought to be equal and reciprocal,' any Infringement or Encroachment upon the Rights of either, is a Diminution of the Strength of both; which, kept within their due Bounds and Limits, make that jult Balance which is necessary for the Honour and Dignity of the Crown, and for the Protection and Prosperity of the People: What depends upon me shall, on my Part, be religiously kept and observed; and I make no Doubt of receiving the just Returns of Duty and Gratitude from them.

I mult, in a particular manner, recommend it to you, and, from your known Afle&ion, do expect, that you will use your best Endeavours to heal the unhappy Divisions of the Nation, and to reconcile the Minds of all who truly and finfcerely with the Safety and Welfare of the Kingdom: It would be the greatest

Satisfaction to me, to fee a perfeCl Harmony restored amongstthem that have one and the same Principle at heart; that there might be no DillinClion, but of such as mean the Support of our present happy Constitution in Church and State, and such as willi tofubvert both; this is the only DistinClion that ought to prevail in this Country; where the Interest of King and People is one and the fame, and where they cannot fubfiit but by being so: If Religion, Liberty, and Property, were never at any time more fully enjoyed, without not only an Attempt, but even the Shadow of a Design, to alter or invade them, let not these sacred Names be made use of as artful and plausible Pretences to undermine the present Establishment, under which alone they can be safe.

I have nothing to wish, but that my People may not bemilguided; I appeal to their own Consciences for my Conduct; and hope the Providence of God will direct them in the Choice of such Representatives, as are most tit to be trusted with the Care and Preservation of the Protestant Religion, the present Establishment, and all the Religious and Civil Rights of Great Britain.

May it pleaseyour most Excellent Majesty,

The Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, have, in pursuance of your Majesty's Direction, and according to their ancient Right, proceeded to the Election of One of their Members, to be presented to your Majesty, for their Speaker.

And their Choice, Sir, has again fallen upon me for this important Trust.

An Office, Sir, which, almost in all times, has been deemed too important and difficult for any Person to undertake, without expressing his Fears and Dread of not performing his Duty in it, and of the State thereby receiving Detriment through his Inabilities.

A Caution, Sir, none can use better than they who have experienced the Difficulty; nor your Majesty’s Power, of remitting your Commons to another Choice, be better exercised, than where joa. Sir, have experienced a former Insufficiency.

My knowledge suggests the one, my fears the other.

Both make it a Matter of Duty in me to be an humble Suitor to your Majesty,

withdtit Loss of Time, bur joint arid earnest Instances to bring Matters to a, speedy and happy Accommodation, before we should coriie to a Determination upon the Succours demanded by the Emperor: These Instances did not at first produce such explicit Answers, from the contending Parties, as to enable us to put immediately in Execution our impartial and sincere Desires for that Purpose: Resolved, however, to pursue so great and salutary a Work, and to prevent our Subjects from being unne-cefikrily involved in War, we renewed the Offer of our good Offices in so effectual a manner, as to obtain an Acceptation of them.

In consequence of this Acceptation, and of our Declaration made thereupon to the respective Powers engaged in the War, no time has been loft in taking such Measures, as should be most proper, to make the belt use of their good Dispositions for re-establishing the Tranquillity of Europe; and I have the Satisfaction to acquaint you, that Things are now brought to so great a Forwardness, that I hope, in a short time, a Plan will be offered to the Consideration of all the Parties engaged in the present War, as a Basis for a general Negotiation of Peace, in which the Honour and Interest of all Parties have been confuted, as far as the Circumstances of Time, and the present Posture of Affairs, vrould permit

I do not take upon me to answer for the Success of a Negotiation where so many different Interests are to be considered and reconciled; but when a Proceeding is founded upon Reason, and formed from such Lights as can be had, it had been inexcusable not to have attempted a Work which may produce infinite Benefits and Advantages, and can be of no prejudice, if we do not suffer ourselves to be so far amused by Hopes that may possibly be afterwards dilappointed, as to leave ourselves exposed to real Dangers.

I have made use of the Power, which the late Parliament intrusted me with, with great Moderation; and I have concluded a Treaty with the Crown of Denmark, of great Importance in the present Conjuncture: it is impossible, when all the Courts of Europe are busy, and in Motion, to secure to themselves such Supports as Time and Occasion may require, for me to fit (till, and neglect opportunities, which, if once loft, may not only be irretrievable, but turned as greatly to our Prejudice, as they will prove to our Advantage, by being seasonably secured; and which, if neglected, would have been thought a just Cable of Complaint: This necessary Confidence, placed in me, has given great Weight to my Endeavours for the publick Good.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

1 have ordered the Accounts and Estimates to be prepared, and laid before you, of such extraordinary Expences as wefe incurred last Year, and of such Serviced as I think highly necessary to be carried on, and provided for; and whatever additional Charges shall be found necessary, shall be reduced, as soon as it can be done consistently with the common Security.

And, as the Treaty with the Crown of Denmark is attended with an Expence, I have ordered the same to be laid before yon.

I make no Doubt but I shall find, in this House of Commons, the same Zeal, Duty, and Affection, as I have experienced through the whole Course of my Reign; and that you will raise the necessary Supplies with Ciiear-fulness, Unanimity, and Dispatch.

The sense of the Nation is best to be learned by the Choice of their Representatives; and I am persuaded, that the Behaviour and Conduct of my faithful Commons will demonstrate to all the World the unlhaken fidelity and Attachment of my good Subjects to my Person and Government.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is our Happiness to have continued hitherto in a State of Peace; but, whilst many of the principal Powers of Europe are engaged in a War, the Consequences must more or less affect us; and, as the best concerted Mea-lyres are liable to Uncertainty, -we ought to be in a Rea-

A. 1734.

diness, and prepared against all Events; and if our Ex-peuces are, in feme degree, increased, to prevent greater, and such as, if once, entered into, it would be difficult to see the End of, I hope my good Subjects will not repine at the necessary means^of procuring the Blessings of Peace, and of universal Tranquillity, or of putting ourselves in a Condition to act that Part, which it may be necessary and incumbent upon us to take.

Most gracious Sovereign,

We, your Majesty’s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament aliem-bied, beg Leave to return our hurablelt Thauks for Vox.. 22.

3.

your Majesty’s most gracious Speech from the Throne; and to acknowledge, in the most grateful manner, your Majesty’s tender and affectionate Concern for the Welfare of your People, in steadily pursuing such Measures as have teuded towards Peace and Accommodation, rattier than to involve too precipitately this Kingdom, and all Europe, iu a general and bloody War.

Among so many differing Interests, and contending Powers engaged in the present War, it is your Majesty’s :.

Wisdom and Goodness alone which could have secured to us our present happy Situation; and the Crown of Great Britain could never appear with greater Honour and Lustre, than by your Majesty’s interposing your good Offices between the contending Parties; and, as they have received them with due Respect, we cannot: but hope their own Prudence will help to complete so desirable a Work.

It is our Duty, and we beg Leave, to express the greatest Gratitude to your Majesty for the Care and Concern which must have attended your unwearied Endeavours both in beginning and carrying on those good Offices, which, being accepted, have broughtThings to so great a Forwanlncfs, that n Plan, in Concert with the Slates General, may, in a lliort time, be offered to the Consideration of all the Powers engaged in the War; which, notwithstatidi/ig the great Difficulties that must attend so great a Work, may serve for the Basis of a general Negotiation of Peace, consistent with the Honour and Interest of all Parties, as far as the Circumstances of Time, and the present Situation of Affairs, will permit.

If these Measures, concerted for the common Repose and Tranquillity of all Europe, should unhappily meet with any Difuppointment, your Majesty’s Wisdom and Care must be acknowledged to have deserved that Suc-eels which the wisest Counlels cannot always command; but, whatever the Event may be, we beg Leave to af-sure your Majesty, That this House will chearfully and effectually raii'e such Supplies as shall be necessary for the Honour and Security of your Majesty, and these kingdoms; and enable your Majesty to act that Part which Honour and Justice, and the true Interest of your People, ilia.ll call upon your Majesty to undertake.

The said Address. being read a Second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

A Petition of several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and many Hundred Freemen of the City of Covtnhy, was presented to the Ilonfe, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners, being Freemen of the said City, and having an undoubted Right to vote for Members to represent them in Parliament, hoped they should have had Liberty to give their Votes freely, and without Molestation, for such Candidates as they thought best qualified for fc» great a Trust: That, by groat Riots and Tumults at the said Election, and oilier indirect Practices, contrary to the Laws of this Kingdom, some of the Petitioners, and many Hundred other Freemen of the said City, in the Interest of John Neale Esquire, were not suffered, nor was it possible for them, to come up to give their V otes, notwithstanding the y used their utmost Endeavours so to do, through the Violence of the Mob, made up of more People that had no Votes than of those that had, w hose Business there was chiefly to keep off and thrust away, such Freemen as were not in the Sitting Members Interest, and were relieved from time to time the whole Day; so that Mr. Neale could only get about Two hundred and Forty of his Friends polled, while iliey polled upward of Five hundred; and the Constables, placed within and without the Bar, instead of obeying the Magistrates, and suppressing the Mob, drove back Mr. NeaPs Men as they endeavoured to come up to poll; so that great Numbers, who came from London, and other remote Parts, were obliged to return home unpolled, being by these means, deprived of their just Rights; and a Return was made without Consent of the Candidates, and without calling up the Books; when, at the same time. Hundreds of unpolled Freemen demanded a Poil: That by these, and many other illegal Practices, particularly most barefaced Bribery and Corruption, the Petitioners humbly conceive they are deprived of their lawful Representative: And praying such Relief as to the Iloui'e shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matters thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of Alexander Macdcwall, of Garthlandy Esquire, waspresented to the House. and read; setting forth. That, at the late Election of a Representative to Parliament for the Shire of Wigtoun, upon the 23d Day of May 1734, the honourable Colonel IVm. Dairy tuple, and the Petitioner, flood Candidates: That the said Colonel Wm. Dalt ymple (l>eing sensible how necessary it was, for the Purpose of his Election, to have the Prafes and Clerk chosen of such as he could depend upon to be entirely under his Direction and Influence; and being likewisr* certain, that he should not be able to carry either of these, if the Votes of such were fairly demanded, as had an unquestionable Right to vote in the Choice of Prafes and Clerk) did, as Commissioner to the last Parliament, and, as such, authorized by Law to preside in any Meeting of Freeholders, in order to their Election of a Representative to Parliament, before choosing of Prafes and Clerk, in Concert with some others oT his Associates, take upon him to call the Votes for choosing of Prafts and Clerk by the Roll of the last Election in the Year 1727; excluding all other undoubted Freeholders of the County, for no Reason but because they were not present at the last Election; though, as there was then no Struggle in the Country, that Meeting did consist mostly of Colonel Daltymple's own Friends, who came there at his Desire; while other undoubted Freeholders, who had voted at former Elections, and flood upon the Roll, were not present: That the Act of Parliament in Scotland, 1681, expressly directs the Freeholder^ in the respective Counties to convene at Michaelmas yearly, to make up the Rolls of Freeholders: That, agreeable to the Terms of this Act, it was, by a late Resolution of the House of Commons, declared, That the Right of Election of a Prafes and Clerk is in such Persons as fraud upon the Roll last made up by the Freeholders at the Michaelmas Head Court, or at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament: That, iu consequence of the said ACT and Ilefo-lution, the Rolls were regularly made up, by the Freeholders of the said County, at Michaelmas before the said Election: That these Rolls were the last made up, and every Person there inrolled was entitled to a Voice in the Choice of Prafes and Clerk at the said Election; notwithstanding of which, the said Colonel William Dalrymple refused to call these Rolls, though often required, or to take the Vote of any Freeholder, but such as voted Vol. 22.

at his last Election in the Year 1727: That a Protest being taken in Form agaitift this arbitrary and tmjufti-fiable Proceeding; and the said Colonel William Dtil-rymple being determined not to exercise, according to Law, the Power given him, as last Representative, to preside over the Freeholders in the Choice of Prafes and Clerk; the Majority of the Freeholders nrefent, legally qualified to vote, empowered Patrick Slackie, Provost of the Burgh of Wigtoun, to supply his Place, and to take the Votes of all who had Voices for choosing Prafes and Clerk: That thereupon John Sleuart of Castle Stenart was duly clected Prafes; and John Dun, Writer iu Wigtoun, was duly eiefted Clerk: That, by this, the only regularly constituted Meeting of Freeholders at the said Election, the Petitioner was chose the Repre-fentative of the said County in this present Parliament; and was accordingly returned, by the said John Dun, to Captain Andrew Agnezv, of Lochnaw, the High Sheriff; who refused to accept of a Return of the Petitioner from the said John Dun, but took a Return of the said Colonel William Dalrymple from Patrick Ag~ neic, which he has annexed to the Writ, and returned into the Court out of which the Writ issued; though the Fleftion of the said Patrick Agnezo to be Clerk, and the Constitution of that Meeting of Freeholders, by which the said Colonel William Dalrymple pretended to be chose, were founded in Violation of a positive Act of Parliament, and in Defiance of a Resolution of the House of Commons: And praying the House to take the Premises into their immediate Consideration; and give the Petitioner such Relief as the Circumstances of the same requires.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Liverpoole A Petition of Thomas Bootle Esquire was presented to

Election. House, and read; fell in" forth, That the Petitioner, together with Foster Cunliffe, Richard Gild art, and Thomas Brereton, Esquires, itood Candidates at the last Election of Burge lies to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Liverpoole, in the County Palatine of Lancaster; and, by a Majority of legal Votes, the Petitioner was duly elected, and ought to have been returned a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough: That the said Richard Gildart, by himselfand his Agents, has been guilty of several corrupt and illegal Practices, and unwarrantable Proceedings, and, by means thereof, has procured himself to be returned a Burgess for the said Borough: That William Pole, who took upon himself to act as Mayor of the said Borough, without any Bight, or legal Authority; and John Brooks and Owen Prichard, who took upon themselves to act as Bailiffs of the said Borough, without any Right, and who all presided at the said Election, have acted in a very partial, illegal, and arbitrary manner, at the said Election, in favour of the said Rickard Gildart, by admitting Persons to vote for him, who had no Right to-vote; and have taken upon them, without any Foundation of Bight, to return the said Richard Gildart a Burgess for the said Borough, although he was not duly elected; to the Injury and Prejudice of the Petitioner: And praying the House to take the Premises into Confederation; and grant the Petitioner such Relief as shall seem meet.

Pitto. A Petition of John Cobham, George Dickens, Thomas Summers, and others, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, Burgesses of the Borough of Liverpool, in the County Palatine of Lancaster, on behalf of themselves, and divers other Burgesses of the said Borough; alleging. That the said Thomas Bootle and Foster Cunliffc Esquires were duly elected, and ought to have been returned, Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Borough; and that the said Richard Gildart and Thomas Brereton . Esquires, at the times of the said Election and Return, were not, nor either of them, qualified to be elected Burgesses for the said Borough; was presented to the House, and read.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

Property A Petition of William Hogarth, George Vertue, George

Right of Lambert, Isaac Wai'e, John Pine, Gerrard Vandergucht,

Prints, &c. j0fin G&itpy, Artists and Designers of Paintings, Drawings, and Engravers of original Prints, in behalf of themselves, and others, was presented to the House, and read; alleging, That the Petitioners, and others, have, with great Industry and Expence, Severally invented, designed, or engraved, divers Sets of new Pictures and Prints, in Hopes to have reaped the Benefit of such their own Labours, and the Credit thereof; but that divers Printfellers, Printers, and other Persons, both here and abroad, have, of late, too frequently taken the Liberty of copying, printing, and publishing, great Quantities of base, imperfect, and mean, Copies-and Imitations thereof; to the great Detriment of the Petitioners, and such other Artists, and to the Discouragement of Arts and Sciences in this Kingdom: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given for a Bill to be brought into the House, for preventing such Frauds and Abuses for the future, and securing the Properties of the Petitioners, as the Laws now in being have preserved the Properties of the Authors of Books; or in such other Manner as by the House shall be thought fit.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House:

The House being informed, That Sir Alexander Mur* ray Baronet, who was returned in the Double Return for the Shire of Peebles, desires not toconteft the Matter of the Election and Return for the said Shire with Sir Janies Nafmyth Baronet, returned also in the said Double Return.

Ordered, That the said Sir James Nafmyth be at Liberty to withdraw his Petition, complaining of an undue'Election and Double Return for the said Shire.

Ordered, That the Committee of Privileges and Elections he discharged from proceeding upon the Matter of the said Petition and Double Return.

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown do attend this House upon Monday Morning next, with the Return for the Shire of Peebles, to amend the fame, by taking off the Indenture, by which the said Sir Alexander Murray is returned.

The House, according to Order, resolved itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Mr. Speaker left the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner took the Chair of the Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Sir Charles Turner reported from the Committee, That they had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed him to report, when the House will please to receive the same.

Ordered, That the Report be received upon Monday Morning next.

Sir Charles Turner also acquainted the House, That he was directed by the Committee to move, That they may have Leave to fit again.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolve itself into aCommittee of the whole House, to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Ordered, That all Committees be adjourned.

And then the House adjourned till Monday Morning, Nine of the Clock.

which Lands, subject to the said Limitations, were, by Letters Patent of the same Date, granted to the Trustees in the said Articles named, by his late Majesty King James the Second; upon whose Abdication the Petitioner's laid Father, being one of his menial Servants, followed him into France, and thereby incurred an Outlawry for High Treason; having before, in the Month of October 1688, purchased, in Fee-simple, other l*ands, not subject to any of the said Limitations; but that, afterwards, his Majesty King William, thinking the same extremely compassionate, was graciously pleased, by his Letters Patent dated the Sixth Day of November 1696, to grant the said Fee-simple Lands, as well as the said other Lands, during the Life of the said Randal, in Trull, among other Things, to secure to the Petitioner’s Mother her separate Annuity, and several other Advantages: That this Grant, with other Grants of the same Nature, was resumed by an Act, made in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of the Reign of his said Majesty, whereby the said several Estates and Interests were veiled in Trustees in the said Act named, for the Purposes therein mentioned; by whose Decree, upon a Claim made the Fifth Day of March 1701, by the Petitioner’s Mother, on the behalf of her Children, the Remainders in Tail, limited by the said Articles, were finally and conclusively established: That, by a private Act of Parliament, made in the First Year of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for the Relief of Hannah Macdonel with relation to the forfeited Estates in Ireland, it was, amongst other Things, enacted, That the said Hannah, who was the Petitioner’s Mother, and her Children, should enjoy the full Benefit of the said Grant, and of the said Marriage Articles: That the Petitioner having lately entered into a Treaty for the Disposal of Part of the Premises, in order to pay off some Debts contracted by himself, and to discharge Incumbrances affecting the whole Estate, it hath been objected to Ins Title, that no common Recovery could bar the Reversion iu Fee expectant upon the Determination of the said Remainders in Tail which w as vested in the Crown by his Father’s Attainder; The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the Tenth Instant, have examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And to prove the Allegations.of the fame, Witnesses were called; viz.

Thomas Smith Esquire: Who said, That the Roads mentioned in the Petition are Part of the Great Road leading from London to Bath, Bristol, and other considerable trading Towns in the Western Parts of this Kingdom; and lead from the End of the Turnpikes ereCled, by former Acts of Parliament, at the Devizes, and Sandy-lane; which Roads, so directed to be repaired, meet at Sheppards Shord, over the Down to Back-hampton\ as also the Road from the End of Cain Turnpike Road, over the Top of Cherh ill hill, where the upper and the lower Roads meet and cross; and that the Roads from Beekhampton, through Kennel, to tire 'Pop of Overton-hill, in the Parish of Avebury, and so on to St. Peter*s Church in Marlborough, as also from the Cross-way to the farther End of Avebury, leading to Marlborough; are so very bad, that the same are become dangerous for Travellers to pass and repass: And he said further, That the Inhabitants of Avebury, through which the Roads desired to be repaired lead, have constantly done their Statute-work, and raised Six Pence and Seven Pence Halfpenny in the Pound, and laid out the same in amending the Roads; notwithstanding which, the Parish hath been indicted on account of the Badness of the Highways there: And he also said. That, if the Parish i oners of the several Parishes were to do and raise twice as much as they are obliged to do and raise by Law, the Road could not be effectually amended:

That the upper and lower Roads, particularly the Lane in the upper Iload leading from the Cross-way at Backhampton, to the further End of Avebury, towards

Green-fireel, were so very bad, that the Farmers were several times obliged to cut Bullies, and lay them in the Roads, and cover them with Flints and Pebbles, in or* der to make the same passable: Tjiat the Bristol and Bath Waggoners have this Year oftentimes hired Horses at Cher lull-hill, and put Four or Five additional Horses to their Waggons, to draw them over the Down; which additional Horses, on the Return of the Waggons, have met them at Backhampton, to draw the Waggons to Cher lull-hill; and the Inhabitants of Avebury Parish, knowing their Roads not to be passable without such additional Strength, did not dare to take off any of the additional Horses, ns they might legally do; but have often taken their Horses out of the Ploughs, to help to draw ,the Waggons out of the Sloughs, and demanded no Consideration for the fame, fearing the y should be indicted by reason of the Badness of the Roads: That they paid, in One Year, £. 100 Fine, befuies Fees; and havefeldom escaped a Year without an Indictment:

That, upon the Justices of Peace last Summons to the Surveyors of the Parish of Avebuiy, to give in their Accounts, they were satisfied, that the inhabitants iiad done every thing that was ia their Power to do towards repairing the Roads: That Indictments have been threatened against the Inhabitants of the Parishes leading through the upper and the lower Roads, on account of the Badness thereof; and, unless some further Provision be made for amending those Iloads, they mufi unavoidably be exposed to frequent Indictments; and it will be impoHibie for Travellers to pass and repass that Way with Safety, sufficient Provision being not made, by the Laws in Force, to keep the same in Repair.
