The Truncation of the said Treaty is aa follows; w.

BE it known unto all to whom it appertains, That his Majesty the King of Great Britain on one Side, and his Majesty the King of Denmark and Norway on the other, having considered that, in the present Situation of the Affairs of Europe, their reciprocal Interests require, that the ancient Friendship and Confidence which has been at all turns cultivated between their Majesties and their glorious Ancestors, to the great Advantage of the Two Nations, should be renewed, and strengthened by the most strict Ties, and by a new Treaty of a Defensive Alliance; their Majesties have thought fit, reciprocally, to order their Ministers, that is to say, His Majesty the King of Great Britain, his Privy Councilors, Thomas Holies Duke of Newcastle, One of his principal Secretaries of State, iniliam Baron of Harrington, the other of his principal Secretaries of State, and Sir Robert Walpolr, Knight of the most noble Order of the Garter, First Commissioner of his Treasury, and Chancellor and Under Treasurer of his Exchequer; and his Majesty the King of Denmark, and of Norway, the Sieur Christian August de Johttn, his Councilor of Justice, and his Resident with his fald Majesty the King of Great Britain; being provided with the necessary full Powers, to confer thereupon; who, after having exchanged their full Powers, agreed upon the Points and Articles following:

Article I.

There shall be a finccrc Amity, and a most drift U’luii, between their Majesties, their Successors and Heirs, Kingdoms and Subjects; lb that the one shall look upon the Inter* fts of the oilier, as if they were his own; and shall faithfully employ himself to promote them as mud) as poflihle; and to prevent and keep oft' from each other, mutually, all Trouble and Dumuge.

Article II.

To that End, it is agreed, That all the preceding Treaties of Peace, Amity, Guaranty, Navigation, and Commerce, without excepting any, shall be taken to be renewed and confirmed by this present Treaty, in all their Points, Articles, and Clauses; and they shall have the tune Force as if they bad been hero inserted Word for Word, as far as there shall have been no Alteration made therein by the present Treaty.

Article III.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain having desired that his Majesty the King of Denmark would hold in ReuJincfs u Body of his Troops, for the Service of his Britannick Majesty, in case the Good of his Kingdoms and Dominions Oiould require such a Succour, his Majesty the King of Denmark has been willing to content thereto; promising and engaging, by virtue of this Article, to hold in Kcadinels, for that Purpose, during the Space of Three Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of this present Treaty, a Body of Six thousand Men; that is to Iky, One thousand Horse, and Five thousand Foot, provided with General Officers, and the necessary Subalterns, fitly mounted and armed, and in a Condition to march, for the Service of his Majesty the King of Great Britain, Two Months after Reqmfttion thud have been made, or sooner, if it be possible, unless there be Need of them for the immediate Defence of the Kingdoms and Dominions of his Britannic Majesty; in which Cate they shall march immediately after the Requisition has been made; and the said Troops shall take the Oath of Fidelity to his Britamuc Majesty, when they shall have passed the Frontiers of the Territories belonging to the Crow n of Denmark, without prejudicing that which they have taken to his Majesty the King of Denmark; his said Danish Majesty, however, preserving to himself the conferring all the Places that shall become vacant in that Corps; and the Administration of Justice being regulated in the same manner as it was practised in that which went into the Service of England and Holland^ by virtue of the Treaty of 1701.

Vox.. 22.

Article IV.

As his Danish Majesty is engaged to fend considerable Treaty w*lh Succours to other Powers* his Friends and Allies; and as* DL‘uls, ar,u in order to fumish his Majesty the King of Great Britain with the abovesaid Body of Troop^, without leaving hirn-self naked of such Forces as are requisite for the Security and Preservation of his own Kingdoms and Dominions, he must be at great Charges in augmenting his IjukI Forces; his Majesty the King of Great Britain, towards defraying such Charges, promises to pay his Majesty the King of Dettmark, for every Horseman, fitly armed and mounted, Fourfcorc Crowns; and for every Foot Soldier,

Thirty Crowns; One Half immediately after the Signing this Treaty, and the other Half when the Troops shall be delivered} besides, his Majesty the King of Great Britain engages to pay to his Majesty the King of Denmark, without any Abatement, or Delay, an annual Subsidy of Two hundred and fifty thousand Crowns Banco, during the time that the Troops shall be at the Charge of the Treasury of his Majesty the King of Denmark; which Subsidy shall commence from the Signing of this present Treaty, and shall coutinue to the Expiration of the Three Years above mentioned; but when thefeTroops shall aftu&lly be taken into the Pay of his Ma icily the King of Great Britain, his Majesty the King of Denmark shall then be contented with an annual Subsidy of One hundred and fifty thousand Crowns Banco; which Subsidy shall continue during the whole time that the said Troops shall be in the Service of his Britamuc Majesty; the Payment of tive one, and of the other, shall be made regularly every Quarter, in the Town of Hamburgh, to such Persons as shall be authorized by his Majesty the King of Denmark to receive it: That if his Majesty the King of Great Britain lets the aljovcsaid Three Years pats, without demanding the Body of Six thousand Men, his Majesty the King of Denmark shall not be any longer obliged, after that, to fumith the lame; and the Subsidies shall entirely cease, at the feme time, at the End of those Three Years, unless the Two contracting King®

shall agree otherwise.

Article V.

His Majesty the King of Great Britain shall take upon himself the Pay and Entertainment, as well ordinary as extraordinary, of the Officers, Horsemen, and Foot Soldiers, of that Body, from the Day they shall begin their March for his Service; and this Pay, both ordinary and extraordinary, shall be regulated upon the tame Foot with that of the Danish Troops made over by the Treaty of 1701; and it shall be put into the Hands of the Danish Commissaries, without any Abatement or Diminution, to make the Distribution thereof: That if it should, by Miffortune, happen that forae of the Regiments, or Companies, of the abovesaid Corps should be ruined or de-llroyed, in the Whole, or in Part, his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall cause to be paid, without Delay, to the Officers to the said Body of Troops, the Charges of the necessary Recruits for putting the Regiments, or Companies, speedily again in a good Condition; and these Recruits shall be, in like manner, regulated upon the Foot of those that were furnished to the Officers of the Danish Troops, by virtue of the Treaty of 1701; to the end that this Corps may always be preserved, and lent back One Day, in as good Condition as it was received.

Article VI.

It is to depend upon his Britannic Majesty as to the keeping of this Corps in his Service all the time of the Duration of this Treaty, to make use of it wherever he shall have Occasion, provided it be not neither in Italy, nor upon the Fleet, nor to be transported, in the Whole or in Part, beyond Sea, after it is come out of the Territories of his Majesty the King oiJDenmark, except for the Defence of the Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland; in which Cafe, these Troops shall wholly enjoy the same Pay which the English Troops enjoy; and when his Majesty the King of Great Britain shall be desirous of fending back the said Troops, he shall acquaint his Majesty the King of Denmark with it Three Months beforehand;

th hand; and shall cause to be paid to them a Month’s Wages for their Return.

Article VII.

In case his Majesty the King of Denmark should be attacked or troubled in the Possession of his Kingdoms, Dominions, Lands, Provinces, or Cities, his Britamiick Majesty promises to fend the said Body of Troops speedily back to him, paying them a Month’s Wages for their Return; and furthermore, to give his Danish Majesty all the Assistance, by Sea and by Land, that the same shall require; which Assistance shall be continued to him till he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace; as his Majesty the King of Denmark, on his Part, also promises, that in case his Majesty the King of Great Britain should be attacked or troubled, as is abovesaid, he will give him immediately all the Assistance, by Sea and by Land, that the same shall require; which Assistance shall, in like manner, be continued to him, until he shall have obtained a good and advantageous Peace: Furthermore, his Majesty the King of Denmark expressly reserves to himself the Liberty of Commerce for his Subjects trading as well to France as every where else, during all the time that this present War shall last; and his Majest y the King of Great Britain promises, that, on his Part, they shall not, in anywise, be troubled therein.

Article VIII.

In order to make this Alliance and Union the more perfect, and to leave the Parties no kind of Scruple, as to the Certainty of the Assistance which they are to expefit from each other, it is expressly agreed, That, for judging, hereafter, whether the same of this Alliance exists or not, it shall be sufficient that either of the Parties be actually attacked by Force of Arms, without that Party’s having before used open Force against him who attacks.

Article IX.

This Treaty shall last for the Space of Three Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of it, and, if their Majesties shall think fit to continue, prolong, or change it, that Matter shall be treated of Three Months before it expires, according to the Exigency of the Cafe.

Article X.

The Ratification of this Treaty shall be exchanged London, within Two Months after the Signing, or sooner, if it be possible.

In Witness whereof, we the under-written, being furnished with the full Powers of the most Serene Kings of Great Britain and of Denmark and Norxvay, have, in their said Names, signed the present Treaty, and have caused our Seals to be set thereunto. Done at Westminster, the Day of September, 1734*

(L. S.) Holies Newcastle.

(L. S.) Harrington.

(L. S.) R. Walpole.

Whitby Mr. Cholmley Turner reported from the Committee, Harbour. to whom the Petition of the Burgesses, Matters, and Owners of Ships, and Inhabitants of the Town of Whitby, in the County of York, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition 5 and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, in pursuance of the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the CommitteeThree Acts of Parliament; One passed in the First Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for the Rebuilding and Repairing of the Piers of the said Town and Port of Whitby; by which Act several Duties were imposed, for that Purpose, upon all Ships and Vessels which should come into the said Harbour, and all Goods and Merchandize which should be landed there; and the said Duties were to continue for the Term of Nine Years, commencing from the First of May 1702:

Another Act, which passed in the Seventh Year of her said late Majesty’s Reign; whereby the said First Act, and all the Duties thereby granted, were further continued until the ift of May 1723:

Another Act, which passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for better preserving, and keeping in Repair, the Piers of the said Town and Port:

By which last mentioned Act several other Duties, after the Expiration of the Payment of those Duties granted and continued by the said Acts of the ift and 7th Years of her late Majesty’s Reign, were laid upon all Ships and Vessels entering the said Harbour, and upon several Sorts of Goods and Merchandizes mentioned in the said Act of the 7th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, which should be landed or delivered at the said Port of Whiltiy; which Duties are, by the said Act, made perpetual.

Then the Committee examined the following Witnesses; viz.

Jonathan Lacey and Geo. Prijfeck: Who severally said, That they very well remember the building the Piers of the Harbour; and that the same are substantially built, and are at present in very good Repair; and that, since the building thereof, the Shipping of the Town has very much increased; and that there are at present above 1 ao Sail, and most of them the largest Ships, that are employed in the Coal Trade.

Colonel Peregrine Lafcclls, being also examined, confirmed the Evidence of these Witnesses, and added further, That the Number of Ships was increased, they being near One half more than formerly.

The laid W'itnefl'es, being examined as to the Obstruction of the Entrance into the said Harbour, mentioned in the Petition, said. That, of late Years, the Entrance into the said Harbour has been rendered very *7

difficult and dangerous, by reason of a large Bank of Sand gathered behind the West Pier; and that, if the Wind blows hard, the Tide drives great Quantities of Sand into the said Harbour, which would be prevented by lengthening the said West Pier; and that, the Harbour being choaked up with such Sand, Ships are fre* questly forced against the Head of the East Pier, and there bulged, or are driven upon the Bank.

Colonel Lafcells said further. That lie has known the said Bank to have remained so high for Three Months together, that 150 Men have been frequently employed to dig a Channel through it; and that several Ships, not being able to enter into the said Harbour, have been obliged to fail into Burlington Bay.

Then a Plan or Map of the said Harbour and Piers, and of the Addition proposed to be made to the Western Pier, being laid before the Committee, and the said Colonel Lafcells and Jonathan Lacy being further examined thereto, they said, That if the said Pier was to be lengthened to low-water-mark, which is about 100 Yards further towards the Sea, it would efl'e&ually prevent the Sand coming in to choak up the Entrance of the said Harbour, and render the Passage of Ships into, and out of the fame, much more easy and safe, and also be a further Encouragement to the Navigation of the said Town and Port; and the Petitioners delivered to the Committee an Estimate of the Charge of the additional Work proposed to be made to the said West Pier, being One hundred Yards in Length, 18 Yards broad, and 16 Yards high, and to be built of Stone; which Estimate amounts to the Sum of £.10,800.

The Committee then proceeded to inquire what the Duties granted for Repair of the said Pier and Harbour amounted to.

It appeared to the Committee, by an Account laid before them of the Produce of those Duties, and signed by the Trustees appointed to collect and apply the fame, That the Surplus of those Duties, over and above what has been expended in keeping the said Piers in Repair, and making some necessary Additions, amounts, for the last Ten Years, to no more than the Sum of £. 58. 15.9. 3$d. so that the Petitioners have no Reve nties to enable them to raise the said Sum of£. 10,800.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for lengthening the West Pier of the Harbour of Whitby, in the County of York, and for improving the said Harbour: And that Mr. Cholmley Turner, and Sir Francis Boynton, do prepare, and bring in the fame.

as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 13th Instant, have exam in ed the Matter of the said Petition:

To prove the Allegations whereof, the Petitioners laid before the Committee the Act of Parliament mentioned in their said Petition; whereby it appeared, That several Tolls and Powers were granted and given, for the Term of 21 Years, for repairing the said Road; and also a Power was given to the Trustees to borrow Money on the Credit of the said Tolls.

Then Witnesses were called, and examined; viz.

Mr. William Thomas: Who said, That, when the Act of Parliament passed, the said Road was in so ruinous a Condition, That the then acting Trustees were under a Necessity of borrowing a considerable Sum of Money on the Credit of the Tolls, to make all Parts thereof passable for Coaches and Wheel-carriages; which Money, so borrowed, and also what was from time to time raised by the Tolls, had been duly applied, according to the Directions of the said Act; but that, nevertheless, several Parts of the said Road, by reason of many heavy laden Waggons, and other Carriages, frequently passing through the fame, arefcarce passable in the Winter-season.

Then the said Mr. Thomas laid before the Committee a Hated Account of the Money received and paid, on account of the said Act, from Midsummer 1721 to Christmas 1734; whereby it appeared,

That there had been laid out in repairing this Road, from Midsummer 1721 to £. s. d.

And the said Mr. Thomas also said, That the Tolls granted by the said Act are very final!, and that they are much less than any other Tolls laid by any Act of Parliament for repairing Roads about this Town; and that, the Toll being so small, the Trustees are obliged to apply One-half towards paying the Interest of the Money borrowed; and that therefore there is not a sufficient Fund to repair the Road effectually, and to repay the Money borrowed; so that the Road cannot be amended, and kept in repair, unless the Toll, Term, and Powers, granted by the former Act, be inlarged.

John Milner Esquire, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Thomas; and further said, That Oxford Road, leading from St. Giles's Pound, to a Place called The Lord Mayor'sBanquetting-houJ'e Bridge, hath been partly paved with Pebble-Hones by the Trustees, partly by the Inhabitants, and that other Parts thereof are unpaved; whereby, and by the Inhabitants not repairing and cleaning their Pavements, and the Trustees being not impowered by the said Act to pave the said Street, it is become full of deep Holes, and dangerous to Passengers.

And he also said, That the said Street is incapable of being repaired and cleansed, as it ought to be, unless some further Provision be given.

And the said Mr. Milner further added. That the Trustees are under great Difficulties to get the Compo-lition-Money paid in lieu of the Statute-work, by reason of the Poverty of the Inhabitants, who very often leave their Habitations before or as soon as the Year is out.

of The Copy of his Majesty’s Warrant, whereby letters

g are permitted to pass free from the Duty payable upon Post Letters, which was prefonted to the House upon the Nineteenth Day of this Instaut February, was read* and is as follows; viz.

GEORGE R.

Whereas we arc given to understand, that the Revenue anting by the General letter Office, or Office of Postmaltor General, bath heretofore suffered great Prejudice by the free Carriage of a great Number of Letters and Pacquets, from time to time, which ought to have been paid for according to the Acts of Parliament in that behalf; and that, for rettraining the Mif-chief attending fuel) Practices, our Royal Pnedecessors have directs!, from time to time, by Warrant under their Royal Sign Maituui, to whom the said Freedom of fending or receiving free any I-ethts or Pat quets should be granted or allowed: Our Will and Pleasure, therefore, is, and we do hereby require and command, That, from henceforth, you permit and fnffer no Person or Persons whatsoever to fend or receive free any Letters or Pacquets, which, by virtue of the said Acts of Parliament, or any of them, ought to be paid for, as aforesaid; Kxcept, our Principal Secretaries of State for the time being, the Com mi lii oners of our Treasury now being, and our High Treasurer, or the Commissioners of our Treasury, for the Time being, anti the Secretaries to the Treasury for the Time being, the Secretary at War, the Secretary of our Admiralty, our Lieutenant General, or oth» r Chief Governor or Governors, of onr Kingdom of Ireland, for the Time being, and his or their Secretary; excepting also the Members of both our Houses of Parliament, during every Sessions of Parliament, and for Forty Days before, and Forty Days after, every SolTion; so as the Letters or Pacquets to be franked, by virtue of this our Authority, for the Members of Parliament of either House, do not exceed the Weight of Two Ounces: And our further Pleasure is. That our said Secretaries of State, Commissioners of our Treasury, and our High Treasurer, and the Secretaries of the Treasury, our Secretary at War, and the Secretary to our Admiralty, our Lieutenant or Chief Governor of our Kingdom of Ireland for the Time being, and his Secretary, or any of them, now or for the Time being, shall not, at any Time or Times, permit or suffer any Person or Persons whatsoever to fend any private Letters, under Cover, to them, the same not being for our Service, but what they shall immediately send to the said General Post Office, to be taxed, and delivered from thence; and shall not cover any Persons Letters whatsoever, other than their own; and that they shall give strict Orders to the respective Secretaries and Clerks under them to govern themselves accordingly: And we do also will and require you to make our Pleasure known to the Members of our said Houses of Parliament, That, for preventing the Abuses, which, as we have been informed, have been frequently practised by divers Persons, who, not being Members of either of our said Houses of Parliament ‘themselves, have yet presumed to indorse on their Letters the Names of inch as were; as also to direct their Letters to Members of Parliament, when, at the same time, such Letters do not really belong to or concern the Members to whom the same are directed, we do expect, that the Members of both Houses do conllantly indorse their own Names on their own Letters, with their own Vol. 22.

Hand-writing; and that they do not suffer any Letters whatsoever, other than fuel) as concern themselves, to pass under their Frank, Cover, or Direction, to the Diminution and Prejudice of our said Revenue; and, for so doing, this shall be your Warrant.

Given at our Court at St. James's, this 18th Day of October 1727, in the Firil Year of our Reign.

By his Majesty’s Command.

To our trusty and well- /?. Waljjole,

beloved Edward Carteret Cha. Turner,

and Edward Harrijbn Geo. Dodington,

Esquires, our Postmaster Geo. Oxenden>

General. Will. Clayton.

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, being informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Ti.en the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That there being no Provision of Fabrick-rents, or other Emoluments, to enable the Dean and Chapter either to complete the iinfmitlied Parts of the said Collegiate Church, or to keep in Repair what was erected; and they lowing annually expended considerable Sums upon the many other laige and pubbek Buildings within their Precinct, which it is incumbent on them to keep up; the Parliament, by Two Acts, made in the Fighth Year of the lteigu of his late Majesty King William the Third, and in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, allotted them inch an annual Sum, out of the Duties upon Coals, for a certain Number of Years, as hath enabled them to repair the most ruinous Parts, and to make good about Two-thirds of the whole Fabrick; but that, the said annual Allowance ex pinner, and the Money arising therefrom being all expended about Michaelmas 1728, and a further Supply being necessary to support a considerable Part of ttie Church, with the Chapel of King Henry the Seventh, Hill remaining in a ruinous Condition, the Sum of Four thousand Pounds, upon Application made to the last Parliament, was, in each of the Two last Sessions thereof, granted for this Purpose; an Account of the Disposal and Application whereof hath been laid before this House; but that a further Supply, lor repairing and finishing the said Collegiate Church, is still wanting: And therefore expressing their Hope, That so great and good a Work, carried on, and so far advanced, by the Aid of former Parliaments, will be continued by the present: and that this venerable Pile, wherein the Remains of the Royal Family, the Nobility, and chief Gentry, of these Realms, are deposited, will be esteemed a publick Concern, and be it length finished according to its intended Model.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

St. James, A Petition of the Vestrymen, and other the Inhabi-

Wt stminster, tants of the Two Parishes of St. James and St. George,

Watch^&c Hanover-square, within the Liberty of Westmiiijler, was

' presented to the House, and read; setting forth the

Importance and Necessity of keeping a sufficient, strong, and well-regulated Watch, in the Night-time, within the several Parishes of this great and populous City, Burglaries, Robberies, and other Outrages and Disorders, in and about the fame, having, of late, much increased; and that, by the Laws now in being, no effectual Provision is made for establishing, ordering, or well-governing, any such Nightly Watch, or for the due levying and coilecting Money for defraying the necessary Charges thereof, or for enforcing a due Application, and just Account, of Money so levied and collected; and farther representing to the House, That, for want of a proper Regulation of the Beadles appointed and employed within the said Two Parishes, who have been of great Charge, and little Use, to the fame, the Streets have been every Day more and more pestered with idle vagrant Beggars, to the great Annoyance of Passengers, and Reproach of our Laws and Government: and that the Methods hitherto practised, for railing Money to maintain the said Beadles, have been very precarious and unwarrantable: And therefore, and in order to remedy the Mischiefs and Inconveniencies aforesaid, praying the House, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for the better regulating the Nightly Watch and Beadles within the said Two Parishes of St. James, Westminster, and St. George, Hanover square.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; alledging, That the Expence of making commodious, beautifying, and repairing, the Church of the said Parish, which this House, and their Predecessors, have made Choice of to honour with their Presence, having their particular Appointment of Seats therein, to attend divine Service, together with the Purchase, Repairs, and Furniture, of a vVorkhouse, has created so great a Parish Debt, yet remaining unsatisfied, and occasioned such heavy annual Rates, to which a much finaller N umber of Inhabitants are now subject, since the great Increase of Buildings in the Upper Liberty, and the Removal of great Numbers of the liest and wealthiest Inhabitants of the said Parish, that the Petitioners are unable, without the greatest Difficulty, to go through a further Charge, however necessary; and, as the Tow er of the said Church, and some late discovered Defects in the Roof, are the only Parts of the Building which want Relief, and the said Towfer is in a ruinous Condition; therefore, and in regard to the Circumstances of the said Parish, and their having formerly received Favours from an House of Commons, to repair their Church, praying the House to grant them such Assistance, as will enable them to make Repairs suitable to the Church which has the Honour to receive the Representatives of the People of Great Britain, the Expence w hereof, by Computation, will amount to about Three thousand Five hundred Pounds.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

>lonvof A Petition of the Trustees for establishing the Colony eor^ia* of Georgia, in America, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, being informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners, by the Atliftance of this House, in the last Parliament, in 1733, together with the Contributions of well-disposed Persons, have been enabled to proceed so far in the Execution of the Trust reposed in them, that, at Lady-day 1734, there were settled, in the Province of Georgia, above One Thou-fond Persons, who, until the Ground is cleared, and produces a Crop, must necessarily, for the greatest Part, be subsisted at the Expence of the Trull: That the principal Town, named Savannah, is already built, consisting of a great Number of Houses, and daily increasing and a County laid out, of the same Name, ia Vol. 22.

which several Villages and Settlements are begun; and Forts already built upon the principal Passes, for the Defence of the Whole: That* lor the maintaining of good Government in the Colony, proper Courts of Judicature have been erected, and Civil Magistrates appointed; and that, for the Conveniency of Ships frequenting that Coast, a Beacon is begun, and near finished, upon the Point of Tybee Istand, lying at the Mouth of the River Savannah; and alleging, That the Soil and Climate of Georgia are proper for producing Wine, Oil, Silk, and other valuable Commodities, which at present are purchased from Foreigners with ready Money; and representing to the House the Importance of the Situation Of this Province; and expressing their Hope, That, the Premises considered, the House will enable them to carry on the good Work so happily begun, on which so greatly depend the increase of the Trade of this Kingdom, the Security of our Colonies on the Continent of America, the providing a comfortable lletreat for persecuted, and other indigent, industrious, foreign Protestants, as well as many of our own unfortunate Countrymen, who cannot fuhfift at home: And therefore praying the House to give the Petitioners stich Afliftauce in the Premises as the House shall think meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee’of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty.

Ordered, That an Account of the Monies received, applied, and expended, by the Trustees for establishing the Colony of Georgia, in America, from the 9th Day of June 1732 to the gth Day of September 1734, laid before this House.

Rejoiced) That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, there be issued and applied the Sum of One Million, out of such Monies as have arisen, or shall or may arise, lor the Surpluses, Excesses, or overplus Monies, commonly called the Sinking Fund.

And the said Petition was read:

And the Order of the House, made Yesterday, for rettraining the Counsel at the Bar of this House, or before the Committee of Privileges and Elections, from offering Evidence touching the Legality of Votes for Members to serve in Parliament for any County, Shire, City, Borough, Cinque Port or Place, contrary to the last Determination in the House of Commons, wa9 also read:

And the Counsel for the Petitioners were heard:

And the last Determination of the House, made the Eighteenth Day of April 1729, concerning the Right of Election of Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City of Wells, which is thereby resolved to be in the Mayor, Masters, Burgesses, and Freemen of the said City, who are admitted to their Freedom, in any of the Seven Companies within the said City, being the reunto entitled by Birth, Servitude, or Marriage, was read.

And the Counsel for the Petitioners having produced a Copy of the Poll taken at the said Election, and having, in order to disqualify several Persons who voted for the Sitting Members, delivered in several Lifts, containing the Names of such Persons, examined several Witnesses, in order to prove, that the Mayor was guilty of Partiality, in favour of the Sitting Members; and did examine many of the Electors, upon Oath, concerning their Right of Voting; and examined Witnesses, also upon Oath, in Contradiction to the Oaths of several Electors; and refused to admit the Votes of several Electors, who refused to take the Oath required.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners offered to produce Evidence, in order to disqualify the Persons named in One of the said Lifts, upon account of their not being legaJL Burgesses of the said City.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Members having objected to the said Evidence being produced;

The Resolution of the House, made the Eighteenth Day of February, in the Eighth Year of the Reign of King William the Third, concerning the Right of electing Citizens to serve in Parliament for the said City, was read.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioners proceeded to examine several Witnesses, concerning the Usage of the said City, in respect to the Admission of Burgesses and Freemen, and their respective Rights:

And the Resolution of the House, made the 30th Day of May 1716, concerning the By-law made by the governing Part of the Corporation of the said City, in 1712, was read.

Then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

The House divided.

And, upon the Whole, it appeared to the Committee,

That the said Church is in a very ruinous and decayed Condition; and that there is a Necessity for rebuilding the fame.

Which Act declares* That the Author of any Book or Books, his Assignee or Assigns, shall have the 1‘ole Liberty of printing such Book or Books, for the Term of 14 Years, commencing from the Day of Publication j and provides against any other Persons re-printing, importing, or expofuig to Sale, such Books, within that time; unless the Consent of the Proprietors be first had; and, by a Proviso in the said Act, the foie Right of re-printing or diipofing of Copies, At the End of the said Term of 14 Years, is to return to the Authors, if they are then living, lor the like further Term;

The Petitioners alleged, That, notwithstanding the Provision in the said. Act, the good Intentions thereof have been frustrated and evaded, of which there are numerous Instances; and they called One Witness, to prove the great Labours of the Authors of Books, and the Expences thoie Persons are at, to whom such Authors alienate or transfer their Property therein; viz*

Mr. John Goland, of Bond-street, St. George's Parish being examined, said, That within these Four or Five Years last pail, he had been robbed Three times of Lead, to the Value of4o.r. or 50 each time, notwithstanding the Watchman’s Box is within 20 Yards of his House: That on his Return home in the Evening, he generally finds the Watchman drunk, and wandering about with lewd Women: That, one Morning after Christmas last, he found him so drunk, that he.was forced himself to take him out of the Kennel*, and in that Condition several of his Neighbours saw him.

Mr. Samuel Seddon, being examined, said, That he was concerned as an Attorney in prosecuting a Servant of a Gentleman, for breaking open the House of Mr. Fox, in the Parish of S'. George, Hanover Square, and for stealing some Plate of his Walter, who lodged in Mr. Fox's House; of which Crime the Servant was convicted.

Oliver Lambart Esquire, of St. James's Parish, being examined, said, That he had frequently Complaintsmade to him, being One of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace, of Watchmen not being at their Stands; and that Robberies, and other Outrages and Disorders, were committed in the Streets; whereupon he had often made Complaint thereof to the Burgesses, and applied for an Increase of Watchmen; but without Success.

The Petitioners then laid before the Committee the Statutes following; viz. An Act of 13th of King Edward id, called the Statute of Winchester; and also an Act of the 5th of King Edzoard the 3d , and also an Act of the 5th of King Henry the 4th; and so much of the said Statutes as relate to nightly Watches, were read; the Petitioners alleging, That noProvision is made by either of the said Acts, orby any other Law, for theestablishing, ordering, or well governing, of nightly Watches, except from Ascension-day to Michaelmas-daij, or for the due raising and collecting of Money, to defray the necessary Charges of a nightly Watch, or for enforcing a due Application, and just Account, of such Money as had or should be collected for that Purpose.

It appeared to the Committee, by the Evidence of Mr. Samuel Seddon and Mr. Thomas Caigozo, formerly a Constable of the Parish of St. James, That there are in that Parish 81 Streets, Four Lanes, and 38 Alleys, containing, in all, upwards of 3,000 Houses, and but Thirty-two Watchmen employed to take care of the whole Parish.

And Mr. Simon Parry and Mr. Matthew Panic, being severally examined, said, That in the Parish of St. George there are 56 Streets, 16 Courts, or thereabouts, and Two large Squares, that the Streets, Courts, and Squares, contain, in all, near 2,000 Houses, and but 14 Watchmen, most of whom are very old and infirm, being appointed by the Burgesses, for the Care of the whole Parish; 14 or 15 were paid by the voluntary Contribution of the Parish.

Mr. Nicolas Humphreys, One of the Collectors of the Rates for the nightly Watch, laid before the Committee a Book, wherein are entered the Rates and Assessments, made by the Burgesses of Westminster, for defraying the Expence of Watchmen, each-of whom is paid 7id. per Night, or thereabouts:

4 22

The said Mr. Humphreys, being examined as to the Collecting of the Money afi'efled on the Inhabitants, said. There being no Power to enforce tile Payment of those Assessments, a great many of the Inhabitants refused to pay them, complaining the y were not half watched,

The Committee then proceeded to inquire into that Part of the Petition, which complains, That there is a Want of a proper Regulation of Beadles appointed and employed within the said Two Parishes, in order to assist the Constable.

And the said Mr. Humphreys, being again called, said,

That in the Parish of St. George, Hanover Square there are Three Beadles employed, who usually have each £. 30. per Annum, or thereabouts.

And Mr. Seddon, being examined, said, Th^t in the Parish of St. James there are Seven Beadles, who have, as he has been informed, either £. 30per Annum, with a Coat, or £. 35 without one; and that the Money to pay them is taken out of the Watch-money, raised by the Assessments of the Burgesses; and therefore precarious and unwarrantable.

It appeared to the Committee, That One Inhabitant of the Parish of -57. James paid 16 s. per Annum Watch-money, for a House f£. 60 per Annum.

The said Mr. Lambart, being again called, and examined, said, That he has frequently spoke to Beadles, and desired them to remove Beggars; Imt to no Purpose:

That a Lady of Quality once desired iiis Assistance therein, when her Daughter had been frightened, being with Child, by a Beggar, who had loft his Hand, and having only a Stump, thrall it into the Chair to her Daughter:

That he thereupon wrote to Mr. Green, One of the Burgesses, to desire that he would fend a Beadle or Two to remove the Beggars; but the said Mr. Green took no manner of Notice of his Request: That lie spoke at that time to one of the Beadles himself, to turn the Beggars away; and the Beadle excused himself from doing it, saying, That it was not within his Ward.

M r. James IJaJtings, Sexton of the Parish of St. James's, was called, and, being examined, said, That he had often met Beadles, and iliewed them Beggars-, and complained of their being an Annoyance, and troublesome to the Inhabitants; and the Answer the Beadle gave was, That it was not their Business to remove t hem; and if they did remove them from thence, they would go into fom*e other Street.

Mr. Thomas Rea, Churchwarden of the Parish of St.

George, Hanover Square\ said. That he had taken great Pains with the Beadles for the Removal of Beggars; and that, after his Complaints, they had llaid Montiis in the Parish: That finding his Applications to the Beadles ineffectual, he made Complaint to the Burgesses; but met with no Success. /

Dr. Andrew Trebeck, being examined, confirmed the foregoing Evidence given of the Remiflhefs of Beadles in their Offices, and of the Complaints that had been made thereof to the Burgess’esCourt: But said. He never heard that any Redress was given upon such Complaints.

Mr. Willimott reported from the Committee, to Exportation whom the Petition of the Matters, Workmen, and other of Wool. Persons, concerned in the Woollen and Silk Manufactures within the Cities of London and Westminster, and Borough of Southwark, in behalf of themselves, and all other Persons concerned in the said Manufactures throughout Great Britain; and also the several Petitions from the Cities of Peterborough, Exeter, and Coventry, and the Towns of Bampfon, Chumleigh*

Kighley, Barkway, Northampton, Barnstaple, and Whitchurch; complaining of the unlawful Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland, and of Woollen Goods completely manufactured from Ireland to foreign Countries; were referred; and who, by an Instruction to them given by the House, were ordered to consider the Laws in being to prevent the clandestine Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland, and what further Provisions may be necessary for the better preventing thereof: That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions, and had considered the said Laws; and had directed him to report the Matter of the said Petitions, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Report and Resolutions are as follows; viz.

The Committee have, in pursuance of the Orders of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and have also, pursuant to the Instruction given to the said Committee, considered the Laws in being to prevent the clandestine Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland, and what further Provisions may be necessary for the better preventing thereof:

To prove the First Allegation, contained in the first-mentioned Petition, which complains of unlawful Exportation of great Quantities of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland, the following Witnesses were examined; viz.

Samuel Webber: Who said, That |ie had followed the Business of a Serge-maker ever since the Year 1696, and had travelled through several Parts of France, and seen the Woollen Manufactures there; and that at a Place called Rochelle, they worked up Irish Wool, which he had Reason to believe, because he was informed by an Irish Merchant there named White, that he, the said White, came to reside at Rochelle as a Factor for Wool, which Wool, he told the Examinant, they had from Ireland: That he was at another Town called Poieters; and happening to be at a Weaver’s, the Examinant emptied a Pair of Combs of French Wool, which was verycoarfe: That the fined Sort of that Wool has a coarse Bottom, and can only be worked up into Broad Cloth, Serges, or Goods of that Sort; but that, unless it was mixed up with English or Irish Wool, it was impracticable to work it up in the making of Camblets, Callimancoes, Crapes, and such kind of Goods, with which the French now supply foreign Markets.

Henry Oland said, That One-third Part of the Wool of Ireland, wrought up with Two-third Parts of the French Wool, would make up the several Sorts of Goods enumerated by the said Mr. Webber; but, without Irish or English Wool, the French cannot*work up these Sorts of Goods.

Mr. John Munn said. That, being at Dunkirk on the Third Day of November last, he saw near 2,000 Tod of "Wool landed there out of a Dutch Ship arrived from Amsterdam: which Wool, he said, was landed in the new Harbour, where it was not usual to land Goods*

That the Reason of landing it there, the Examinant apprehended, was to prevent being observed by the English in that Town; and that the said Wool was packed up in Linen, according to the Method used in

packing

V

8 Geo. II. 190 Mar 423

packing tip W ool in England, and was put into Waggons to be carried to Lijle, where there is a Woollen Manufactory established.

The Examinant produced to the Committee a Lock of the said W ool, which he and Mr. Webber positively asserted to be either Englisht or Irish \ but they said, that Wool of the Growth of some Fart of England, being of the same nature with Irish Woo], it was im-polltble to distinguish which of the Two Countries it was the Growth of.

The said Mr. hlunn likewise said. That he had Information, about Two Years ago, from a Correspondent of his at Dunkirk, that several W aggon Loads of English or Irish W ool, had been then lauded there in the Night time.

Upon further Examination he said likewise, That the Manufactory at IJjle was supported by English and Irish Wool, where they made several Sorts of Stuffs and Stockings: That, ns he was informed, a Fund had been raised by the City of St. Omers, for letting up a Woollen Manufactory, in that City, for making Shalloons, Baragons, Sagathu s, Dnroys, Sc. which Manufactory, the Examinant said, within these Three Years lad pod, had urifen to lb considerable a Figure and Improvement, that, to his Knowledge, now almod every Shop in Dunkirk was docked with fume of the Goods made there.

That, at another Town in France called Abbeville, the Examinant said, he saw Six Combers working together upon English or Irish W ool, besides the Factor Royal, w ho was established in that Town: That the Sagathies, Duroys, Tamies, and divers other Species of Goods, had been wrought up there, and several Hales of Baragons had been fold from thence to English Merchants, who had put them on hoard their Ships at St. Talere, in order to carry the same to Spain and Portugal.

Then, iu order to prove that Quantities of Goods, completely manufactured, have been exported from Ireland to foreign Parts,

Mr. John Wenham, Merchant, was examined: Who said. That, in the Year 1 720, he went to Lt/bon, where he fund Seven Years: That, the Fu ll Part of the lime he was there, largo Quantities of Caiublets had b»*en usually imported into Portugal from England: That afterwards Irish Camblets were introduced by degrees, until it became usual to import large Quantities of them, and other Sorts of Woollen Goods; inso much, that when the Examinant left Lisbon, the Norwich Manufactures were then quite out of Use there, because the same Sorts of Goods were brought from Ireland, and fold 10 per Cent, cheaper.

The Examinant likewise said, That he has been informed, That the Method of conveying the Woollen Manufactures on board Ships from Cork, and other Places in Ireland, was this: Several Warehouses are erected near the Sea Shore, in which great Quantities of these Manufactures are put; and though, when Ships clear out of Port, they have none of these Goods on board, yet there are Boats, which lie ready in wait, to convey the said Goods, out of the Warehouses, on board such Ships, when they are run off to Sea, in the Nighttime, or as Opportunity offers; and he said. That there was not a British Ship that came to Lisbon from Ireland, but what had Quantities of the said Manufactures on board.

It also appeared to the Committee, by an Account delivered in to them, transmited from Lisbon, dated the 28th of May lad, and signed Walrave Lodwick, Vice Consul, who certifies the said Account to be a true Copy token from the original Manifetis, that, from May 1733 to the latter End of May 1734, there had been imported into the Port of Lisbon, from Cork in Ireland, Seven Bundles and Four Packs of Goods, One hundred and Nineteen Dozen of Stockings, Forty-four Pieces . Stuffs, Four thousand Nine hundred Thirty-one Pieces of Camblets, and Sixty-four Pieces of Frizes and Ratteens.

The Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Vol. 22.

That further Provisions are necessary to prevent the clandediue Exportation of Wool from Great Britain and Ireland, and of Woollen Goods completely manufactured from Ireland to foreign Parts.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee*

That a most proper Way to prevent the Running of ’Wool from Ireland, will be by encouraging the Importation of Wool, Worded, Woollen, and Bay Yarn* from thence into this Kingdom.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That further Encouragement be given to such Persons as shall inform against the Running of Wool out of Great Britain, and of Wool, and Woollen Manufactures, out of Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Part of the Act, passed in the Ninth and Tenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, which directs, That all Wool, of the Growth of England, shall be regidered in the Counties of Kent and Safer, he extended to all Parts of the united Kingdom, within Ten Miles of the Sea Coads.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table.

Ordered, That it be an Indruftion to the said Committee, That they have Power to consider of the Duty upon Woollen and Bay Yarn imported from Ireland into England.

And the Counsel on both Sides were called in.

And the said Petition was read.

And the lall Determination of the House, concerning the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Town, made the 26th Day of April, in the x6th Year of the Reign of King Charles the Second, was read; whereby it was resolved, That the Inhabitants of the Town of Northampton, being Houfholclers, and not receiving Alms, are the proper Electors of Burgestes for that Town; and that the sharing in the charitable Gift, appointed to be distributed at Christmas, is a taking of Alms.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner was heard; and infilling, That the Freemen of the said Town have usually voted at former Elections, submitted it tothe House, whether the said Freemen are excluded by the said Resolution.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Member was also heard; and iniifting, That the said Ilesolution has declared the Inhabitants of the said Town, being Householders, and not receiving Alms, to be the proper Electors of BnrgelTes to serve in Parliament for that Town, submitted it to the House, whether the Right of Elec tion is not in them only.

Then the Counsel for the Petitioner acquainted the House, That, if it was their Opinion, that the Right of electing Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the said Town was, by the said Resolution, confined to the Inhabitants thereof, being Housholders, and not receiving Alms, he was not prepared to maintain a Majority of Votes for the Petitioner, and would, in that Cafe, give the House no further Trouble.

And then the Counsel on both Sides were directed to withdraw.

Resolved, That the honourable George Compton Esquire, is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Town of Northampton, in the County of Northampton.

Upon the Petition of Sir William Irby Baronet, complaining of an undue Kitction and Return of the honourable John King Esquire, now Lord King, to serve for the Borough of Dunhexid\ alias Launceston, in the County of Cornu all:

The Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

The Counsel for the Petitioner insisted, That this is an ancient Borough by Prescripiion, as appears by the Charter of King Philip and Queen Mary, dated 15th February, in the Second and Third Year of their Reign; which grants, That the Borough or Town of Dunhevid, alias Launceston, shall be, and remain for ever thereafter, a free Borough; and creates the Burgctlcs thereof a Body Corporate and Politic, by tire Name ot tire Mayor and Commonalty of the Borough of Dunhevid, alias Launceston; and grants to them, and their Successors, together with the Aldermen of the said Borough, for tiro Time being, or tire major Part thereof, a Power to cleft, and admit, so many, and such of the more discreet, prudent, and quiet. Men, and Inhabitants, of the said Borough, to be Burgesses and Freemen of the said Borough, as shall fresh to them to be necessary and fit, from time to time, with Power to remove, for Offences committed within the said Borough, and, in their stead, to admit other Inhabitants, at their Discretion.

A Petition of the Merchants, and Planters, trading to, and interested in, his Majesty's Sugar Colonies, was presented to the House, atul read; setling forth. That by Two Acts, passed in the i ath and 22d Years of King diaries the Second, the Inhabitants of the said Colonies are rertrained from fending any Sugars to foreign Markets, before they are firli lauded in Great Britain; and that the Sugar Islands, now being in a declining Condition, chiefly by the Increase of the French Settlements, it would be highly beneficial to Great Britain, as the Petitioners apprehend, to put the British Subject in a Capacity of disputing foreign Markets with the French, and to permit him to carry his Sugars earlier and cheaper to these Markets, than he now can do; and that the Sugar Colonies import yearly, into this Kingdom, Sugar enough for our HomeCon-fumption, ami also a large Surplus for Re-exportation to foreign Parts; but that the Demand from abroad has greatly decreased within these few Years; and the Markets for that Commodity have been forestalled by the French, not only to the Prejudice of the Sugar Trade, hut also of the general Trade of Great Britain; and that, if British Ships were permitted to go to foreign Markets, without unloading here, under proper Restrictions, the whole Charge, and, in a great Measure, the Risk of a double Voyage, would be saved; and that the obliging such Ships to return to Great Britain to unload, and take their Clearance here, before their proceeding on another American Voyage, would be attended with this farther good Effect, that they xnuft afford to carry Freight at the cheapest Rates, or return home empty; so that this Regulation, as the Petitioners conceive, would extend our Navigation, Vol.22.

— V Apr ills. 439

and contribute to make us the Carriers of Europe, without prejudicing the Revenue, all the Duties on Sugar being drawn back on the Re-exportation of it to foreign Parts; And therefore praying, That a Liberty may be granted of carrying British Sugars, from our Sugar Colonies in America, directly to any foreign Markets to the Southward of Cape Finisterre., under such Rertrictions asdhall be thought reasonable; and also of carrying such Sugars to any foreign Markets to the Northward of Cape Finisterre, after first touching in Great Britain, giving in a Manifeli of their Cargo, and entering into Bond to return to Great Britain before they proceed on another JEcJl India Voyage; or such other Relief as to the Hotife shall seem meet.

Resolved, That this House will, Tomorrow Fortnight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Petition.

SI R Fronds Child reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Proprietors and Inhabitants of the Houses in Lincoln's-mn-Jields, in the County of Middlesex, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove what is alledged therein, the following Witnesses were examined; viz.

Mr.Bevan: Who laid, That Lincoln s-inn Jields have lain, and do now lie, in a very bad Condition; and that he has known the said Fields 40 Years, and upwards, when they were in Grass: That, about 30 Years ago, that Part thereof, which lies against the Terrals Walk belonging to the Society of Lincoln s-inn, was raised in; but, of late, great Quantities of Rubbish and Earth have been laid on, all over the Fields, and the Ground considerably raised; and that a Week seldom passed, but Earth, or Rubbish, w’us carried and laid on some Part or other of the Fields: That, in that Part of the Fields which lies next to Holbourn Row, near Turn Style, Boys frequently ride, giving a Half-peny a-piece for the same: And he said, That he had seen several Boys thrown off, and some of them had their Legs and Arms broken; and, from that Part of the Fields which lies next to the Duke of Newcastle's House, he himself law a Woman, who had been run over by a Horse that was airing the re, which occasioned her Death; and that Accidents of that kind Very frequently happened: And that other great Disordera are therein committed by great Numbers of Thieves, and other loose and disorderly Persons frequently resorting thither, whom he had endeavoured to keep from thence, but could not, although he had a Warrant from Five Justices of the Peace, impowering liim to clear the said Fields of loose artd idle Persons, and to keep out all Ilorfes: That he had executed the Warrant as far as he could, and taken up Three or Four of such loose People as frequented the Fields, whom he carried before a Justice, who bound them over; and that he has attempted to take up more, but was relifted therein, and in Danger of loling his Life: The said Mr. Bcvan further said,

That Robberies are frequently committed in the said Fields; and that Mr. Jessop, who was a Member of this House, and lived in Lincolns-inn-jiclds, but is since dead, was attacked there, and with great Difficulty escaped with his Life.

Mr. Mono ton laid, That, within these Three Years that he has lived with Mr. Bigg, Surgeon, he, the said Mr. Bigg, has sent upwards of 30 Persons, who have had their Limbs broken by Accidents in the said Fields, to Hoipiials: That, about Three Quarters of a Year ago, a poor man, eroding the Fields, was tun over by a Horle/ and carried to a publick House, where he attended him; and that he could not be recovered, so as to speak, for Three Hours; and that a Child was run over about a Fortnight ago, whom he now attends: That hardly a Week palfes, but some Accidents of this kind happen: lie further said, That he has frequently seen great Number of Hories airing in all Parts of the Fields.

Mr. Ely on said, as he was coming through Lincolns-inn-fields one Night, he was knocked down, and robbed of Nine Guineas, and received a Cut on his Head, by which his Life was in Danger; and that it was done near Sir Francis Child's House.

And it appeared to the Committee, That the present Matter of the Rolls was, Tail Summer Twelve-month,

The By-law, dated the 18th of November 1730, was read; and is as follows:

" Against the illegal Making of Burgesses.

" Whereas the Method of electing Burgesses of this Town has been several times varied, and the Charters of the Town being iilent in whom the Right of Elec-

44 tion coniiits; for preventing the refore of ail Inconve-

4i niencies that may arise touching such Right, and settling and establishing a certain Rule therein, for the 4t future, it is this Day unanimously agreed and deter*

44 mined, as inoli conformable to the Custom and Con* lt stitution of the Town, That the Right of Election of Burgesses of this Town is in the Common-council " only; and it is agreed, determined, and ordered, That no Man shall from henceforth be elected a Burgess of this Town, unless he shall have been first proposed to " the next preceding Common-council, held Six Days at least before his Elefition, and the Day of putting the Question for his Election fixed at such preceding Com*

44 mon-council; and that if any Person be elected a 44 Burgess in any other manner, his Election shall be reputed null and void.

44 Provided, nevertheless, That a Nobleman may be " admitted and sworn a Burgeii, at a Common-council,

" confilting of Nine at the least, without any previous u Proposition."

Mr. Edward Byotlin, Clerk to the Trustees: Who, being examined, said. Then the Petitioners laid before the Committee the said Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament; whereby the Surveyors, and other Officers of the Parishes, through Which the Roads lead, are directed to prepare Lists of the Names of the Persons, who, within each Parish, are obliged by Law to do Statute-work on the Roads in the several Parishes, and to give in such Lifts to the Justices of the Peace of the County, at their petty or special Sessions, to be held for any of the Di* visions in which the Roads do lie; out of which Lifts the Justices {halt and may allot and appoint such and so many Persons to do their Statute-work on the Roads, as they shall think fit; which Work is to be done by such Persons, on such Days, and at such Times, and in such Parts of the Roads, as the Trustees, or their Surveyors, shall appoint.

And, by the said last mentioned Act, Provision was intended to be made for the Recovery of such Sums of Money, as the Inhabitants of any Parish had compounded for, or shall agree to pay, in lieu of the Statiite-work to be done by the Inhabitants of such Parishes upon the Roads.

The said Edward By oil in, being again called, said.

That the Surveyors of the Highways, and other Officers of some of the Parishes, have neglected to give in such Lists of the Names of the several Persons, who are obliged by Law to do their Statute-work; and the Justices of the Peace, at their Petty Sessions, have neglected to allot the Statute-work to be done upon Fart of the Roads within some of the Parishes, although he had, by Order of the Trustees, applied to them for that Purpose: And helsaid further, That no Cornposition had been made, or paid, in lieu of such Statute-work so neglected to be done.

It appeared, by the Evidence of the said Edward Byollin, That the Provisions, made by the said Act of Parliament, passed in the last Session, for obliging the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, to which the Roads belong, to do and perform their Statute-work upon the Roads, or to pay such Money as they have already compounded for, or shall hereafter agree to pay, in lien of such Statute-work, are defective and insufficient.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better Regulation of Pilots for the Conducting of Ships and Vessels from Dover, Deal, and the Isle of Thanet, up the River of Thames, and Medway, which was to continue in force for Seven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and a Clause for further regulating the Pilots of Dover, Deal, and the Isle of Thanet, in an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, was to be in force for so long as the said Act, of the Third Year of his said late Majesty was to have Continuance; and the said Act, of the Third Year of his said late Majesty’s Reign, together with the said Clause, were, by an Act passed in^Jje Tenth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty, continued in force for the further Term of Eleven Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament \ which said Term is fit to be further continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the better paving and cleaning the Streets in the City and Liberty of Westminster, and other Places within the Limits of the weekly Bills of Mortality, in the County of Middlesex, which expired at the End of the Session of Parliament 1733> is fit to be revived.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That so much of an Act, made in the Fifth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act against clandestine Running of uncustomed Goods", and for the more effectual preventing Frauds relating to the Customs, as relates to such foreign Goods, Wares, and Merchandises, as shall be taken in at Sea, out of any Ship, or Vessel, in order to be landed, or put into any other Ship, Vessel, or Boat; and so much of the said Act as relates to Goods not reported, and found after clearing Ships; and so much of the said Act as provides further

Remedies against relanding Goods prohibited to be worn in this Kingdom, and foreign Goods ffiipped out of Parts beyond the Seas; and so much of the said Act as relates to the opening or altering the Package of Goods on board Ships oiitward-bound; and so much of the said Act as relates to hovering Ships or Vessels, of the Burden of Fifty Tons, or under; and so much of the said Act as concerns the Bales, or Package, in which the Coffee shall be exported, which was to continue in force for Three Years, from the Twenty-fifth Day of March 1719, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and so much of the said Act as relates to Rum imported in Calks or Vessels, not containing Twenty Gallons at the least, which was to continue in force for Three Years, from the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1719, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and so much of the said Act as relates to Certificate Goods entered in order to be exported to Ireland, which was to continue in force for Three Years, from the First Day of May 1719, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; which said several Clauses, contained in the Act aforesaid, by an Act, made in the Ninth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, were further continued, from the Expiration of their said several and respective Terms, for the further Term of Five Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; and which said Clauses, by an Act, made in the Second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, were further continued, from and after the Expiration thereof, until the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1734, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; are near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, made in the Eighth Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, intituled, An Act to prevent theclan-destine Running of Goods, and the Danger of Infection thereby; and to prevent Ships breaking their Quarantine; and to subject Copper-ore, of the Production of the British Plantations, to such Regulations as other enumerated Commodities, of the like Production, are subject, which was to be in force for Two Years, from the Twenty-fifth Day of March 1722, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; which Act, except the Clause obliging all Ships or Vessels to perform Quarantine, by an Act, made in the Eleventh Year of his late Majesty’s Reign, was further continued, from the Expiration thereof, for Three Years, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; which Act, except the Clause obliging all Ships or Vessels to perform Quarantine, was, by an Act made in the Second Year of the Reign of his present Majesty, further continued, from the Expiration thereof, until the Twenty-ninth Day of September 1734, and from thence to the End of the then next Session of Parliament; is near expiring and fit to be continued.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That an Act, passed in the Second Year of the Ileign of his present Majesty, intituled, An Act for the Relief of Debtors, with respect to thelmprisonment of their Persons, is near expiring, and fit to be continued.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard, at the Bar of this House, at the same time the Matter of the several Petitions, complaining of an undue Election and Return for the City, and County of the City, of Bristol, is appointed to be heard.

Ordered, That the Report from the Committee of Canterbury Privileges and Elections* touching the Election and Return for the City and County of Canterbury, be now received.

Mr. Earle, accordingly, reported from the said Committee, the Matter, as it appeared to them, touching the said Election and Return, and the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Report and Resolutions are as follow; viz.

Upon the Petition of Sir Thomas Hales Baronet, complaining of an undue Election and Return of Sir Wm. Hardress Baronet, and Thomas May Esquire, for the City and County of Canterbury, in the County of Kent.

The Committee have examined the Merits of this Election.

The Right of Election not having been settled by this House, it was agreed, by the Counsel on both Sides, to be the Usage and Custom,

That the Right of eleCling Citizens, to serve in Parliament for the City and County of Canterbury, is in the Mayor, Sheriff, Aldermen, Common-council-men, and Freemen, of the said City, being entitled thereto either by Birth, Marriage, or by serving Seven Years Apprenticeftip to Freemen of the said City, or by Purchase, or Gift.

And it appeared, by a Copy of the Poll, which was proved, and delivered in, that the Votes were.

For Sir Wm. Hardress Baronet - - 645.

Sir Thomas Hales Baronet - - 503.

Thomas May Esquire - - - 643.

And the Counsel for the Petitioner alleged, That 159 Persons appeared, and offered to poll for him; and that Seven of the said Voters offered to poll for Thomas May Esquire, but they were prevented by the Crowd, and Insolence of the Mob; and that, with this Addition, the Petitioner would have a Majority, and the Numbers would (land,

For Sir Wm. Hardress - 643.

Sir Thomas Hales - 662.

Thomas May Esquire - 650.

And the Counsel for the Sitting Members desiring a Sight of the said Lift, it was shewed to him at the Bar; and he, having perused the fame, allowed them to be good Votes; and that the Numbers, as above, were truly dated, and thereby a Majority did appear for Sir Thomas Hales and Mr. May.

Then the Counsel were directed to withdraw.

And the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Sir Wm. Hardress Baronet is not duly elected a Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the City and County of Canterbury, in the County of Kent.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Thomas May Esquire is duly elected a Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the City and County of Canterbury, in the County of Kent.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That Sir Thomas Hales Baronet is duly elected a Citizen to serve in this present Parliament for the City and County of Canterbury, in the County of Kent.

The said Resolutions being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Committee, to whom the Copy of his Majesty’s Warrrant, whereby Letters are permitted to pals free from the Duty payable upon Post Letters, was referred, have met; andf pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter thereof: To which-Purpose,

The Committee, in the First Place* thought it necessary to inquire, from what Time the Privilege of franking Letters commenced, and in what manner it had been enjoyed, by the Members of the House of Commons; and having examined the First Steps of the Act, which granted the Post Revenue to his Majesty King Charles the Second, they find, in the Paper Bill, which remains in the Custody of the Clerk of this House, a Clause, providing and en-aSing;

" That all the Letters, which at any time hereafter,

" be sent by or unto any of the Knights, Citizens, and " Burgesses, chosen, and continuing, to be Members " of the Parliament of England, and fitting in Parliament, shall be freely, and without any Charge unto " them, safely carried and conveyed, by all and every " Letter Polt established by this Act, according to the " Directions of the said Letters; any thing in this Act P to the contrary notwithstanding."

Which Clause was left out by the Lords, as appears by the Journals of the House of Commons; as your Committee suppolc, because there was no Provision made for their Letters passing free; and because as it was a Money Bill, they could not make any Addition to it, though they took upon tllem to leave out Part of it; which occasioned some Difficulty in the House of Commons, about passing the Bill; to facilitate which, your Committee have Reason to believe, that the Persons who had then the Honour to lerve the Crown, and who were Members of the House of Commons, gave the rest of the Members

Your Committee, considering that the Duke of York enjoyed this Revenue under the Crown, conceive, that this must be looked upon as the strongest Acknowledgement, That the Franking of Letters was a Privilege of this House; and that the Poftinafters then were so far from thinking themselves at Liberty to strike out the Names of Members signed by themselves, that they thought themfeUcs obliged to desire the Assistance of the House of Commons, when the Name of a Member appeared upon a Letter, though counterfeited.

Your Committee thought it not necessary to make their Report tedious, by inferring all the Orders they found upon the Journals, relating to the Post Office, not doubting, but that thelfc already mentioned were sufficient to fetisfy the House, That the Privilege of having their Lel> Vol. 22.

44 his Predecessor in the Office, under whom he learned the Ait of finding out falle Franks, as he termed them; which still continues a Mark among them for that Purpose: That another Motive for his charging the Letters of Members is, when he know s the Mein- ber to he in Mourning, and his Letter is not sealed with black Wax: That he frequently guesses; and Members Letters may sometimes be charged, through Mistake; but that then they ore always ready to return the Members the Money so charged: That when he is in doubt, he always thinks it better to tax, bearing in mind the Postmaster General's Maxim,

44 We can give Redrels at any time, but can never recover what is slipt: That he has observed the Franks increase with every new Parliament: That as the new Members do, and have a Right to, frank Let- ters, those who were in the last Parliament do not w ill- ingly part with that Privilege, and, by the Acquaint- ance they still have in the House of Commons, they get blank Franks, which being superferibed by the said old Members, whole Hand-writing he is acquainted with, he apprehends it to be the Business of the Mem- ber of the lait Parliament, and then strikes off the Frank."

Your Committee cannot help observing, upon this Evidence, That the Methods by which Mr. Cave pretends to distinguish whether Letters concern the Business of the Members themselves, or not, are very uncertain, and tending to give a great deal of unnecessary Trouble to the Members; but that if he has any surer Methods, which lie did not think fit to disclose, they must still be of infinitely worfc Consequence.

Your Committee then proceeded to peruse a Paper, intituled,

An Account of the Diminution of the Revenue, by franking of Letters, from the Year 1715 to the Year 1734:

Which they have hereunto annexed, N* I, by whiclv there appears a great gradual Increase of Franks: And they examined Mr. John Searle, the Accomptant General of the Poll Office: Who said, 44 It was a general Account; and not of the Diminution arising from Members franking only?’
