of " though he owned they franked a good deal, to make u them amends for the Smallncfs of their Salary: lhat £< what was called an Account of the Diminution of the " Revenue, by Franking, was rather an Estimate, and " taken in the following manner: That they weighed " all the Letters, franked at the Office, once, twice, or " perhaps at most thrice, in the Year; and, taking an " Account of that Weight, they concluded, that the u Franks of every Night, till the next Weighing, should " be the fame: That they endeavoured to take their " Weighing at as equal times as they could, when they " had no particular Reason to believe the Postage higher <£ or lower than ordinary; as when the King's Speech, " or any such Publick Paper, came out: That there " could be no Distinciion of the Franks of Lords, Com-u mons, or State Offices, they being all weighed together."

Your Committee, for further Information in this Affair, called for a Paper, intituled,

An Account of the net Revenue of the Post Office from the Year 1715 to the Year 1734:

Which they have hereunto annexed N® II.: And as this Account is a certain Account, and not an Estimate, they find by it the Revenue is not really diminished, in any Proportion to what it appears to be by the former Estimate; and Mr. Bell explained that, by acquainting the Committee, " That he did not apprehend, that Onethird of the Letters, which are franked, would go by " the Polt if not franked."

Your Committee, having thus stated the Fa&s, have thought fit, as well for prelcrving the Privilege of this House, as to guard the Revenue against any unlawful Diminution, to come to the following Resolutions:

1. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Privilege of Franking Letters, by the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, cholen to represent the Commons in Parliament, began with the erecting a Post Office, within this Kingdom, by Act of Parliament.

2. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Letters, not exceeding Two Ounces, ligned by the proper hand of, or directed to, any Member of this House, during the Sitting of every Session of Parliament, and Forty Days before, and Forty Days after, every Summons, or Prorogation, ought to be carried and delivered freely and lafely from all Parts of Great Britain and Ireland, without any Charge of Postage.

3. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is an high Infringement of the Privilege of the Knights,

Citizens, and Burgesses, cholen to represent the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament, for any Post-master, his Deputies, or Agents, in Great Britain or Ireland, to detain or delay, open or look into, by any means whatsoever, any Letter directed to, or signed by, the proper hand of any Member, without an express Warrant, in writing, under the hand of one of the Principal Secretaries of State, for every such detaining, delaying, opening, or looking into.

4. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That all Letters, directed to any Member of this House, at any Place within the Bills of Mortality, be carried by the proper Officers of the Post Office to the House or Lodgings of such Member, or to the Lobby of the House of Commons.

5. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is a notorious Breach of the Privilege of die House of Commons, for any Person to counterfeit the Hand, or put the Name, of any Member of the House of Commons, upon any Letter, in order to prevent its being charged with the Duty of Poltage.

6. That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Persons as shall preiume to do the fame, ought to be proceeded against with the utmost Severity.

And Four Receipts were produced, and proved under Mr. Robert Jacomb's Hand, of several Sums received of Lady Torringtmi, which Ihe received from Lord Mon-tratk, and paid to the same Mr. Jacomb, for the U£e of John Botder Esquire.

And then,

Edward Mathews being again called, and examined, laid, That, before 1729, he killed Two or Three Bucks for Lord Mont rath, which were paid for, and the Money brought to Account: That he served Lord Montrath alter wards, when he took the Park into his Hands: That he killed a few Deer for him ;. but none were sold by my Lord:

And since be gave an Account, as in his former Evidence, of 19 Brace; and, upon Recollefilion, he said, he believed he killed 25 Brace that Seafbn, for there were many old Bucks: but could give no Account of what was killed for Three Years* after.

And farther said, That, from 1722 to 1729, he killed the Vension, and sent it to the Cooks in London, who, he believes, accounted to Mr. Boteler:

That, in 1722, there were about 300 Head of Deer: That he left a better Stock in 1729

That he knew nothing of any Bargain with Lord Mon-troth, except that his Lordship hired the House and Gardens several Years before he hired the Park; and that then he paid for Rabbets:

That the Land, one Acre with another, may be worth Fifteen or Sixteen Shillings an Acre.

That, from 1722 to 1729, no Horses, or other Cattle, were kept in the Park, but what his Master Botder had die Profit of: That he had Ten Pounds a Year for Wages, said Seven Shillings a Week, and a Man at Six. Shillings-a Week.

And being, asked. How many Deer the Park would keep I he said, About Five hundred; and1 how many he could kill out of every Hundred ? he said, Six Brace of Bucks of the First Head, and Does in Proportion.

After which,.

The Counselfor the Petitioner aHedged, That the said Estate would not bear the former Allowance to Mr. Bote-kr of £. 400 per Annum; and produced a Copy of a decretal Order of the Court of Chancery, made 2 2d December, 90 Geo.; and the same was read; wherein ijt is ordered and declared, That no Part of the said £.400 ought to be allowed to the Defendant John Botder and doth therefore order, that the Payment thereof, for the future, to the said John Boteler, do cease.

The Order of the Day being read, for resuming the adjourned Debate, upon the Third Resolution of the Committee, to whom the Copy of his Majestys War-

rant, whereby the Letters are permitted to pass free from the Duty payable upon Post Letters; was referred;

The laid Resolution being again read;

And a Motion being made, and the Question being proposed, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That it is an high Infringe-tnent of the Privileges of the Knights, Citizens, and Burgefi’es, chosen to representthe Commons of Great Britain in Parliament, for any Polt-master, his Deputies or Agents, in Great Britain or Ireland, to detain or delay, open or look into, by any means whatsoever, any Letter directed to, or signed by, the proper Hand of any Member, without an exp refs Warrant, in Writing, under the Hand of one of the principal Secretaries of State* for every such detaining, delaying, opening, or looking into;

An Amendment w^as proposed to be made to the Question, by leaving out the Words " detain or delay:"

And the Question being put, That those Words stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to thfe Question, by leaving out the Words " detaining, delaying.

And the Question being put. That those Words stand Part of the Question;

It passed in the Negative.

Another Amendment was proposed to be made to the Question, by adding, at the End thereof, thele Words,

" or to detain or delay any Letter directed to, or signed " with the Name of, any Member, unless there shall be " just Reason to suspect some Counterfeit of it, without " an express Warrant of a principal Secretary of State*

" as aforesaid, for every such detaining or delaying

And the Question being put, That those Words be added;

It was resolved in the Affirmative.

Resolved, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, so amended; That it is an high Infringement of the Privilege of the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, chosen to represent the Commons of Great Britain in Parliament, for any Post-master, his Deputies or Agents, in Great Britain or Ireland, to open, or look, into, by any means whatsoever, any Letter directed to, or signed by, the proper Hand of, any Member, without an express Warrant, in Writing, under the Hand of one of the principal Secretaries of State, for every such opening or looking into; or to detain or delay any Letter directed to, or signed with the Name of, any Member, unless there shall be just lleafon to suspect some Counterfeit of it, without an express Warrant of a principal Secretary of State, as aforesaid, for every such detaining or delaying.

The rest of the Resolutions of the said Committee, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. Hay reported from the Committee appointed to consider the Laws in being relating to the Maintenance and Settlement of the Poor; and to consider what further Pro\ ilions may he neccftary for their better Relief and Employment, That the Committee had considered t h o ft Laws; and had come to several Resolutions, which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and the Refohilions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

lle/olved. That it is the Opinion of this Committee; That the Laws in being, relating to the Maintenance of the Poor of this Kingdom, are defective; and, notwithstanding the y impose heavy Burdens on Parishes, yet the Poor, in most of them, are ill taken careof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Laws relating to the Settlement of the Poor, and concerning Vagrants, are very difficult to be executed, and chargeable in their execution, vexatious to the-Poor, and of little Advantage to the Publick, and ineffectual to promote the good Ends for which they were intended.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is neccftary, for the better Relief and Employment of the Poor, that a publick Workhouse or Work-houses, Hospital or I lospitals, House or Houses of Correction, be estabiillied in proper Places, and under proper Regulations, in each County.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in such Workhouse or Worklioufes, all poor Persons; able to labour, lie set to work, whofliail either be sent thither, or come voluntarily, for Employment.

Resolved,

Laws.

Preventing wrongous Imprisonment, &c. in Scotland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in such Hospital or Hospitals, Foundlings, and Mother poor Children, not having Parents able to provide for them, be taken care of> as also all poor Persons that are impotent or infirm.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in such House or Houses of Correction, all idle and disorderly Persons, Vagrants, and such other Criminals, as shall be thought proper, be confined to hard Labour.

Refoloed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards the Charge of such Workhouses, Hospitals, and Houses of Correction, each Parish be assessed or rated; and that proper Persons be im powered to receive the Money so to be assessed or rated, when collected, and also all voluntary Contributions, or Collections, either given or made for such Purposes.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Workhouses, Hospitals, and Houses of Correction, be under the Management of proper Persons, Regard being had to such as shall be Benefactors to so good a Work.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such Persons, as shall be appointed to*.he Management of such Workhouses, Hospitals, and Houses of Correction, be One Body Politick in Law, capable to file and be sued, and of taking and receiving charitable Contributions and -Benefactions for theufeof the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, for the better understanding, and rendering more effectual, the Laws relating to the Maintenance and Settlement of the Poor, it is very expedient that they be reduced into One Act of Parliament.

Ordered, That the said Report be taken into further Consideration upon Wednesday Morning next.

Resolvtd, Nemine contradicente, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the Law’s in being relating to the Maintenance of the Poor of this Kingdom are defective, notwithstanding the y impose heavy Burthens on Parities, yet the Poor, in most of them, are ill taken Care of.

The Second Resolution being read a Second time;

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That the Laws relating to the Settlement of the Poor, and concerning Vagrants, are very difficult to be executed, and chargeable in their Execution, vexatiou^ to the Poor, and of little Advantage to the Publick, and ineffectual to promote the good Ends for which they were intended.

The Third and Fourth Resolution, being severally read a Second time, were, upon the Question severally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

The Fifth Resolution being read a Second time:

Resolved, Nemine contradicente, That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution, That in such Hospital or Hospitals, Foundlings, and other poor Children, not having Parents able to provide for them, be taken care of, as also all poor Persons that are impotent and infirm.

After which his Majesty was pleated to make a most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I am glad the Business of this Session of Parliament The King1* is brought to such a Conclusion, That I have now an Speech. Opportunity of giving you same Reeels, after the great Pains you have tAkcn in the Service of your Country:

On this Occasion I must in Justice return you my Thanks for the many Instances you have given me of your Duty and Afteftion to my Person and Government, and for the necessary Provisions you have made for the publick Security, as far as the immediate Circumstances of Affairs might require.

I have considered, with great Care and Attention, the present Situation of Europe, and duly weighed the Consequences that may arise from the Progress of the War, either by means of its becoming more general, or continuing only to be carried on between the Powers already engaged.

An Accommodation of these unhappy Troubles appeared to be the best means to prevent the Dangers that are to be apprehended on either Side: In this View, a Plan of Pacification was concerted between me and the States General, with great Impartiality, and not without reasonable Grounds to hope for Succels, although it hath not had the deli red Effect.

But all further Resolutions, to be taken in this important and critical Conjuncture, must be principally determined by future Events: This makes it inpoffible for me at present to take the previous Advice and Concurrence of my Parliament, in such Meal:ires as may become ubfolutely necessary to be entered into: But you may be allured, that my constant Concern for the Publick Welfare, the Liberties of Europe, and, in particular, for the Felicity and Security of these Kingdoms will never suffer me to take any Steps, but such as the Honour and Interest of my Crown and People shall call for and justify; and, in the Pursuit of these great and desirable Ends, I do, with the best grounded Conlidence, promish myself your zealous and affectionate Support

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my hearty Thanks for the Supplies you have, with so much Chearfulness and Dispatch, granted for the Service of the current Year; which have been so effectually raised, and accompanied with so feasonable an Augmentation of our Forces by Sea and Land, That I shall be in a Condition to make use of them in the most advantageous manner for the publick Service, as any Occasion, that may happen to arise, shall require.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Conduct and Prudence of this Parliament, in at time osso great Difficulty, cannot be enough commended; the Polture of Affairs before us required all possible Resolution, joined with Caution, neither to be unwarily involved in the present Disturbances, nor to remain unprovided against those Dangers, which are too obvious to standingneed of any Explanation, and may either directly or remotely affect us.

As I think it necessary this Summer to visit my Dominions in Germany, it is my Intention to appoint the Queen Regent here, during my Absence, of whole just and prudent Administration you have, on the like Occa-lion, had Experience: Let me earnestly recommend it to you to render the Burden of this weighty Trust as easy to her as possible, by making it your constant Study and Endeavour, as I am fore it is your Inclination, to pveferve the Peace of the Kingdom, and to discountenance and suppress all Attempts to raise groundless Discontents in the Minds of my People, whole Happiness hath always been, and shall continue, my daily and uninterrupted Care.

Proclamation for Meeting of Parliament

By the KI N G,

A PROCLAMATION.

GEORGE R.

WHEREAS our Parliament stands prorogued to Tuesday the Eleventh Day of this instant November, V*?, with the Advice of our Privy Council, do hereby publish and declare, That the said Parliament shall be further prorogued, on the said Eleventh Day of November, to Thursday the Fifteenth Day of January next ensuing: And we have given Order to our Chancellor of Great Britain to prepare a Commission for proroguing the same accordingly: And we do hereby further declare our Royal Vo l. 22.

Will and Pleasure, That the said Parliament shall, on the said Fiiteenth Day of January next, he held, and fit, for the Dispatch of divers weighty and important Affairs; And the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are hereby required to give their Attendance accordingly, at Westminster, on the said Fifteenth Day of January next.

Given at our Court at St. James s, the Sixth Day of November, in the Ninth Year of our Reign.

GOD save the King.

The King’s Mr. Speaker reported, That the House had attended Speech re- his Majesty in the House of Peers: Where his Majesty ported. %vas please(j to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker laid he had, to prevent Mistakes, obtained a Copy: Which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The happy Turn which the Affairs of Europe have evidently taken, fmee the End of the last Session of Parliament, must, I am persuaded, give you all, as it does me, the greatest Satisfaction.

I acquainted you then, That a Plan of Pacification, concerted between me and the States General of the United Provinces, had been proposed to the Parties engaged in the War, which had not the Effect to prevent the Opening of the Campaign: The Armies took the Field, and the War was carried on, in some Parts, in such a manner as to give very just Apprehensions, that it would unavoidably become general, from an absolute Necessity of preserving that Balance of Power, on which the Safety and Commerce of the maritime Powers so much depend.

This Consideration determined me to persevere, jointly with the States, in repeating our most earneit Instances to the contending Parties to agree to an Armistice, and to enter into a Negotiation for obtaining a general Peace, upon the Basis of the Plan we had proposed to them.

Whilst Affairs continued in this State of Deliberation, the Heat and Fury of the War abated; and the Emperor,

and the most Chrifrian King, in canfequenoe of their repeated Professions of afmoere Disposition to put an End to the War by an honourable and lblid Peace, concerted and agreed upon certain preliminary Articles to answer that most desirable End: An Armistice is since agreed to by all the Parties engaged in die War; and the contracting Powers, in regard to the good Offices employed by me and the States, have communicated to us, by their respective Ministers, the Preliminaries, desiring our Concurrence for effectuating a general Pacification upon the Terms thereby itipulated.

It appearing, upon due Examination, That these Articles do not effectially vary from the Plan proposed by me and the Slates, nor contain any thing prejudicial to the Equilibre of Europe, or to the Rights and Interests of our respective Subjects, we have thought fit, in pursuance of our constant Purpose to contribute our utmost towards a general Pacification, to declare, by a joint Resolution, to the Courts of Vieua and France, our Approbation of the said Preliminaries, and our Reudlnefe to concur inaTreaty to be made for bringing them to Perfection.

These Preliminaries have been like wile communicated to the Kings of Spain, and of Sardinia; and, although those Princes have not as yet, in Form, declared their final Refutations upon them, there is great Reason to believe, that the Love of Peace, their avowed Dispositions for putting an End to the Troubles of Europe, and the amicable 15

Interposition of common Friends, will prevail upon then! to agree to what has been thus concerted, upon reasonable Security given them for die peaceable Possession and Enjoyment of the Countries allotted to them.

In these Circumstances my first Care was to ease the Burdens of my People, as loon, and as far, as Prudence, in the present Posture of Affairs, would permit: I have therefore ordered a considerable Reduction to be made of my Forces both by Sea and Land; and, if the Influence of the Crown of Great Britain, and the Respect due to this Nation, have had any Share in com poling the preterit Troubles in Europe, or preventing new ones, I am persuaded you wiH be of Opinion*, that it will be necessary to continue some extraordinary Expence, until there be a more perfect Reconciliation among the several Powers of Europe.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I have ordered the proper Officers to lay before you the Estimates for the Service of the current Year; and I make no Doubt, but my Delire to make the Charge of the Public as low as possible, will find in you the same Rea-dinels to grant the necessary Supplies with Chearfulness and Unanimity.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

I am willing to hope this pleasing Prospect of Peace Abroad will greatly contribute to Peace and good Harmony at Home. Let that Example of Temper and Moderation, which has so happily calmed the Spirits of contending Princes, banilli from among you all intestine Discord and Diffcnlion. Those, who truly with the Peace and Prosperity of their Country, can never have a more favourable Opportunity, than now offers, of distinguiiliing themselves, by declaring their Satisfaction in the Progress already made towards restoring the public Tranquillity, and in promoting what is still necessary to bring it to Perfection.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm hath any Right urual to give his Vote in the Election of any Member to serve Ordera. in Parliament.

Resolved, That where the House shall judge any Petition, touching Elections, to be frivolous and vexatious, the House will order Satisfaction to be made to the Person petitioned against.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, That any Person hath procured himself to be eletted or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured lb to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt Practices, this House w ill proceed, with the utmost Severity, against such Person.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, That any Person hath been tampering with any Witness, in respect of his Evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any Person from appearing, or giving Evidence, the same is declared to be a high Crime and Misdemeanour, and this House will proceed, with the utmost Severity, against such Offender.

Resolved, That if it shall appear, That any Person hath given false Evidence, in any Case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed, with the utmost Severity, against such Offender.

Resolved, That it is an high Infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of Great Britain, for any Lord of Parliament, or any Lord Lieutenant of any County, to concern themselves in the Elections of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Mr. Fax reported from the Committee appointed Yesterday to draw up an Address to be presented to his Majesty, That the Committee had drawn up an Address accordingly; which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the same in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: W here the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

Most gracious Sovereign,

Wre, your Majesty s most dutiful and loyal Subjects, the Commons of Great Britain, in Parliament assembled, return your Majesty our unfeigned Thanks, lor your most gracious Speech from the Throne.

We are truly ienlible of your Majesty’s early Endeavours to put an end to the War; and can never enough admire the Iteady Application with which you purlued that great Work, by the joint Interposition of the good Offices of your Majesty and die States General.

And it is with the warmest Gratitude we acknowledge your Majesty’s particular Care and Circumspection in all your Proceedings, not to involve this Nation unnecefllirily in the War, w hen, at the same time, your Majesty shewed you were not insensible of the imminent Danger that threatened the Liliertics of Europe, from a longer Continuance of it upon lb unequal a l oot; a Conduct wherein your Majesty plainly proved you equally consulted the immediate Interests of your People, and that Balance of Power in Europe, upon which the Safety and Commerce of this Nation lo much depend; at once lkving this Nation from all the present Calamities of War, and trying to avert the future Necessity of its being at last obliged to take its Share and Hazard in them.

We cannot but be fenlible of your Majesty s Wisdom and Impartiality in forming the Plan of Pacification, proposed by your Majesty and the States General to the Powers engaged in the War; which, although not immediately accepted by the contending Parties, nor an-ftvering the desired Effect, by preventing the Opening of the Campaign, has been so far adopted, that the most material and essential Parts of it have been agreed to by the Princes originally and principally concerned in this Rupture, and recommended by them to their Allies, as preliminary Articles to a general Pacification.

Upon this happy Turn the Affairs of Europe have taken, we most heartily congratulate with your Majesty; and when we consider the Assurances your Majesty hps been graciously pleasec! to give us, That these Preliminaries do not essentially vary from the Plan or Pacification concerted byyour Majesty and the States General, and the ready Approbation your Majesty and the States General have given of them; a just Confidence in yoyr Wisdom, and the Experience we have of your coiistant and paternal

Care of the true Interest of your People^ through the whole Course of this great and intricate Work, leaves us not the least Room to entertain a Doubt, but that the preliminary Conditions of this Pacification, so founded, and so approved, will give general Satisfaction; in which Persuasion we are further confirmed, by the great Probability there appears to be of their being accepted and agreed to by all the Powers engaged in the War.

The early regard your Majesty has been graciously pleased tofhew to the Welfare of your People, in taking the First Opportunity, on this great and fortunate Event* to5 lighten the Burden of their Expences, by making a Rddu^tioiVof your Forces, both by Sea and Land, is such ft Mark of your same in confuting their Interest; and of your tender Concern Tor their Ease, that we should - be as ftdjuft to our own-Gratitude, as to your Majesty’s Good-fief^, if we fail to testify the one, and acknowledge the dther, in the strongest and most dutiful manner; arid as we look ripon1 this; added to dll the other Measures of your glorious and happy Reign, as a Proof that the Estimates fbi* !tb& preferitJ Year will be proportioned to the Situation of jAffiirs, and the Pur^oses to which they shall be fotirid necessar^;’ so webeg leave to assure'your Majesty-that we will chearfully and effectually raise such Supplies, as the Posture of our present happy Circumstances shall vj: ’' ' require, and sufficient to support the Dignity of the Crown,

Weight, in making us persevere in our Endeavours to give a Lustre to your Majesty’s Reign abroad, equal, if possible, to the Happiness we enjoy from it at home.

A Petition of James Brodie, of Spynie Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That John Campbell, of Calder, Esquire, having been elected to serve in this present Parliament for Pembrokefure, and also for the Shire of Nairn, made his Election to serve fovPembrokeshire: That, aWrit having been issued for a new Election for the Shire of Nairn, Sir Archibald Campbell, Sheriff Principal for Life of the said Shire, appointed Monday the Seventeenth of March last past for the Day of Election, and made the proper Intimations to the Freeholders to assemble betwixt the Hours of Twelve and Two of that Day, in the Tolbooth of Nairn, the usual Place of Election: That accordingly several of the Freeholders came to Nairn on the Day appointed, in order to elect a Member to serve in Parliament, in Place of the said John Campbell of Calder: That; to their great Surprize, a Body of Highlanders in Arms, to the Number of 140, or thereby, amongst whom were several Soldiers of the Independent Companies, and many others, not Inhabitants of the County of Nairn, appeared that Day, about Eleven a Clock, in the said Town of Nairn, placed themselves before the House of the Sheriff in that Town; That Colonel Alexander Rose, Provoll of the Town, and Alexander Brodie, of Brodie, Justices of the Peace for that County, forthwith demanded the Meaning of such an Appearance in Arms; but received no other Answer, than that some Gentlemen behind would tell the Meaning of it; whereupon the said Alexander Brodie read the Proclamation against Riots, and required them to disperse: This appeared the more extraordinary, that Colonel Alexander Rose, Provost of the Town, had, the Day before, notified to the Sheriff, in Person, That there was no ground to suspect any Disorder: and that he was sufficiently able to keep the Peace of the said Town, without any armed Men being brought into it: That, after this, some of the Freeholders, finding the Sheriff in the Midst of those armed Men, asked to know what the Meaning of this was ? to which he answered, They were his Guard: Upon which a Protest was taken, and the Proclamation read a Second time: That the said Sheriff, intending to carry on the Election in a clandestine Manner, thought fit, about Eleven of the Clock, to require, from one of the Magistrates, the Keys of the Tolbooth; and received for Answer, that there was then a Prisoner there, but that the Room should be forthwith cleared 6 O before

and Hugh Rose of Geddes, and Hugh Rose of Clava, junior,'were afterwards admitted upon the Roll: That Alexander Brodie of Brodie, and the other Freeholders in the Petitioner’s Interest, to the Number of Six, elected the Petitioner to serve as Member in thus present Parliament, and offered a Return to the Sheriff in his Favour, under form of Instrument: That there was another Freeholder, viz. James Sutherland, of Kinjle-rie, then in Town, ready to have voted for the Petitioner, who was violently laid hold on by a Party of the said armed Men, commanded by a Serjeant of one of the independent Companies, on Pretence of assisting a Messenger, who had a Caption, or Capias, against him for a eivrl Debt; and, notwithstanding the Money was immediately tendered to the Messenger, which he aknow-ledged was a sufficient Stop to his further Proceeding, and which he was willing to have received, if he had not been hindered by the said armed Party, and notwithstanding that the Money was offered to be deposited

Spanish Depredations on British Trade.

23° Januarii. 1735*

Ordered, That the said Estimates do lie upon the Table, to be perused by the Members of the House.

Sir Thomas LyttletoP, from the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, presented to the House, pursuant to their Address to his Majesty, of the 14th Day of May, in the last Session of Parliaments Copies of the several Repre-fentations, Memorials, or Petitions, made to the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, fmce the 25th of March 1725, which have not already been laid before this House, relating to any Losses sustained by his Majesty’s Subjects, by Depredations committed by the Spaniards, in Europe or America; together with all Copies or Extracts of any Letters, from any of the British Governors in America, Consuls in Europe, or any Commanders in Chief, or Captains of his Majesty’s Ships of War, to the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, which have not already been laid before this House; and also, Copies or Extracts of all Letters written, or Instructions given, by the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, to any of the Governors of the British Plantations, or any Commanders in Chief, or Captains of his Majesty’s Ships of War, which have not already been laid before this House, relating to the said Losses sustained by the said Depredations; together with a Schedule of the said Copies or Extracts.

A Petition of Alexander Macdmvall, of Garthland, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, at the late Election of a Representative to Parliament for the Shire of Wigtown, upon the 23d of May 1734, the honourable Colonel JV?n. Dalrymple, and the Petitioner, flood Candidates: That the said Colonel William Dalrymple, being sensible how necessary it was for the Purpose of his Election, to have the Prcefes and Clerk chosen of such as he could depend upon to be entirely under his Direction and Influence; and being likewise certain, that he should not be able to carry either of these, if the Votes of such were fairly demanded, as had an unqueflionableRight to vote in the Choice of Prcefes and Clerk; did, as Commissioner to the last Parliament, and, as such, authorized by Law toprefide in any Meeting of Freeholders, in order to their Election of a Representative to Parliament, before choosing of Prcefes and Clerk, in Concert with some others of his Associates, take upon him to call the Votes for Choosing of Prcefes and Clerk, by the Roll of the last Election in the Year 1727, excluding all other undoubted, Freeholders of the County, for no Reason, but because they Were not present at the last Election, though, as there was then no Struggle in the County, that Meeting did consist mostly of Colonel Dalnpnple's own Friends, who came there at his Desire; while other undoubted Freeholders, who had voted at former Elections, and flood upon the Roll, were not present: That the Act of Parliament in Scotland, 1681, expressly directs the Freeholders in the respective Counties to convene at Michaelmas ^yearly, to make up the Rolls of Freeholders: That, agreeable to the Terms of this Act, it was, by a late Resolution of the House of Commons, declared, That the Right of Election of a Prafes and Clerk is in such Personsas stand upon the Roll last made up by the Freeholders at the Michaelmas Head Court, or at the last Election of a Member to serve in Parliament: That, in Consequence of the said Act and Resolution, the Rolls were regularly made up, by the Freeholders of the said County, at Michaelmas before the said Election: That these Rolls were the last made up, and every Person there inrolled was entitled to a Voice in the Choice of Prafes and Clerk at the said Election; notwithstanding of which, the said Colonel Dalrymple refused to call these Rolls, though often required; or to take the Vote of any*Freeholder, hut such as voted at his last Election in the Year 1727: That a Protest being taken in Form against this arbitrary and unjustifiable Proceeding; and the said Colonel IVm. Dalrymple being determined not to exercise, according to Law, the Power given him, as last Representative, to preside over the Freeholders in the Choice of Prafes and Clerk; the Majority of the Freeholders present, legally qualified to vote, empowered Patrick Mac/cie, Provost of the Burgh of Wigtoun, to supply his Place, and to take the Votes of all who had Voices for choosing Prafes and Clerk: That, thereupon, John Stewart, of Cafle Stewart, was duly elected Prafes, and John Dun, Writer in Wigtoun, was duly elected Clerk: That, by this, the only regularly constituted Meeting of the Freeholders at the said Election, the Petitioner waschofethe Representative of the said County in this present Parliament; and was accordingly returned, by the said John Dan, to Captain Andrew Agnezo, of Lochnaw, the High Sheriff, who refused to accept of a Return of the Petitioner from the said John Dun, but took a Return of the said Colonel William Dalrymple from Patrick Agnew, which lie has annexed to the Writ, and returned into the Court out of which the same issued; though the Election of the said Patrick Agnew to be Clerk, and the Constitution of that Meeting of Freeholders, by which the said Colonel Wm, Dalrymple pretended to be chose, were founded in Violation of a positive Act of Parliament, and in Defiance of a Resolution of the House of Commons: And praying the House to take the Premises into their

immediate Cousideration; and give the Petitioner such Relief as the Circumstances of the same require.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof, and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Merchants, Tradesmen, Freeholders, and Inhabitants, of the City of York, was presented to the House, and read; alleging. That the River Ouze and Swale is capable of being made navigable from St. Mary's Gate, in the City of York, to the Town of Richmond, in the County of York, for Boats, Barges, Lighters, and other Vessels; and that, for the better carrying on the said Navigation, and for opening a Trade between the said River and the River Dun, up to the Towns of Doncaster, Rotherham, and Sheffield, it will be necessary to improve the Navigation of the said River Dun, from Wilfick-house, to a Place called Sike-house Ferry; and that the improving and making navigable, the said River, will not only be a great Advancement to the Trade of the said Towns, but like-wife for the publick Good: And therefore praying, That the House will give Leave, that a Bill may be brought in for improving, and making navigable, the River Oitze and Swale, from St. Mary's Gate, in the City of York, to Richmond; and also to improve the Navigation of the River Dun, from Wilfick-house, to SikeAwufe Ferry.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

and thereby excluded many Freeholders, formerly inrolled, w'hose Names had never been struck off the Roll, and to whose Qualifications there could not be the lead Objection pretended, feme of them having the very best Estates in the Stewartry: That the said Patrick ficron absolutely and peremptorily refilled, though formally required, to tender the Oaths by Law appointed to every Freeholder, before he should be admitted to vote for Prafes or Clerk; neither would he suffer the Oaths to be administered to, or taken by, any one Voter whatsoever, before the Election of Prafes and Clerk: That the said Patrick Heron persisting thus to act, contrary to the positive Directions of many Acts of Parliament, in such a manner, that no Prafes or Clerk could, upon the Question by him put, be legally chose, nor, consequently, any Member regularly elected; and the Stewart Cleric refuting to collect the Votes for Prafes and Clerk, tte Freeholders were under a Necessity to authorize feme other Person, who would aft impartially to take the Roll, and preside over them, while they chose their Prafes and Clerk: That, accordingly, Sir Thomas Gordon, of Earlstoun, at the Desire, and with the Approbation, of the Majority of the Freeholders present, legally qualified to vote, took the Roll, and called the Names of all the Freeholders formerly inrolled, and received their Votes for Prafes and Clerk: That, thereupon, William Muir, of Caffencarry, was duly elected Prafes, and James Broun, Writer, in Dumfries, was duly elected Clerk, to the Meeting of Freeholders: That the Meeting being thus regularly constituted, the Rolls settled, and all the previous Steps taken which are by Law required, the Freeliolders proreeded to the Election of their Repre-fentative, and the Petitioner was duly elected: That the find James Promt* Clerk of the Meeting, and, consequently. Sir Charles Turner, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Number of effective Men to be provided for Guards and Garisons in Great Britain, and for Guernsey and Jersey, for the Year 1736, be, including One thousand Eight hundred and Fifteen Invalids, and Five hundred Fifty-five Men, which the Six Independent Companies consist of, for the Service of the Highlands, Seventeen thousand Seven hundred and Four Men, Commission and Non-commission Officers included.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee. That a Sum, not exceeding Six hundred forty-nine thou* land Two hundred Seventy Pounds and Two Shilling?, be granted to his Majesty, for defraying the Charge of the said Seventeen thousand Seven hundred and Four Men; for Guards and Garisons, and other his Majesty's Land Forces, in Great Britain, Guernsey, and Jersey, for the Year 1736.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, hot exceeding Twb hundred sixteen thousand Two hundred Twenty-eight Pounds Ten Shillings hnd tleven Pence, be granted to his Majestyi for maintaining his Majesty s Forces and Garisons in the Plantations, Minorca, and Gibraltar, and for Provisions for the Garisons at Annapolis Royal, Canso, Placentia, and Gibraltar, for the Year 1736.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Seven Ufoufand One hundred Forty-four Pounds One Shilling and Eleven Pence Farthing, be granted to his Majesty,: for defraying several extraordinary Expences and Services incurred Anno 1735, and not provided forty Parliament.,.

The said Resolutions, being severally read a Second time, were, upon th6 Question severally put thereupon; agreed to by the House.

A Motion was ma’dd, and the Question being put, fteduffion of That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to the ^rmy* acquaint him with the Readinels wherewith his faithful Commons have agreed to the Continuance of that extra* ordinary Expence, which he hath thought necessary, ill the present Jutfohire; in which Resolution they have concurred with the greater Chearfulness and Willingness, as a suitable and grateful Return to his‘Royal Goodness, in ordering so coriliderable a Reduction of his Forces, both by Sea and Land, as loon as the present Posture of Affairs would permit, and in full Confidence, that it is his Royal Intention, as soon as there shalt be a more perfe6l Reconciliation among^ the several Powders of Europe, to make such further Reduction of his Forces as may be consistent with the Security and Dignity of his Majesty’s Royal Per* foil and Government, and with our present happy Constitution; not doubting, but that, from his fatherly Com-pafftorr to his People, he will be graciously pleased to direct, That whatever Land Forces thall hereafter be thought necessary, be established in such a manner as shall make the Saving more feniible> and the future Burden less grievous to the Nation;

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the following Witness was examined;

Mr. Richard Ellison; Who said, That he surveyed the River Owze and Swale, from St. Mary's Gate, in York, to Richmond, and found it capable of being made completely navigable; a Plan of which River he produced to the Committee; adding, that the same is already navigable from York to Myton, except in very dry Seasons, and may easily be made navigable to Moreton Bridge.

He likewise produced a Plan of the River Dun; and said. That the Navigation thereof from Wilfikc-hvufe to Sikehouse Ferry, is at present imperfect; but that the said River is capable of being made conitanf ly navigable, by cutting near Two Shallows in the said River, which occasion Boats to lie thereon Seven Days out of Fourteen.

He further said, That great Quanties of Goods are carried by Land from Sheffield to Borough Bridge, the Carriage whereof now cods 50 s. per Ton; but that, when the said Navigation shall be completed, and a Communication opened between the River Dun and the River Owze and Szcale, the Price of the Carriage of the said Goods will be reduced to 10 s. per Torn Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to improve, and make navigable, the River Owze and Swale from St. Marys Gate, in the City of York, to Moreton Bridge, in the County of York; and to improve the Navigation of the River Dun, from Wilfike-house, in the Parish of Barmby Dun, to Sikehouse Ferry,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

A Petition of the Provost, Bailies, and Council, of the Burgh of Irvine, in the Shire of Air, in behalf of the Community of the said Borough, and of the Burgesses and Inhabitants thereof, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the said Borough of Irvine lies very commodioufty for Trade, at the Mouth of a River; oncf, for feme time, has been much employed in Exportation of Coal, which was of Advantage to the Place, and increased his Majesty s Revenue; but, of late, the Trade Of that Town has been very much impaired, and in Ha-rard of being entirely loft, by reason of the Decay of their Pier or Harbour, the same being almost filled with Sand Banks daily increasing.; and that the Petitioners have been at considerable Expences in cleansing the aforesaid Harbour, and repairing the Pier; which they have not been able to make effectual, for want of fuflicienl Fund for answering that and the other publick Works of the Town, the upholding their Bridge, which wants to be renewed, the Townrhouse, Church, and Steeple, and making and keeping the Roads, Streets, and Avenues, of the Town, together with the Payment of the Minister’s Stipend, and other Expences: And therefore praying the House, to order, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for impoling, for a certain Term of Years, a Duty of Two Pcnies Scots, or One-Sixth of a Peny Sterling, on each Scots Pint of Ale or Beer brewed or brought into the said Tow n for Sale, and a Duty of Two Pence Sterling on every Twenty Loads of Coals carried to and shipped at the said Port and Harbour, for Transportation to Ireland, or other Places beyond Seas; to be levied and applied to 'the deanfing the aforesaid Harbour, and preventing the Sand Banks arising the rein; for deepening of the Chanel, and paling the River; for repairing the Harbour, repairing, and, if needful, rebuilding the Bridge; and for defraying the Charge of their other publick Works; and for paying their Debts already contrafted; the said Duties to be vetted in the Magistrates and Town Council, as Trustees, and to be under the Inspection of Overseers, to be named in the usual manner; or to grant such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Owners, Ship-matters, and Mariners, in and about the Borough of Irvine, in the County of Air, for themselves, and in behalf of many Sailors employed by them, was also presented to the House, and read; representing the Decay of the Coal Trade betwixt the Port of l'vine and Ireland, occasioned by the bad Condition of the Pier and Breast-work, and by the Foulness of the Harbour there, and by the Inability of the Magistrates of the said Borough to answer the Expence of repairing, cleansing, and keeping in Repair, the said Harbour, and the annual Expences of their other publick Works and Affairs: And therefore praying. That a Bill may be brought in, according to the Prayer of the Petition of the Provost, Bailies, and Council, of the Burgh of Irvine, in the Shire of Air, in behalf of the Community of the said Borough, and of the Burgesses and Inhabitants thereof.

Places adjacent, vhofe Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and other the Manufacturers , of Fustian, and Dealers therein, in the several Counties of Lancaster, Chester, and Derby, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, together wit! 1 the Ilesolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read: And the Report and Resolutions of the Committee are as followeth; viz.

The Committee, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 9th lnstant, have examined the Matter of the Petition:

And the Petitioners, to prove the Allegations thereof, laid before the Committee,

An Act of Parliament, made in the 7th Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act to preserve and encourage the Woolen and Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, and for more effectual employing the Poor, by prohibiting the Use and Wear of all printed, painted, stained, or dyed Callicoes, in Apparel, Houshold-stuff, Furniture, or otbenvife, after the 23d Day of December 1722, except as therein is excepted; which was read:

By which Act it was, amongst other Things Enacted, That the Prohibition of Callicoes intended, and the Penalties inflicted for wearing or uling printed, painted, stained, or dyed Callicoes, in Apparel, Houshold-stuff, or Furniture, after the 25th Day of December 1722, contrary to the said Act, should respectively extend to prohibit, and should be levied and recovered for wearing or using in Apparel, lloufhold-stuff, or Furniture, after the 25th Day of December 1722, any Stuff made of Cotton, or mixed therewith, which should be printed or painted with any Colour or Colours, or any Callico chequered or striped, or any Callico stitched or flowered in foreign Parts, with any Colour or Colours, or with coloured Flowers made there, Mullins, Neckcloths, and Fustians, excepted.

The Petitioners called the following Witnesses, viz.

Mr. Robert Livefay: Who, being examined, said, That he knows that there are large Quantities of Fustians made in the several Counties of Lancaster, Chester, and Derby; and that great Numbers of Families have been brought up in Manufacturing of Fustians, in the several Branches thereof; and several Thousands of Poor are employed in the said Manufactures, and maintained and supported thereby; and that himself, and his Brother, employ upwards of Six hundred Looms in the Weaving of Fustians; and that one Weaver employs Four Spinners, at lead; which amount to upwards of 3,000 Persons employed by them.

Air. Isaac Clegg confirmed Part of the Evidence given by Mr. Livefay, as to great Quantities of Fustians manufactured in the aforesaid Counties; and said, That Persons from Five Years of Age to Seventy are employed in the said Manufacture; and that the Cotton used therein is the Growth of his Majesty s Plantations; and that great Quantities of Linen Yarn, the Product of Great Britain and Ireland, are also used therein; and that he bought as much Linen Yarn at one time, of a Person in Northumberland, as cost about £. 1,000, and fold the greatest Part thereof to the Manufacturers of Fustians.

Mr. Livefay, being asked, If great Quantities of Linen Yarn from Germany were not made use of in the said Manufacture? laid, That small Quantities of Brunswick Yarn are made use of sometimes in making of printed Fustians, when English, Scotch, or Irish Linen Yarn is Icarce to be had; but it is not lo good, or so cheap, as the other; and not One-tenth Part of the Quantity is used as formerly, since their own Poor are lb much improved in the Spinning of Linen Yarn as they now are.

And also said, That the Warp of the Fustian is of Linen Yarn, and the Shoot is of Cotton imported from the British Plantations; and that there are many different Sorts of the said Manufacture, which are called Fustians.

20

A. 1735.

Air. John Hardman, Merchant, said, That he lives at Liverpoole, and trades confnlerably to Guinea, and the British Plantations; and freights the Ships, which he fends to those Parts, with all Sorts of English Woolen Manufactures; viz. Perpetls, Long-ells, Bays, Broadcloths, Plains, Worsted Cruels, home-made Spirits, and Spirits taken in at Cork; and that, with these Goods, Negroes are ptirchafed; and the rest of the Freight is of Cloths, Druggets, Sagathies, Caliimancoes, <§(?. and Cantaloons, which he apprehends to be manufactured at Norxvich; and also Iron Hoes, S;c. and Toys fit for the British Plantations in the West Indies; for which, in Return, he receives the Produce of those Islands, and particularly Cotton, which is taken in last, and is Ono-fourth Part of the Loading of most of the Ships which come from thence, and is chiefly made use of in the Manufacturing of Fustians.

Being asked, Where the Merchants of Liverpool took in their Gunpowder for Africa; he laid, Both in England and Holland; but the Reason of their buying it of the Dutch, he said, is, that, when the East India Company raise the Price of their Salt-petre, sometimes the Price of Gunpowder is 20 or 30 Shillings per Barrel above what the Merchants can have it for in Holland.

Mr. Slingsby Bethell laid, That he trades considerably in the English Woolen Manufactures, and fends great Quantities to the Coast of Guinea, hut no Money; and that of a Freight that cost £. 2,300 for the Gold Coast, One-half was Woolen Goods of Great Britain, with which Negroes are purchased, and carried to the British Plantations; and that he, in return, receives the Produce of the said Islands, and particularly Cotton, the greatest Part whereof he disposes of to the Manufacturers of Fustian; that he never deals in any other Cotton Wool but what is brought from the said Islands.

Air. Livefay and Air. Hardman severally said, That, in making of a Piece of Fustian, in which-J-as is of Cotton from the British Islands, and 4-d of Flax, the prime Cost is Six Shillings; but, by the Number of Poor employed in manufacturing the fame, viz. picking and cleaning, carding and spinning, winding, warping, weaving, whitening, printing, and the Duty, which is 3 d. per Yard, the same is fold for 40 s. per Piece, on an Average; and that the Profit arising from the same is by the Labour of the Poor employed therein.

And Air. Hardman further said, That, in 1735, there was imported at Liverpool, from the British Plantations, as much Cotton Wool, according to the foregoing Computation, as, when manufactured, would amount to about the Sum of ,£. 400,000.

And the said Mr. Livefay also said, That great Quantities of the said Manufactures have, for several Years last past, been printed, and when so printed, have been used in Apparel and Furniture; and that Eight Parts out of Nine of the Goods he manufactures are printed, and, according to the heft of his Judgment, One-half or Two-thirds of the Cotton Wool brought into this Kingdom from the British Plantations is used in the Fustians that are printed; and that the greatest Part of them are sent up brown, from the several Countries in which they are made, and printed in or about London.

Air. Thomas Dyer, being examined, said, That the said Fustians were printed and worn before the said Act passed for prohibiting the Wearing of Callicoes; and that they have gone by the Name of Fustians ever since he has been in Trade; and that Mr. Movillon has printed great Numbers of them for him.

Mr. Hardman also said, That he has seen the said / Manufacture, when fold, entered by the Name of Fustians in the Books of Air. John Sudall, of Black bourn.

Mr. Thomas Smith junior confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Dyer, as to their being called Fustians, and their having been printed and worn for several Years past.

Air. Dyer further said, That, about Seven or Eight Years since, he fold many Pieces of German Linen printed; but that, since the Fustian Manufacture is so much improved, he fells but very few them.

And lie also said, That, under Pretence that* lhch Persons as ute or wear the said Manufactures, when printed or painted, are liable to the Penalties laid by the (kid Act, fume Prosecutions luive been lately let on Foot, and several Advertisaments published, insinuating, that the same are prohibit* d by tiic said Act; which Advertisements have been indultrinully bunded about, in order to deter People from wrnring or utiuii the fame; whereby the farther Improvement of the said Manufacture* is not only discouraged, but the said Trade is wholly at a Stand; and Numbers of Poor, usually employed ti. rein, are deprived of their Livelihood, and the Traders thru in dare not carry on the said Trade, unlcb the said Act be explained.

Then he produced to the Committee Two of the said Advertisements complained of in the Petition; one of which is infortrd in a printed Paper, intituled, The Norwich Gazette, from Saturday, May the 10th, to Saturday, May the 17th. 1735: Norwich; printed by Henry Crofigrove, in St. Giles'.v Parish, 173^; and abb One other Advertisement, Norwich, May 31;/, 1735. subscribed by the Letters E. And he further said, That, fmee these Advertisements have been spread abroad, several of his Cultoiners have refilled to dml u id) him for the said Manufacture; and that be made hi* Agreement with One of the Manufacturers of the said Fustians, with whom lie deals, mid of whom lie bought upwards of boo Pieces of the said Manufacture, that, if the said Act was not explained in favour of the said Manufacture, he w as to return diem again, and had the said Fustians upon no other Terms: And further said, That the said Manufufturc was very much incivaled, till the Advertisements and Prosecutions put u Stop to the fame.

Mr. Livefay further said. That he has great Quantities of the said Manufacture by him, which he cannot fall, and diercforc is obliged to dilclmrge several poor Families which he used to employ.

Mr. Harthnan n\io laid, That for several Years together, he has fold 100 Hags of Cotton Wool per Mouth, which was of the Growdi of the British Plantations, each Hag weighing, on an Average, about 200lb. Weight; but this W inter lie has not Ibid.20 Bags in Ten W eeks; and that die Price of the said Cotton, this Year, L fallen a Peny, and a Pony Halfpeny, per Pound, which, as he apprehends is occasioned by die Discouragement this Manufufturc lies under.

Mr. Dax id Jenks, of ATM-street, London, being examined, said, That, as he was upon his Journey in the Gnintry, at Settle, in Yorkshire, he applied to one of his Customers, for Orders to fend him the said printed Fustians; whereupon l»e produced an Advertisement, which he had received in a Parcel of Goods sent him from Noncich; in which Advertisement was infer ted, That the said Fustians* were prohibited, and therefore would give him no Orders; and the Witness has not received any Orders finer, though, before that time, he used, every Journey, to receive Orders for large Quantities of the said Manufacture.

It appeared to the Committee, That several Informations have been laid, and Prosecutions commenced, against Persons who wear the said printed Fustians.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That die Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the House be moved for Leave to bring in a Bill to explain an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act to preserve and encourage die Woolen and Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, and for the more effectual employing the Poor, by prohibiting the Use and Wear of all printed, painted, stained, or dyed Callicoes, in Apparel, Houshold-stuff, Furniture, or otherwise, after

A Petition of the Dean and Chapter of the Collegiate Westminster Church ol St. Peter, in ! Test minster, being offered to be e^‘ prefanted to the House;

Mr. Pelham, by h:-> Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That his Majesty, being informed of the Contents of the said Petition, recommends it to their Consideration.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; fattin" forth. That there being no Provision, or Fabrick Rents, or other Emoluments, to enable the Dean and (-hupter eitiier to complete the unanilhul Parts of the said Collegiate Church, or to keep in Repair what was erected; and they having annually expended considerable Sums upon the many other large and publick Buildings w ithin their Preciivt, which it is incumbent on diem to keep up; the Parliament, by Two Acts, made in the Eighth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King /f illiam the Third, and in tin Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Quefcn Anne, allotted them such an annual Sum, out of the Duties upon Coals, for a certain Number of Years, i.adi enabled them to repair the most ruinous Parts, and to make good about Two-thirds of the whole Fabrick; but diat, the said annual Allowance expiring, and the Money arising therefrom being all expended about Michaelmas 1728, and a further Supply being necessary to iiipport a considerable Part of the Church, with die Clmpcl of King Henry the Seventh, full remaining in a ruinous Condition, the Sum of Four thousand Pounds, upon Application made to the last Parliament, was, in each of the Two last Sessions thereof, granted for this Purpose; and, upon Application made to the prefant Parliament, the like Sum of Four thousand Pounds was likewise granted; an Account of the Diij>o/ai and Application whereof hath been laid before the House; but that a further Supply, lor repairing and linishing the said Collegiate Church, is still wanting; And therefore expressing their Hope, that To great and good a "Work, carried on, and so far advanced, by the Aid of former Parliaments, will be continued by the present; and that this venerable Pile, wherein the Remains of the Royal Family, the Nobility, and chief Gentry, of thele Realms, are depositud, will be esteemed a publick Concern, and be it length fmished according to its intended Model.

A Motion was made, and the Question being put,

That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of die whole House, to whom it is referred to consider further of the Supply granted to his Majesty;

A Petition of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Commonalty, of the City of Exon, was presented to the House, and read; Getting forth, That the Citizens and Inhabitants of the said City have frequently represented unto the Petitioners, That, to cleanse and enlighten the Streets of the said City within the Walls thereof, and to keep a strongand regular Watch within the same, will be of great Service and Importance for the Preservation of the Persons, Properties, and Health, of the Citizens and Inhabitants thereof, and very necessary to prevent as well the Mischiefs which may happen from Fires, as Murders, Burglaries, Robberies, and Felonies, and other Violences, Outrages, and Disorders, in the Nighttime, within the Walls of the said City, and for apprehending the Persons concerned therein, and arresting suspected Persons, Night-walkers, and the like evil Persons, and securing them, so as they may be brought to Justice; the said City being very large, and many Strangers resorting thither; and it being, as the Petitioners conceive, very necessary and useful to cleanse and enlighten the said Streets, and keep a strong and regular Watch in the Night-time, throughout the Year, within the Walls of the said City, for the Purposes aforesaid: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for cleaning and enlightening the Streets of the said City, within the Walls thereof, and for keeping a strong and regular Watch therein in the Night-time.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

consfield Mr. Harry Waller reported from the Committee, Roads, to whom the Petition of the Trustees, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, appointed to put in Execution an Act, passed in the Fifth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for repairing the Roads from Bcconsfield, in the County of Bucks, to Stoken Church, in the County of Oxon, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the

House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof.

The Act for repairing the Road from Becon field, in the County of Bucks, to Stoken Church, in the County of Oxo?i, was laid before the said Committee.

And several Clauses thereof were read:

And the Petitioners called,

Mr. Thomas Jues, who produced a Deed, dated Jidy 6th, 1720; whereby it appeared, That the Toll, granted by the former Act, was mortgaged to Mr. Edmund Barllet, for £. 500, which he afterwards adigned over to Mr. Thomas Shrimpton and Mrs. Mary Shrimp ton.

Mr. Jer. Stevens, Receiver of the Tolls, was examined: Who said, That he had paid the Interest of the said Mortgage half yearly; and that, at Lady-day next, there will be Haifa Year’s Interest due thereupon.

Mr. John Hawes, being examined, said. That notwithstandingMen are continually employed in repairing the said Road, yet many Parts thereof are in a ruinous Condition; and that it is necessary to widen the fame: And he also said, That if the waste Water of the River running by the said Road could be so turned, as that it might run along the said Road, it will be of great Use to the fame, and little or no Detriment to the Owners of the Mills upon that River.

Ordered, That Leave1 be given to bring in a Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for repairing the Roads from Beconsfield, in the County of Bucks, to Stoken Church, in the County of Oxon: And that Mr. Harry Waller, Mr. Waller, and Sir Charles Vernon, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

)yal AflTent A Message from his Majesty, by Sir Charles Dalton, to Buis. Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this honourable House to attend his Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Mr. Alderman Perry reported from the Committee, improving to w hom the Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, the Street* and Commons, of the City of London, in Common of Loudoa« Council assembled, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the llesolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read: And the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, are as followeth; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, thinking it unnecessary to call E\ idence, to prove the First Allegation of the Petition, with regard to the many Street Robberies, Burglaries, and Murders, charged to have been of late committed in the City of London, the Notoriety of which was unhappily too glaring to need any oilier Proof than what every Man's own Knowledge supplied him with;

The Committee proceeded to inquire into the causes, as laid down in the Petition, of those Difordors so dangerous to the Lives and Properties of his Majesty’s Subjects.

And, in order to prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

Leonard Belt was examined, as to the present Manner of enlightening the Streets of London: Who said.

That the Lights used for that Purpose were the convex Lights: That the Number of these, throughout the whole City, was about 81.5, which was about One to Sixteen Houses: That these were light only One-half of the Year, from Michaelmas to Lady-day; and were to continue burning from the Dulk of the Evening till Twelve of the Clock at Night: That in that Halfyear were included about 64 Moon-light Nights, when no Lights at all were made use of; which, deducting the Number of Hours these Lights were computed to continue burning, was about 925; the which appearing insufficient to light so large a City, both from. the Number of Lights, and the small Time they burn, as well as the Kind of Lights made use ofi the fame

being.

J-IJIS-

being, as appeared by the Evidence of Sir Robert Godfchall, rather productive, than preventive, of the Disorders complained of, from the glaring, dazling Light that they gave.

The Committee proceeded to inquire into the Improvements proposed to be made by the Petitioners: To which Purpose,

Sir Robert Godfchall was examined: Who said. That he had made as nice an Inquiry as he could, concerning the Extent of the City, and the proper Places for erecting of Lamps; and, by the Computation he had made, he imagined, That about 4,000 globular Lamps would completely light the City: That the Distance of these from each other, on the same Side of the Way, would be, in the high Streets, about Twenty-five Yards, and, in the Lanes and Alleys, about Thirty-five: but, it being proposed to have Lamps on both Sides of the Way, it would be so contrived, in the Position of them, that each Lamp on one Side of the Way should cut Two on the opposite Side; so that, taking one Side with the other, the Distance of the Lights, throughout the whole Streets, Lanes, and Alleys, would, at a Medium, be about 15 Yards: That it was proposed these Lamps should continue burning from Sun-setting to Sun-riling throughout the whole Year; which will make the Hours they shall be burning, in the whole Year, 4,380.

He then proceeded to lay before the Committee the Expence of maintaining these 4,000 Lamps, how it was proposed the Money for defraying it should be raised, and under what Regulations the same should be put; and said.

That he had made Experiments of the Consumption of Oil; and imagined, That the said,000 Lamps would consume, in the Year, about 450 Tun of Oil; which, reckoning Oil at £. 17 per Tun, one time with another, would amount to £. 7,650: That One hundred Men to be employed, each in the Care of 40 Lamps, at £. 20 per Annum each, would cost £. a,000: That Cotton, Wicks, Breaking of Lamps, Repairs, and Ac-cid» n s, might, one Year with another, be computed at £. 600 per Annum, which would make the whole annual Expence £. 10,250:

That, in order to make the bed Computation of the Houses from whence this Money is to be raised, he had applied to the Surveyor of the Window-lights, and finds there are 14,400 Houses, distinguished into the following Classes j which it is proposed to tax in the following manner j

2.000 Houses under £.10 per Annum, the

Inhabitants of which pay to Church and Poor, at 7 s. per Annum, 700

4,800 Housesat;£.io and under£.20, at ns. 2,880

That the Committee had qonfidered of the said Petition; and had come to several Resolutions; which they had directed hitn to report to the House; and’ he read the Report ih his Place; And afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the said Resolutions were read; and are as follow; viz.

Rt/blved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the low Price of spirituous Liquors is the principal Inducement to the-excessive and pernicious Use thereof.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, in order to prevent the excessive and pernicious Use of spirituous Liquors, a Discouragement be given thereto, by a Duty to be laid on all such Liquors sold by Retail.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Vending, Bartering, or Uttering, of the said Liquors, be reftfained to Persons keeping public Brandy {hops, publick Victualling-houses, Coffee-houses, Ale-houses, and Inn-holders, and to such Apothecaries and Surgeons as {kail make use of the same by way of Medicine only.

Refokved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That no Person keeping a publick Brandy*(hop, a publick Victualling-house, Coffee-house, or Ale-house, or being an Innholder, be permitted to vend, barter, or utter, the said Liquors, but by a Licence, with a Duty made payable thereupon.

A Petition of John Sinclair, eldest Son of Henry late Lord Sinclair, deceased, being offered to be presented to the House;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer, by his Majesty’s Command, acquainted the House, That the same of the Petitioner having been humbly represented to his Majesty, his Majesty gives his Consent, That the House may do therein as they think fit.

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, in the Life-time of his Father, by virtue of an Act, made in the First Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for the Attainder of George Earl of Marischal, William Earl of Seaforth, James Earl of Southejhue, James Earl of Panmuir, and others, of High Treason, unless they shall render themselves to Justice, by a Day certain, therein mentioned, was attainted of High Treason, by the Description of John Sinclair Esquire, commonly called Matter of Sinclair; and that his said late Majesty, by Letters Patent, bearing Date the 21st Day of October, in the Thirteenth Year of his Reign, was pleased, in his great Mercy, to pardon and idischarge the Petitioner of and from Imprisonment, and Execution of his Person, on such Attainder; but that the Petitioner, by reason of the said Attainder, is exposed to many Difficulties, being inca-

pable to sue, or maintain any Action or Suit; and is likewise wholly disabled to take or inherit any real or personal Estate that shall or may hereafter defeend or come to him; and is thereby excluded from the Means of providing for himself, and his unfortunate Family:

And therefore praying, That the House will give Leave to bring in a Bill for removing the Disability and Incapacity occasioned by the said Attainder; or to grant him such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to enable John Sinclair, eldest Son of Henry late Lord Sinclair, deceased, to sue,. or maintain any Action or Suit, notwithstanding his Attainder; and to remove any Disability in him, by reason of his said Attainder, to take or inherit any real or personal Estate that may or shall hereafter defeend or come to him: And that the Lord Glenorchy and the Lord Advocate of Scotland do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses, and of the Gentlemen, Traders, and principal Inhabitants, of the Town of Kendall, and Places adjacent, in the County of Westmorland, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That large Quantities of the Woollen Cloths, called Kendall Cottons, and of Cloths of Woollen and Linen, called Linfeys, are made in the said Town of Kendall, and Places adjacent, and in other Parts of the said County; and that, in the manufacturing thereof, very large Numbers of poor Families have been brought up, and are constantly employed therein, and depend thereon for their Maintenance; and that great Quantities of the same Manufactures are exported into the British Plantations; and that the Return for the same Goods is chiefly Cotton Wool, of which large Quantities are brought back, and have always been manufactured, in several Parts of this Kingdom, into printed, chequered, stripedj and other Fustians; and representing to the House the ill Consequence of prohibiting the said Manufactures of Linen and Woollen made in this Kingdom, or any Branch thereof: And therefore praying. That the Manufactures of this Kingdom, as well those of Linen and Cotton as others, or any Improvement thereof, may not be restrained, but preserved free, by having the Act, made in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, explained, in such manner as to ' the House shall seem most meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the Bill to explain an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act to preserve and encourage the AYoollen and Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom; and for more effectual employing the Poor, by prohibiting the Use and Wear of all printed, painted, Rained, or dyed Callicoes, in Apparel, Iloulhold Stuff, Furniture, or otherwise, alter the 25th Day of December 1722, except as is therein excepted, lb far as relates to Goods made of Linen Yarn and Cotton AVool manufactured in Great Britain; be read a second time.
