A PETITION of the Mayor, Bailiffs, and Bur- Kew geffes of the Town and Borough of New Windsor, AVindfo

in the County of Berks, was presented to the House, and Bridge read; setting forth, That, in the Town and Borough of New Windsor, in the said County, there is, and has been time out of mind, a large publick Bridge over the River of Thames, leading from New Windsor aforesaid to the Town of Eton, in the County of Bucks, and Parts adjacent; which, during all the said Term, has been maintained by the Corporation of New Windsor, by the Money arising from the several customary Tolls, which are due, and payable, for loaded Carriages passing over, and Barges passing under, the said Bridge; and that there is no other Provision made for the maintaining the said Bridge, other than the aforesaid customary Tolls; and that the Petitioners have, of late, laboured under very great Hard-ship and Difficulty in collecting the said Tolls, which are very small and incontiderable, several Persons passing with loaded Carriages over the said Bridge refusing to pay the same, pretending that the same is a free Bridge; whereby the Petitioners are reduced to the Necessity either of acquiefeing in the Lois of the said Tolls, or asserting their Right to the same by a tedious and expensive Course of Law, which the Petitioners are discouraged from pursuing, in regard they must bring separate Actions against every particular Person so refusing to pay the said ac-customed Tolls; and the said Bridge being now in a very ruinous and decayed Condition: Therefore praying, That the Petitioners may be enabled to maintain and repair the said Bridge; and that their Right to the said Tolls may be established; and that the Quantum due, and payable upon all Occasions, may be settled and ascertained, and a more speedy and easy Remedy given, for the Recovery of the same; and such other Relief given as to the House Rial! seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Confi derat ion of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A Petition of the Merchants and Planters trading to, and interested in, his Majesty's Sugar Colonies in America, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That great Quantities of Woolen, Linen, and other Goods, being, for the most part, our own Manufactures, are exported annually, as well to Africa, for the Purchase of Negroes, as to the Sugar Colonies, for the Use of the Inhabitants; and that, with such Goods and Negroes, imported into these Colonies, are purchased Sugar, Cotton, Ginger, and other the Produce of the Plantations; of which, Cotton is a very beneficial Article to the Navigation of this Kingdom; and representing to the House, the Advantage arising from the Plantation of Cotton in the said Colonies, and the Inconvenience arising from any Discouragfement to the same: And therefore praying, That the Bill, now depending in this House, to explain an Act, passed in the Seventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, an Act to preserve and encourage the Woolen and Silk Manufactures of this Kingdom, and for more effectual employing the Poor, by prohibiting the Use and Wear of all printed, painted, stained, or dyed Callicoes, in Apparel, Houshold-stuff, Furniture, or otherwise, after the 25th Day of December 1622, except as is therein excepted, so far as relates to Goods pade of Linen Yarn, and Cotton Wool, manufactured in Great Britain, may pals into a Law.

A Petition of the Master and Wardens of the Company of Bakers, in the City of London, on behalf of themselves, and the rest of the Bakers within the Bills of Mortality, was presented1 to the House* and read; setting forth, That the Meal Weighers, who are Officers appointed to bring in the Prices of Wheat to the Alagi-strates, in order to fix tile Assize of Bread within the City of London, make their Cockets, or Returns, of the Prices of Three different kinds of Wheat, as sold at the Market of Bear Key only; from which Three Prices of Wheat, the Assize of the Three Sorts of Bread, distinguished by the Names of White, Wheaten, and Houshold, is always ascertained; and that the best kind of WLeat at Bear Key is generally fold, in Parcels, with

Wheat of inferior Quality, at One common Price; so that the Aleal Weighers are not able to distinguish the true and real Price of the best kind of Wheat; and that the First Sort of Bread in the Assize Table, distinguished by the Name of White Bread, being that kind of Bread commonly called French Rolls, is, of late Years, greatly improved; and, in making such White Bread, the Petitioners use only the very lined Part of the Flour, produced from the choice!! kind of Wheat, collected not from Bear Key only, but from all the adjacent Markets; and even inch selected Wheat affords but a very small Quantity of this Sort of Flour, which is also used in making the fmeft kind of Fade; and that, although the fin eft Sort of Wheat, mentioned in the Cockets of the Meal Weighers, is not of a Quality fine enough to make the first Sort of Bread, called White Bread, yet the Assize of such White Bread is fixed from the Price of the First Sort of Wheat, inserted in thol’e Cockets; and that the Second Sort of Bread in the Assize Table, distinguished by the Name of Wheaten Bread (which is the best kind of large Bread, wherewith the Families within the City oi London, and Bills of Mortality, are daily served) is made intirely of the First Sort of Wheat mentioned in the Cockets ut the Aleal Weighers; and the Second Sort of Wheat, contained in those Cockets, is not of a sufficient Goodness to make such Wheaten Bread; nevertheless, the Assize of that Wheaten Bread is ascertained according to the Price of that Second Sort of Wheat, as returned by the Aleal Weighers; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that the Assize of Wheaten Bread ought to be settled according to the Price of the First Sort of Wheat mentioned in the Cockets of the Meal Weighers, being the -very Grain of which the Wheaten Bread is made, and that the Assize of the White Bread ought to be advanced in proportion; and that, although the Expences attending the Trade and Business of the Petitioners are very greatly increased since the making tire Table of Assize, yet they have had 110 Allowance in respect to such Increase of Expences; and that, by these means, much the greatest Number of the Petitioners are reduced to very low Circumstances; and the most considerable amongst them, notwithstanding all their Fains, Application, and Frugality, find their Substance daily diminishing: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may he brought in for explaining and amending the Laws now in being for regulating the Price and Assize of Bread; or to give such other Relief to the Petitioners in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee; and that they do examine the A1alter thereof, and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

And it is referred to Mr. Braw/lon, Mr. Bacan, Colonel Bladen, Mr. Alderman Heathcote, Mr. Holland, Lord Pohcarth, Mr. Archer, Lord Sidney Beauclerk, Six James Grant, Mr. Yorke, Lord Gage, Mr. Gybbon, Sir Geo*

Then the said Petition was brought up, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner was a considerable Dealer in the Tobacco Trade; and imported from Virginia very large Quantities of Tobacco, for the Duties whereof he paid to his Majesty several Thousand Pounds per Annum: That the Petitioner, having sustained great Lodes in Trade, became considerably indebted, upon several Bonds given to the Crown, for the Duties on Tobacco; which the Petitioner, and his Sureties, who also had sustained great Lodes, being unable to discharge. Extents ifi’ued thereupon; and they, and their Effects, were seized, and the Petitioner, and his Sureties, were long confined, and their Effects made over for the payment of the said Debt, whereby great Part thereof hath been satisfied; but a considerable Sum still remains unpaid, as appears by the Report of the proper Officer, annexed; which Debt, so remaining due, the Petitioner, and his Sureties, are utterly unable to discharge; and that the Petitioner, and his Sureties, are, by reason of the said Extents, unable to follow any Business, in order to support themselves, and their numerous Families; but hope, in case they shall be allowed their Liberty, that they dial I, by their industry, and Assistance of Friends, be able to raise some Money, in order to compound the said Debt, if they might be permitted so to do: And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in to impower the Commissioners of his Majesty sTreasury, or the Lord High Treasurer, for the Time being, to compound with the Petitioner, and his Sureties, for the said Debt; or that the Petitioner may be otherwise relieved, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon Tomorrow Se-Vennight, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Pet ition.

A Petition of the Merchants of London trading to,

Cadiz, and Port St. Afary's, in the Kingdom of Spain, 1 Acadia was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

That it has been customary, Time immemorial, for the Consul, with the Majority of the British Merchants and Factors residing at Cadiz, and Port St. Mary's, to receive certain small Sums upon Tonnage, and Bale Goods imported into that Bay in British Vessels; which Sums have been applied for answering and defraying the common and unavoidable Expences of the said Merchants and Fabtors, in the Defence of their Privileges, and for Relief of fliipwrecked Mariners, and others his Majesty’s Subjects in Necessity and Distress, and for other charitable Purposes; and the likeCustom is observed by the Factors and Merchants of other Nations, pursuant to Edicts of their respective Sovereigns, granted for that Purpose: That, although this Design, so carried on, hath been found to be of great Lfe and Benefit for the Purposes aforesaid, yet several Persons trading to those Places, have, of late Years, refused to comply with the Payment of the said small Sums, the said Custom not having beenestablished by Authority sufficient to compel an Obedience to it; and, for want of such Authority, the Money collected hath very much diminillied, the Collection fallen very unequal upon several of the said Fabiors and Traders, and the publick Fund arising therefrom hath proved insufficient for answering all the good Purposes intended by it; which occasions the Affairs of the said Factory to suffer very much, and several of his Majesty’s Subjects fliipwrecked, or otherwise distressed, to be reduced to the greatest Extremities, who otherwise might be supported, were the Powers sufficient for the more equal and effectual collecting the small Sums necessary for such publick Uses and Services: And therefore praying. That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid, or that such other Relief may be given as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: and that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House.

Mr. Brampston reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Owners and Occupiers of Lands and Mills adjoining to, and near, the River Stozver, in the Counties of Essex and Suffolk, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and other Owners and Occupiers of Lands and Mills near the said River, was referred, That the Committee, had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows: viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, of the 12th Instant, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the Committee, an Act of Parliament, passed in the 4th and .5th Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for making the River Stozver navigable from Maningtree, in the County of Essex, to the Town of Sudbury, in the County of Suffolk; by which Act, Undertakers were appointed to make the said River navigable, under certain Directions, Restrictions, and Limitations; and Commissioners were also appointed to settle and determine all Differences between the Undertakers, and such Persons whose Lands or Properties might be injured by such Navigation; and upon the Death of any of the said Commissioners, or their Refusal to act, any Fifteen of the surviving Commissioners w'ere impowered to appoint others in their stead: Then,

Thomas Burman Esquine, being examined, said, That, in pursuance of the said Act, the Undertakers cut the Banks and Land adjoining to the said River, without making Satisfaction to the Owners and Occupiers of such Land, as thereby is directed; and have likewise erected Locks, Stanches, and other Works, in order to carry on the said Navigation; and thereby have done, and full continue to do, great Damage to the said Owners and Occupiers:

That the said Undertakers have neither purchased nor set out Towing-paths upon the Banks of the said River: 16

but that the Bargemen frequently make new, and vary their Haling-paths through the Grass, when fit to be cut down.

But he said, That the said Undertakers had compounded with some few of such Owners and Occupiers for Haling-paths; but that, being threatened, by others of the said Occupiers, with the Commencement of Suits, on account of Damages, done, as aforesaid, they made Answer, That they would fell out their Shares in the said Navigation, and that then such Owners and Occupiers might get Satisfaction as they could.

The laid Mr. Burman further said, That most Part of the Commissioners named, in the said Act, for awarding Satisfaction, and adjusting Disputes, as before-mentioned, being dead, others were nominated in the Year 1719; which Nomination was deposited in the Hands of one Mr. Hooper, then a Servant to the fair! Undertakers, with Directions to have it registered with the Clerk of the Peace either for the County of Essex or Suffolk, as the Act: required; but it doth not appear, that it was lo registered:

That the Examinant hath been at Law, on account of Damages he sustained; and, in 1721, brought a Bill in Equity, to discover who were the Undertakers; but was long delayed by means of the Undertakers evasive Answers, and frequent Disposal of their Shares to Pei Ions whole Names he could never find out (there being no Direction in the Act for a Registry in that Cafe), until he obtained an Order of the Court of Chancery to inspect their Books; upon which they agreed with him, and made him Satisfaction:

That, in the Year 1719, about So Commissioners were nominated; and that about 27 of those named in the Act were living in the Year 1731, when a new Nomination w as then made: That, at a Meeting held in the Year 1 733. by the Commissioners ehofe in 1731, many Disputes arose in relation to the several Nominations and Appointments of the Commissioners so made, by reason wdiereof the Owners and Occupiers of Lauds have been, and are, deprived of the Means of ascertaining their Damages by the Mediation of the Commissioners, or Assessments of Juries; and that the Methods and Rules prescribed, in the said Act, for giving Recompence for Damages, as aforesaid, and for recovering the fame, have been found defective.

He said further, That the Commissioners nominated in 1731, at a Meeting, allowed Time to the Undertakers, for One Year, to agree with the Owners of Lands for the Damages done; but, the Undertakers only agreeing with some few of such Owners within that Time, a Jury was summoned and impanelled, as the Act directs; who gave in their Verdict; but the Undertakers gave no Regard to it, telling the Commissioners, That the Nomination in 1731 wgs irregular, as it exceeded the Number limited by the Act; not regarding the Nomination in 1719, which is not registered as the Act requires.

Joseph Hankey Esquire said, That, by the Nomination in the Year 1731, he, with several others, were appointed Commissioners; and that publick Notice was given to the Owners and Occupiers of Lands, and to the Undertakers, of the said Commissioners meeting in 1733; who met several times to mediate, settle, and determine, all Damages, and to adjust all other Matters, about which any Disputes had arisen, concerning, the Premises; and the Commissioners recommended to the Undertakers to compromise the same with the said Owners and Occupiers, and allowed them some time for that Purpose; which the said Undertakers neglecting, further Application was made, by such Owners and Occupiers, to the Conmiissioners; who met again; apd, when the Undertakers fouild that the Commissioners were going to proceed to order Satisfaction to the said Owners and Occupiers, who had long suffered by the Navigation, they told them, That there had been a Nomination of Commissioners in 1719; which most of the Commissioners present, till then, were ignorant of:. Whereupon they ordered Mr. Paris, who acted as Clerk, to look for that Nomination amongst

The CotfMiktee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the following Witnesses were examined; viz.

Mr. James Church: Who said, Thai; the Manufacture of Sail-cloth of this Kingdom is, of late Years, brought to lo great Perfection, that it is of equal Goodness, and in many Respects superior, to the Cloth of any other Country, the Thread being spun finer, struck closer, and much evener, and made of better Materials: That he had exported several Bolts of Ejiglish Sail-cloth to New England, and St. Christophers where it was highly approved of; but that the same cannot be fold so cheap as Jtuffia Sail-cloth, though it is now fold £. 20 per Cent. -cheaper th&n what it was 3,0 Years ago:

That the Witness had 500 Bolts of Sail-cloth lent him from Russia to dispose of; but, it being much inferior to the Sail-cloth manufactured in England, he refused the said Commission, becausb he would encourage the English Manufacture.

Mr. William Blakeway, Sail-maker, and Captain 'Thomas King, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. James Church, as to the English Sail-cloth being of equal Goodness, and in many Respects superior, to the Sail-cloth of any other Country.

Mr. Blakeway further said, That, if further Encouragement was given to the said Manufacture, the Poor of all Sorts might be employed; and £. 200,000 per Annum would be saved to the Nation, which is now paid for the Imports of foreign Sail-cloth.

And Captain King added, That the English Sail-cloth is better than foreign; he having experienced the Goodness of it by binding a Sail made of the best Holland's Duck to one Yard, and English Sail-cloth to another Yard; and that the English Cloth lasted as long, and wore better than the Holland's Duck.

Mr. Samuel Gower, Manufacturer of Sail-cloth, said, That Persons of both Sexes, from Seven to Seventy Years of Age, are employed in the said Manufacture, and get a Livelihood, who otherwise, some, by reason of their tender Age, and others, by reason of the Infirmities of old Age, being incapable of other Labour, must necessai ily become burdensome to their several Parishes:

That there are great Numbers of the said Manufacturers in this Kingdom, many whereof live in or near tooft of the Sea Ports; and employ great Numbers of poor Children in spinning of Yarn, and turning the Wheels-, and the ancient stople ia spinning, and winding of Quills for the Weavers.

Mr. John Garwdy feid, That, about a Year and Half since, hefet up a Manufacture of Sail-cloth at Worcester, where formerly a Woolen Manufacture had been carried on for making Broad Cloths for the Turkey Trade; which falling to Decay, he had reason to believe, that the Persons employed in the Woolen Manufacture would easily faH into the Method of making Sail-cloth; and, upon Tryal, he found, that the Weavers of the Woolen Cloths soon made themselves Mailers of the Weaving of Sail cloth; and that, if he had not set up this Manufacture, great N umbers of Poor of that Place, now employ-fed, must have become burdensome to their respective SParishes:

That Boys, Girls, old Men, and Women, are employed in Spinning of Yarn, Turning of Wheels, and Winding of Quills, and get the same Wages as they used to do when employed in the Manufacturing of Woolen Goods; and that he works upwards of 50 Looms, and each Loom employs upwards of 20 Persons, in the several Branches Of the said Manufacture.

Mr. John Pincock, Manufacturer of Sail-cloth, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Gower and Mr. Gar-1my, of Persons ot both Sexes being employed in the said Manufacture, from Seven to Seventy Years of Age: And he further said, That, some time since, he worked 38 Looms; but, finding the Trade decline, he has reduced them to 28: That he could have fold great Quantities of English Sail-cloth to Merchants, for Exportation; but

4.1735.

they would not havfe it, because they could have Sailcloth of Raffia Two Pence per Yard cheaper, even with the Benefit of the present Bounty considered; and that the Russia Sail-cloth is not so good as the English; and that, if the English Manufacturers were enabled to reduce the Price of their Cloth 2 d. a Yard, it would have the Preference of foreign Sail -cloth, and there would footi be Looms and Hands sufficient to supply all Merchants for Shipping, and for Exportation.

Then the Petitioners laid before thfe Committee, an Act, passed in the Twelfth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, and also another Act, passed in the Fourth Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for theincreasing and making the said Manufacture more extensive in this Kingdom; Which said last mentioned Act being rfead;

Mr. Geo. JFaple, Factor for English Sail-cloth, said, That, notwithstanding the Encouragement given by the said Acts, the same is found* by Exjxjrience, not sufficient to reduce the Price of British Sail-cloth to dn Equality with the Sail-cloth imported from foreign Countries; and that he has always been defeated in his Attempts to fell thfe English Sail-cloth; the Russia Sail-cloth being 2 d. per Yard cheaper, though not lb good; That he had received Orders from several Merchants to lend them English Sail-cloth; but that their Sail-makers persuaded them to the Use of Russia Sail-cloth, it being so much cheaper.

And he further said, That the best English Sail-cloth is 24 Inches wide, and each Piece 40 Yards long, and can^ not be sold for less than 15 d. per Yard; but is better and more durable, than the Russia, each Piece of which is about 30 Inches wide, and 38 Yards long, which is fold for 12 d. per Yard, or under.

Mr. Blakeway confirmed the last Part of the Evidence given by Mr. JVaple; and added, That the last Contraft made with the Commissioners of the Navy, for Sail-cloth, was at the Price of about Fourteen Pence Halfpeny per Yard; but that it was the lowest they ever made; and that the English Sail-cloth is so much better in Quality than the Russia, as the Difference is in Breadth; and that Sail-cloth 24 Inches wide is stronger than that of Thirty; for that, the more Seams there is in a Sail, the stronger it is.

Ordered, That the said Report be referred to the Consideration of a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, upon this Day Seven-night, resolveitfelfinto a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report.

Mr. Serjeant Belfield, Recorder of the City of Exon, was examined: Who said, That he had known the said City above Fifty Years; and that, at the time when the Incendiaries sent Letters about the Country, Application was made, by the Inhabitants, to the Mayor and Aldermen, to enlighten the Streets of the said City, and to keep a strong and regular Watch therein, as the most effectual Means to (ecure their Lives and Properties against the Violences then threatened; and that thereupon a Con-

fultation was had with him, how to raise Money to defray that Expence; and his Opinion was, That a Bye-law should be made, for railing such Money upon the Inhabitants, the Corporation having, before that time, fold almost all their real Estate, in order to preserve the Navigation of the River Ex, very near the City, and were many Thousand Pounds in Debt: That, in pursuance of his Advice, a Bye-law was accordingly prepared, an8 offered to the Judges of Assize, for their Allowance; but it being to charge the Subject with the Payment of Money, they were of Opinion, That it was a Matter proper only for the legislative Power to do:

And he further said, That the Streets of the City were kept so dirty, that they were a Scandal, as well as a Nuisance, to the Inhabitants; and that he knew of no compulsory Means to oblige the Inhabitants to cleanse the fame, or to provide Lights, and a Watch; for want of which, several Persons have been tempted to take ill Courses, and were brought before him, as Recorder, and have been convicted of Felonies; some of which Persons, he believed, would not have had an Opportunity of committing those Crimes, had there been a sufficient Quantity of Lights in the Streets, and a strong Watch.

Mr. Thomas Heath, being examined, confirmed Part of the Evidence of Mr. Serjeant Belfield', in relation to the Dirtiness of the Streets, and the Want of Lights therein, and a regular and strong Watch: And said further, That he was One of the Four Bailiffs of the City, at the time that the Incendiaries sent about Letters 5 and that the Citizens being called together by the Mayor, upon that Occasion, it was their unanimous Opinion, That the only Way to preserve the Properties of the Citizens, and Persons resorting to the City, was to provide a sufficient Quantity of Lights in the Streets thereof, and a strong Watch within the same.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better cleansing and enlightening the Streets of the City of Exon, within the Walls thereof and for keeping a strong and regular Watch therein, in the Night-time: And that Sir Henry Northcote, Mr. Rolle, Sir Wm. Courtenay, and Mr. Bampjylde, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Upon the Petition of Smile Cujl Esquire, complaining of an undue Ejection and Return o {John Pro by Esquire, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Stamford, in the County of Lincoln;

The Committee have examined*the Merits of this Election.

The Counsel for the Petitioner alleged. That Slam-ford w as a Borough by Prescription; and that no Right of Election had hitherto been settled there:

That the Right of FJeftion is in the Housholders, Inhabitants within the Borough, paying Scotland Lot there, and not receiving Alms or publick Charities.

The Counsel for the Sitting Member alleged. That the Right of FJeftion is in the Inhabitants, paying Scotland Lot, and not receiving Alms or public Charity.

The Petitioner's Counsel, to prove the Right of Election to be as itated by them, called the following Witnesses; viz.

Thomas lialviflon, aged Seventy-four Years: Who said, That he had known the Borough of Stamford 52 or 53 Years; and had been present at several Elections there; and that he had taken the Poll twice; and was present at the Election, when Sir Pury Cujl and Mr, Vol. 22.

Bertie stood Candidates: That all Persons, being Hous-holders paying Scotland Lot, voted: That, at the Two next Elections after the Convention, One Person for each House only voted: That he remembered four or Five Persons, who then offered to vote, were rejected, as not paying Scotland Lot.

But the Witness said, That he had left Stanford about 36 Years: That no Inhabitants were admitted to vote that were not Housholders.

Being asked, If he knew'any Instance of Inhabitants paying Scotland Lot, refit fed for not being 1 Joufh<»lders? lie said. That one Warrington, who rented a Shop in St. Michael's Parish, was not admitted to vote at the Election after the Convention.

John Hand, aged Seventy-two Years, said, That he was born at Stamford, and lived Twenty-five Years there; and was present at Three Elections: That he remembered the Elections of Mr. Noel and Sir Pury Cujl, in the latter End of King Charles's Reign, when Mr. Noel was chose: That none were then admitted to vote hut Houftkeepers who paid to the Poor, and but One Vote for each House, was allowed to poll: That at the Ejection ol Sir Punj Cujl. the Right ot Vt;ng was the faint*; and that he never knew any hut Housekeepers admired to poll; nor did he ever know Two Votes admitted for One House, or Persons who kept Shops only, or Inmate*, admitted to poll; but that all who Wciv not Housholders were always rejected.

Bring cross-examined, he said, That he never knew any Person paying Scotland Lot refused.

John Clan anti IVm. Walgrave, the Eirft aged 66, the other 72 Year?, and both horn in Stamford, gave Evidence, That they have always lived in the! own; and r« membered Mr. Noel's Elen ion about 58 Years ago: That the Right of FJeftion was in lloul.-keepers paying to Church and Poor: And Walgrave laid, That though a Lodger or Inmate paid the Rates, yet they had no Right to vote.

Nathanael Wild, aged 77 Years, said. That he had known Stamford all his Life-time: That the Right of Lien ion is in Housholders paying to Church and Poor: But he laid, That he had left Stamford about 20 Years, John Blake said, That lie had known Stamford 34 Years; and that the Right of Election is in Housholders paying Scotland Lot; and that Lodgers and Inmates paying Scotland Lot have no Right.

Being asked, If he remembered Mr. Bertie's Election? he said, lie did, and then took the Poll: That Inmates claimed to vote, and were queried: That they were about 36 in Number, and some of them paid Scotland Lot; and that all that voted were queried, if not Housholders:

That, at the Election Seven or Eight Yrears ago, 400 and Eight Voters were polled.

Being cross-examined, he said, That about Seven or Eight voted at that Election, who were not Housholders, and were therefore queried: That there were about 16 or 18 queried on each Side; but that some were not queried, who were Partners in Business; and, he believes, some of them w^ere polled.

And being asked, Why he had asserted, in the Firfi Part of his Evidence, That about 36 Inmates had voted, and were queried ? he said, He spoke at random.

That he never remembered Two or Three Persons voting for One House; but that he believed that Two may have voted for the same Hpufe.

Being asked, Whether Alderman South and Mr. Whitfield were queried at the Election of Mr. Bertie ? he said, That some w ere queried; but he could not remember the particular Objections; but believed, that Alderman South had a Right, and that he boarded, at that time, with Mr. Gardner; and that Mr. Whitfield lived with Mr. Lock% and carried on Trade on one Side of his Shop.

That feieral Consultations have been had, relating to the Condition of the Church, and it was always determined to lie irrcpairable . , which occasioned some of the principal Inhabitants, about a Month before the Meeting of the Vestry in July to subscribe to-

That publick Notice was given of the Vestry that was held July 2id, 173.), at which the Committee was appointed to view the Church; who, taking Workmen to their Abidance, scarclied into its Defects, and reported their Opinions thereof.

Mr. Adam Lugg, being examined, gave Evidence, the same in Subdance with Huttons; and said further, That Divine Service is not now performed in the Body of the Church, but in the Three Quires of the Chancels, lit the East End, which were fitted up by the Archdeacon’s Order, on his View, and after Presentment m;ide by the Churchwardens: That One of the Three Chancels belongs to Sir Sc oil Hickman; the other to the Bishop of Lincoln*, and the 1 bird to the Town, which they used as a School, till the Archdeacon’s Order: That he has for many Years heard several of Vo t. 22.

the Inhabitants of Gainsborough express their Desire for a new Church, because of the Badness and Inconvenience of the old one, the Floor whereof lies so near the Springs, that sometimes the People are reduced to the Ncccfiity of walking upon Planks, to get to their I*e\vs; but, as the Poor’s Rate of the Town was very high, being often 3*. or jjt. and 6 d. in the Pound, the Inhabitants were unable to enter upon Measures to rebuild the fame: That, as to the Method of rating Lands there, they are charged but at Half Value; but how personal Estates are taxed, the Witness could give no Account.

Iking examined. Whether certain Lands, called Thunnock, were rated to the Repair of the Church; he said, That he had seen some of the old, and some of the late Rules, wherein the Names of the Occupiers of those Lands were put, hut no Charge or Sum was set against them j hut that he believed, that Thunnock Eliate is charged to the Poor, but not to the Church; because it repairs that Part called Thunnock's Quire, which is not One of the Three Quires before-mentioned, but a Part of the Church proposed be rebuilt, and which the Hamlet of Thunnock is afterwards to repair, in the same manner as now.

Upon further F.xamination, he said, That, in his Opinion, the Church is not worse now than it was 12 Years ago; but, upon opening the Drawing of the Church, many Cracks were discovered quite through iii the Walls, and also some Settlements:

That, at a publick Meeting, it was proposed to raise Money for defraying the Expence of an Act of Parliament to rebuild the Church; and a Title of aSubfcrip-tion, for that Purpose, was wrote in the Presence of several Inhabitants, and ligned by all present, in the Year 1 731: That the Examinant went round the Town with the said Subscription; and believed he saw the several Subscribers sign their Names, or order them to be signed.

Mr. Fume is Smith of Warwick, said, That, in No-vcmhtr 1731, lie came to Gainsborough, to examine the Condition of the Church: That, ha\ ing taken Workmen to his Abidance, he turned the Lead oft*the Beams in several Places, and likewise from the Corvels of Wood, their Supports: which he found so much decayed, that he could thrustliis Stick through the Ends of 1 he Beams; and that he found the Beams of the Out Kies likewise v< rv much decayed: That the Middle of the Beams, he said, are found; but the Ends are rotted lo far liom the Wall, and so much, that they cannot be repaired; which has been partly occasioned by the ill Laying of the Gutters from the first: That he plumbed the South Pillars, which are ab&ut lo Feet high, but do not exceed Two Feet Two Inches in Diameter, and found them Two Inches out of the Upright in every Three Feet and Half, leaning to the South: That those at the West End, joining to the Tower, which are arched over, are Three Inches out of the Upright iri every Three Feet and Half, leaning to the West: That the North Pillars are the fame; and all lean to the West One Inch in Three Feet and an Half, which he takes to have been occasioned by the Badness of their Foundations: That he perceived that the Church in general was built with bad Materials, the Stoncsover the Arches being very i’mall, and the Mortar bad: That there are several Cracks above the Arches, over the Pillars, though none, as he remembered, in the Pillars themselves: That, on plumbing the South Wall, which is 20 Feet high, he found it overhung One Foot: That the Middle Ille Wall on the South Side, which is 35 or 36 Feet high, overhung, from Top to Bottom, One Foot Seven Inches: The North Wall of the Middle Ille, of the same Height, overhung, towards the South, One Foot Four Inches; and the North Outside Wall inclines the same way, from an Upright, Nine or Ten inches: That there are Two Timber Props in the Inside of the Church, which are footed to the Bottom of the South Wall, and run through the South Roof into a Piece of Timber; and there are Laces from thore Props, which spread Four or Five Feet on each Side, for the

The Witness said, That, in taking this Survey, he had Four other skilful Persons to assist him; who agreed in Opinion with him, and signed a Report he had drawn up, to be presented to the Parishioners who employed him: That he was Two Days in taking the said Survey; and which he could not have beeu exact in, without turning the Lead off the Timber, and taking the Plaister off the Walls, and plumbing them, and the Pillars:

That he had made a Computation of the Expence of building a new Church (but not the Steeple) capable of containing 1,400 People, according to the Price of Materials at Gainsborough; and he laid before the Com-ihittee the Plan and Estimate thereof, which amounts to 2,834 js. od.; but he said, That, leaving out the Ornaments, if it was to be built plain with Stone, it would abate £. 100 or something more; and, if of Brick, it would save much more:

That Thunnock's Quire is the strongest Part of the Church; but the Witness thinks itfhould be pulled down, if a new Church is built; and that it would Jeffen the Expence considerably to pull down the Chancels, and not to rebuild them, they being built of better Materials than the red of the Church, and, in lieu of them, to erect a semicircular Alcove for the Communion Table: That, if they arekept up, it will be necessary to raise them Three Feet; which will occasion a further Expence of£. 218 by making new Windows, 8Cc.

Mr. Hutton, being again examined, said. That the Committeeappointed by a Vestry to examine the State and Condition of the Church, after the Survey by Mr. Bickerton and Mr. Smith, met, and agreed upon a Report, which was communicated to many of the principal. b^t, notwithstanding the Regulations made; by that'AH, and tile many Penalties the Smugglers of Tea, and their Accomplices, are liable to by Law, the Petitioners have fatally experienced the c]Laude(tine Importation of this Commodity is so far from being prevented, that it is carried on to such a Degree, that the Petitioners have theftrongeftReafon to believe, that near One-balf of the Tea consumpd in this Kingdom pays no Duty; and that the very high Duty of 4 v. per Pound, as well as the Inequality of its being laid, are the principal Foundation of the pernicious Practice of Smuggling, the coarser Sorts bearing much too gi-eat a Proportion of the said Duty, and by the Smugglers bought abroad at One-third of the Price it will Hand the fairTrader in at home; and that unless some Remedy be applied, effectually to prevent this known Evil, the Petitioners, and all fairTra-ders, will be under extreme Difficulties in carrying on their Trade, by reason of the Di fad vantages they are under, from the Practices of Smuggling, as well as from the Hardships they endure, and the Trouble they arp put to, by the Execution of the said Act; and that IhePetitioners conceive the most effectual Means of putting a Stop to the clandestine Importation of Tea, will be to alter the present Duty of 4,$*. per Pound, to a certain Rate ad valorem, according to the Prices Tea shall fell for at the East India Company’sSale; by which Alteration the Pe* titi oners apprehend, the Amount of the Duty to the Publick will be equivalent, considering the Quantity now fraudulently imported will be then added to the Revenue: And therefore, for the Preservation of this Trade to the Petitioners, by putting an End to the Practice of Smuggling, and for securing a Revenue to the Publick, by the Importation of this Commodity, in British Ships, from China, and other Parts of India; and give the Petitioner? such Relief as to the House shall feeni meet.

The Witnesses said, That the City had been put to great Expence at the time of the Rebellion in the Year 1715; and, being brought under a great Load of Debt were lately necessitated to fell off their Lands, to discharge the fame.

That the public Buildings of the City want Repair, particularly the Church called The Wynd, which, from its ruinous Condition, must of Necessity be rebuilt; and, the City becoming very populous, there will be a Necessity for building another Church:

That the Expence of the City hath been increased, by paving the Streets of the Village of Garhells, upholding the Bridge over the River Clyde, and other Bridges and Avenues leading to the said City:

Thai the said Village holds Feu of the City; and its Inhabitants are entirely supported by the Trade thereof, enjoying almost every Privilege equal with the Citizens:

That the Village of Port Glasgow likewise holding Feu of the City, and paying to it upwards of £.100 in Fee-farm, was anciently purchased, and the Harbour built at the Charge of the City:

That the said City voluntarily employed the above Sum in repairing and enlarging the Harbour, and supporting the other Works of the Village of Port Glas gozoy and in pacing the Ministers Stipends; but that this Sum is not sufficient for these Purposes, without putting the City to an additional Charge.

Upon Examination of the whole Matter, it appeared to the Committee, That the Debt of the said City will inevitably increase by the Deficiency aforesaid; and that the City will be unable to prevent the fame, or carry on the Works aforesaid, unless the Term in the said Act, which expires the iff Day of November 1738, be prolonged, and unless the Duty be extended over the said Villages of Garbells and Port Glasgow, holding Feu of the said City.

Avon O IR Abraham Elton reported from the Committee, to Navigation. whom the Petition of Edward Heylin and Thomas Fane Esquires, John Wynne, Walter Hawksworth, Edward Gregory, and Onesiphorus Tyndal, Merchants, on behalf of themselves, and several other Merchants and Traders within the City of Bristol, and Parts adjacent, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the lame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the Committee, An Act of Parliament, passed in the Tenth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, for making the River Avon, in the Counties of Somerset and Gloucester, navigable, from the City of Bath, to or near Hanham’s Mills. Then,

Mr Hen. Parker was examined: Who said, That, in pursuance of the Powers given by the said Act, the Navigation of the River Avon was completed about Eight Years ago, from a new Quay at or near the City of Bath, to Hanhams Mills; and that the same is capable of being further extended to or near the Towns of Bradford, Melksham, La cock, and Chippenham, in the County of Wilts.

Mr.# Smith, being examined, said, That in 1734, a Survey was taken of the Ground through which the Navigation was intended to be carried; and that the same Was found practicable.

The said Mr. Hen. Parker, and Mr. Timothy Gr if cold, being severally examined, said, That, in and near the Towns of Bradford, Melksham, Lacock, and Chippenham, considerable Manufactures in the Cloathing Trade are carried on; and that the extending the said Navigation to those Towns will be of great Benefit to the fame, and will reduce the Price of Carriage of all the Materials made use of in the said Manufactures, 40$. a Load being now paid for the Carriages of such Manufactures to some of the Places to which the Navigation is intended to be carried.

And they further said, That the said Navigation will also be of great Advantage to the Landed Interest, by reason the Farmers will be able to carry their Corn, and particularly Barley, to the Markets, much cheaper than they can now- do; and that, in case the said Navigation is carried on, the Roads will be preserved, which, at this time, are in a very ruinous Condition, particularly the Road leading from Bath to the Towns of Bradford and Melksham.

Then the Petitioners laid before the Committee, Articles of Agreement bearing Date the 17th Day of Feb. i?35; whereby it is agreed, That the Navigation of the said River shall be extended to the Towns before-mentioned, under certain Conditions and Restrictions, in case an Act of Parliament can be obtained for that Purpose.

Mr. Hervey reported from the Committee, to whom Bury St. the Petition of the Aldermen, Recorder, capital Burgesses, Edmund's and Burgesses, of the Common Council of the Burgh of Streets, &e. Buiy St. Edmunds, in the County of Suffolk, and also the Petition of the principal Inhabitants of the Burgh of Bury St. Edmunds, in the County of Suffolk, were referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petitions; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as folio weth; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matters of the Petitions:

And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Reverend Mr. John Bat ley was examined: Who said, That the Streets and Highways within the said Town are very much out of Repair, and that several Parts thereof want paving: That Surveyors every Year are regularly appointed, to see that the said Highways and Streets kept in good Repair; and have constantly done their Duty, as far as they were able; but, the Number of Inhabitants being upwards of 7,000, he apprehends it to be impossible that the Surveyors should know when the Statute-work is done; and that, if the Laws relating to the same were rigorously put in Execution, they would be attended with very great Hardship to the poorer Sort of People.

And he further said, That the Streets of the said Town cut one another at Right Angles; so that the enlightening of them would thereby be considerably less expensive, inasmuch as one Lamp would throw a Light into several Streets.

The Petitioners then proceeded to lay before the Committee, so much of the Statute of Windufter, 13* Edit;.

Imi, as rebates to the Watch and Ward to be kept in great Towns.

And Mr. Batley, being again examined, said, That the said Statute had been complied with in the Town of Bury; but that the Watch and Ward, kept in pursuance of it, is of little or no Ule, and of a considerable Expence to the Inhabitants of the said Burgh.

Sir Charles Turner, according to Order, reported from Ways and the Committee of the whole House, whom it was refer- Mean*; red to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, for all spirituous Liquors which any Retailer thereof shall, from and after the 24th Day of June 1736, be possessed of, there be granted to his Majesty a Duty of Twenty Shillings per Gallon.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That, from and after the Q 4th Day of June 1736, the Sum of Fifty Pounds yearly shall be paid to his Majesty for a Licence to be taken out yearly by every Person keeping a publick Brandy-lhop, a publick Vi&ualing^house, Coffee-house, or Alehouse, or being an Innholder, who shal vend, barter, or utter, any such spirituous LiqUors. \

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Duty and Revenue which shall ariseby Licences for vending Brandy or Spirits, as also the present Duties on low Wines, strong Waters, Brandy, Rum, Arrack, and all other Spirits, whether foreign or British, and such Duties as shall arise by retailing the fame, be united to, and made Part of, the General or Aggregate Fund established by the Act of the First of King George the First, and be issued and applied to the Uses to which the said Fund is or shall be made applicable.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That all the several Annuities, Payments, and other Appropriations, which are now charged upon, and pay-:

able out of, the said several Duties on strong Waters,

Brandy, Rum, Arrack, or any other Spirits, be charged upon, and made payable out of, the said Aggregate Fund.

n ®e* of Watermen and Lightermen, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the said Company, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That in case the Bill, how depending in this House, for erecting a Bridge cross the River Thames, should pass into a Law, it will tend to obstruct the Navigation of the River Thames, and will highly prejudice the Members of the said Company, by greatly lessening, if not totally destroying, several Ferries between Vauxhall and the Temple, which, by an Alt of the 1 ith and 12th of King William, they have a Power to work on Sundays, and produce a very considerable Sum yearly, which is applied towards the Maintenance of poor decayed and aged Watermen and Lightermen* their Widows and Children; and many Hundreds, who are able and willing to work on the other Days of the Week, will be deprived of their daily Livelihood, in carrying Passengers, Goods, and Merchandizes, as well up and down, as cross, the said River; by which means , the Old and Decrepit will become chargeable upon their

respective Parishes, and the Young and Aide must be obliged to seek their Bread in foreign Parts; And therefore praying the Ifoufe to t ike the Premises into Consideration; and that they may be heard, by themselves, or Counsel, against the said Bill,

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the Borough of South-tvark, in the County of Surrey, was presentec! to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners apprehend, that, should the Bill, now depending in this House, for building a Bridge cross the River Thames, pass into a Law, the Trade and Estates of the said Borough will be greatly affected, and the Inhabitants thereof rendered unable to support themselves under the heavy Taxes they now pay, which must be increased by the Poverty of great Numbers of Watermen, who are Parishioners and Inhabitants of the several Parishes, within the said Borough, who, for want of Employment, must become a Burden to the said Parishes; and representing also to the House, That, by the late great Flood which happened in February last, innumerable Damages have been sustained by a great Number of the Petitioners, and others; and that, as the Petitioners apprehend, should such a Bridge be built, as intended by the said Bill, it would greatly obstruct the Navigation of the said River, and thereby occasion frequent Inundations, to the great Damage of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, as well as the Publick in general: And therefore praying the House, That they may be heard, by their Counsel, agaiilft the said Bill, before the same pass into a Law.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table until the said Bill be read the Third time; and that the Petitioners, if they think fit, be then heard, by their Counsel, against the said Bill.

tegiftry of Mr. Alderman Willimot reported from the Committee, Ships. the Petition of the several Persons, whose

Names are thereunto subscribed, being Merchants, Owners, Part Owners, Commanders, or Mailers, of Ships and Vessels employed in the Trade of Great Britain, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerks Table: Where the same was read; and the Report, and R/elblutions of the Committee, are as followeth; viz.

The Committee have, perfuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof, the following Witnesses were examined; viz.

Mr. Thomas Hopkins said, That his Father, now deceased, had had a Bill of Sale made to him of Three Eighth Parts of a Ship, called The Yeoman's and Saucolt; which Bill the Witness produced; but that the same being found not valid, the whole Property therein w ill be loft.

Mr. Samuel Bonham said, That he advanced £. 1,120, in the Year 1734, upon the Credit of the before-mentioned Ship; and it was found afterwards, that the same had been mortgaged Four times over to different Persons; whereby the Witness, and several others, must be considerable Losers, it being apprehended, that, if a Law Suit was commenced, the First Bill of Sale would be

adjudged to have the Preference.

Mr. Slingsby Bethell, Merchant, said. That he had advanced 815 on the said Ship, and took a Bill of Sale for One Moiety thereof; but will be in Danger of losing his Property by the prior Mortgages.

Mr. Richard Gapper said, That, about Five Years ago, he bought One Sixteenth Part of a Hoy, of Daniel Simons, Malter, deceased, who before had fold One Sixteenth Part of the said Hoy, more than he had a Right to do; by which means the Witness loft his whole Money: And he further said, That lie had purchased the Sixteenth Part of a Ship, the Matter of which paid him several Dividends of Profits arising therefrom; but, after the Death of the said Master, it was discovered that the Ship was sold by the Person who had the grand Bill of Sale made to him; by which means, the Examinant, with Two others, having each One Sixteenth in the said Ship, loft the Parts that they had purchased.

Mr. Samuel Bonham being asked, If that when Ships are registeredat the Custom-house, the Owners Names ard registered ? heanswered. That they were: But said, That he is of Opinion, That the Intent of such Registry is only to notify, that the Ships are British built, and have British Owners, the Mailer then making Oath, That no Foreigner is concerned therein; and he does not think that such Registry will prevent the Frauds committed by the Ow ners of Ships.

And being aiked, Whether it is not usual for Persons, when they purchase any Part of a Ship, to have Recourse to the grand Bill of Sale ? he said, It was not usual, unless they have an ill Opinion of the Seller; it sometimes happening that the grand Bill of Sale is beyond the Sea, and the Seller in England; and that every Person having a Share or Part in any Ship, has a different Bill of Sale made to them; and that Shares are often branched out into Halves, Quarters, or lesser Parts, which are not indorsed on the grand Bill of Sale.

And being aiked, If the Part of a Ship being indorsed on the grand Bill of Sale, will make it a Security agffinft a Bill of Sale of a Part not indorsed, though prior in Time to that indorsed ? he answered, That it would not; for the Person who had not his Part indorsed on the grand ' Voj*. 22L

64}

Bill of Sale, if it appeared that it was prior in Date, would have the Title:

That if the Captain, who has the grand Bill of Sale, takes it with him abroad, the Buyer of any Part of a Ship is prevented having Recourse thereto.

Mr. Slingsby Bethell, being further examined, and aiked, What Ships are registered at the Custom-house, and in what manner ? He said, That those trading to the Plantations are obliged to be registered; but it is only to notify, that they are British built, and have British Owners; but that he don’t know' that the Owners are particularly named in the Register; and that the Register does not ascertain the property they have in the Ship.

Mr. Ephraim Haden said, That he purchased Part of a Ship, which being fold more than once over, he loft his Property therein: And he, and Mr. Gapptr, and Mr.

Bonham, severally said, That Persons are greatly discouraged from lending Money on Ships, or Parts of Ships, the Security for the same being so precarious.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the Petitioners have proved the Allegations of their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That the House be moved. That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the establishing an Office within the City of London, and in any otl^cr Port or Ports, which shall desire to have an Office erected within their respective Ports, for the Register ing of Bills of Sale of trading Ships, and Parts of such Ships and Vessels built, and hereafter to be built, to prevent the Frauds and clandestine Sales therein committed.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the establishing an Office within the City of London, for the Registering Bills of Sale of trading Ships, and Parts of such Ships and Vessels built, and hereafter to be built, to prevent the Frauds and clandestine Sales therein committed:

Sail-cloth Mr. Alderman Willimolty according to Order, reported Manufacture. from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Report from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Makers of Sail-cloth, and others, in behalf of themselves, and many Thousands Of the Poor in this Kingdom, employed in the manufacturing thereof, was referred, the Resolutions which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place, and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and are as follows; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a further Encouragement be given to the Manufacture of British Sail-cloth.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Duties payable on foreign Sail-cloth imported into this Kingdom be more effectually secured.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That every Ship which shall be built in Great Britain, or in the British Plantations in America, from and after the 24th Day of June next, shall, upon her first setting out, have One full Set of Sails made of British Canvas.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That no Sail-cloth, from and after the 24 th Day of June next, he exported to the British Plantations in America, but such only as is manufactured in Great Britain or Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, from and after the 24th Day of June 1738, all British Ships or Vessels of 200 Tons Admeasurement, or upwards, be fumished with One full Suit of Sails made of British Sail-cloth.

And the Titles of the said Copy and Translation were read.

The Translation is as follows; viz.

Whereas the most Serene and most Potent Prince George the Second, by the Grace of God King of Great Britain, Fram e, and Ireland, Defender of the Faith, Duke of Bmnfwkk and Lnncnberg, Arch Trea-fnrer and Prince Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, S c. and the most Serene, most High, and most Potent, Prineefs Anne, likewise by the Grace of God Czarina and Great Duciiefs of all the Great, IJttle, and White Raffias, Sole Monarch of Muscovia, Kiovia, Ulodomiria, Xovogardia, Czarina of Cazan, Czarina of AJiracan, Czarina of Siberia, Lady of Pfcovia, and Great Duciiefs of Smolcn/ko, Tueria, Jugoria, Permia, lr\atkia, Bolgaria, and other Places, Lady and Great Ducbefs of the Lower Xovogardia, Tzemihovia, Rezania, Ro-Jtovia, Jaroffivia, Belooforia, I?doria, Ohdoria, Condinia, and Empress of all the Coasts of the North, Lady of the Lands of Iberia, Cartalinia, and Gruzinia, Czarina of Caberdinnia, Circoffin, and the Dukes of the Mountains, and of many other Dominions and Countries East, West, and North, Hcireft, Successor, Lady, and Ruler, e£c. have considered, that there has been, for a very long time, an Intercourse of Commerce and good Friendship between their Territories and Subjects reciprocally, without having been regulated and established by any fixed and particular Convention; and being defirousto render this Correspondence more firm and lifting, by such Regulations and Conditions as might remove some Difficulties that have arisen therein, and put the Trade and Navigation upon a Foundation that might better answer the mutual good Intelligence that fubiifts between the said King, and the said Czarina, and their Dominions and Subjects, they have thought fit to name and authorize Ministers on the one Side, and on the other, for that Purpose; that is to say. His Majesty the King of Great Britain, 8Cc. has named, for Commissary and Plenipotentiary on his Part, the Sieur Claudius Rondeau, his Resident at the Court of her Czarish Majesty; and her Majesty the Czarina of all the Rujffias, tfc. hath named, for Commissaries and Plenipotentiaries on her Part, her Cabinet Minister, actual Privy Counsellor, and Knight of the Order of St. Andrtry, Henry John Frederick, Count of Overman, as also her Cabinet Minister, actual Privy Counsellor, and Knight Vo l.

647

of the Order of St. Andrew, Prinfce Alexti Czercafcoy', Commercial ai likewise her actual Privy Counsellor, Senator, and with President of the College of Commerce, and Knight of Ru the Order of the White Eagle, Baron Peter de Schap-hirojf; who having conferred together by virtue of their respective full Powers, have agreed upon the Articles following:

1.

The Peafce, Friendship, and good Correspondence, which happily subsist between their Majesties of Great Britain, and of all the Rujffias, shall be confirmed and settled by this Treaty; so that from this time forward, and for the future, there shall be, between the Crown of Great Britain, on the one Side, and the Crown of all the Rujffias, 00 the other, as also between their States,

Countries, Kingtloms, Dominions, and Territories, which are under their Obedience, a true, sincere, firm, and perfect* Peace* Amity, and good Intelligence, which shall last for ever*and be inviolably preserved, as well by Land as by Sea, and upon firelh Waters; and the Subjects,

People, and Inhabitants, on the one Side, and on the other, of what Degree or Condition soever they may be, shall mutually treat each other with all Sort of Kindness,

Aid, and Assistance, possible, without doing any Wrongs or Damage whatsoever to each other.

2.

There shall be a perfect Liberty of Navigation and Commerce in all the Dominions of either of the Two High contracting Parties, situated in Europe, where Navigation and Commerce is at present allowed, or shall hereafter be allowed, by the High contracting Parties, to the Subjects of any other Nation.

3*

It is agreed, That the Subjects of the High contracting Parties may at all times enter into the Ports, Places, or Towns, ofeitheroftbe High contracting Parties, with their Ships, Vessels, and Carriages, loaden or empty, into which the Subjects of any other Nation are allowed to enter, trade, or abide; and the Seamen, Passengers, and Vessels, as well English as Russ, although the Subjects of some other foreign Nation should be fdund among their Crew, shall be received and treated as the most favoured Nation; and the Seamen or Passengers shall not be forced to enter into the Service of either of the High contracting Parties, except the Subjects of that contracting Party which shall have Occasion for their Service: And it is agreed, That the Subjects of ilie High contracting Parties may buy all Sorts of Necessaries, which they may want, at the current Prices, refit and repair their Ships, Vessels, or Carriages, and buy all Sorts of Provision for their Subsistence or Voyage, stay or go, as they please, without Molestation or Hindrance; provided that they conform themselvesto the Laws and Ordinances of the respective Dominions of the High contracting Parties into which they shall come, or where they shall relide.

4-

It is agreed, That the Subjects of Great Britain may bring, by Water or by Land, into all or any of the Dominions of Rujffia, where the Subjects of any other Nation have Permission to trade, all Sorts of Goods or Merchandizes, whereof the Tradeor Importation are hot prohibited; and, in like manner, the Subjects of Russia may bring into all or any of the Dominions of Great Britain, where the Subjects of any other Nation are permitted to trade, all Sorts of Merchandizes of the Produce or Manufactureof the Dominions of Russia, whereof the Trade and Importation are not prohibited, and; in like manner, the Merchandizes of the Produce or Ma-nufadure oiAfia, provided that the same be not actually prohibited by any Law at present in Force in Great Britain; and that they may buy and export, out of the Dominions of Great Britain, all Sorts of Goods and Merchandizes which the Subjects of any other Nation may buy in the Dominions, and export out of the Dominions, of Great Britain, particularly Gold and Silver wrought or unwrought, the coined Money of Great Britain being excepted: And to the end that an Equality may be preserved, with respect to the Exportation of

AH Ease and Dispatch shall be given according to the Regulations for that Purpose, at the Entry of English Vessels, to load and unload their Merchandizes belonging to the Subjects of Great Britain, and they shall not be in any-ways detained under the Penalties specified in the Regulations; and, if the Subjects of Great Britain make any Contract with any Chancery or College, to deliver any Goods or Merchandizes, upon making Declaration that the Merchandizes are ready to be delivered, they shall be received according to the Time specified in the Contract; after which the Account shall be regulated and liquidated, in such time as shall have beep agreed in the Contract between the Chancery, or College, and the English Merchant. It is agreed, That the Subjects of Great Britain may import into Russia all Sorts of Goods or Merchandizes, and carry them through the Dominions of Russia, by the shortest and most commodious Way* into Persia, paying Three percent, in Rix Dollars, ad valorem, for the Duty and Transit of the said Merchandizes, and not any more, under any Pretext whatsoever; nevertheless the English Merchants shall be obliged to agree with the Russian Subjects for the Charge of Transportation, as well by Water as by Land, and to give them areasonable Price for the same; and the most precise Orders shall be issued, that the English Merchants may meet with all Expedition and Facility upon the Road; and, in like manner, that they may bring all Sorts of Goods an Merchandizes from Persia, and carry them through BuJJia, with the same Liberty and Ease, paying only Three per Cent, ad valorem, for the Duty and Transit, reckoning the Rix Dollars in the manner as usual in the Russian Cudom-houses: And, for preventing all Frauds on the Part of the English Subjects, and all Vexations and Delays on the Part of the Russian Officers, the English Merchants shall declare the Merchandizes deigned to pass through Rujffia, and to go to Perffa, and also those which they bring from Persia, at the Fird Placewhere they come into Rujffia; and they shall be received according to their Bills of Lading, Policy, or Register, and according to their declared Value; on which a Duty of Three per Cent, shall be paid, without opening or unpacking the Merchandizes, more than is absolu.tely necessary to satisfy the Russ Officer, that the Merchandizes specified in the Bill of Lading, Policy, or Register, and no other, is or are contained in the Packs or Bales wherein the Merchandizes are put; but in case that the Russ Officer has Reason to fuf-16

pe#, that the Merchandizes are not declared according to their full Value, by 20 per Cent. in such same the Russ Officer, paying the Merchant the declared Value, and 20 per Cent, more, without any Deduction, may take the Merchandizes, and dispose of them: When the Russ Officer has made his Visitation, which shall be done without any Vexation or Injury to the Merchandizes, or the Package, he shall affix a Piece of Lead on the Bales or Packs wherein the Merchandizes are contained; he shall number them, and mark them;and shall give the Merchants a Certificate of the Payment of the Duties, and, by this Certificate, Lead Mark, and Numero, they shall pass through Russia, to go to Per-fia, or to come from thence, without any other Hindrance or Molestation; but in case the Merchant does not carry all or any of the Bales through Russia, according to the Declaration, or if he breaks the Leads, and takes out'any of the Merchandizes in Russia, if there be any Reason to suspe# that it was done contrary to the clear Sense and Intention of this Article, lie shall be fined, and shall pay the full declared Value of such Bale or Pack as shall be wanting, or shall have the Lead broke.

/ 9-

That it shall be allowed reciprocally to the Subjects of the Highcontracting Parties, at the usual Places of Transportation, to load, upon their own Ships, Vessels, or Carriages, or on any others, the Merchandizes that they have bought, except suchonly as are prohibited to be exported, and to carry or fend them out freely; provided that they pay the Customs, and that the Ships, Vessels, or Carriages, be cleared according to the Regulations.

10.

That the Subjects of either the ope or the other of the Parties shall not pay more Customs or Duties for the Importation or Exportation of the Merchandizes, than what is paid for the Importation or Exportation of the same Merchandizes by the Subjects of any other Nation; and, for the Preventing of all Frauds in the Customs, on the one Side and the other, the Merchandizes that have flipped by the Custom-house, to avoid the Payment of the Duties of Importation, shall be contifcated; and no other Punishment shall be inflicted on the Merchants of either the one or the other of the Parties.

11.

It is agreed. That the Subjects of the one or the other of the Parties may freely go, come, and traffick, in all the Dominions that are, or that shall be hereafter, at Enmity with either of the Parties, except only the Places which are actually blockaded or besieged, provided that they do not carry any warlike Stores to the Enemy; as to all other Goods, the Vessel, the Passengers, and Effects, shall be free and unmolelied.

' 12.

Cannon, Mortars, Fire-arms, Pistols, Bombs, Gra-nadoes, Cannon-ball, Bullets, Fufees, Flints, Match, Powder, Salt-petre, Brimstone, Armour, Pikes, Swords, Belts, Pouches, Cartouch-boxes, Saddles, and Bridles, in any Quantity beyond what is necessary for the Provision of the Shi p, or what may belong to, or be judged necessary for each Man belonging to the Ship, or for the Passengers, shall be deemed warlike Stores, and, if they are found, they may be seized and confiscated, according to Law; but neither the Ship, Passengers; nor the rest of the Efte&s, shall be detained on that Account, or hindered from pursuing their Voyage.

13-

That in case of a Rupture between the High coning Parties (which God forbid 1) the Persons, Effects, or Ships, of the Subjects of the one or the other of the Parties shall not be detained nor confiscated; but, at kail, a Year’s Time shall be allowed, that they may fell, dispose of, carry, or fend away, their Effects, and remove their Persons.

14.

The Merchants, Seamen, Ships, or Este#s, shall not, on either Side, be seized, or forced to enter into the Service, under any Pretence whatsoever, without their ow*

Content;

Consent 5 and, if any Servant or Seaman deserts his Service or Ship, he shall be given up, it being understood, that nothing in this Article tends to hinder the ordinary course of Justice of the one Side or the other.

That in case of Shipwreck in any Place of the Dominions of the High contracting Parties, all Manner of Assistance shall be given to the Unfortunate; no Violence shall be offered them, nor shall their Effects, which have been saved by themselves, or by others, or cast on Shore by the Sea, be concealed or detained from them; nor shall any one do Damage to them, under any Pretence whatsoever, but they shall be kept safe for them,# and they shall pay a reasonable Price for the Assistancethey shall have received, towards helping them to save their Persons, Ship, and Effects.

16.

The Engli/k Merchants may build, buy, or hire, Houses, and sell or dispose of them in any Place at St. Petersburgh, at Moscow, in the German Slabod, in AJiracan, and in Arch Angel, and nobody shall be quartered upon them in their Houses in those Places 5 in all other Places, though they shall have Liberty to buy, fell, or'hire, Houses, they shall not however be exempted from Quartering, but they shall bear the same equally with the other Inhabitants: It is likewise agreed, That the Russ Merchants may build, buy, or hire, Houses, in Great Britain and Ireland, and sell or dispose of them; they qualifying themselves for that Purpose in the same manner as the Subjects of any other Nation, the most favoured, are obliged to do; and that they shall be exempted from Quartering; and that they shall have the free Exercise of the Greek Religion in their Houses, or in such Places as shall be appointed for that Purpose.

PafTports shall be given to all the English Subjects, who desire to leave the Dominions of Rufia, Two Months after they shall have given Notice of their Design to go away, without obliging them to give any Security, if in that time there does not appear any just Cause for detaining them, or without obliging them to apply for their PafTports any-where else than to the College of Commerce, or to that which shall hereafter be substituted in the room of that College: The same Dispatch and Facility in going away shall be given to the Russ Subjects in all the Dominions of Great Britain, according to the Custom of the Country on such Occasions.

18.

The English Merchants, who take into their Service, or Hire, Servants in Russia, with such PafTportsas the Civil Policy think fit to register, shall not be afterwards obliged to pay more for them, to the Mailers of those Servants, than that which shall have been agreed upon between the English Merchant and the Servant; but the English Merchant shall not keep those Servants longer than the Term which was allowed for their Service by their Mailer’s Passport; but, without Pokermojlinoys, no Servant shall be taken into Service, or hired: And in case that the Merchant takes a Bond of Security for the Probity and Fidelity of the Servant, if it happens that such Servant does not behave himself well, and cheats any one, the Merchant shall not be responsible for it, but the Security: Aud there shall be the same reciprocal Security and Justice for the Russ Merchant residing in the Dominions of Great Britain, who shall hire Servants there, according to the Laws of the Country.

All the Affairs of the English Merchants in Rufia shall be under the Cognizance of the College of Commerce only, or of such other Court as shall hereafter be appointed, instead of that College, to take Cognizance of the Affairs of foreign Merchants, and no other: The Russ Merchants in the Dominions of Great Britain shall be under the Protection and Justice of the Laws of that Kingdom, as all other foreign* Merchants, and they shall be treated as the moll favoured Nation.

20.

The English Merchants shall not be obliged to shew Commercial their Books or Papers to any one whatever, except for Treaty with making Proof in Law; neither shall their Books or Papers be taken away from them, or detained; neither shall their Goods be taken in Execution, or fold, under any Pretence whatsoever, unless in case of Bankruptcy, and then by Judgment of the College of Commerce only, or of such other Court as may be appointed hereafter, in the room of that College, to take care of the Affairs of foreign Merchants: And the Russ Merchants in the Dominions of Great Britain ^shall be protected by the Laws, as in the preceding Article.

21:

That, in case of a Law-suit, Four Persons, of unble-mished Reputation among the foreign Merchants, shall be named by the College of Commerce to examine the Books and Papers of the Prosecutor, as Occasion shall require; and the Report of the Examiners to the College of Commerce, of what they shall have found upon examining the Books or Papers, shall be held for good Evidence in the Cafe.

22.

The Custom-house shall take care to examine the"

Servants of the Russ Merchants, when they write Bargains, if they have Orders, or Letters of Credit, from their Mailers, for so doing; if they have none, they shall not be trusted: The same Thing shall be done towards the Servants of the English Merchants; and the Merchandizes shall be written on the Account of the Masters; who, if they have given Orders, or Letters of Credit, to their Servants, shall then be responsible, as if they had written the Merchandizes themselves: In like manner all the Russ Servants employed in the Shops shall be registered; and their Masters shall be responsible for their Transactions in point of Commerce.

In case that Russ Merchants, being indebted to Eng-lifi Merchants, shall leave the Place where they are, and remove into the Country; if it should happen, that, while they are absent, Petitions should be given in against them, with Proof of the Debt; then the College of Commerce shall cite them Three different times, allowing a sufficient Time for their Appearance before the College, but, if they do not appear, the College of Commerce shall condemn them, and fend a Person express, at the Charge of the Prosecutor, to the Governors, or Chief Magistrates, to put the Sentence in Execution, and oblige the Debtor to pay that which is demanded.

That the Russ Merchants, which come with the Merchandizes, shall be obliged to enter them at the Custom-house as soon as possible; and, when they flialji have been fold, they shall write the Quantity, the Weight, and the Measur, according to the Regulations.
