There shall be Regulations made for correcting the Abuses that may happen in the Bandage on Hides and Hemp: In the mean while, if there happens any Dispute between the Buyer and the Seller, concerning the Tare of any Merchandizes, the Custom-house shall decide it, without Delay, according to Reason and Equity.

27.

For the greater Ease and Encouragement of the Trade of Great Britain, it is agreed, That, for the future, the Woolen Stuffs of England, hereafter specified, shall not pay any more Duties on Eutry, than what is specified in this Article; that is to say,

/ 8 C English

240 Martii. A. 1735.

C rnimercial English Cloth for Soldiers shall pay no more than Two Tr ity with Copecks in Rix Dollars by the Archine, for Duty on Entry. 3

The coarse Cloth of the County of York, known in the Russian Tariff by the Name of KoftroJJcy, shall pay no more than Two Copecks in Rix Dollars by the Archine, for Duty on Entry.

The Broad Flannel shall pay but One Copeck in Rix Dollars by the Archine, for Duty on Entry.

The narrow Flannel shall pay but Three Quarters of a Copeck in Rix Dollars by the Archine, for the Duty on Entry.

28.

It is agreed and concluded between the High con-trading Parties, That the Subjects of the one and the other Side shall be considered and treated always as the moil favoured Nation in their respective Dominions; and that the Subjects of Ruffa, who shall go into England, to learn their Arts or Trade, shall be protected, favoured, and inftriicted: In like manner the Ritfs Ships, when they are at Sea, upon their Voyage, shall not in anywise be hindered by the English Ships, when they shall meet each other, provided that, in the Brit iff Sea, they demean themselves according to Custom; but they shall be favoured, and shall receive all Assistance possible; and the same shall be done in the Ports or Havens under the Dominion of Great Britain.

29-

The Peace, Amity, and good Understanding, shall lad for ever between the High contracting Parties; and as it is customary to fix a certain Time for Treaties of Commerce, the said High contracting Parties have agreed, That this, of Commerce, shall last for the Space of Fifteen Years, to be reckoned from the Day of the Signing of this present Treaty; and, before that Term be expired, they may agree together for renewing and prolonging the fame-3°-

This present Treaty of Navigation and Commerce shall be approved and ratified by his Bntaww/c/; Majesty, and by her Czarish Majesty; and the Instruments of Ratification, in due Form, shall be exchanged on each Side, at St. Petersburgh, within the Space of Three Months, or sooner, if possible, reckoning from the Day of Signing.

Iu Witness whereof, we the Underwritten, provided with the full Powers of their ft\id Britannick and Czarish Majesties, have, in their said Names, signed this present Treaty, and have let our Seals thereto. Done at St. 'Petersburgh, the 2d December 1734.

ecovery of A Petition of Peter Burton, James Mount, Geo. a lindon*8 G'rew> William Calvert, on the behalf of themselves, and Edward Hajled, Henry llatty Edmund Newton, and Thomas Sheppard, Clerk Sitters of the Sheriffs Courts of the City of London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Office of a Clerk Sitter is a most ancient Office belonging to the Courts of the Sheriffs of London y and that the Petitioners gave upwards of £.8,000 for their Places; and were all of them admitted to their said Offices by the Court of Aldermen of the said City, to hold and enjoy the fame, with all Fees and Profits thereunto belonging, quamdiufe bene gefferint; and that the Petitioners have not any Salary annexed to their said Offices, the foie Profits whereof arise from several ancient and small Fees; and that almost all the Actions brought in the said Courts, and entered by the Petitioners, at their respective Offices in the Two Compters belonging to the said Sheriffs of London, are for Debts between 40s. and Ten Pounds; and that many of the said Actions which are entered for more than Five Pounds, are removed, by Habeas Corpus, into the superior Courts; so that if the Bill, now depending in this House, for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts within the City of London should pass into a Law, the Petitioners Freeholds will be greatly-prejudiced, if not entirely destroyed; the superior Courts taking away, by Habeas Corpus, all the larger Actions, and this new-intended Court all others: And therefore, as the Petitioners, and their Predecessors, have been, for Time immemorial, the proper and only Officers for issuing out the First Process for Recovery of the said Debts above 40 Sh. as also to take and enter Appearances, administer the Oath to the Jurors, and Vol, 33.

to record the Verdicts given in all Causes tried in the said Courts; and since the Petitioners will be the Persons principally injured by this Bill, if it should pass into a Law; praying, That, in case the said Bill ftionld pass into a Law, they may be appointed the Registers or Officers of such new-intended Court, the Bufmefe of such Register being agreeable and answering to that which the Petitioners, of Right, now exercise in the said Sheriffs Courts, by virtue of their said Offices, and , which will otherwise be greatly abridged, if not totally taken from them; and that such Fees be allowed to the Petitioners, for the Business to be done by them in such new-intended Court, as will, in some measure, compensate to them the Loss they will sustain, by being deprived of the ancient Business and Fees annexed to their said Offices; or that the House will give the Petitioners such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee, to whom the Bill for the more easy and speedy Recovery of small Debts within the City of London, and the Liberties thereof, is committed.

ments and Supports of both; dnd that the University hath, at all times heretofore, been thought worthy of the Countenance of the Legislature, and continually favoured by Persons of all Orders and Degrees, eminent for Wisdom and public Spirit; and that if the Bill to restrain Alienations of Lands should pass into a Law, without Amendment, it will, as the Petitioners , apprehend, be attended with Consequences greatly prejudicial to them at present, and much more so in time to come; because it will, in a great measure, prevent all Donations to supply present or future De-'ficiencies, or for any other wise and great Purposes, how useful and necessary soever they may be thought; and that a confidei;able Part of their Revenue arises from Annuities, and other certain Payments, issuing out of Lands and other Estates; and that many of these Payments being fixed in the Reign of Queen Elizabeth, and Trill continuing invariably the fame, are now, by the great Fall of Money since that time, funk so far below the original Value, as to be insufficient to answer the Purposes for which they were designed; and that several Headflrips are under £.120, some under £.100 per Annum % and that the Salaries of some Professorships are under £.50 per Annum, and others, as those of Botany, Anatomy, and Chymistry, have no Endowment at all; and that the Income of much the greatest Part of their Fellowships is under £.60, of many under £40, of some so low as £.30, £.20, and £.15 per Annum; and that many of their Scholar-ffiips and Exhibitions amount not to above £.6, £.4, and £.3 per Annum; and that some are even under those small Sums; and that many poor Students have neither Scholarship nor Exhibition, to help towards their Maintenance; and that the Number of Advowsons, in most Colleges, is very small, in proportion to the Number of Fellows: And therefore praying the House to except this University, and the several Colleges therein, out of the said Bill.

A Petition of the Chancellor, Masters, and Scholars, of the University of Oxford, in behalf of themselves, and the several Colleges and Halls within the said University, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Petitioners apprehend, that by the Bill, now depending before this House, to restrain the Dif-positions of Lands, whereby the same become unalienable, they and their Successors may be deprived of the Assistance of future Benefactions, and the charitable Donations of such as may be disposed to promote the pious Intentions for which that ancient University was founded; and that the Petitioners are, by their Constitution, entirely founded in Charity, and must ever continue to depend upon it; and that,1 notwithstanding the large Benefactions with which they have been formerly endowed, yet many of the Societies are so meanly provided for, that the pious Designs of their Founders must remain imperfect, without future Benefactions, which have been found, by long Experience to arise by such low Degrees: That the Petitioners hope. That when their same is duly considered, they will not be thought to be within any of the general Mischiefs that may arise from Alienations in Mortmain; and that, as their present Possessions are inconsiderable, in respect of the great Number of Persons that are maintained out of them, and as the Donations they now enjoy, as well as those they may hereafter receive, must be solely appropriated to the Advancement of Religion and Learning, for these Reasons they hope, that no Difficulties or Discouragements will be put in the Way of those, whose pious and charitable Intentions may dispose them to give their Assistance towards rendering the University in general, as well as the several Societies of it, more instrumental in promoting these great and necessary Ends: And that the Petitioners therefore hope they shall be exempted from

That the said Burgh bath been at very considerable Changes in cleansing the said River and Harbour, and repairing the Pier; but that the Revenue thereof is not sufficient effectually to carry on so expensive an Undertaking: That the Town-house, Church, and Steeple, want Repair; and One of the Arches of the Bridge over the River will be entirely loft, unless speedily repaired: That the common Gaol is so much out of Repair, that several Prisoners for Debt have made their Escapes, and the Town hath been thereby subjected to the Payment of their Debts; and that the Roads and Streets belonging to the said Town are become very ruinous, and want Repair:

That the Charge of paling the River, in order to confine the Water in its proper Chanel, and of cleansing the Harbour, and repairing the Pier, will amount to upwards of £.4,000, for which, and the other public Works, Money cannot be raised, unless some Provision be made by Parliament for that Purpose.

The Counsel for the Sitting Member alleged* That, as to Four of them, it La 1 been admitted by the Petitioner’s Counsel, that the Charters produced by those Voters, at the Election, did recite their Lands to be of Extents and Valuations sufficient to intitle them to vote; and that as all Charters proceed upon Inquisitions taken* they therefore infilled, that the Recitals of the Charters mentioned must be presumed to have had a proper Foundation.

As to the Objection made to Henry Cunningham, they referred to Mr. Cunningham's Answer given to that Objection in the Minutes; viz. That the same Objection had been made at former Elections, and over-ruled, in respect that no Decree against his Right was produced; and that it was not competent to object pretended Nulli4 ties uninftrufted, against Infeoftments proceeding upon Charters, on alleged Fasts, when no Nullities appear id the Infeoftment.

and that afterwards, in pursuance of the Powers granted by the said Statute, divers Rules and Orders were settled and confirmed by her said late Majesty, under the Great Seal; by some of which Rules and Orders the Augmentations to be made are directed to be by way of Purchase, and not by way of Pension; and the stated Sum, to be allowed for the Augmentation of each Cure, is limited to £. 200. to be invested in a Purchase at the Expence of the Corporation; and the said Governors are impowered to give the said Sum of £. 200. to Cures not exceeding Five-and-thirty Pounds per Annum (which Sum was afterwards, by th^Authority of his late Majesty King George the First, extended to £. 5Q. per Annum), where any Persons will give the fame, or greater Sum, or Value, in Lands or Tythes; and such Governors are direfited every Year, between Christmas and Eastery to cause the Account of what Money they have to distribute that Year\to be audited; and, when they know the Sum, publick Notice is dirc6fced to be given, that they have such a Sum to distribute in so many Shares, and that they will be ready to apply these Shares to such Cures as want the fame; and are; by the Rules of the Corporation, qualified to receive them, where any Persons, w ill add the like, or greater Sum to it,' or the Value in Lands or Tythes, for any such particular Cure; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that, by the Bill, now depending, before this house, to restrain the Dispositions of:Lands, whereby the same become unalienable, the Rights and Powers vested in them by the same Act, and by the Rules and Orders made in pursuance thereof, may be greatly affc6ted, if some proper Provision be not made to prevent it: And therefore praying* That a; Clause or Clauses, may be added, whereby the said Rights and Powers may be secured.

and that the Children now, and for several Years past, are many more in Number than the Petitioners can provide for by the yearly Subscriptions and Collection, joined to the certain annual Revenues of the said Hospital, which together, at present, do not. exceed Seven hundred Pounds a Year; A Petition of the Trustees of the several Charity Aliening Schools within the Cities of London and WestminfleVy Bo- ^rnt^a-u rough of Southwark, and Bills of Mortality, in behalf of ° upwards of Five thousand poor Children- clothed and educated in the said Schools, and also in behalf of all otherCharity Schools in this Kingdom, for the Education of the Children of the Poor in the Principles of the Church of England, as by Law established, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That if the Bill, now depending in this House, to restrain the Dispositions of Lands, whereby the same become unalienable, Uiould pass into a Law, without Amendment, it will prevent many charitable Donations for the Promotion of the said Schools, which are so far from having any large Endowments in Land or Money, that very few have so much as a School House; and that, as the voluntary Contributions do not equally and regularly answer the conffant Expences, the Trustees in several Places have been obliged to reduce the Number of their Children, and in others, the Schools have been entirely laid down, for want of Means to support them; and representing to the House the great Usefulness of thefeSchools; and alleging, That, during the Continuance thereof, the Petitioners have placed out upwards of Seventeen thousand Children, within the said Bills of Mortality, to Apprenticeships in the lower Trades, and to menial Services, whereof above One Half have been put out to such Services, besides near 400 bound to the Sea Service: And therefore praying the House to except the said Charity Schools out of the said Bill, or to grant them such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

,n America, was presented to the House, and read; feting forth. That the greatest and principal Branch of their Trade consists in the Exportation of Manufactures, the Produce of Great Britain, to our Colonies in America, and bringing Muscovado Sugars in Return for the fame; Three Fourth Parts of which Sugars cannot be consumed without being first refined; and Two Fifth Parts, when refined, are drawn into Melasses, whereof near Two Thirds are distilled into Spirits; and that, if the Bill brought in, upon several Resolutions of the House, jn order to lay a Duty of Twenty Shillings a Gallon upon all Kinds of spirituous Liquors retailed within this Kingdom, Rum from his Majesty’s Plantations not excepted, should pass into a Law, the greatest Consumption of refined Sugars would be entirely loft; and Rum, which is near a Fourth Part in Value of the Produce of our Sugar Colonies, would also be rendered of little or no Value, and Two Thirds of the Melasses produced from refined Sugars mud become useless; to the inevitable Ruin of our Sugar Plantations, and Definition of the Two most valuable Branches of our foreign Trade to the British Colonies, and the Coast of Africa: And therefore expit fling their Hope, that the Legislature will not hazard so beneficial a Trade, to cure an Evil that never would have happened from Rum, or any other Liquor of that Value; but will be able to find Means elVedually to suppress the fame, without extending it to any of the Liquors that are distilled from the Produce of our own Plantations; and praying, That the 1 Soule will be pleased to take their same into Consideration, and give fuel) Relief therein as the House rtiJill find mofl meet.

A Petition of the Merchants, Owners and Matters Sail ed of Ships, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in Manure, beliatf of themselves, and all otluers concerned in the British Navigation, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioners are informed, J

that by a Bill, which has been brought into this House, Forgiving farther Encouragement to the Manufacturers of British Sail-cloth, and for more effectually securing the Duties now payable on foreign Sail-cloth imported into this Kingdom, all Matters and Commanders of Ships or Vessels, which shall be built in this Kingdom^ or the British Plantations in America, will be obliged to furnish the same with Sails made of British Sailcloth; but that there is no Provision in the said Bill, with respect either to the Quality or Price of such British Sail-cloth, which even the Manutttfturers allow to be not so cheap, and the Petitioners hav$ found, by Experience, not to be so good, as the Cloth of other Countries, nor any further Encouragement given to the Manufacturers, whereby they may he enabled to reduce the Price to an Equality with that of other Nations; and expressing their Apprehensions, that the Taid Bill, if passed into a Law, will not only he attended with very great Hardships to the Petitioners, but wifi prove highly prejudicial to the British Navigation, aail be of dangerous Consequence to the Trade and Interest of this Nation in general: Arid therefore praying to be heard, by themselves, or Cohn Cel, against the said Bill; or that the Petitioners may shave such other Relief as to the House shall feern meet.

Anne Gofton: Who said, That since the last Election, one Mr. Stockdale, and Francis Pate, came to her, and told her, That if ftie, or her Husband, w'ould lpeak for the Petitioner, and declare, that the Freemen had never voted, they (liould be wjell gratified; and that her Iiuf-band should be admitted into Greenwich Hospital:

Being asked, 1 f it was a contested Election ? (he answered, It was; or otherwise there would have been no Occasion for a free Vote; and that (he had heard a Talk, several Years, of bringing in the free Votes.

Martha Spicer, aged 76 Years, gave the same Evidence, in relation to that Election, and to the Freemen s Right of voting.

William Hodgson, aged 80 Years, said, That he had known Scarborough Sixty-eight or Sixty-nine Years, and remembered the Election of Sir Philip Mon&on: That Freemen voted at that Election, his Father being One that gave his Vote; and he believed Fourscore or One hundred more might vote like wife; and that, after that Election, the Freemen voted for a great many Years:

The Committee came to this Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right of Election of Burgesses to lerve in Parliament for the Borough of Scarborough, in the County of York, is in the Common House, or Common Council, of the said Borough, consisting of Two Bailiffs, Two Coroners, Four Chamberlains, and Thirty-six Burgesses only.

Upon which the Sitting Member acquainted the Committee, That, the Right of Election being thus determined, he admitted, that the Petitioner had a Majority upon the Poll.

Thereupon the Committee came to the following Resolutions;

Resolved, That it is the opinion of this Committee, That the Right honourable Thomas Hay Esquire, commonly called Lord Dupplin, is not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Scarborough, in the County of York.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That William Ojbaldeston Esquire is duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Scarborough, in the County of York.

A Petition of Henjhaw Halsey Esquire was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That at the last Election for a Knight of the Shire to serve in this present Parliament for the County of Hertford, in the room of Sir Thomas Saunders Sebright Baronet, deceased, the Petitioner, and Charles Ccefar Esquire, were Candidates; and the said Charles Ccefar is returned a Representative in Parliament for the said County: That the said Charles Ccefar, at the time of such Election and Return, was not qualified to be elected, according to the Statute made in the Ninth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, to serve in Parliament as a Knight of the Shire, he not having an Estate in Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, over and above what will satisfy and clear all Incumbrances that may affect the fame, of the annual Value of£. 600; for which Reason the Petitioner does insist, that the Election and Return of the said Charles Ccefar is contrary to the said Statute: That the Petitioner was duly elected, and ought to represent the said County instead of the said Charles Ccefar: And praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and to give the Petitioner such Relief as shall seem just.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections, And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House;

Edward Hobcrts, being examined, said, That Saturday was Three Weeks Wm. Mills asked him to go over the Water to Rai/ner the Printer; and told him he had a Copy of the Gin Bill, with thcClause offered, relating to Punch; and, if lie succeeded in felling it, they w ould live well:

Edward Roberts, being asked, If he was positive that he saw Mills, Rayner, and Ilive, together, he averred his former Evidence was true, notwithstanding what Ilive said to the contrary.

William Rayner, being examined, and the said Pamphlet being shewn to him, acknowledged that it was printed at his House, but without his Privity; and that he knew nothing of it till after the same was published:

That he gives Leave to his Servants to print some small Pamphlets, without knowing what the Contents are.

After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a most the Kin. gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament, as fol- Speech, loweth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

The Dispatch you have given to the publick Bufinefe,

and the advanced Season of the Year, make it proper to put an End to this Session of Parliament.

1 acquainted you, at your first Meeting, That Preliminary Articles had been concluded between the Emperor and the most Christian King: since which time, a further Convention, concerning the Execution of them, hath been made, and communicated to me, by both those Courts; and Negotiations are carrying on by the several Powers engaged in the late War, in order to settle the General Pacificaition.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return you my Thanks for the Provisions you have made for the Service of the current Year: You can never better recommend yourselves to my Esteem, and to the good Opinion of those you represent, than by raising the Supplies necessary for the support of my Government, and for the Service of the Publick, in a Maimer the most effectual, and the least burdensome to my People.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is a great Concern to m6 to fee such feeds of Diffcntion sown among my good People, as, if not timely prevented, may prove very prejudicial to the Peace and Quiet of my Kingdoms: It is my desire, and shall be my Care, to preserve the present Confutation in Church and State, as by Law established, perfect and intire, and not to countenance any Attempts to the Prejudice of either; Good Harmony and mutual Affection among all the Protestants of this Nation, have been the great Security of the present happy Establishment, from the Resolution to this Time:

By this united Strength, they will be able to refill the secret and open Attempts of our common Enemies; but, divided, they may become a Prey to them: My Protection shall be impartially dispensed to all my Subjects, in the full Enjoyment of their Religious and Civil Rights: Let it be your Care, by your Conduct in your several Stations, to make my Endeavours for your common Happiness effectual.'

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It being necessary for me to visit ray Dominions in Germany again this Year, I have resolved to appoint the Queen Regent here during my Absence: The Experience you have already had of her just and prudent Administration, will, I doubt not, engage you all to make the Weight of the publick Affairs as easy to her as her wife Conduct will render the Government agreeable to you: And this I recommend to you in a particular manner.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by his Majesty's Command, said;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is his Majesty’s Royal Will and Pleasure, That Parliament this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday the Twenty- prorogued, ninth Day of July next, to be then here held.

And this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to

Thursday the Twenty-ninth Day of July next.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

We are commanded by his Majesty to let you know, That, as it is not convenient for his Majesty to be prefers here this Day in his Royal Person, he has been pleased, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal, to authorize his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, and several Lords, therein mentioned, to do every thing in the Name of his Majesty, which ought to be done on the Part of his Majesty, in this Parliament, as may more fully appear by the Letters Patent.

That then the said Letters Patent being rejad* which were to the Purport of what the Lord Chancellor had said, the Lord Chaucejlor, as One of the Com mifiio iters, made a Speech to both Houses of Parliament; of which Mr. Speaker said he had, to prevent Mistake*, obtained a Copy; which he read to the House; and is as followeth; viz.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

In Pursuance of the Authority given us, by his Majesty’s Commission under the Great Seal, amongst other Things, to declare the Causes of his holding this Parliament, we are, by his Majesty’s Command, in the First place, to observe t<? you* That-his Majesty acquainted you last Year, That he had, in Conjunction with the States General,< given hijj Approbation ofcet tain preliminary Articles opnperted and agreed upon between the Emperor and France, fer reftofing tha Peace of Europe \ ap^(that.,a further Convention, concerning the Execution of them, hdd bfep communicated to him, by both those , Court$v and, Negotiations Were carrying on by the several, Ppyrpns engaged in the late War, in order to settle the general Pacification.

We are now commanded, by hisit Majesty, to inform you, That the respective Acts of Cession being exchanged, and Orders given for the Evacuation and Possession of the several Countries and Places by the Powers concerned, according to the Allotment and Disposition of the preliminary Articles, the great Work of re-establishing the general Tranquillity is far advanced: However, it is his Majesty’s Opinion, That common Prudence calls upon us to be very attentive to, and observe the final Conclusion of, this new Settlement of such con-

The Copy of tht Letters Patent is entered at the End of the Journal of this Dav.

My Lords and Gentlemen,

His Majesty has been graciously pleased to direct us to acquaint you, That he hath seen, with the greatest Satisfaction, the unwearied Application of this Parliament in framing good Laws, for advancing the Prof-perity, and securing the W elfare, of his loving Subjects; and that it hath been one of his Majesty’s Principal Cares to enforce them, by a due Execution, with the strictest Regard to the Rights and Properties of his People; no Invasion whereof can, with any Colour, be suggested byvthe most malicious Enemies of the present Establishment: Whilst this hath been our Condition, his Majesty cannot but observe, that it must be Matter of the utmost Surprise and Concern to every true Lover of his Country, to see the niany Contrivances and Attempts carried on, in various Shapes, and in different Parts of the Nation, tumultuously to refill and obstruct the Execution of the Laws, and to violate the Peace, of the Kingdom: These Disturbers of the, publick Repose, conscious that the Interests of his Majesty and his People are the fame, and of the good Harmony which happily subsists between him and his Parliament, have levelled their Sedition against both, and, in their late Outrages, have either directly opposed, or at lead endeavoured to render ineffectual, some Acts of the whole Legislature: His Majesty, in his great Wisdom, thinks it affords a melancholy Prospect, to consider to w hat Height these audacious Practices may rife, if not timely suppressed; and that it deserves no small Attention, that they may go on to aflfect private Persons in the quiet Enjoyment of their Property, as well as the general Peace and good Order of the Whole: His Majesty apprehends it to be unnecessary to inlarge upon a Subject of this Nature; and therefore hath commanded us barely to mention it to you, who, by the constant Tenor of your Conduct, jrave shewn* that you consider the Support of his Authority, and the Security of his Government, as inseparable from the Preserv ation of the publick Tranquillity, and your own Safety.

A Petition of John Scott, of JVardropcrtoun, Esquire, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, upon the 28th of May 1 734, being the Day appointed for the FI eft ion of a Commissioner to serve in this prefen t Parliament for the Shire of Kincardine, IVm. Burnett, of Crigie, Esquire, was duly elected Pnrfes, and Mr. John Maulc was duly elected Clerk, by the Majority of Freeholders, who had a Right to vote in furh Election: That the Minority of the Freeholders thereupon fpparated themselves from the Majority: That the Freeholders who continued together, after having adjusted the Roll, unanimously, to the Number of Thirteen, voted for the Petitioner, to be Commissioner for the said Shire; and the said Mr Mauley who was Clerk, and the proper Returning Officer, did, agreeable to Law, tender a Return of the Petitioner’s Name to Arthur Shepherd, Deputy Sheriff of the said Shire, there being no Principal Sheriff, and required him to receive such Return, and annex it to the Writ; but that the said Arthur Shepherd, in the manifest Violation of the Vol.

Right of Elections, hath taken upon himself, by Indenture between him and one John Young, who had no Colour of Right to join in such Indenture, to return John Falconer, of Phefdo, Esquire, to be Commissioner for the said Shire: That the said John Falconer was not capable of being so elected, not being seised or possessed of such an Estate as in titled him cither to elect or be elected; That several Persons, who pretended to vote for the said John Falconer, had no Right or Title to vote; and they refused to take the v Oatiis appointed by Law to be taken by the Electors of Members to serve in Parliament: That the Persons who pretended to vote for the said John Falconer, having withdrawn and separated from the duly elected Prafes and Clerk, could not regularly choose any Commissioner for the said Shire: That, as well before as at the Election, many undue and illegal Practices were made use of by, for, and in favour of, the said John Falconer, in order to procure him to be elected and returned to serve in Parliament for the said Shire f and though he was not duly chose, yet he hath been returned, by a Person who had no Right to make such Return, though the Petitioner was duly elected, and who, as tiic proper Officer tendered a Return of hitn to the Sheriff, ought to have been returned accordingly:

Ami praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give the Petitioner such Relief as to the House flirtll seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of Privileges and Elections: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the lame, with their Opinion thereupon, to the House.

A Petition of the Inhabitants of the City of New Sarum, in the County of Wilts;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; alleging. That the Highways, Streets, and Watercourses in the said City, are much out of Repair, and want Paving; and that the Laws now in force, in relation to the Highways, are not sufficient to repair the fame, and cannot be put in Execution, as ’tis apprehended, without great Hardship to the poorer fort of the People; and that the Streets of the said City, for the most part, are very strait and regular, and may be enlightened at a small Expence; and that the Watch and Ward, which is now set, and kept there, pursuant to the Statute at Winchester, is of little or no Use, and of a considerable Expence to the Inhabitants of the said City: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill to impower the Mayor, Justices of the Peace, and Inhabitants, of the said City, to order the cleansing, and repairing, and paving, the Highways, and Streets, and Water-courses, and enlightening the said Streets, and the Lanes and Passages, and to appoint the Watch, at such Times in the Year, and in such manner, as they shall think proper; and that the Money to be raised for the Purposes aforesaid be raised by a Pound Rate, or by such other Ways or Means as the House shall think fit.

Sir Charles Turner, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of the Supply granted to his Majesty, the Resolutions which they had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his Place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same were read; and are as follow; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Ten thousand Men be employed for the Sea Service, for the Year 1737, beginning from the First Day of January 1736.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Sum, not exceeding Four Pounds per Man per 16 Month,

A P E T IT IO N of the Magistrates and Town Council " Clyd jl\ of the Burgh of Lanark, in North Britain, under Bridge, the Common Seal of the said Burgh, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Burgh of La- nark contributed considerable Sums of Money towards building a Stone Bridge, of Three Arches, over the River Clyd, at Clydjholm, to the great Benefit of the Inhabitants of the adjacent Country; and that the Keeping of the said Bridge in Repair being burthensome to the Community of the said Burgh, in 1703 an Act passed in the Parliament of Scotland, granting to them a Toll or Custom of One Peny Sterling for every Horse and Load, and Two-third Parts of a Peny for every Cow or Horse, and the Sixth Part of a Peny for -every Sheep, or Foot Passenger, that should pass over the said Bridge, for the Term of Nineteen Years; and that this Bridge has appeared so useful to the Neighbourhood, and the Toll so moderate, that though the Term granted by the said Act expired in 1722, yet they have voluntarily paid it, till feme Persons, of late, objected to the Payment thereof, whose Example others will probably follow, though the Country, in general, desires the Continuance of the said Toll; but that the Produce thereof is so very low, no Wheel-carriages being taxed, though these give the greatest Occasion for Repairs: That the Petitioners are not able to defray, the continual Expence of Repairs out of the Toll and if it is not renewed-to them, by reason of the great Debts and low* Circumstances of the Community of the said Burgh, the Petitioners will not be able to preserve this useful Fabrick;

And therefore praying the House to give Leave, That a Bill may be brought in to continue the Toll granted by the said Act; and to give the Petitioners such other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the JVfatter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

A PETITION of the Provost, Baillies, Dean of Dumfries Guild, and Treasurer* of the Town of Dumfries, Town Im-for themselves, and in Name of the Town Council and pavement, Community thereof, was presented to the House, and read; reciting an Act of Parliament, passed in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a Peny Sterling, upon every Pint of Ale or Beer that shall be vended or sold within the Town of Dumfries, and Privileges thereof, for paying the Debts of the said Town, and for building a Church, and making a Harbour there; and setting forth. That the Petitioners, expelling the Money arising from this Duty might answer the Purposes for which it was appropriated by the said Act, did, in a few Years after the Commencement thereof, in virtue of the Credit and Powers thereby granted to them, borrow, upon Interest, a considerableSum of Money, and have therewith built a Commodious new Church for the performing of Divine Service, and endowed the famd with a Maintenance to a Minister; and that, though the Money arising from the Duty has been duly collected, and regularly applied, in the First Place, towards paying the Debts formerly owing by the Town, as directed by the said Act, yet a considerable Part of these dill remain undischarged, besides the large Debts contracted since; and that the other publick Funds of the said Town having been of late much exhausted in rebuilding their free Prison, Council-house, and Part of their old Church, which were become ruinous, and in other publick necessary Works, the whole Revenue of the Town is not sufficient to pay the Interest of the Debts now owing by the Town, and suppoi t their other necessary Expences, which will be increased by a Necessity of rebuilding their publick School-house, that is become ruinous, and repairing their other publick Works, now in Decay, and improving the Navigation of their River, which is become so dangerous, that their Trade of late has greatly suffered, without Aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into their Consideration; and that Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for continuing the said Import Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth of a Peny Sterling, over and above the Duty of Excise, on every Scots Pint of Ale and Beer that shall be either brewed, or brought in, and vended, tapped, or fold, within the said Town, and Privileges thereof, in the same manner as the same was granted by the aforesaid Act* for such Term of Years as shall be thought meet, and some small Town Dues on Goods imported, and Tonage on Shipping coming into their Port; or grant such other Relief as by the House shall be judged proper.

To prove the Allegations of the Petition, the Petitioners laid before the Committee,

An Act of Parliament, passed in the Fifth Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for laying a Duty of Two Penies Scots, or One-sixth Part of a reny Sterling, upon every Pint of Ale or Beer that should be vended or loid within the Town of Dunbar, for improving and preserving the Harbour, and repairing the Town-house, and building a School, and other publick Buildings there, and for supplying the said Town with fresh Water; by which Act the said Duty was to commence from the lft of June 1719, and to continue payable for the Term of Nineteen Years.

Then the Petitioners called,

Mr. Alexander Wallace: Who, being examined, said, That considerable Sums of Money have been laid out, according to the iMreftions of the said Act, in repairing the Town-house, and other publick Buildings, and for improving Part of the Harbour.

He also said, That Part of the Rock remaining in the Bottom of the Harbour intended to be taken up, has not been touched; and that nothing is done towards the carrying out of the great Pier to the Beacon Rock, or

cutting down to a Perpendicular the Slope of the Island, for making the Entry into the Harbour safe and secure, or towards supplying the said Town with fresh Water.*

And he further said, That the Money to be raised by the said Duty, during the Continuance of the said Act, which expires in 1738, will not be sufficient to answer the Purposes aforesaid; and, unless the Tenn and Powers granted by the former Act be further continued, the said publick Works must remain unfinished.

Then he produced an Account of the annual Receipts and Payments, from the 15th of November 1719 to Martinmas 1733, which, he informed the Committee, he had compared with the Town Books of Dunbar; by which it appears, that there is a Debt now standing out, amounting to the Sum of £. 1,183. 3. if.

Mr. Robert Hacks reported from the Committee, to Paving, Sec; whom the Petition of several of the Inhabitants living Street* in within the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, in the County of Middleje.r, and Borough of Southwark; in the County of Surry, on behalf of themselves, anil others, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had diverted him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the I Ioufe 1 and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read j and is as follows; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the following Witnesses were examined; viz.

John Milner, Thomas Ilucks, Esquires, and Mr. Daniel Bolton: Who severally said, Tlmt the Streets within the Limits aforesaid are in a very ruinous Condition, occasioned by each lloufekeoper having the Liberty of directing the Pavement before his own Door in what manner lie thinks proper, the Method whereof is generally left to the Paviour; and tin* Pavements before Two Houses adjoining, being frequently laid by different Workmen, are ieldom level; by means whereof the Water settles on the lower Pavement, and soon destroys the same; and the Channels are lb much deepened, as to btcomo a Nuisance, and frequently occasion the Overturning or Breuking down of Coaches, and other Carriages:

That the Paviours employed by the Proprietors of the several Waterworks, who have it in their power to break up Pavements at their pleasure, seldom make good such Pavement with proper Materials, but nfe Allies and Dirt instead of Gravel; which not being well rammed, the Pavement soon links, and wears into Holes:

That the Number of empty Houses is another Cause of the bad Pavements; the Owners of such Houses, not being cafilydiscovered, living frequently indiAanl Parts:

That t lie J nAices of Peace cannot refuse the Scavengers returned by the Inhabitants, however improper or unfit: nor cau such Scavengers be called to account till the Expiration of the Year; whereby many Inconveniencies have arisen, and large Sums of Money have been loA:

That the Builders, in order to make their Mortar, frequently lay Rubbish in irregular Heaps in the said Streets; which are often the Means of Coaches, and other Carriages, being overturned; and that the Night Carts frequently pals through the said Streets by Nine of the Clock in the Evening, without regard to the Season of the Year, and continue passing till late in the Morning, to the great Annoyance of the Inhabitants.

That Polls, Rails, Bulks, Sheds, and other Incroach-ments, are daily erected in the Streets within the Limits aforesaid; and that Spouts are often so placed, that the Rain-water falls into the Foot-way.

Upon reading several Clauses in the Statute of the Second Year of the Reign of their late Mnjefiies King William and Queen Mary, Chapter the 8th, it appeared to the Committee, that there was not sufficient Power to compel the Scavengers or Rakers to carry the Dirt or Filth out of the Streets; and that there are not sufficient

Mr. Robert Hucks also reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Inhabitants of the City and Liberty of Westminster, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behaifof themselves, and others, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the following Witness was examined; viz.

Nathanael Blackerby Esquire: Who said. That the Pavements of the Streets within the said City and Liberty of Westminster are in a very ruinous Condition, for want of sufficient Powers in the Act passed in the 2d Year of the Reign of their late Majesties King William and Queen Maiy, Chapter 8th, to oblige the Owners of empty Houses to keep in repair the Pavements before such Houses; or to oblige the Occupiers of Houses to make life of proper Materials, or to observe proper Levels, in paving the said Streets; it being left entirely to them to have it done in what manner they think fit; or to oblige the Scavengers and Rakers to take up, and carry away, the Filth and Soil out of the Streets, or the Dirt, Dust, or Coal-Allies, made in the Houses of the several Inhabitants, tinless such Inhabitants shall carry1 the same to their Carls, which, in many Cafes, is impossible to be done.

He further said, That there are many Incroachments and Nuisances in the said Streets; for that Bulks, Sheds, and Cellar-doors, are frequently carried so far into the said Streets, that it is not only inconvenient, but dangerous, for Foot Passengers, Coaches, and other Carriage?, to pass; and that in many Places, the Rain-water is conveyed from off the Tops of the Houses by open Spouts, or Gutters, so that it falls immediately into the Streets, and is a great Annoyance to Persons going through the same; all which Incroachments and Ntii-fances cannot be effectually remedied without some further Provision by Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better paving and cleansing the Streets within the City and Liberty of Westminster, the Liberties and Pa-riflies within the Limits of the Weekly Bills of Mortality, in the County of Middlesex, and in the Borough of Southwark, in the County of Surry; and for preventing Nuisances and Incroachments therein: And that Mr. Robert Hucks, Sir William llealhcote, and Sir William Jollijjfe, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

That an humble Address be presented to his Majesty, to express the just Sense of this House of his Majesty’s great Goodness and tender Regard for the lading Welfare and Happiness of his People, in the Marriageof his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales; and asthis House cannot omit any Opportunity of shewing their Zeal and Regard for his Majesty’s Honour, and the Prosperity of his Family, humbly to beseech his Majesty, That, in Consideration of the high Rank and Dignity of their Royal Highnesses the Prince and Princess of Wales, and their many eminent Virtues and Merits, he would be graciously pleased to settle One hundred thousand Pounds a Year on the Prince of Wales, out of the Revenues cheerfully granted his Majesty for the Expences of his Civil Government, and better supporting the Dignity of the Crown, and for enabling his Majesty to make an honourable Provision for his Royal Family, in the same manner tiis Majesty enjoyed it before his happy Accession to the Throne; and also humbly to beseech his Majesty to settle the like Jointure on her Royal Highness the Princess of Wales, as her Majesty had when flie was Princess of Wales; and to allure his Majesty, that this House will enable him effectually to perform the fame, as nothing will more conduce to the Strengthening of his Majesty’s Government, than honourably support ing the Dignity of their Royal Highnesses, from whom we hope to fee a numerous I flue, to deliver down the Blessings of his Majesty’s Reign to latelt Posterity;

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer said to the House* That he was commanded by his Majesty to acquaint this House, That his Majesty Yesterday fentaMeffage to his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales, by the Lord Chancellor, Lord President, Lord Steward, Lord Chamberlain, Duke of Richmond, Duke of Argyle, Duke of Newcastle, Earl of Pembroke, Earl of Scarborough, and Vojl. 22

759

Lord Harrington; which Message, so sent by those Lords, being in Writing, was as follows; viz.

His Majesty has commanded us to acquaint your Royal Ilighuefs, in his Name, That, upon your Royal Highness's Marriage, he immediately took into his Royal Consideration the settling a proper Jointure upon the Princess of Wales; but his sudden going abroad, and his late Indisposition since his Return, had hitherto retarded the Execution of these his gracious Intentions; from which ftiort Delay his Majesty did not apprehend any Inconveniences could arise, especially since no Application had in any manner been made to him upon this subject by your Royal Highness; and that his Majesty bath now given Orders for settling a Jointure upon the Princess of Wales, as far as he is enabled by Law, suitable to her high Rank and Dignity; which he will in proper time lay before his Parliament, in order to be rendered certain and effectual for the Benefit of her Royal Highness.

The King has further commanded us to acquaint your lloyal Highness, That although your Royal Highness has not thought fit, by any Application to his Majesty, to desire that your Allowance of Fifty thousand Pounds per Annum, which is now paid you by Moutkly Payments, at the Choice of your Royal Highness, preferably to Quarterly Payments, might, by his Majestyvs further Grace and Favour, be rendered less precarious *, his Majesty, to prevent the bad Consequences which he apprehends may follow from the undutiful Measures which, his Majesty is informed, your Royal Highness has been advised to pursue, will grant to your Royal Highness, for his Majesty’s Life, the said Fifty thousand Pounds per Annum, to be issuing out of his Majesty’s Civil List Revenues, over and above your Royal Highness's Revenues arising from the Duchy of Cornwall; which his Majesty thinks a very competent Allowance, considering his numerous Issue, and the great Expences which do and must necessarily attend an honourable Provision for his whole Royal Family.

And that, to this Message, his Royal Highness the Prince returned a verbal Answer; which, according to the best Reeolledion and Remembrance of the Lords, was, in Substance, as follows; viz.

That his Royal Highness defined the Lords to lay him, with all Humility, at his Majesty's Feet; and to allure his Majesty, that he had, and ever should retain the utmofc Duty for his Royal Person; that his Royal Highness was very thankful for any Instance of his Majesty’s Goodness to him, or the Princess, and particularly for his Majesty’s gracious Intention of settling a Jointure upon her Royal Highness; but that, as to the Message, the Affair was now out of his Hands, and therefore he could give no Answer to it.

After which, his Royal Highness used many dutiful Expressions towards his Majesty; and then added, " Indeed, my Lords, it is in other Hands; I amforry " for it 5" or to that Effect.

His Royal Highness concluded with earnestly desiring the Lords to represent his Answer to his Majesty in the most respectful and dutiful manner.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

An Act, passed in the Parliament of Scotland'm 1703, was produced, and read; whereby a Toll was granted to the said Burgh of Lanark, for the Term of Nineteen Years, for repairing a Stone Bridge of Three Arches, which the Town had been at a very considerable Expence in building over the River Clyd, at Clyd/holm.

Then the Agents for the Petitioners laid before the Committee several Certificates, duly attested and proved; whereby it appeared, that the Expence of the Repairs annually exceeded the yearly Income of the Tolls granted by the said Act.

And it also appeared to the Committee, that the Bridge has been, and is, of so great Ufeand Service to the Neighbourhood, and the Toll so moderate andeafy, that, notwithstanding the Term granted by the said Act has been expired ever since the Year 1722, yet the Passengers have voluntarily paid for passing over the said Bridge, till of late, when some refused to pay the same; and the Petitioners are apprehen five that others will follow their Example, though the Bridge is and will be very useful and beneficial to the Country in general; which Bridge cannot be rebuilt, if there itoould be Occasion, nor repaired, or supported, if the fame should gojo Decay,'by the said Burgh of Lanark (their Debts being already large, and the Circumstances of the Community low), unless the said former Act be revived, and the Term and Tolls thereby granted continued and enlarged.

The said Report is as follows; viz.

IN Obedience to the Directions of an Act, passed in the First Session of this present Parliament, intituled, An Act for the Application of the Rents and Profits of the Estates forfeited by the Attainders of James late Earl of Derwentwater and Charles Radcliffe;

Requiring the Commissioners or Governors of the Royal Hospital for Seamen, at Greenwich, to contract and agree with able and sufficient Tradesmen, Artificers, or other Persons, for finishing and completing the said Royal Hospital in a workman-like and substantial Manner, on the easiest and most reasonable Terms, according to the Plan laid before the House of Commons, in the said Session of Parliament; and to lay their Proceedings therein with their annual Accounts, before his Majesty, and both Houses of Parliament, respectively;

The Commissioners or Governors of the said Hospital do humbly report as followeth:

' £. s. d.

There has been received, between the 31st of December 1735, and 31st December 1736, out of the

Rents of the Estate 1 - - - ... 5,063 11 — {

E?V/rtry Petition of the Right honourable George Fitzroy e ion% Esquire, commonly called Earl of Ettfton, was presented to the House, and l ead; letting forth, That on Tuesday the Fifteenth of February lait, came on the Election of a Member to serve in Parliament for the City of Coventry, in the room of Sir Adolphus Oughton Knight and Baronet, deceased: That the Petitioner, and John Neale Esquire, stood Candidates: That the said Sir. Neale, and mgny of . the Officers of the Corporation of Coventry, in his Interest, being sensible of the Petitioner's having a Majority of legal Voters (notwithstanding many partial and undue Proceedings of the Mayor and Council of the said Corpora: ion, with regard to the (wearing and inrolling the Freemen, previous to the said Election), and that there was no Way to prevent the Petitioners being duly elected, but by hindering the Freemen in his Interest from polling, did, with this View, employ several Agents to bring from different Parts of the Country great Numbers of Colliers, and others, who had no Pretence of voting, to surround the Place of polling, and to prevent any Freeman in the Interest of the Petitioner from giving his Vote: That the said Colliers, and others, by the Direction and Encouragement of the said John Neale, or his Agents, and of the Officers of the said Corporation, and their Agents, in a most riotous manner, drove from the Place of polling all the Freemen suspected to be in the Petitioner's Interest, and beat and wounded several of them, to the endangering of their Lives; which Riot proceeded to Inch a Height, that the Petitioner apprehended he and his Fronds, if they ft aid any longer at the Polling Booth, would be in imminent Danger of their Lives; and therefore the Petitioner, with all his Agents and Friends, left the Polling Booth, declaring he could not continue there, or proceed any further in the Poll, and loon afterwards lelt the Town: That, had it not been for these riotous and tumultuous Proceedings, the Petitioner would have had a clear and unquestionable Majority of legal Voters: That many other undue, illegal, corrupt, partial, unwarrantable, and indirect Practices, were mafic life of by the Officers of the Corporation of Coventry, and their Agents and Servants, and likewise by the Returning Officer, and by the Agents and Servants of

the said John Neale, in order to procure the said John Neale to bci elected and resumed a Member for the said City; and by means whereof the said John Neale procured himself to he returned a Representative for the said City, to the great Prejudice of the Petitioner, and in Violation of that Freedom which ought to be preservd at Elections for Members to serve in Parliament: And therefore praying, That the House will be plealed to take the Premises into Consideration, and give the Petitioner such Relief therein, as in their great Wisdom and Justice Hi all be thought meet.

Ordered, That the Matter of the said Petition be heard at the Bar of this House, upon Tuesday the 2 2d Day of this initant March.

A Petition of his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace fop l*)e County of Middlesex, in their General Sessions assembled, was presented to the House, and read; ferting forth, That the Petitioners have used their utmost Endeavours to cause the Statutes made and provided for the Repair of County Bridges, Parting of Vagrants, and Repairing of Gaols, to be duly put in Execution; and, in order thereunto, the Petitioners have caused several Rates to be made for the Purposes aforesaid, which have been made in the usual Form practised for many Years last past in this and other Counties; and, particularly, a Rate was lately made for Repairing of Brentford Bridge, which was then greatly decayed, and in Danger of becoming impassable in a very short time, and was so presented to be by the Grand Inquest of the County; and that several of these Rates have been lately removed by Certiorari, and Two of them quashed, and Actions have been brought against the Officers for collecting One of the said Rates, whilst such Rate was in Force; and others of the said Rates, particularly the said Rate for Repairing of JBrentford Bridge, are now removed by Certiorari\ and are liable to be quashed, considering the great Niceties and Forms requisite in such Cases, although the Petitioners have, by themselves and Counsel, used their utmost Care and Caution therein; whereby it is become extremely difficult, if not? im-Vol.

Mr. Earle, according to Order, reported from the Weobley Committee of Privileges and Elections, the Matter, £ie^loft* ns it appeared to them, touching the El-ftion and Return for the Borough of Weobien/> in the Gotnfty of Hereford, and the Resoluiions of the Committee thereupon; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table; where the same was read: And the Report, and Resolutions of the Committee, are as follow; viz.

LTpon the Petition of James Cornewall Esquire, complaining of an undue Election and Return of John Birch Serjeant at Law, deceased, to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Weobley, in the County of Hereford;

The Committee have examined the Merits of this Election:

The Counsel for the Petitioner alleged. That Weobley is an ancient Borough by Prescription: That the Two Constables are the Returning Officers; and that the Right of Election is in the Inhabitants of the ancient Vote-houses of 20J. per Annum Value, or more, residing in the Borough Forty Days before the Election, and paying Scotland Lot; and also in the Owners of ancient Vote-houses not inhabited, such Owners paying Scotland Lot.

The Counsel, w ho appeared to support the Election and Return of Mr. Serjeant Birch, deceased, alleged,

That the Right of Election is in the Inhabitants of Houses of 20s. per Annum Value, or more, paying Scotland Lot.

To prove the Right of Election to be as alleged by the Petitioner's Counsel, the following Witnesse#

W'ere examined; viz.

John Newcomb, Mr. Charles Lloyd* and James Williams: Who spoke to Twenty-nine and Thirty-two Years; and said, That the Right of Election was always understood to be in the Inhabitants of ancient Houses of 20s. per Annum Value, or more, residing within the Borough Forty Days before the Election, and paying Scotland Lot; and also in the Owners of aucient Vote-houses, paying Scotland Lot:

That if the Owners of Vote-houses are resident at any time, even the Night, before the Election, such Jftefidenoa ie> ftaficient to entitle them to vote: That 91Z all

77° 3° Mart173^.

obley {Ji Persons claiming to vote, whether4 Owners or Inhabi-iUeftton. tantSj must pay Scotland Lot.

And Mr. Lloyd and Mr* Williams added farther. That this Right is confined to the Owners or Inhabitants of such Houses only as are ancient Vote-houses, or Houses built upon ancient Foundations; there being other Houses, within the Borough, of much greater annual Value, the Owners and Inhabitants whereof are excluded from voting, as not being Owners or Inhabitants of ancient Houses.

And Mr. Lloyd iaid, That this had been the constant Usage, and was never disputed, or so much as questioned, during the Time which he had known the Borough.

The Counsel on the other Side producing no Evidence to support what they alleged to be the Right of Election;

The Committee came to the following Resolution;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Right Of Election of Burgesses to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Weobley, in the County of Hereford, is in the Inhabitants of the ancient Vote-honfes of 20s. per Annum Value, and upwards, residing in the said Houses Forty Days before the Day of Election, and paying Scotland Lot; and also in the Owners of such ancient Vote-houses paying Scotland Lot, who shall be resident in such Houses at the Time of the Election.

That the Numbers on the Poll were.

For Sir John Buckworth Baronet - - 9°

For Serjeant Birch - - - - 55

For the Petitioner - - - 37

That no Objection was made to the Election or Return of Sir John Buckworth.

But the Petitioner’s Counsel alleged, That the Majority in favour of Mr. Serjeant Birch was obtained by Bribery.

And Mr. Lloyd, being again examined, said. That 14 Persons, whom he named, and who voted for Mr. Serjeant Birch, came in a Body to him, and told him, That they had rather vote for the Petitioner than Mr. Bivfh, if they might have a Gratuity for so doing; and that, if the Examinant would but give them a Promise of a Gratuity, the Petitioner should have their Votes; but he refusing it, they replied, They would go to Mr. Birch's House: That accordingly they went; and, upon their Return from thence, said, Mr. Birch had satisfied them, and therefore should have their Votes.

The Counsel for the Petitioner offering to proceed ip their Evidence;

The Counsel on the other Side acquainted the Committee, That the Right of Election being determined as dated by the Petitioner’s Counsel; and, as the Pc*

titioner’s Evidence Jiad and would affe6fc many of the late Sitting Members Votes, they, to prevent giving the Committee any further Trouble, did admit, that the Petitioner had a Majority.

Upon which the Committee came to the following Resolutions:

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That John Birch, Serjeant at Law, deceased, was not duly elected a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Weobley, in the County of Hereford.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee,

That James CornewallXiLqn'ne'is dulyeledted a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough of Weoblei/.

A Petition of the Merchants and Ironmongers of this Kingdom, in behalf of themselves, and many others trading to his Majesty’s Plantations in America, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That there are Premiums settled by Acts of Parliament, upon the Importation of Tar, Pitch, Turpentine, Hemp, Mails, Yards, and Bowsprits, but not any Encouragement upon the Importation of Iron into this Kingdom, from our American Colonies, where k is capable of being produced, in every respect, equal in Goodness to, the best Iron from Sweden, from which, and other foreign Countries, are annually imported into Great Britain upwards of Twenty thousand Tons, the greatest Part of which is paid for in ready Money; and that the Inhabitants of the British Colonies having already erected several Furnaces and Forges for the making of Bar Iron, Great Britain may, in a Course of Years, be supplied, and rendered independent of any foreign Country, for a Commodity so essential to the Support of our Navigation; but that it is to be feared, if some Encouragement be not given for the Importation of it into Great Britain, that they will be induced to work up the said Iron themselves; to the great Decay and Prejudice of the Iron Trade in this Kingdom, which at this time employs more People, especially of the poor laborious Sort, than any other Trade, that of the Woollen Manufacture only excepted: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration; and to give such Encouragement for the Importation of Bar Iron, Pigs, and Sows, from America, and to lay such a Restraint on their Manufacturing, as to the House shall seem reasonable.

And the Question being proposed, that the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee;

And a Debate arising in the House thereuDon;

Ordered, That the Debate be adjourned until this Day Seven night.

Ordered, That the Lord Sundon have Leave to make Westminster a Motion, it being after Two of the Clock. n

And he moved accordingly: And presented to the House,

and that, if it should happen the Lottery should not prove effectual, by a Day certain, to be named by this House, notwithstanding these further Advantages, the Commissioners may be empowered to raise Money by a Toll, as was done in the same of Fulham Bridge, or by such other Ways as this House shall think fit, for building a Bridge: And therefore praying the House to take the Premises into Consideration, and grant them such Relief, by explaining ami amending the said Act, as may enable them to build the said Bridge, and to repair and maintain the same when built.

A Petition of insolvent Debtors confined in Aylesbury Gaol, in the County of Bucks, on behalf of themselves, and some Thousand others in the several Gaols of this Kingdom; and also,

A Petition of several poor Prisoners, now confined in the Prison for the City and County of Exon, for Debt, in behalf of themselves, and many others, in the like unhappy Condition, in the several Prisons of this Kingdom;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; complaining of their Distress: And praying Relief.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Petition of sundry Iron-masters and Ironmongers, in behalf of themselves, and many others trading to his Majesty’s Plantations in America, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That the Inhabitants of Nezo England have, within these few Years, erected several Forges and Slitting-mills, and do annually make a great deal of Bar Iron, and manufacture the said Iron into Axes, Nails, and sundry other Species, and do now not only supply themselves with great Part of their Nails and Iron Ware, but export great Quantities to many other of his Majesty’s Plantations; to the great Decay and Prejudice of the Iron Trade in this Kingdom, which, at this time, employs more People, and especially of the poor laborious Sort, than any other Trade, that of the Woollen Manufacture only excepted; and that, unless their Slitting-mills are destroyed, and some Stop put to their manufacturing, our Trade mull soon be utterly ruined, and great Numbers of People employed in the Making and Manufacturing of Iron . will be unavoidably deprived of the Means of their Subsistence: And praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to the House thall seem reasonable.

A Petition of sundry Iron-masters and Ironmongers, concerned in the Iron Manufactory of the County of Worcester, in behalf of themselves, and others, was also presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That, in that and other adjacent Counties, there has long been established the greatest Manufactory of Iron Ware in this Kingdom; and that their Manufactory owes its Original, as well to the several Forges ereCTed in the Neighbourhood, for making Bar Iron suitable to particular Purposes, as to the great Plenty of Pit Coal, and the Conveniency of Severn for Exportation; and that their Trade has always increased and flourished, till lately, in proportion to the American Plantations, but now greatly declines, for want of its usual Demands; and that they can ascribe this to nothing but the making of Iron and Iron Wares in that Part of the World; and that many of their Artificers and Workmen have, of late, gone off, and, as ’tis to be feared, have removed themselves thither; and that they are apprehensive, by a free Importation of Bar Iron from America, the Evil complained of will be rather increased than remedied: And therefore praying the House to take their same into Consideration.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table, until the adjourned Debate of Thursday last, upon the Question proposed for referring to a Committee the Petition of the Merchants and Ironmongers of this Kingdom, in behalf of themselves, and many others trading to his Majesty’s Plantations in America, be resumed.

A Petition of the High Sheriff and Grand July assembled at the Affixes holden at Aylesbury, in and for the County of Bucks, the Second Day of March One thousand Seven hundred and Thirty-six, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the County of Bucks, which is large and populous, not having any County Gaol for many Years, was obliged to rent a House to be used for that Purpose, which House so rented was situated in Aylesbury, a Market Town, lying about the Middle of the said County, in which Towa

the Assizes, Sessions, and other publick Meetings for transading County Business, had been usuallykept; and that the House so rented for a Gaol becoming iusufficient for the safe Custody of the many Felons, Debtors, and Offenders, thereunto, from time to time, committed, after divers Presentments of Grand Juries of the said County, of Inch insufficiency, his Majesty’s Justices of the Peace of and for the said County assembled, in their open General Quarter Sessions, of the Peace, at Midsummer Sessions One thousand Seven hundred and Twenty-two, did resolve and agree to build a Gaol in the said Town of Aylesbury, for the Use of the County, and purchased Ground for that Purpose; and were also of Opinion, That a Court Room, or Shire House, for holding the Assizes and Sessions, was much wanted; am! that the building such Court Room, or Shire House, with the said Gaol, at Aylesbury, would be very much for the Benefit of, and was even necessary for, the said County, there being no such Place, but what was the Property of a Private Person, and used with Leave only; and that a considerable Progress was made in such Building, and a large Sum of Money was raiserl, and paid, by the said County, for that Purpose; but that, by including such Court Room, or Shire House, in the said Building, the Justices found they had no Power by Law to assess and levy such a Sum as was necessary to complete the same, whereby t he said Gaol,

Court Room, or Shire House, remain unfinished, and the Families of many of the Workmen employed in such Building are now in extreme Want, for the Money due to them for Work done, and Materials used in the said Building: And therefore, in Consideration of the Premises, and of the Neceftity there is of fin ifiling the said Gaol and Shire House, for the Convenience of the Judges of Assize anti Justices of the Peace, in Sessions to beafsembled, and for the Use of the County in general, as first intended, as well as for paying the Workmen, who are under the greatest Neceflily for want of their Money, praying the House to take the Care of the said County into their Consideration, and to grant, by some Law for that Purpose, such Powers as shall be thought proper, for the assessing and levying, on the said County, such Sum or Sums of Money, for paying the Workmen their just Debts, and also such farther Sums as shall be necessary for completing the said Gaol and Court Rooms, for the Use of the said County; or otherwise to give such Relief therein as to the House flia.ll seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of a Committee: And that they do examine the Matter thereof; and report the fame, as it shall appear to them, to the House:

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the Iloufr, of the 2d Instant, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, the Petitioners laid before the Committee the said Act, pafi’ed in the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty, for repairing the said Highways; and allb the Act, passed in the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for inlarging the Term granted by the said former Act for repairing the said Highways: And several Clauses in both the said Acts were read.

And it appeared by the first-mentioned Act, That several Tolls were granted, and divers Pow ers given, to the Tmftces thereby appointed, or to be appointed, for repairing the said Highways, for the Term of Twenty-one Years, from die First Day of May 170S; and, by the last-ineutioned Act, the former Tolls and Powers were frirther continued for a Term of Twenty-one Years, to commence after the Expiration of the said former Act.

Then die Petitioners called,

Mr. Thomas Barker: Who produced a Book, w herein is entered the Accounts of the Money that had been received and paid yearly by the Treasurer of die Turnpikes erected in pursuance of the aforesaid Acts; whereby it appeared, That about £. 450- was received one Year with another; and that the Disbursements always exceeded the Income of the Tolls: And it also appeared by the said Book of Accounts That there is now due and owing the Sum of £. 2,400. which was borrowed on the Credit of the said Act.

And the said Thomas Barker, being examined in relation to what die Condition of the said Roads now are in, as to the Repairs thereof, laid, That the said Roads are about 29 measured Miles in Length, and that Materials proper 9 N for

for repairing the fame, lie at a DHtance from the greatest Part thereof; and that many Parts of the said Roads are still so very bad, that the same arc dangerous to Passengers in the Winter Season, especially that Part which leads from Dunchurch to Daventry; and that no Materials, fit for repairing the fame, are to be had nearer than Three Miles and a Half; and that the Trcfftees are obliged to pay 12d. pei' Ton for the Stones brought to amend that Part of the Road; and that there is not any Sand or Gravel fit to repair the fame, but what is fetched several Miles.

And he also laid, That the Money cohered, and £. 2,400. which was borrowed upon the Credit of the Acts, as aforesaid, hath been duly laid out and applied according to the Direction of the said Acts; and that the Trca-surer of the Turnpike did last Year lay out a considerable Sum of Money more in repairing the said Roads than the Tolls produced.

And he further said, That a great many Waggons and Carts travel through these Roads (being the Road to Chester, and other considerabte Towns), and that several of the Waggons carry between 50 and 60 Hundred Weight, and that Carts carry in proportion; which extraordinary Weights contributed very much to the making and continuing the Roads to be in so very bad and ruinous Condition as they are now in; and that, if it were not for the'Foils collected from the Drivers of Packhorles,. (great Numbers frequently travelling through the Turnpikes), the said Roads would have been in a much worse Condition than they now are.

And Mr. Barker added to his Evidence, That the Tolls arising by virtue of the said former Acts will not be sufficient to amend the Roads effectually, and to keep them in Repair, if the Inhabitants of the several Parishes, through which the Roads lead, do their Statute-work, which, he said, thoy had constantly done; nor can the Debt due on the Credit of the said Acts, and the Interest thereof, be paid off, unless the Tolls, and the Term now in being, be further continued, and the Powers inlarged.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for making more effectual Two Acts of Parliament, one of the Sixth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, and the other of the Eleventh Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Highways from Old Stratford, in the County of Northampton, to Dunchurch, in the County of Warwick: And that Mr. Cartwright, Sir Charles Mor daunt, and Mr. Digby, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.
