Mr. Alderman Willimot reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of several Merchants, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and others trading to Leghorn, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the feme, as it appeared to them, to the House; and lie read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the Hoofe, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof,

ChrUopher Craw was called: Who, being examined, laid. That he had lived Fourteen Years at Leghorn; and that, during his Residenoe there, it was cuflnmary fer his Majesty’s Consul, with the Majority of the British Merchants, to receive certain small Sums of Money; rfe-Nine Pence per Ton on all Tonage Goods, and Three Pence per Bale on all Bale Goods, imported, to British Ships or Vessels, into the said City; and that the Money so arising was disposed of by the Conlul, with the Confeot of the Majority of the FaAory of that Place, to the Relief of Mariners shipwrecked, or taken in War, and ft rip t, by which they were prevented from going into foreign Service, and to distressed Persons, and other charitable and publick Uses: And said. That be never beard of any Person’s disputing the Pay* meats of the said Rates and Duties; but that there it no legal Authority to compel the Payment thereof, and that it was only founded upon Agreement amongst themselves.

Brenfy Skinner, being examined, confirmed the Evidence given by Mr. Crow: And added further, That, during his Stay at Leghorn, several Persons did refuse the Payment of the said customary Sums of Money; and that, fmee such Refuse!, several distressed Persons, who applied to the Consul for Relief, were denied the fame, there not being a sufficient Fund for that Purpose.

Captain Win. Clerk, and Captain Andrew Elton: Who, being severally examined, said, That they having used the Leghorn Trade upwards of Twenty Years, never heard of any Refiifal being made for the Payment of the said customary Sums of Money, by Persons trading to the said City of Leghorn, till the Year 1726; and that since the Year 1729, it has been totally refused; and that, since such Refusal, several Mariners, his Majesty’s Subjects, have been in very great Dirtrefs, and have been reduced to very great Extremities, for want of having Assistance as formerly; which hath obliged many of them to enter themselves into foreign Service.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for collecting, at the Port of Leghorn, in Italy, certain small Sums of Money, for Relief of Mariners ship-wrecked and taken inWar, and other distressed Persons, his Majesty’s Subjects, and for other pious and charitable Uses, to which the Merchants trading the re have usually contributed: And that Mr. Alderman Willi* moll, Mr. Alderman Ferry, Mr. Yates, Sir John Barnard, and Mr. Alderman Parsons, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Importation A Petition of sundry Iron-masters and Ironmongers, °America>,n *n themselves, and'many others trading to his Majesty’s Plantations in America, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Inhabitants of New England have, of late Years, erected several Forges and Sfitting-mills, and do yearly make a great deal of Bar Iron, and manufactureit into Axes, Nails, and sundry other kinds of Goods, and do now not only supply themselves with a great Part of their Nails, and other Iron Wares, but export great Quantities to many other of his Majesty’s Plantations, to the great Decay and Prejudice of the Iron Trade in this Kingdom, which, at this time, employs more People, and especially of the poor laborious Sort, than any other Trade, that of the Woollen Manufacture only excepted; and that, unless their Slitting-mills are destroyed, and some Stop put to their Manufacturing, our Trade mull soon be utterly ruined, and great Numbers of People, employed in the Making and Manufacturing of Iron, will be unavoidably deprived of the Means of their Subsistence: And therefore praying the House to take the same of the Petitioners into Consideration, and grant them such Relief as to the House shall seem reasonable.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table, until the adjourned Debate of Thursday last, upon the Question proposed for referring to a Committee the Petition of the Merchants and Ironmongers of this Kingdom, in behalf of themselves, and many others trading to his Majesty’s Plantations in America, be resumed.

Lea A Petition of the Mayor, Recorder, Aldermen, and Navigation. Inhabitants of the Town of Hertford, and of the Inhabitants of the Town of Ware, in the County of Hertford, and of several Farmers, Maltsters, and Barge Owners, living in or near the said Towns, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, on behalf of themselves, and several Hundreds of other Persons residing near to, and concerned in, the Navigation on the River Lea, running from Hertford to Ware, and from thence to the River of Thames, near the City of London, and of the Governor and Company of the New River brought from Chadwell and Amwetl to London, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth. That the Navigation of the said River Lea is an ancient Navigation, and hath been very useful to the Publick, by conveying great Quantities of Grain, and other Goods, to and from the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof; and that the Petitioners, the Governor and Company of the New River, have usually had and taken, find still take, great Quantities of Water out of that Part of the River Lea which runs 20

from Hertford to Ware, for supplying the said Cities,

Suburbs, and Liberties thereof, with Watery touching which, many Controversies have arisen between thfe Petitioners the Governor and Company, and the Navigators, and other Persons concerned in the Navigation of the said River Lea, which have lately been accommodated; and that although the Settling of such Disputes will be of great Advantage to the Publick, by ascertaining and improving that Part of the Navigation on the River Lea running from Hertford to Ware, and will very much contribute to preserve and improve the Navigation of that Part which runs from Ware to the River of Thames, and enable the Petitioners the Go-, vernor and Company to supply the said Cities, Suburbs, and Liberties, with good and wholeforae Water, and tend very much to the Increase of Trade; yet such Agreement cannot be established and made effectual without the Aid and Authority of Parliament: And therefore praying, that the House will please to give Leave to bring in a Bill for ascertaining, preserving, and improving the Navigation of the said River Lea-, and to enable the said Governor and Company the better to fUpply the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof, with good Water.

A Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the Company of Watermen and Lightermen, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the said Company: Which was read; letting forth, That by an Act, passed in the First Year of the Reign of King James the First, it was, amongst other Things, enacted, That no Wherryman or

Waterman

&c.

792 ioe — i

Waterman should take any Apprentice unless of the Age of Eighteen Years attheleait, except the Son of a Waterman, who might betaken Apprentice at the Age of Sixteen Years; and that, in pursuance of another Act, passed in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of the Reign of King William the Third, several Rules, Orders and Conltitu-tions, were, by the said Company, made and confirmed, in the manner thereby prescribed; One of which directs, " That no Waterman shall have more than One Appren-c< tice at one time; nor shall be capable of taking any " Apprentice until such Master hath been a Freeman " Seven Years; nor shall take a Second Apprentice till " his First be dead, or the Term expired; and that no " Lighterman shall take any Apprentice, until he is a " real Owner of Two Lighters, nor shall have any more " than One Apprentice atone time;" under the Penalties therein mentioned; and that, by an Act passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of Queen Anne, the said Clause in the l ft of King James the lft, and the said recited Rule, Order, and Constitution, and all and every other Rule, Order, and Constitution, made for restraining any Waterman, Wherry man, and Lighterman, taking and breeding Apprentices, were repealed, and made void; and that, by a Clause in another Act,-of the same Year of her said late Majesty’s Reign, it is enacted, That in case any Waterman, Bargeman, Wherry man, or Lighterman, being duly summoned, by leaving Notice in Writing, at the Place of his usual Abode, in pursuance of Notice given to the said Company of Watermen by the Lord High Admiral, or the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral, for the Time being, shall not appear before the Rulers of the said Company within Ten Days after such Summons to be sent on board the Royal Fleet; such Person, being convicted thereof, is to suffer One Month's Imprisonment, and to be disabled from working on the River Thames, or enjoying any of the Privileges of the said Company, for Two Years; and that, in consequence of the said Act of the Fourth of Queen Anne, great Numbers of such Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, for the Sake of small Sums of Money, have taken Apprentices at Twelve and Thirteen Years of Age, not having Strength, nor being of Size, sufficient for the Labour required in such Occupation; and have taken more than they had Employment for, so that the Number of Masters and Apprentices is increased to upwards of Eight thousand; am!, many such Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, having no settled Habitation, or Place of Abode, such Apprentices are not only unskilful, but too frequently become vagrant, idle, and profligate; by means whereof the Lives and Goods of Passengers have been, and are frequently, in imminent Danger, and often lolt; and many Robberies have been, and arc daily, committed on the said River; and the good Intention of the said Laws has not been answered, in providing able and fuflficient Seamen for the Royal Navy; in that many of them are unlit, or of very little Use, when employed in the Service of the said Royal Navy; and in that many of such Watermen, having no settled Place of Abode or Residence, the Summons for their Appearance before the Rulers of the Company cannot be served in the manner directed by the said last recited Act; whereby they avoid the Penalty, they are thereby liable to, and withdraw and hide themselves in secret Places, at Times of the greatest Necessity for their Service; so that it has often happened, when Five hundred have been summoned, not Fifty have appeared, to be sent on board the Fleet: Aud therefore praying the House, to take the Premises into . Consideration; and that Leave maybe given to bring in a Bill to limit the Number of Apprentices to he taken by each Waterman, Wherryman, or Lighterman; to ascertain at what Age they shall be bound; and to reltraiu any Waterman, Wherryman, or Lighterman, from taking any Apprentices whatsoever, unless he shall have some known or settled Place of Abode, in such manner as to the House shall lean meet.

very prejudicial to the Landholders, within the said Counties; and that a large Tract. of Meadow Ground, containing many Thousand Acres, besides Arable and Pasture, lying on the River Soar, will be much more liable to be overflowed, by raising the Water with Locks and Flood-gates, which are oftentimes broke down by great Floods; and great Discouragement will fail upon the Breeders of large Horses for Draught, and the publick Service, in time of War; and that there is a Navigation within Twelve Miles of the Place whither it is intended to be carried; and that bringing in great Quantities of Deals, and foreign Timber, will low'er the Price, of the "Woodlands, and discourage Planting; and that these, and other Injuries greatly apprehended, will render the Landholders unable to pay the Taxes, and Parliamentary Subsidies: And therefore praying the Floufe to do therein as to the House shall seem meet.

Hedxcorth reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Commissioners of the River IFear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fume, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk s Table: Where the same was read; and is as followed]; viz.

The Committee h ive, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the Committee, an Act, made in the Third Year of the Reign of his late Majesty King George the First, intituled, An Act for Preservation and Improvement of the River /fear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland, in the County of Durham; and fume Clauses therein wcrercud, whereby it appeared. That certain Powers were granted to the Commissioners thereby appointed, for and during the Term of Twenty-one ^ears; and certain Duties were also imposed, payable from and after the 24U1 Day of June 1717,^and for the Space of Twenty-one Wars then next following.

And another Act, made in the 13th Year of the Reign of his laid lute Majesty, was laid before the Committee; and Part thereof was read, whereby it appeared, That several additional Powers were granted to the said Commissioners.

Then the Petitioners called,

Mr. Smith: Who said, That the Duties granted by the first-menlioned Act had produced annually about X- 1,boo, or X- L700> which had been duly laid, out in preserving and improving the said River Wear, and Port and Haven of Sunderland; but that the same had been found insufficieut for the Purposes for which they were intended.

The Committee then proceeded to inquire what was further necessary to be done, towards preserving and improving the said River, Port, and Haven: Upon which,

Mr. John Thomas was called: Who laid before the Committee, a Draught of the said River, Port, and Haven; whereby it appeared, that, on the South Side of the said Port, a large Pier had been erected; and he laid, that another on the North Side was absolutely necessary. Ships being frequently (trended on the Sands there, for want of the same; One Infiance of which he himself had seen.

The said Mr. Thomas then laid before the Committee, an Estimate of the necessary Expence of erecting a large Pier on the North Side of the said Harbour, which amounts to X- 12,000 or thereabouts; and cannot be raised during the Continuance of the Term granted, which is near expiring.

It appeared likewise to the Committee, by the Evidence of

Mr. Samuel Gowland\ That the Duties, Penalties, and Forfeitures, payable by virtue of the said last mentioned Act, frequently cannot be effectually levied, by reason that the Power thereby given to the Commissioners to direct their Warrants, is only to the Constable of the Place, where the Offence is committed; by which means the Distress upon Goods for Offences committed is frequently evaded by the Offenders removing their Goods into such different Parts; and where Constables, to whom the Warrants are directed, cannot execute the same; and the Constable is the only Person particularly appointed, by the said first-mentioned Act, for the Execution of such Warrants.

Sir IVMiam Stanhope reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the High Sheriff and Grand Jury, assembled at the Assizes holden at Aylesbury, in and for the County of Bucks, the 2d Day of March 1736, was referred, That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

Mr. William Hay ton was examined: Who said, That the County of Bucks, which is of a considerable Extent, had no County Gaol; but the Prisoners for Debt, and the Felons, were confined in a House, rented for that Purpose, in Aylcsbui'y, which h a Market Town, situated, as near as can be, in the Middle of the said County; and that, over and above the annual Rent, the County was yearly at great Charge and Expence in strengthening and repairing the fame; notwithstanding which, there were frequent Escapes; and for want of convenient Room, the Debtors and Felons were often confined together: That, after several Presentments of divers Grand Juries at the Assizes, and frequent Complaints made at the Quarter Sessions held for the said County, of the Insufficiency of the House so rented, and considering the Money that had been annually laid out in repairing the fame, the Justices, at their General Quarter Sessions in the Year 1722, agreed to purchase the said House so uled for a Gaol, and the Soil and Ground thereunto belonging, whereon to erect a new Gaol, with proper Conveniences, the Ground being commodious and convenient for that Purpose, the Freehold of which House and ..Ground has been conveyed to several Trustees, for the Use of the said County:

That it had been agreed upon, by the said Justices, in their General Quarter Sessions, That, in erecting the said Gaol, Part thereof, which is in the Centre of the said Building, should be appropriated for a convenient Court Room, or Shire Hall, there being no Place in the said Town of Aylesbury fit for holding the Assizes and Quarter Sessions, but in the Market-house, which is the Property of a private Person, very incommodious for such Purpose, being much out of Repair, and no ways under the Controul, or subject to any Alteration to be made by or for the Use of the County:

And Mr. Hayton added, That, in order to pay the Purchase-money, and defray the necessary Charges and Expence of such Building, the said Justices did afterwards affels the Sum of Five Pence in the Pound, at Three Assessments, made at Three several Quarter Sessions for the said County, within the Space of Three Years; which Assessments were laid on the several Hundreds and Divisions of the County, according to the Proportions of the Land Tax, and amounted, in the Whole, to the Sum of £.4,918 or thereabouts, whereof the Sum of £.4,578 and upwards, was collected and paid; and there still remains about the Sum of £. 340 in Arrear, from several Parishes, who refuse to pay the same; alleging the y are not obliged to pay such Assessments by Law, neither have the Justices a Power to compel the Payment thereof:

And he also laid, That upon the Credit of the said Assessments, fj ordered to be made, several Workmen, Artificers, Labourers, and others, were employed in and about the said Building, and a very considerable Progress made therein > and that an exact Account was taken by several of his Majesty s Justices of the Peace for the said County, who, at different times, examined the Bills and Accounts relating thereto, and, after many Dedu6tions were made out of the said Bills and Accounts, there remained due to such Persons, for what they have done in and about the said Building, upwards of £. 1,900 over and above what there has been paid to them already: And the said Mr. Hayton further said, That divers of the Workmen so employed, and their Families, are reduced to great Poverty, for want of their Money for the said Work, which has been done above Twelve Years; and that one of the Workmen was arrested, and carried to Gaol, being not able to pay the Debt.

And, upon the Examination of Mr. Hayton, it also appeared, That the said Building remains untiniflied, and stands in a very ruinous Condition; and that a further Sum was wanting to complete the said Building; and that the Sum necessary for defraying the said Expence cannot be effectually raised, and levied on the said County, without the Aid and Authority of Parliament.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill to impower the Justices of the Peace for the County of Bucks to raise Money to discharge the Debts incuncd on account of building a Gaol and Court Room, and for finishing the fame, for the Use of the County: And that Sir William

but that, in the said Acts, there is 110 Direction to oblige the Governor, Consuls, and Assistants, of the said Company, to hold General Courts at any fixed Time, or upon any Emergencies; whereby great Inconveniencies have happened, as w ell as from Want of a Power to restrain the Number of Votes given in the Election or Removal of the Company's Officers and Servants, and in the Disposal of their Money to Persons under certain Qualifications; and that the Petitioners apprehend, that, if such Quali-lication was confined to such Members of the said Company only as have traded upon thfeir own Account, so far as to have paid Impositions to a certain Amount, and within a certain Time, towards the public Expences of the Company (there being, in most public Companies, Limitations of the like Nature), the same w ould greatly encourage the Trade, and tend to the better Regulation of the Government of the said Company: And therefore praying, That Leave may be given to bring in a Bill for effecting the Purposes aforesaid; and frivolous Pretences, the Petitioner has been kept several Years in Suspence; when the Society being prelfed for a categorical Answer, they, by their Treasurer, acquainted the Petitioner, in Writing, "That they are advised, that " a Renewal at present will be greatly prejudicial to the " Interest and Good of the College; for which Reason " they are not willing to treat about any Renewal f and that the Petitioners Family have been the Lessees of the said Estate for more than Two hundred Years; and that the Petitioner, upon Assurance given him, by the Provost and Fellows of the said College, that they would renew the Lease with him as soon as they were impowered by Law so to do, was induced to expend upwards of Nine hundred Pounds in such Improvements as he was not obliged to make, for which he has received no Advantage exceeding the Interest of the principal Sum; and has also paid, to and for the Use of the College, the Land Taxes for One hundred Pounds per Annum, and otherwise, amounting to Six hundred Pounds, and upwards, which Sum he was not obliged to pay; and therefore, and in regard the Petitioner was not obliged to pay the said Sqm, and the now subsisting Term expiring at Michaelmas 1747, expressing his Hope, that the House will be pleased to relieve him, inasmuch as a very large House has been built upon the said Leasehold Estate, and more than thje Value of the Fee-simple of the said Estate has been paid by the Petitioner, and his Family, Lessees thereof, the Addition of Forty-two Pounds per Annum being imposed upon them by the Act: of Parliament aforesaid, contrary to the original Contraft: And therefore praying, That the House will take his same into Consideration, and give him such Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

A Petition of the Mayor, Justices, Burgesses, and Okeharaptou other principal Inhabitants, of the Town and Borough Market, of Okehampt.on, in the County of Devon, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Town and Borough have, by virtue of several Charters, Grants, and Conveyances, held a Market weekly, and several Fairs yearly, in the said Town; and received such Tolls, Rents, and Sums of Mone\% as are made payable by the said Charters, Grants, and Conveyances, for Stallage and Standings, or otherwise, there, for a long Continuance of Time, amounting annually to a considerable Sum of Money; and that good Part thereof arises from the Weighing of White Yarn, commonly called M hite Shute; for which Purpose the Mayor and Burgesses of the said Town, for the Time being, keep publick Scales and Weights, and proper Servants to attend, in order that no lnjustice be done either to the Buyer or Seller, and to receive for every Score Four Pence, the Income whereof generally amounted to Eighty Pounds per Annum, or upwards; and that, out of the Produce of this, and other Revenues belonging to the said Town, a Chaplain and Grammar Schoolmaster is allowed a Salary, and the Chapel, School-house, Bridges, and Streets, repaired, and other necessary Officers maintained; but that, for about Ten Years last past, there hath been a great Abatement in the Revenue arising from the said Markets and Fairs, by reason of a great Number of Spin-ning-houses being set up in the Neighbourhood, whereby the Dealers in Wool set out certain Quantities thereof to the Poor for Spinning, at a very low Price; and, instead of setting out Sixteen Ounces, generally allot such poor People Eighteen or Twenty Ounces to the Pound, which is never brought to any publick Market; and that such Dealers frequently, instead of prompt Payment in Money, oblige the Spinners to take Goods at an extravagant Price, by way of Barter, contrary to the Laws now in being; whereby the poor People are much opprested, and coufequently the Yarn not so well lpun as it ought to be, and the berg^s not brought to their usual Peifeftion: And therefore praying the House to give Leave to bring in a Bill for redressing the Grievances aforesaid, or to give the Petitioners such Other Relief in the Premises as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Regulating A Petition of several Merchants of London, whose Merchant Names are thereunto subscribed, was presented to the eamen. House, and read; letting forth, That an Act was passed in the Second Year of his present Majesty’s Reign, for the better Regulation and Government of Seamen in the Merchants Service; wherein several useful Regulations and Provisions were made, which apparently shew, that the Intention thereof was to redress the many Inconveniencies that Merchants, Owners and Masters of Ships, at that time laboured under from the Irregularities of Seamen in their Service; notwithstanding which, as the Petitioners conceive, the good Design of that Law is in a great nicafure frustrated by a Clause therein, which gives Liberty to Seamen belonging to Merchants Ships to enter into the Service of his Majesty, without incurring the Forfeiture of their Wages, or being deemed Deserters; and that this Liberty occasions the Petitioners t<* be put under great Difficulties; frequent Instances having happened, where Seamen have entered thomselves on board Men of War when they have been in remote Countries, and thereby eecafioned several Masters of Ships to be detained from

pursuing their Voyages, by obliging them to Hop in foreign Ports, till they could have other Seamen to navigate their Vessels; and that the Delays so occ a tinned have been attended with treble the Lx pence which ot her-wife would in the said Voyages have been incurred; and that, l»v reason of the aforesaid Hardships, Expences, and Delays, the Navigation and Commerce of this Kingdom is discouraged, and injured greatly: And therefore praying, That the said Act may be so explained and amended, as that no Seamen, hired on board any Merchant Ship or Vessel, dial I be at Liberty to quit such Service after the Sailing or Departure of such Ships or Vessels from any Port or Place in this Kingdom, on the Penalty of forfeiting the Wages due to him; or that the Petitioners may have such other Relief as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. Richard Shirgold, sworn Broker, was called, and examined; and, being asked, W hat he apprehended to be the Reasons that the Lottery did not fill ? he informed the Committee, That the Conditions thereof were generally esteemed to be so very di('advantageous, that the moneyed People did not think it their Inteielt to engage therein; and that, in order to make it effectual, he apprehended there should be a Premium of Two per Cent. given to the Suhlcribers of Fifty Pickets, and upwards.

And said, That the Clause, in the late Ad, for prohibiting the DispofaJ of Chances of Tickets for the said Lottery, for any lei's Time than the whole Time of drawing thereof, was another Reason why the said Lottery did not take Effect; and that he believed, if Liberty was allowed for disposing of the Chances of Tickets for an unlimited Time, it might be a Means of making the said Lottery effectual.

And he said, That it might be necessary that the Clause in the late Act of Parliament, subjecting any Office-VpL. 22.

keeper to the Penalty of £. 500 for taking a Premium for the Repayment of any Sum of Money on any Ticket or Tickets which shall be drawn fortunate, should extend only to such Office-keeper that should sell and dispose of the Chance of any Ticket or Tickets, which he had not the actual Po Hellion of during the whole Time of drawing the said Lottery, or till such Ticket or Tickets was or were drawn.

And said, That bethought the Commissioners should have a dilcretionary Power granted them to lock up, and stand the drawing of, such Tickets, for the Account of the said Bridge, which should remain feribed.

And also. That the Subicrihers under the lass Act should have the faing Advantage astheSubscribers tinder this intended Act; and that, if the whole Number of Tickets were not subscribed or accepted by the Commissioners for the Account of t he Bridge, lb that the Subscription should he entirely closed in One Month after the Books should be opened at the Bank; then, and in such Case, the Subicrihers should have their Money returned again, on Demand.

And, being asked by the Committee, Whether lie had communicated these Observations to any Persons; said. That he had to several; and that it was the general Opinion of those who were likely to be large Subscribers, that, if the foregoing Particulars were granted, the Lottery might be (bon filled.

And being further aiked, Whether he believed, that, if the said Allowance of Two per Cent. Premium to the Subicrihers of Fifty Tickets, and upwards, might not make the said Lottery effectual, without having the Liberty of disposing of the Chances of Tickets for such au unlimited Time as afore-mentioned ? gave for Answer, That Six per Cent, would not be sufficient for that Purpose, without such Liberty.

Thomas Ripley Esquire, Comptroller of his Majesty’* Works, being then examined, and asked, What the Charges might amount to, in building a Stone Bridge at Palace-yard, Westminster ? said. That there were Two Ways of building a Stone Bridge; the one Way was, by making a solid Bed of Piles, duff-tailed together; drove Eight or Ten Feet deep, or as deep as the nature of the Soil would permit, and to he Eighteen Inches below Low-water Mark, and from thence wholly Stone, and Thirty Feet wide in the Clear, with the Recedes on each Pier, would cost the Sum of Eighty thousand Pounds, and he a convenient Bridge for Man, Horse, and all other Carriage; and that the said Bridge might be completely finished in Three Summers, if not in Two.

And being aiked. If there were any Person or Persons that would undertake to build and complete the the said Bridge for that Sum, and give sufficient Security for executing the same ? said, There were Persons that would undertake to do it, and give sufficient Security.

And also informed the Committee, That the other Way of building a Stone Bridge was, by carrying down Piers to the Bed of the River; and that only laving the Foundations thereof would cost One hundred thousand Pounds at lead, betides the Charge of building the said Bridge.

And being aiked, What the Charge of building a Stone Bridge, on duff’tailed Piles, at the Horse-ferry, would be, said, That it might be built for Seventy thou-f.uul Pounds at most; the River being the re but 850 Feet w ide, and at Palace-yard, Westminster, 1,072 Feet.

And being asked. What the Charge of building aTim-ber Bridge at Palace-yard, Westminster, would be, upon the same Plan that Fulham Bridge was built? said, There would be great Difficulties in buildingaTimber Bridge at Palace-yard, by reason the Waterat Low-water Mark was Ten Feet deep, and flowed 14 Feet perpendicular; whereas at Fulham Bridge it was only Six Feet at Low-water Mark, and flowed Eight Feet only at High Water; so that the Charges of a Bridge at Palace-yard, Westminster, could not ealily be compared to that at Fulham; but believed, that a Timber Bridge might be built at Palace-yard, Westminster, for the Sum of Twenty-lix thousand Pound, or thereabouts; and that the same could not be finished in less than Two Years, by reason such Scat!ings

Westminster Timber, nefceflary for building the fame, could not Bridge. be provided in less than One Year: And being asked, What the Charges would amount to in building a Timber Bridge at the Horse-ferry? said, He believed it might be completed in Two Years for Twenty thousand Pounds.

And further said, That, if a Stone Bridge was erected either at Palace-yard, Westminster, or at the Horse-ferry, there are Materials in Town sufficient (if wanted) to begin the same forthwith.

And being asked, What the clear Profits of the Toll at Fulham Bridge might amount to? said, He believed Two thousand Pounds/vr Annum, or thereabouts: And then being asked, What the Toll of the Bridge built at the New Palace-yard, Westminster, or at the Horse-ferry, might produce, if the same Toll was granted as at Fulham f said, That he believed the Income would be at Jeaft Three or Four times as much as that at Fulham; and that, in Conversation with others, he found that they were of the same Opinion with him.

And then being asked, How long Fulham Bridge was building? said, That it was begun in March 1728, and finished in Christmas following: And being likewise asked. How long it might stand, before any considerable Repairs would be wanting to be done thereto; said, That there had been feme Repairs donefir.ee the building the said Bridge; and, in Seven Years more, it will want considerable Repairs.

And being asked, How long a Stone Bridge would stand, without any considerable Repairs ? said, Five hundred Years, if built in a plain and substantial manner, as proposed.

And being then asked. How wide the River was at Fulham, and at the Horse-ferry ? said. That the River at Fulham was 847 Feet, and the Horse-ferry 850 Feet, wide: And being asked, If a Stone Bridge was built at the Horse-ferry, whether there would be sufficient Waterway left ? said, That he believed that a Stone Bridge might be built there, and leave 720 Feet clear Waterway; which he supposed would be sufficient, by reason that the River at Peter borough-house was but 740 Feet wide between Bank and Bank; so that there will be al-xnoft the same Water-way though the Bridge as there Was between Bank and Bank at PeterIwrougk-house.

And being asked, How long a Timber Bridge might stand, if kept in Repair; and what the Charges of keeping the same in Repair Fifty Years would be ? he said. It would be equal to the Building of it twice over in the same time, allowing it was as completely finished as that at Fulham.

Nathaniel Blackerby Esquire, being asked, What he thought the Charges of making a clear Passage from Channell R010 to the Privy Garden would amount to ? said, That the purchasing the Houses and Ground ne-~cessary to be pulled down, to make a Way 30 Feet wide to the Bridge, by Computation, would cost Ten thousand Pounds, or thereabouts.

Thomas Ripley being called again, and asked, What he thought the Charges might be in making a free Passage to Palace-yard, Westminster ? said, That the Houses which must be purchased, to open a passage of 100 Feet wide to the Banqueting-house, the Rents thereof being Fifteen hundred Pounds per Annum; and the old Houses would be valued as he believed, at Twenty Years Purchase, and amount to Thirty thousand Pounds, but leave a Ground-rent of£. 600 per Annum, which would make a considerable Abatement in the Purchase-money, and reduce it to the Sum of 15 or 16 thousand Pounds.

And being asked. What the Charges might amount to, in making a clear Way on the other Side of the Water, if a Bridge was built at New Palace-yard? he said, At present there was only a bad, narrow Cart or Bridleway; and to purchase the Ground, to make a good Road through the Marshes, would amount to Seven thousand Pounds, or thereabouts; but, if a Road might be permitted to be made under the Shore from Slang ale to the Stairs of Lambeth, it might be done for

jf.bjpoo.

And being asked. What the Charges might amount to in opening and making the Road at the Horse-ferry ? said, That lie had not very well considered it; but that there were but a few old Houses in the Way in Dhiy-lane, which, he supposed, might be purchased for about £. 3,000, as near as he could compute.

And being further asked, When any Persons came over the Bridge at the Horse-ferry, who were Inhabitants of the Upper Liberty, whether they would not have a convenient Passage or Way to the fame, without coming to the Old Palace-yard? he said, He believed the Inhabitants would make it their Choice to go round by Hide-park Corner to the Upper Liberty, rather than by Old Palace-yard, and through the other Streets which lead to the Upper Liberty; and that little or no Charges would be necessary to make a Road good that Way.

And further acquainted t he Com mi ttee. That a M iddle Way might be found for building a Bridge of Timber and Stone together, thus: By building Walls Two Foot thick upon Two Rows of duff-tailed Piles, and laying Timber from Pier to Pier, and covering the same with Lead, which would keep the Timber dry, and preserve it from the Weather, so as to continue Fifty Years, at lead, with small Repairs; and would cost at Palace-yard, Westminster, besides purchasing Ways and Passages, Thirty-eight thousand Pounds, and at the Horse-ferry Thirty thousand Pounds, or thereabouts.

Surcfiafed with ready Money; and that, for want of a ue Encouragement, the Inhabitants of those Colonies have already negun to erect and set up Slitting-mills, and will be the more induced to work up and pianu-facture the said Iron themselves; which, as the Petitioners conceive^ will greatly tend to the Decay, ^lejudice, and Discouragement of the Trade and Navigation of this Kingdom: And therefore praying the House to take the same into Consideration, and grant such Encouragement to the Importation of Bar Iron, Pigs, and Sows, from America, and to lay such ILdiraiut on their Manufacturing of Iron there, as to the House Audi seem most reasonable.

Colchester Captain Martin reported from the Committee, to Streets, whom the Petition of the Mayor, Aldermen, Assistants, and Common Council, of the Borough of Colchester, in the County of F.ffex, in behalf of themselves, and other the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and the Liberties thereof, was referred, That, the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof, George Wegg Esquire, Colonel John Price, and Wm. Mahew, were called: Who, being severally examined, said. That the Pavements of the Streets and Lanes of the said Town, a Mile of which is the direct Road from London to Harwich, are in a very bad and ruinous Condition; and mull so remain, unless further Powers are given than what, by the Laws now in being, the Corporation are at present inverted with; the same having, as they apprehended and believed, been duly put in Execution, but found ineffectual; which, as they thought, in some measure, arose from this, that several Houses in the said Streets had of late Years been pulled down, and others were untenanted; so that the Work that used to be done by the Inhabitants ofthofe Houses, in repairing of the Streets, was now so much Loss to the said Town.

They further laid, That it would be of general Convenience to Travellers, as well as to the Inhabitants, to have the Streets well enlightened, as also to have a regular Watch and Ward kept; the Watch and Ward, as now kept in pursuance of the Statute at Winchester, being of little or no Use; but that there was no Law now in being, to enable the Inhabitants to make a Sufficient Assessment or defraying the necessary Charges that mud arise from so great Conveniences being procured to the said Town.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for the better Cleaning, Paving, Repairing, and Enlightening of the Streets and lLanes in the Town of Colchester, in the County of Esse:r, and for appointing a regular Watch within the said Town: And that Captain Martin, Mr. Houblon, Sir Robert Abdy, Mr. Brain-Jion, Colonel Bladen, Mr. Parsons, Mr. Leafhes, and Mr, Charles Stanhope, do prepare, and bring in, the lame.

The said Administrators have been at great Charges and Expences in obtaining the Letters of Administration, and in prosecuting and defending several Suits at Law, and in otherwise carrying the said Trust, repoled in them by the said Act of Parliament, into Execution: the several Accounts whereof have not yet been delivered to them, the Caules being still depending.

Mr. Bostoc/c Toiler, being called, said. That he appeared as Agent for the Petitioners the Corporation and Inhabitants of the Town of Hertford. and also for the inhabitants of the Town of If are, and for the Navigators on the River Lea; and that he, about Four Years ago, was directed by those Petitioners to inquire what Right the New River Compuny lmil to take so large a Quantity of Water out of the River Lea, as they constantly did; and, about a Year and Half since, he came to the Knowledge of the lame.

That the Governor and Company of the New River should take away their great; Pipes, then lying in the River Lea, and, dnstead thereof, should lay Two lefier Pipes, the one of Eight, and the other of Six, Inches Bore, at or -near the Places where, the great Pipes lay, and to place and contrive them, that they might be coniiantly fervad with Water to supply the New River; and, if, upon Trial, it should be found that the Water in the River Lea would not always rife high enough to fill the said Pipes, that the Governor and Company might, and they were thereby authorized, to set up and use a Turnpike,

L*i And Mr. Toller further fa Id, That when he had col-

ligation. Ic&ed all the Fasts together, he recommended it to the , Inhabitants of the Towns of Hertford and lVare, and the

Navigators, to take the Opinion of some eminent Coun-fel; whereupon a same was stated, a Copy whereof was laid before the present Lord Chancellor, then his Majesty’s Attorney General, and another Copy before the late Lord Chief Justice Reeve; and they both advised, That, as the same was a publick Concern, proper Application should be made to the Legislature; and thereupon he waited on the New River Company, from time to time, by Directions of the Persons he was concerned for, that an amicable Agreement might be entered into.

Dr. Defeguliers, being called, and examined, said, That, in August last, he was sent for into the Country, by the Navigators on the River Lea, but did not know for what Purpose: That, whilst he (laid there, he measured the Gage, or new-made Instrument, belonging to the New River Company, through which the whole Water* passed out of the River Lea, and found that lnftru-mentto measure Six Feet wide, and Two Feet deep, and the Top thereof to be 28 Inches above the Cill at the Water-houfo; and then he measured the Quantity of Water below the Gage, and found, that it run about 2,400 Tun in an hour, with small Allowances for the Eddies: That, on the 28th of the same Month, he went down again, and, not trusting to the First Experiment, he then made several others, in Presence of many Persons of the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and of one Mr. Mill, a Gentleman belonging to the New River Company, who also made a Calculation; and that, after making several large Allowances, he found the Quantity of Water diverted or taken out of the said River to be 2,100 Tun per Hour.

He also said, That, by the Pipes which were directed to be laid down by the before-mentioned Order of Council, about 200 Tun of Water an Hour would be taken out of the River, the Surface of the Water being just over the Pipes; but if the Pipes were square, 250 Tun of Water per Hour would be taken out.

And he further said, That the fall of that River is very cdnsiderable, and if a Compensation was given for erecting Locks, and making other Conveniences for the Navigation, not only that Quantity of Water which is now taken, but half as much more might be taken, without any Prejudice to the Navigation.

Mr. Thomas Pettit, and Mr. James Fordham, Barge-Owners, being severally examined, said. That they had known the River Lea, the one 45, and the other 47 Years; and that there is a greater Difference in the Navigating of Boats and Barges now, than when they tirft used the River:

That formerly they navigated to and from London to Ware in a considerable left time than they now do, and at a much less Expence; and the Rcalon they gave was, because the Lock-keepers cut the Weeds, which makes the Water to run quicker away, and thereby the River becomes more shallow, and great Quantities of Gravel and Stones being thrown into the River by the Weir-keepers and Millers at the Wares, occasions so many Shoals, that they cannot now pass, without paying at the several Locks for Flashes of Water frequently in the Summer-leafon, by reason great Quantities of Water are taken out of the River, for the Use of the New River Company: And for those Reasons, the Witnesses said, That the Navigation is become very tedious and expensive.

They also said, The Owners of Boats and Barges, and the Navigators, had raised, amongst themselves, the Sum of £. 3,000. which had been expended in removing of Shoals: which, if ib large a Quantity of Water had not been taken away, and such Shoals thereby made, they should not have been at so great an Expence; and that, before the Weeds were cut, and Gravel and Stones thrown into the River, the Boats and Barges, when they got below Waltham Abbey, were frequently towed to Old Ford9 without any Obstruction, or the Assistance of any Weirs; which cannot now be done.

And they likewise said. That there had been, in their Memory, Two Commissioners of Sewers taken out, in relation to this Matter; and, during the time the Coin-missioners fat, and executed the Powers given by those Commissioners, the Navigation was carried on much ealier, and at a less Expence, than at other times.

And they severally added to their Evidence, That if a Fund was established for removing the Shoals, and a con* stant Commission of Sewers established, it would make a double Recompence for the Water now taken out of the River by the New River Company; and that the several Nuisances complained of would thereby be remedied: and that such a Quantity of Water, as is now taken out, be the better spared.

Mr. Toller, being again called, said, That the River Lea is divided into Two or Three Branches, between the Towns of Hertford and Ware, and unite again into One Stream, a little below Ware Mill: That the ancient and right Way of navigating Boats and Barges between the said Towns, was, and is, through One of the said Branches, called Manifold Ditch; but the Navigation is now carried on, and has been for many Years past, through another Branch of the said River, called, the Mill Stream, running to Ware Mills, and from thence, through a Lock or Cistern there, into the main Stream running to Ware Bridge; but this Navigation is carried on by Agreement between the Navigators and the Owners of Ware Mill; but may be refilled by the Owners of that Mill; and, if they should, the Navigators must have Recourse to their ancient ami right Way through Manifold Ditch; which will oblige the New River Company to pull up their Turhpike or Jetty erected cross the fame, for conveying the Water they now take, which is now agreed they may take out of the said River Lea, whereby the Company will be less able to supply the Cities of London and Westminister with the Quantity of Water they now do; but, that the Company may be enabled to supply the Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof, the Company have agreed to purchase Ware Mills, and the Lock belonging’to the fame, with the Stream of Water running to the fame; and to declare, That the Stream through the Lock there into the main River, shall be the indifpu table right Way for navigating Boats and Barges for the future between Hertford and Ware; and when the same flmH be so purchased, and declared, the Navigators have, on their Part, agreed to relinquifti all their Right and Title to the Navigating of Boats and Barges through Manifold Ditch; by which the Company will have the sole Use of the Turnpike or Jetty already erected, and will thereby be the better enabled to supply the said Cities of London and Westminster, and the Suburbs and Liberties thereof, with good fresh Water.

Mr. Jasper Bull, Clerk to the New River Company, said, That he had Directioqs from the General Court of that Company, held the 17th Instant, to attend, and acquaint the Committee, That the Company had agreed to certain Proposals made to them; which were, That the Corporation of the Town of Hertford should have £.500. Premium, and £. 50. per Annum, to commence from Michaelmas 1734; and that the Sums of £. 1,000 Premium, and £. 300. per Annum, were to be for the Town of Ware, and for the Improvement of the Navigation only, to commence from the same time; and that the several Sums were to be paid to certain Trustees, on condition that such a Quantity of Water was given to the New River Company, out of the River Lea, as will pass through a Trough of Six Feet wide, and Two Feet deep; and the same was confirmed by Act of Parliament.

It appeared to the Committee, That there has been a Navigation for Boats and Barges, from the Town of Hertford to the Town of Ware, Time out of Mind: But the Witnesses said, That the Navigation was not always carried through the same Branch of the River as it is at this time.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for ascertaini.ng, preferring, and improving, the Navigation

the County of Middlesex, in behalf of them selves, and the rest of the Inhabitants and Landholders within the said Hamlet, was referred. That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read; and is as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, in order to prove the Allegations thereof,

Mr. William Hoare was called: Who, being examined, said. That the Road desired to be repaired by the Petitioners is the only Road out of the Counties of Essex and Middlesex into the County of Kent, by the Ferry or Passage into the TJle of Ducks; and that the same is become exceedingly ruinous and bad, from the Number of Cattle continually passing that Way to the Isle of Ducks; to the Detriment indeed of the Roads of the Petitioners, but to the great Increase of Tolls arising thereby to the Turnpike, from whence they hope to have some assistance for the better Repairing of them.

The Committee then proceeded to inquire how far the Inhabitants were able to repair the fame: And it appeared, by the Evidence of

Mr. Henry Hall9 That the Hamlet of Poplar was in very different Circumstances from what it had been in his Time, who had known it for Forty Years: That Lands, that lett for £3. 10s. od. per Acre, were reduced to Forty Shillings; and that a Yard, that used to be lett for £ 100. per Annum, it was with some Difficulty that he now got£ 10. per Annum for:

That a Fifth Part of the said Parish was uninhabited; and such as are Inhabitants, are now in l'uch mean and low Circumstances, that they are unable to bear any additional Taxes; notwithstanding which, the Sum of Twenty Pounds per Annum has been constantly paid to the Trustees for repairing the Highways from the Stones End at Whitechapel Church to Shenfield and Woodford, in Part of the Composition of £ 150. to be paid by the Parish of Stepney.

He observed likewise to the Committee, That the Badness of the Roads was in some measure owing to the heavy Loads of Gravel passing through the fame, for the Repair of the Highways above-mentioned; which, in a limilar Cafe, with respect to Angel-lane, had beenefteem-ed, in the late Ad forrepairing the Highways from Stones End at Whitechapel Chu rc h, and Shea fields sufficient reason for including the said Lane within the said Act. The Petitioners then proceeded to lay before the Committee, the State of the Revenue arising by the Turnpike afore-mentioned: Upon which,

Thomas Dun, Clerk to the Trustees for repairing the said Roads, attending, according to Order, produced an Account of Receipts and Disbursements of the said Turnpike for these Three Years last past; whereby it appeared, That the yearly Revenue arising therefrom amounted, at a Medium, to upwards of £ 3,700; and the annual Expence attending the fame, at a Medium, to £3,000; so that there was a yearly Saving of £. 700. and more: It likewise appeared to the Committee, by the Evidence of the said Mr. Dun, That the main expensive Work of Bridges and Drains, which had cost the Turnpike near £ 1,000. was now completed ;so that the Expence of repairing the , said Road for some time would be considerably abated; notwithstanding which great Charges, that, at Michaelmas last, there was in Hand above £996; and that, since that time, £. 1,060. of Principal Money had been paid off.

Ordered, That it be an Instruction to the Committee to whom the Bill for enlarging the Term and Powers granted by an Act, passed in the Eighth Year of the JEleign of his late Majesty King George the First, for repairing the Highways from the Stones End at White-chapel Church, in the County of Middlesex, to Shevfidd, and to the furthermost Part of the Parish of Woodford, leading to the Town of Eppingy in the County of Eff'ex; gnd for repairing the Road leading from the causevray, Vol. 22.

Sir George Cafwall reported from the Committee to whom the Petition of the Rulers, Auditors, and Assistants, of the Company of Watermen and Lightermen, in behalf of themselves, and the rest of the said Company, was referred; That the Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, together with the Resolutions of the Committee thereupon, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the same was read 5 and the Report and Resolutions of the Committee are as follows; viz.

The Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition: And, to prove the Allegations thereof,

The Petitioners laid before the Committee several Acts of Parliament made touching Watermen, Wherry-men, and Lightermen, rowiagon the River of Thames^ and for the better ordering and governing the said Watermen, WHierrymen, and Lightermen, upon the said River, between Gravesend and Windsor.

And, upon readingan Act of Parliament, passed in the First Year of the Reign of King James the First, it appeared to the Committee, That no Wherrymen or Watermen shall take any Apprentice under tJie Age of Eighteen Years at least, unless the Son of aVv aterman, who might be taken an Apprentice at the Age of Sixteen Years.

And, upon reading an Act, passed in the Eleventh and Twelfth Years of the Reign of his late Majesty King William the Third, for Explaining and better Executing of former Acts, it likewise appeared to the Committee, That the said Wherrymen, Watermen, and Lightermen, were incorporated into One Company; and were impowered to make reasonable Rules* Orders, and Constitutions, for their Government.

Then the Petitioners laid before the Committee, a Book, containing several Orders and Rules, which were made and confirmed as prescribed and directed by the said last mentioned Act; whereby it appeared to the Committee, That no Waterman shall have more than One Apprentice at One time; nor shall be capable of taking any Apprentice, until such Matter hath been a Freeman Seven Years; and shall not take a Second till his First be dead, or the Term expired; and that no Lighterman shall take any Apprentice until be is a real Owner of Two Lighters, nor shall have any more than One Apprentice at one time, under the Penalties therein mentioned.

And, upon reading the Act of Parliament passed in the Fourth Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, it likewise appeared to the Committee, That the Clause in the said Act, of the First of King James9 for the restraining the taking of Apprentices under the several Ages of Eighteen and Sixteen Years, and also the said Rule, Order, and Constitution, were repealed.

And it further appeared to the Committee, upon reading a Clause in another Act, of the same Year of her said late Majesty’s Reign, for the Encouragement and Increase of Seamen, and for the better and speedier manning her Majesty’s Fleet, it is enacted, That in case any Waterman, Bargeman, Wherryman, or Lighterman, upon Notice being left, in Writing, at the Place of his usual Abode, in pursuance of Notice given to the Company of Watermen by the Lord High Admiral, or the Commissioners for executing such Office, shall not appear before the Rulers of the said Company, within Ten Days after such Summons, to be lent on board the Royal Fleet; such Person, being convi61ed thereof is to iiifler One Month’s Imprisonment and to be 10 B disabled

Regulating disabled from working on the River Thames, or enjoy-Watermen, ing anyv of the Privileges of the said Company, for &c* Two Years.

Then the Petitioners, to prove the other Allegations contained in their Petition, called,

William ChurchyClerk to the said Company of Watermen; Who said. That, in pursuance of the Act of the Fourth Year of the Reign of her said late Majesty, great Number of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, have taken Apprentices, for the fake of small Sums of Money, at the Age of Twelve and Thirteen Years (a List of which he produced to the Committee), who were unlit for such Service, by reason of their not having Strength, nor of Size, sufficient for the Labour required in fuel] Occupation, and have taken more than they had Employment for; so that the Number of Mailers and Apprentices, within these few Years, is increased to upwards of Eight thousand; and that Three Parts of the Apprentices are taken Tor no more than Two or Three Pounds.

And said, That, for want of their Matters having a proper Habitation to retain and keep such Apprentices at, they are not only unikilful, and unfit for their Bufi-nels, but frequently become vagrant, idle, and profligate; and that the Lives and Goods of Passengers have been and are olten exposed to very great Dangers: And added, That frequent Roberies have been and are daily committed on the said River; and that, within these few Years past, great Numbers of such Apprentices have been convicted of Felony.

And likewise informed the Committee, That by reason of such Watermen having no settled Habitation, or Place of Abode, no Summons can be properly served for their Appearance before the Rulers of the said Company, as directed by the last mentioned Act; by which means they wholly avoid the Penalty thereof, and withdraw themselves in secret places when their Service is very much wanted.

John Middle mar fh y Lighterman, being examined, said. He should he willing to take an Apprentice of 17 or 18 years of Age, without having Money with him, and apprehended that was a proper Age to take such an Apprentice at; for then they were able to do their Matters proper Service: And said, There was no Inducement for Matters to take them at the Age of 12 or 13 Years, but the Money which was given with them, and not for any Benefit they might receive from their Service; and confirmed the Evidence given by William Church, relating to the several Robberies being frequently committed by such Apprentices; and that several of them had been, within these few Years, convicted of Felony, some of whom have been hanged, and some transported.

Upon the whole Matter, the Committee came to the following Resolutions; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Petitioners have fully proved the Allegations contained in their Petition.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a Motion be made for Leave to bring in a Bill for regulating the Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, rowing on the River of Thames, between Gravesend, in the County of Kent, and Windsor, in the County of Berks, in regard to their taking Apprentices.

Ordered, That Leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating the Company of Watermen, Wherrymen, and Lightermen, rowing on the River Thames, between Gravesend, in the County of Kent, and WindJbr, in the County of Berks, in regard to their taking Apprentices: And that Sir George Cafzvall, and Mr. Brereton, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

A Petition of Thomas Allen was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Petitioner, being a Person who followed the Art or Business of Distillation for more than Seven Years next before the passing an Act, in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty upon the Retailers of spirituous Liquors, and for licensing the Retailers thereof, had, by virtue of the said Act, from and after the Twenty-ninth Day of September last, full Liberty and Authority to exercise and follow any other Trade, Art, Business, or Manufacture, in any City, Town, or Place, within that Part of Great Britain called England, any Law, Charter, Grant, Custom, or Usage, to the contrary notwithstanding; and that, the said Act having rendered the Petitioner’s Business of Distillation useless to him, he did, for the better Support of himself and Family, since the said Twenty-ninth Day of September last, at his own great Hazard and Expence, hire an House and Wine Cellar in the Town of Cambridge, and Hocked such Cellar with good and wholesome Wines of his own Importation from foreign Parts; and hath ever since fold such Wines at very moderate Prices as a Vintner, in the said Town; and was in hopes that helhould not have been interrupted in such his honest Method of trading; but that he finds that the Chancellor, Mailers, and Scholars, of the University of Cambridge9 are attempting to procure such aClause to be inserted in a Bill, now depending before the House, intituled, a Bill for the more effectual restraining the unlawful Playing of Interludes within the Precincts of the Uni-versity of Cambridge, and the Places adjacent; and for explaining and amending so much of an Act, passed in the last Session of Parliament, intituled, An Act for laying a Duty upon the Retailers of spirituousLiquors, and for licensing the Retailers thereof, as may affect the Privilege of the University of Cambridge with respect to licensing Taverns, and all other publick Houses, within the Precincts of the fame; as will intirely disappoint the Petitioner of the Benefit of the said Act, to his irreparable Injury and Damage: And therefore praying, That the House^will give him such Relief in the Premises as to the House shall fieem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed.

" A Bill . ' I formerly pals the House of Commons, wherein tin I ncouragement proposed for importing Iron in Pig* and Sows from America, was, the taking olT the Duty payable upon it at Importation, which amounts to 3^. 9^/. per Ton; and this Encouragement would, in our Opinion, engage the Plauters to furuith us . ith such Quantities of Iron in Pigs and Sows, as might be futlicient for the Uses of our Ma-nulattures.

" We import annually into this Kingdom about 20,000 Ton of this Commodity, the greateti Part of which is brought from Sweden, and paid for with ready Money; so that, in our humble Opinion, nothing could be more prudent, or indeed more necessary, for the Welfare of Great Britain, than to give such Encouragement to the Importation of Iron from our Plantations, which abound both with Ore, and Wood for the Use of the Furnaces, as might render us independent of our Northern Neighbours, for a Supply of a Commodity lb essential to the Support of our Fleet, and of our Navigation in general.

" We annually import from Sweden only about 14,340 Tons, which, computed at no more than £. 10 per Ton, would amount to upwards off. 143,000 which we pay to that Kingdom in ready Money; and therefore an Encouragement upon the Importation of this Commodity may be the more necessary at this time, because the People of America having discovered several Iron-mines, and set up Forges, it is to be feared, that they will work up their Iron in Manufactures, which may be prejudical to those of this Kingdom, if forae effectual Means be not found out to induce them to import it, in Pigs and Sows, into Great Britain"

Mr. John Bannisters, chief Agent to Mrs. Crowley, was called: Who having laid before the Committee the several Acts of Parliament, whereby Premiums are settled upon the Importation of Tar, Pitch, Turpentine, Hemp,

Malts, Yards, and liowfprits; but wherein not any Encouragement is given to the Importation of Iron into this Kingdom from our American Colonies; proceeded to give his Evidence with regard to the Quality of the American Iron: And acquainted the Committee,

That he had bought] near 50 Tons of the American Iron in Bars, for which he contracted to pay £. 14per Ton: and that what he had seen worked of the same was, in every Respect, equal to the Swedish Iron, and fit for the same Uses, except that of making Steel, wherein, he thought, the Swedish Iron had forae Advantage over the American; though was (till of Opinion, that even Steel might be made out of Bar Iron made from Baltimore and Principio Pigs: That he had sent foine Quantity of it into the North to Mrs. Crouleys Workmen there; and that the Account they gave of it, was, That having tried several Bars of it, which flood the cold Proof, and cut others, they found it to be a good tough Sort of Iron; and that it worked as well as the Swedish Iron, and not red-tliort, but gave general Satbfaction: This, he said, was the Iron lent back from the Navy, as not good: And being asked what the Quantity returned was, he informed the Committee 23 Ton.

Being asked as to the Prices of Swedish, American, and English iron, he acquainted the Committee, That the Swedish Iron, now fells from £. 13 to £. 17per T on; but that that of which Steel is made, 12 or 1,500 Tons of which are annually imported for that Purpose, fills chiefly from £. 15 to £. 17 per Ton: That Bar Iron made of Baltimore and Principio Pigs, which are worth from £. 6 to^. 6. 10^ per Ton, and to the making of which into Bar, a Load and a Half of Coal, or Three Cord of Wood, is necessary, stood Mrs. Crowley in about £. 15 per Ton; and that English Iron, viz. that which is called Ordinary-tough, sold at Bewdley at £. 14 per Ton, which is from £ 3 to £. 3.|io$. less than it used to be, sold at: This he attributed, as well as the great Decrease of the Consumption of English Iron of late Years, to the large Importation of Moscow and Brinfeo Iron, which is fold for £. n per Ton.

I le then proceeded to acquaint the Committee with the State of the Iron Trade, as carred on in America, and the Manner of rendering it subservient to the Trade of this Kingdom; and though he allowed there was some little Manufacture going forward there, and that, as he was informed from Merchants, Nads were imported from Boston to Carolina,'and paid for thexe, in their Currency, yet, he said, that he was persuaded, that Necessity drove them to this; for they had run them-fcJves adrift so in their Trade with us, that, so far from beingable to call forfrefhand larger Recruits of Commodities from hence, they were not able to pay for those they had already had; and that the most effectual Method to prevent their fioking, through Necessity^ deeper into the Way of Manufacturing, was to make it their Interest not to manufacture:

This, as he thought, could be belt effected by the Encouragement of the Importation of Bar Iron into this Kingdom; for that the Dearness of Labour in those Parts, as well as the Inability of the Inhabitants to labour at all, for % great a Part of the Year, on account of the Heat of their Climate, must ever be such an Obstacle in their Way of Manufacturing, as not to make it w orth their while.

He was asked, upon this. Whether more Labour was not required to make Bars than Pigs ? to which he answrered, That he was not much acquainted with the nature of making either Pig or Bar Iron, but that he believed there was; for more Wages were paid for making one than the other.
