Being asked, Whether, if more Labour be required to make Bars than Pigs, and Labour be so very dear in America, it would not be for the Interest of the Americans to import Pigs rather than Bars, and save the Expence of that Labour ? he answered. That he thought not, on account of the Consumption of the Wood in America .* And that further, he observed, that Pigs, English as well as American, had not been of late so saleable as they used to be, the Consumption of both having greatly declined; which he attributed to the great Importation of Russia Iron, and the Cheapness of it: That he himself has large Quantities of Baltimore, Potomocky and Principio Pigs, lying by him, which he could not fell; nor were we able to make Iron so cheap in England, as it could be imported from Russia:

He further said. That there was annually imported from Sweden, about 14,000 Ton of Iron, and that chiefly paid for in Money; which the Importation of this American Iron, though not quite so hard, nor immediately to be sold so cheap, would, in time, chiefly affect: That in Eight or Ten Years time, with the Assistance of the Americans, we should be able to supply ourselves with the Iron imported from Sweden: That the English Iron was as good as the belt Swedish: That in Toys it was preferable to any foreign Iron; and that some Sort or other of it would answer all the Purposes that American Iron was fit for; but, to prevent the English being affected by the Importation of American, and to give the former some Advantage over the latter, it was proposed that 20s. per Ton should remain on all American Bar imported.

He was then asked, Whether we did not fend a great deal of manufactured Iron abroad, and to what Places? and he acquainted the Committee, That a great deal was Cent to our own Plantations, and chiefly to those that produced Iron Ore; but very little to Russia or Szveden, especially the latter, Duties being very high in Sweden on all European Goods.

The Committee then proceeded to inquire, Whether, since this Manufacture begun in some Measure in America, the Exports of manufactured Iron to Virginia, and the Places thereabouts, had not been lessened ? To which he answered. That he believed in nothing but Nails; and gave this Reason why; though Forges were set up, and they were permitted to make Bar Iron, they would not carry their Works any farther; viz. That they could buy their manufactured Iron cheaper from hence, than they could manufacture it there: An Instance of which he gave, in some Axes made at Boston, that he himself imported from Carolina, each of which colt him there, of our Money, 45. and as good as which he could have afforded to have fold here for 2$. and 6d.

He was then desired to inform the Committee, Whether, as the Cheapness of Iron manufactured must depend upon the Cheapness of the Iron first bought, and the Cheapness of that upon the Quantity of Iron brought to Market, it would not affect the English Manufacture to have a Stop put to the Importation of Russia and Swedish Iron? he said. That it would; because there would not be English Iron sufficient for the Purposes for which we wanted it; and that as, on the one hand, to lay an additional Duty upon Rvffiaaxidi Szvedishlvon immediately, would not be advisable, because hurtful to our Manufacture, as we are notripe for such a Resolution at present, so, on the other, to take oft’ the Duties upon American Pig and Bar Iron, at the same time permitting the Importation of Russia and Swedish Iron to continue as before, must greatly affect our English Iron; as there would be such a Glut of Iron at Market, and every one would buy that, whether English or foreign, that came cheapest to his Hands; and that though the Cheapness of Iron might increase our manufacture of it, and thereupon our Exportation of Goods manufactured be greater, yet that our Forges must be flopped thereby, and consequently the Price of ourWoods lowered: the Dear-ness, on the contrary, of foreign Iron, as it would put the English nearer upon a Par with it, must render the use of it less in those Parts where it is dear, and be a Means of preserving the Use of the English.

Being asked, How our Trade with the East Indies flood as to the Iron Manufacture ? he said, That he believed the Exports thither to be about One-fifth of the whole Export from England.

Having mentioned the Difficulties the Manufacturers laboured under, for want of Szvedish Iron, upon a Rupture with Szveden in the Year 1717, he was asked, Whether, should such a same happen again, he thought the American Pigs would answer that Want ? his Answer was, That he believed they would not; for that there was not Wood enough in the Kingdom to supply the Forges.

Having informed the Committee, That the Dutch were the great Competitors with us in our Iron Trade, it was asked him, Whether a Check being put upon the Importation of foreign Iron into this Kingdom, it would not render the said Iron cheaper to the Dutch f he laid. That he believed it might; and that the Smallness of the Duty paid upon Importation of Iron into their Ports, the low Wages paid to Servants, and the small Price given for the Commodity, did, at present, give them great Advantage over us in the Iron Manufacture.

Being asked, Whether the Bar Iron imported from America, and made so there, was as good as the Bar Iron made here from American Pigs ? he said. That it was not.

Captain John Tomlinson, being called, acquainted the Committee, That he had been in New England about Nine Years ago, and had been an Eye-witness of the Produce of Iron in that Country: That he had since been informed, there was an inexhaustible Mine of Iron Ore there, and that as good as any in Europe; and that he had had Two Bars made of it, sent to him from Mafachufetts; and had found no material Difference with regard to Shipping, between the American and Swedish Iron.

He acquainted likewise the Committee, That he had been informed, that a Slitting-mill had been ereCled there: and that there was some Manufacture going forward, such as Horse-thoes, and Streiks for Cartwheels, which he apprehends no Place can subsist without, Axes, and Houghs; but that they are double the Price that he can afford to fell them for in the Gross: And he farther added, That he believed some of them were sent to the Southern Colonies; but was of Opinion, with Mr. Bannisters, that they did no more than what Necessity obliged them to; which being removed, by the Encouragement of the Importation of Bar into this Kingdom, they would, as he imagined, cease to manufacture, or, if not intirely, only so much as was necessary for their Shipping, and what they could not do without: As a Reason why they would proceed no further, he said, That the Difference of Labour here and there being 70 or 80 per Cent. and the Price of Pit Coals being dearer, without which they could not manufacture, a Chaldron there being fold for 4 or. which was fold here for 5s. only, they would not find it worth their While; it being cheaper to have their manufactured Iron from hence, than to manufacture it themselves there: An Instance of which he mentioned, in some Bolts, that, upon his building a Ship there, he once sent over, in Hopes of saving the Expence of their Labour; but they not being fitted to the Ship, and requiring Alteration, it cost him near Half as much, or a Third at lead, to fit them to the Ship, as the prime Cost was here.

He further said. That the Iron he sent to the Plantations was Spanish or Swedish; but never sent himself, nor heard of any English Iron being sent there; for he never knew any English Iron at Market.

The Advantages anting to this Kingdom from the Importation of Bar from America, were, as he thought. That we should be thereby rendered independent of Szveden, or any other Country, for so necessary a Commodity: That their Trade with other Countries, when they had wherewith to deal with us, would be diverted into this: That our Woollen Manufactures would be sent in exchange for their Iron, and the Money they got from

io Geo. II. 20° Aprilis. 853

the Southern Provinces; and that there would, in time, be an additional Trade to this Kingdom for near £. 180,000 per Annum.

Being asked, What the Price of a Ton of Bar Iron made in America would be here ? he said, That the least that it would cost there would be £. 12. 5s. or £. 12. 10$.; lb that, including the Freight, which is 40^. it could not be fold here, for less than £. 15, some perhaps for £. 16 per Ton.

He further said, That it would not be of so great Advantage to import Pigs as Bars; because the Freight upon both was the fame, but the Value greatly different.

The Committee then inquired into the State of the Woollen Manufacture in America; and it appeared, by the Evidence of Captain Tomlinson, That the same was very trifling, and carried on up in the Country at l’o great an Expence, that they would not use it at all, if they had wherewith to purchasethe same from us: He was asked hereupon, Whether the Country, being cleared of its Woods, he did not think it would be fit for feeding of Sheep ? he said, He apprehended it would; and allowed, That it was natural for Colonies to interfere with us in our Manufactories, if we did not take off the grols Produce of their Country.

Mr. IVm.Astell, being examined, said, That our Trade to Sweden for Iron was, as he Imagined, for £. 1,50,000 per Annum; and that, in Exchange for that, they took of our Manufactures about 20 or £. 30,000 worth; so that about £. 120,000 being the Balance of the Trade, was annually paid to them in Money: That he remembered the Difficulties w e laboured under for Iron, at the time of our War with Sweden, and which we mult again labour under, in the like Circumstances, and unprovided v\ith American Iron: That the Dutch, at that time, engrossed all the Iron to themselves; and that he could not think it prudent for such a Natiun as ours to depend upon any but ourfeives for so necessary a Commodity.

Fie then produced a Copy of an Edict of the King of Sweden's, dated 11 th December 1734, and also a Copy of a Tax or Rate to be laid on Goods or Merchandize imported into Sweden, from January the lit, 1735, both received by Mr. Harrison, as himself informed the Committee, from the Secretary’s Office, and by him translated into English; whereby it appeared, that the Importation offeveral of our English Goods wereabfolutely prohibited; and also, that a very high Duty, amounting almost to a Prohibition, was laid upon all the rest, Woollen Hose and Yarn only excepted.

Mr. JVm. Jcvon said, That he had had 10 or 12 Ton of Bar Irun from Philadelphia, and that he had fold it to Birmingham Manufacturers; and that, according to his Information from them, it answered all the Purposes of Swedish Iron, excepting that of making Steel.

Mr. Joseph Farmer, a Manufacturer of Steel Wares at Birmingham, being examined, said, That he had a Parcel of 10 or 12 Ton of Bar Iron from Maryland, and that he had converted the same into Steel; and did not doubt, but that they in America might do the fame, if they had Pit Coal, and experienced Workmen: That he had made thereof Springs for Gun-locks, Sword-blades, Files, and Bits to bore Gun-barrels, and Tower Musket-barrels, all wffiich require the very best of Steel; and that he had found it answer all the Purposes he uled it for, as well as any he ever bad in his Life of the heft Swedish or English Iron: That the Swedish indeed w orked something harder than this; but that he did not look upon it to be the better for that: That he had tried it all Ways, had put (ome at the Top, some in the Middle, and some at the Bottom of the Furnace, and found it, at all Times, and in all Situations, fit for his Wrork: That it worked stiff, but not soft; and, being of a stronger Body, was preferable both to English and Swedish for Gun-barrels, the former of wffiich was chiefly used for that Purpose.

Fie further laid, That he had tried the Potcmc 'ck Iron but had found it too tender, and not tough enough for his Purpose, as he served the Office of Ordnance, though fit for many Uses.

Penjihama Iron he had tried likewise in every thing Importation but Steel, and found it inti rely fit for the Uses lie had of Iron from tried for; and believed it might be converted into Steel, America/ as well as the Maryland; though lie could not speak upon Experience as to that Iron.

He further acquainted the Committee, That, in the Years 1718 and 1719, he w as in the Plantations, and went with a View of trying the Iron Ore there: That, during his Stay there, he made several Experiments of the Ore, in different Places, and in different Manners; sometimes by a Loadstone, and sometimes by I;ire; and that he found good of all Sorts; but on the South-side of Virginia the very heft: That, at that time, there wTere no Furnaces or Forges, but only Two Bloomeries ereCled, where they made Iron for their owm Ule only.

The Committee then proceeded to examine the Matter of the several Petitions against the Importation of American Bar:

To which Purpose,

M. Samuel Barnet, a Slitter at Ridgley, in Stafford-shire, wras called: Who, being examined, said, That he had had about a Ton of Iron from Philadelphia, which he had tried, and found it of a tough, soft, malleable nature, and answering all the Purposes of our English Iron: The Principio and Baltimore Iron, likewise, he said, w*as much of the same nature with our English Ore; the Maryland a good deal so, but not quite so fit for Fri&ion.

Mt. Edward Knight, of Cook by, in Worcestershire, being examin' d, explained to the Committee the nature of the several Sorts of American Pigs, which he had been conversant with; viz. the Bristol Company and Poto-mock, the Tubal, PenJUvania, and the N. B. and F. C.

American Pigs; all which, he said, were of a cold short Kind, and chiefly fit for the Making of Nails: And he further said, That in the Manufacture of Nails, the Second Sort of English Iron had been chiefly used, till the late Importation of Russia Iron, which was fit for the same Purpose. and had greatly broke in upon the Consumprion of the English Iron; to which, if w'as added the Importation of American Bar, which was of the same nature, it uould give such a Blow to the Market for English Iron, as would, in a manner, bring it to nought, and give the American greatly the Advantage over the Swedish, with respect to the English; as, in the Manufacture of American Iron, a Man can do as much Work in Five Days, as he can in the Manufacture of Swedish in Six, or more, on account of its hardness.

He then acquainted the Committee with the best Sort of American Pigs, viz. the Baltimore and Principio Pigs, which, he said, were of a kind malleable nature, and generally foster than any English, except that made of Cumberland Ore: That iron made of these was of a firnilar nature to our English Iron, and, like that, answered all the Purposes of the Szoedish, excepting that of making Steel; and that, if this w>as imported in Bar, it must greatly alfect the English Iron, for that the English sold at Bewdley at £.\bper Ton, and the Swedish at£. 14.10.9. per Ton; Co that the Difference of Price must necessarily bring the first Lois upon the dearer Iron, viz. the English, which must be very considerable, the Value of our English Iron amounting per Annum to upwards of £. 200,000.

Being asked the Expence of making a Ton of Bar Iron, he said. That about 271b. of Pigs, w ere necessary for that Purpose: That working of those into Blooms would take up about Three Cord Six Foot of Four-foot Wood, which cost from 4s1. to 8$. per Cord, as the Distance is from the Forge, after which they might be draw n out by Coals; so that if a Man gives at Bewdley £. 6. 15^. per Ton for Baltimore and Principio Pigs, including the Expence of Carriage, which is about *49. he makes nothing of his Money by felling the Bar Iron made from those Pigs at £. 15. 1 os. per Ton: He said.

There was about 900 or 1,000 Ton of Steel made every Year out of Swedish Iron.

Mr. Abraham Spooner, Importer of Iron, as well as Ironmonger, said, That he had imported Two Sorts of Or grounds Sxvedish Iron; the First made generally into Steel, and fitted for it of all Irons yet discovered, and sold at Bewdley at £. 17. 10$. sometimes £. 18 per Ton; the Second, which had not Body enough to make Steel, if mixed with other Iron, sold at 14. 10$. if by itself, and for ready Money, at £. 15 per Ton; but that the same was harder than English, and took more time in manufacturing:

That he had also, some Years ago, imported Two Sorts of Siberia Iron, the one called Government Sibet'ia, the other Merchants Siberia Iron; but that he had lately heard, that the Czarina had taken that Iron to her own Ul’e, and imported if herself: He likewise acquainted the Committee, That the Iron imported from Petersburg was chiefly paid for in Money, but sometimes in Goods,

He further said, That there were Two other Sorts of Iron imported from Russia, viz. Brinfco or Tuley, and Moscow or Mullarns Irons: That the Brinfco was applicable to the Making of Nails, but was rather too hard, as the Workmen complained; but that iheMofcorcv Iron was used lolely for Nails, and supplied the Place of the English Ordinary-tough: That he had imported Brinfco himself some years ago; and that the Price of Brinfco Iron in Bars, at that time, was 13 per Ton, and that of the English in Kods f. 18 per Ton , but that the Price of Brinfco advancing in Russia, and that of the English falling here, he had left off importing it.

He acquainted likewise the Committee, That he had been conversant with Baltimore Iron, which was of a fbft malleable nature, and came the nearefi of any Iron in Quality to the belt English tough Iron.

He then proceeded to acquaint the Committee with the several Sorts of English Iron, which he divided into the Best-tough, Ordinary*tough, Blend, and Cold-ftiort; and how the same had and might be further affected by the Irons above mentioned.

He observed hereupon, That, by a Computation made in the Year 1718, 18,000 Ton of Bar Iron were then computed to be annually made in England; but that several Forges were now idle, that then worked; that the Price of Wood was lowered; and that now not above 12 or, at moll, 15,000 Ton were computed to be made: This, he said, was undoubtedly owing to the large Importation of foreign Iron; which, if it should be increased, by a further Encouragement to bring it in upon us, must render the Confurnption of our English Iron still less, the Price of our Goods still lower, and drive our Workmen abroad to get their Bread.

He further said, That the heft English tough Merchant Bars are sold at Bewdley at £. 16 per Ton, wholesale Price: and though the same Sort of Goods are made from the Second Sxvedish, and the Two Siberian Irons, aforementioned, that are made of this best English, yet that the fame, being of a harder nature, and requiring more Labour and Coals in the Manufacturing of it, than the English does, do not bear so good a Price at Bewdley as the English: That the Ordinary-tough, Blend, and Cold-short English Iron, are all used for the Making of Nails, which the Russia Iron, being fitted for the same Purpose of making Nails, and sold at a lower Price, has greatly affected England of itself, before the Importation of Russia Iron, having supplied itself with all the Iron wanting for that Manufacture.

He further observed, That one Sort or other of American Iron was of the same Quality with any of our English Iron; whence he inferred, that if Encouragement was given to the Americans to import their Bar Iron into this Kingdom, it would ever affect one Sort or other of English Iron, before any foreign: If they import such Bar

23

as is fit for Nails, it must affect the English before the Russia Iron, because the Russia fells at a lower Price than the English does; if they import such as answers in Quality to the best English Tough, it must affect the English before the Swedish Iron, because the Price of the English is higher than the Swedish; the Consequence of such a Blow given to the Iron Trade, in the Neighbourhood of Birmingham only, were, as he imagined, that 135*000 People would be deprived of their Livelihood; so forced either to seek their Bread abroad, or to become Burdens to their Parishes; which he thus computed, that in Birminghan, and the adjacent Places within Ten Miles, not less than 9,000 Ton of Iron, from the Bar and Rod, were, yearly manufactured: That in the Manufacturing of each Ton, Five Hands were employed, which made the Number of Hands 45,000: That supposing, on each hand. One Woman, and One helpless Child, to depend for Subsistence, it made the whole Number of Dependents on their Trade 135,000.

Being asked, How much of these 9,000 Ton manufactured in Birmingham was English Iron ? he said, He believed that about 6,900 Ton were English Iron, the rest, 220 of which were converted into Steel, chiefly Sxvedish.

The Committee then inquired into the State of the Bir* mingham and Wolverhampton Trade for these last Seven Years, and whether it had, in that time, increased or decreased: And he informed the Committee, That, he believed, there had been an Increase of Manufacture, especially in the Toy Trade, at Wolverhampton, of late Years, but that the Goods so manufactured lay on the Hands of the Owners; which he attributed to the Decrease of the Exportation to America: And that, to the Increase of the Manufacture carried on among themselves, he further said, That he could not think, that an Encouragement given to them to import their Bar Iron into this Kingdom, would make them cease to manufacture; for that it was well known the Number of People in the Northern Parts of America was greatly increased, and he thought they would not choose the Hazard of the Sea, and the Expence of Carriage, w hen they could do w ithout, having already ftiewn a pretty good Disposition to Manufacture themselves, by endeavouring to get some of our Manufacturers amongst them: To prove which, he produced a Letter from an Edge-tooler of Middletown, about 30 Miles from Boston, to one of his own Trade at Birmingham; wherein he desires him to fend him over Three or Four Nailors; for that the Making of Nails was an excellent Trade there, and a Man might get ioj, per Day by it, which would pay for his Board for a whole Week.

Being asked, If we had Wood enough in England to make all the Pigs and Bars that we wanted ? he said, We had enough to make infinitely more than is now made.

Mr. George Rock, Agent to Lord Foley, said, That he had worked both American and English Pigs, and believes the Iron made from Anerican Pigs would answer all the Purposes of the English, being much of the same nature; but that he had observed, that, mixed together, they each received Advantage from the other, though still inferior to the Swedish Iron, being of a foster nature:

He further said. That he paid by the Great, for making a Ton of Ore into Pigs 3s. 4d. and 20$. for making a Ton of Bars from Pigs, which took up of English Pigs 271b. of American, from 281b. to 3olb.: That Three Cord Six Foot of Four-foot Wood was required to make a Ton of Pig from the Ore, and Six Cord Four Foot of Four-foot Wood to make and draw a Ton of Pigs into Bars; though, in some Places upon the River Stower in Worcestershire, they sometimes used Wood only to draw it into Coops and Anchories, which takes up Four Cord only, and from thence they draw it into Bar with Stone Coal; but the greatest Part of Iron is drawn by Charcoal, of w;hicli Two Cord of Wood will make a Load.

Part of the said Sum of £. 13. 4s. should be yearly laid out in Bread, to be distributed on every Friday Morning, after Prayers, to 12 ancient poor People of Abthoipe and Foxcoate, as long as Divine Service should be used and continued in the said Church on Wednesdays Fridays, and Holidays-, and lb long as the Minister, for the Time being, of the Town of Abthorpe, should preach there every Sunday Morning, and read the common Prayers appointed for that Purpose, and cate-chife the poor Children of the Town upon every Sunday in the Afternoon throughout the Year, and should duly administer the Holy Sacrament of the Lord’s Supper at least Six times in every Year; and, whenever Prayers should be discontinued in the said Parish on the several Days, or any of the several Particulars therein mentioned should be omitted, then the said Bread, given to the Poor as aforesaid, was to cease; and that the £. 2. 10 s. other Part of the said Sum of £. 13. 4 s. should be yearly paid to the Parish Clerk of the said Town of Abthorpe, and subject to the Provisoes herein after-mentioned.

And the said Thomas Nicol, by his said Will, gave £. 200 South Sea Annuities to the Town oi Abthorpe, in order to procure Part of the Bounty of her late Majesty Queen Anne, for increasing of Poor Livings; which said South Sea Annuities were given upon Condition that the Town of Abthorpe should, within Three Years next after his Decease, or within Three Years next after the then Incumbent should quit the fame, become a distinct Parish from the Town of Tozvcester; and he the said Thomas Nicol declared by his said Will, That, in such case, he gave 20 Guineas towards the buying of Communion Plate for the Use and Service of the said Church of Abthorpe; and that he also declared the Two several Sums of £.2. 10 s. for Bread for the Poor of the Parish, and £.2. 10 s. for the Parish Clerk of the said Town, should cease, and not be paid, unless Abthorpe should, within the Times limited, become a distiaft and separate Parish from the said Town of Towcester.

A Petition of tile leverstl Gentlemen, Proprietors of Iron -Works and Woodlands; as kllb Freeholders, Landholders, and- Tanners, and divers Miners, Carriers* Woodcutters, Charcoal-holfiets, Workmen, and Labourers, in the County of Gloucester, whose ^Namies are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of thdmselves, and* Thoul&nds of others; and also,’ - -

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Owners and Proprietors of Iron Works, Whod-lands, and Coppices, as also Landholders, Tanners, Wood-cutters, poor Workmen, and Labourers, in the County of Monmouth, whole Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of therof. Ives, and many others; and also,

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Freeholders, Fanners, and others, in the County of Stafford; &nd also,

A Petition of the Gentlemen, Owners and Proprietors of Iron Works, Wood-lhnds, and Coppices, as also Landholders, Tanners, Wood-cutters, poor Workmen, and Labourers, in the County of Hereford, whose Names are thereunto subscribed, in behalf of themselves, and many others;

Were severally presented to the House, and read; complaining of the Importation of great Quantities of Bar Iron into Great Britain from foreign Parts; whereby the Iron Works have, for several Years last past, lain under very great Hardships; and a Stop has, in a great measure, been put to the Making of Iron in this Nation; and many Furnaces and Forges are now- either unemployed, or do not make above Half the Quantity of Iron they did formerly; by which the Demand for Wood is so far obstructed, that the Petitioners cannot dispose of the fame, notwithstanding the Price Wood now fells-for is but little more than Half what they did formerly; and representing to the House the bad Consequences of discouraging the said Iron Works; which, if disused, Coppices (the Nurseries of Oak Timber, for the Support of our Navy, and kept up chiefly for the Support of the said Iron Works with Cord-wood, as also Bark for the Tanning Trade) must be grubbed up, and converted to other Purposes: And therefore praying, That such further Duty may be laid upon foreign Iron imported, or such other Encouragement given to the Proprietors of Iron Works and Woods of this Kingdom, as to the House shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petitions be referred to the Consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom it is referred to consider of the Report from the , Committee to whom the Petition of the Merchants and Ironmongers of this Kingdom, in behalf of themselves, and many others trading to his Majesty s Plantations in America, and the several other Petitions relating to the , Manufacture of Iron, were referred.

The Order of the Day being read, for the House to resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, to consider of the said Report;

Ordered, That the several Accounts and Papers presented to this House, which were referred to the Committee, to whom the Petition of the Merchants and Ironmongers of this Kingdom, in behalf of themselves, and many others trading to his Majesty’s Plantations in America, and the several other Petitions relating to the Manufacture of Iron, were referred, be referred to this Committee.

Ordered, That , the Copy of the Representation from the Commissioners for Trade and Plantations, to the House of Lords, pursuant to his Majesty’s Orders, upon their Addresses of the First and Fifth of April 1734, relating to the State of the British Islands in America, with regard to their Trade, their Strength, and Fortifications, and to what may be further necessary for the Encouragement of their Trade, and Security of those Islands; as likewise to such Encouragements as may be necessary to engage the Inhabitants of the British Colonies on the Continent in America to apply their industry to the Cultivation of Naval Stores of all kinds, and of such other Products as may be proper for the Soil of the said Colonies, and do not interfere with the Trade or Produce of Great Britain; presented to the House the Twenty-seventh- Day of March -ij35; be referred to this Committee.

Ordered, That the Translation of the Treaty of Commerce between his Majesty and her Czarith Majesty, concluded at Petersburg, 2d December 1734, presented to the House the Twenty-fourth Day of March 1735, he referred to this Committee.

Ordered, That the Account Of what Quantity of Woollen Manufactures of England has been exported to JRuffia, from Christmas 1729 to Christmas 1734> distinguishing each Year, presented to the House the Nineteenth Day of Febniary 1735, be referred to this Commiitee. ‘

Committee had examined the Matter of the said Petition; and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his Place; and afterwards delivered it jn at the Clerk's Table: Where the same was read; and is..as follows; viz.

The Committee have, purfoant to the Order of the House, examined the Matter of the said Petition:

And, to prove the Allegations, the Petitioners called,

Thomas Bafemore, Robert Bird\ and Bartholomezc Hill, each of them aged 80 Years, and upwards: Who, being severally examined, said, That they have known the Road between Nonesuch and Worcester Parks, in the Parish of Cuddington, upwards of 50 Years; which is now become so ruinous, that, Eight Months in the Year, Coaches and heavy Carriages cannot travel that Way; and that the Laws in Force, for repairing the Highways of this Kingdom, are not sufficient to amend, and keep the said Road in good Repair, for the Accommodation of Travellers, without some further Provision be made for that Purpose.

And they further said, That, in dry Summers, the Leather head, Epsom, and other Waggons, frequently go that Road, it being Three Miles nearer from those Parts to London, than the Road they now use.

And they also feverdlly laid, That they never knew or heard any Obstruction had been given to Passengers,

Coaches, or Waggons, who travel that Rqad; but the feme was always taken to be a publick Highway.

After which, his Majesty was pleased to make a mol! The King> gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament; as fol- Speech.1 loweth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am come to put an End to this Session of Parliament, that you may be at liberty to retire into your several Countries, and, in your proper Stations, to promote the Peace and Welfare of the Kingdom.

I return you my Thanks for she particular Proofs you have given me of your Aftcdion and Regard to my Person and Honour; and hope the Wifdorn and Just ire which you have shewn, upon some extraordinary Incidents, will prevent all Thoughts of the like Attempts for the future.

The Conduit of this Parliament has been so uniform in all your Deliberations upon publick Affairs, that it would be as unjust not to acknowledge it, as it is unnecessary to enumerate the several Particulars.

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

Your Care, as well in raising the Supplies necessary for the Service of the current Year, as in doing it in the Manner the leal! grievous and burthensome to my People, is a fresh Instance of your equal Concern for the Support of my Government, and for the true Inlereft of your Country.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,
